News.title: Woman, 80, dies after being ‘set on fire with liquid’ – as murder probe launched
News.content:
‘DEEPLY DISTRESSING’ Woman, 80, dies after being ‘set on fire with liquid’ – as murder probe launched







Next

A WOMAN in her 80s who was reportedly set on fire has tragically died days after the horrific incident.

Cops descended on a block of flats in Watford, Hertfordshire at around 12.47pm on Monday, November 9, to reports a woman had been found on fire.



Brenda Raymond was suffering from catastrophic injuries after being raced to hospital.

She was taken to hospital for treatment where she remained in a critical condition.



However, the pensioner tragically succumbed to her injuries and has since been pronounced dead, cops said.

Detectives believe Brenda was attacked as she returned home before she was found in a first-floor communal area of a block of flats.



They also think an accelerant may have been used before she was deliberately set on fire.

A 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life in connection with the investigation, according to cops.

The force confirmed that he has been bailed with strict conditions while enquiries continue.

Detective Inspector Adam Bridges, from the Major Crime Unit, said: “Our thoughts remain with Brenda’s family at this incredibly sad time.



“Her death is now being treated as murder and we continue to work hard to understand the circumstances of what happened to her.

“While an arrest has previously been made, we are still urgently appealing for anyone with information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, to come forward.

“Even the smallest piece of information could prove vital in helping us identify those responsible.

“If you know anything at all, I urge you to contact police immediately. Please do not assume that someone else has already reported what you know.

“Someone knows who carried out this attack. If that person is you, or if you know who is responsible, now is the time to do the right thing and come forward. Brenda’s family deserve answers, and we are determined to get them.”



Evidence recovered at the scene also indicated a flammable liquid may have been poured through the letterbox of another property in the area.

Hertfordshire Police has urged anyone with information to come forward to help them in their investigation.

The force is particularly keen to hear from those who saw someone acting suspiciously in or around the area between 10am and 2pm on Monday.

They also want to hear from anyone who heard any disturbance before emergency services arrived, spotted someone fleeing the scene or wearing a face covering, balaclava or mask.



Anyone who is aware of someone purchasing flammable liquid on the day of or shortly before November 9 is also asked to get in touch.

Speaking at the time of the incident, Detective Inspector Adam Bridges previously said: “Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dash cam footage without realising its significance.

“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.”

News.title: I grilled Baby P’s ‘master manipulator’ mother days before murder… why her move to cushy open prison makes me terrified
News.content:
Next

DETECTIVE Jon Wedger had “master manipulator” Tracey Connelly in his clutches days before her little son Peter – or Baby P – died.

Watching her leave the police station on bail despite clear evidence pointing to her horror treatment of the 17-month-old is one of the veteran ex-cop’s biggest regrets – and now he fears the Parole Board are making the same mistake.





Connelly, 45, is set to move to a cushy open prison 18 years after her toddler son was tortured to death in 2007.

A Parole Board report published yesterday blocked her release but did recommend she move to a Category D open prison, where she will be able to work in the community.

Mr Wedger told The Sun: “If they downgrade her from closed conditions, they’re just sugar coating it and maybe even grooming us into accepting her back into the public domain.

“She’s a deceptive individual and words are cheap. The fruits of her actions are that she’s a danger to children.”

Mr Wedger said being able to work in the community as part of her open prison sentence means “it’s inconceivable to think she won’t come into contact with children”.

“I’m a very victim-focused person,” the ex-cop continued.

“When someone commits the crimes that she did she doesn’t deserve an easier life.

“Her punishment should mirror what she did… She should remain in closed conditions throughout the entirety of her sentence.”





During hearings last year, mum-of-five Connelly spoke for the first on Peter’s death, admitting she’s a “c**p mum” and accepted she was not merely a passive bystander to his abuse.

The mum-of-five was sentenced to an indefinite imprisonment with a minimum of five years after being convicted in 2009 of causing or allowing the child’s death alongside then-boyfriend Steven Barker and his brother Jason Owen.

In her desperate bid for freedom, Connelly said she “failed to protect” her children and instead: “I put my needs first.”

But Mr Wedger believes she is still deflecting blame and it’s the same as her manipulation of authorities, including child services and police, years ago.

He came face to face with Connelly days before 17-month-old Peter’s death.

The toddler suffered months of horrific abuse, resulting in more than 50 injuries, including a broken spine.

It eventualy led to his death on August 3, 2007.

Mr Wedger told us: “She was a very very controlling woman… straight away I knew how manipulative she was.”



Baby P's horror abuse Peter was born in March 2006, though his biological father left the family home in Haringey a few months later. In November, his mum’s new boyfriend, Barker, moved in with her and Peter. The following month, a GP noticed bruises on Peter’s face and chest, with his mum was arrested on suspicion of child abuse and him put into the care of a family friend. The tot was, however, returned to his mum in January 2007. Over the next few months, Peter was admitted to hospital twice, suffering from injuries including bruising, scratches and swelling on his head. Connelly, then 27, was arrested for a second time that May. A month later, a social worker spotted marks on the child and told the police, and a resultant medical examination concluded the bruising was due to child abuse, and he was again placed with a friend for safeguarding. On July 25, Haringey Council’s Children & Young People’s Service sought legal advice, which suggested the “threshold for initiating care proceedings” had not been met. Injuries to Peter’s face and hands were missed by a social worker five days later, after the boy was deliberately smeared with chocolate to hide them. On August 1, Peter was examined by a locum paediatrician at a child development clinic at St Ann’s Hospital. However, a post-mortem following the baby’s death on August 3 showed a broken back and broken ribs that likely went undetected. The day prior to Peter’s death, Connelly was told she would not be prosecuted, but on August 3, an ambulance was called to the family home and the child was found unresponsive in his cot, wearing only a nappy. He was rushed to North Middlesex Hospital but was pronounced dead at 12.20pm, with police immediately launching a murder investigation, and Connelly was arrested. She pleaded guilty to causing or allowing the death of a child or vulnerable person, while Owen, 36, and Barker, 32, were found guilty of the same charge in November 2008. Owen and Connelly were cleared of murder due to insufficient evidence, while Barker was found not guilty of murder by a jury. Connelly received a sentence of indefinite imprisonment for public protection, subject to a minimum term of five years. The mum, now 42, was initially released on licence in 2013 but recalled to prison in 2015 for breaching parole conditions. Parole bids, in 2015, 2017 and 2019, were rejected. She was eventually given parole in July 2022, but again breached her licence conditions and was recalled to prison in September last year.

She’d been called into a police station near where she lived in Haringey, North London, where a decision had to be made whether to hold her on remand or extend her bail, in relation to suspicions she’d been beating little Peter.

Though not his case, as a senior officer on duty at the time, Mr Wedger was given the obligatory opportunity to confront Connelly – just a couple of days prior to Peter’s death.

He said she had put on an act as a caring mum, while giving “ridiculous” excuses for her son’s injuries – before Mr Wedger read to her the paediatric report, which suggested severe physical trauma.

Suddenly, the mask slipped.

“She lost control and she stood up and spat at me and called me a c***,” he recalled.

“She couldn’t control herself. I turned round to her and said ‘that is the monster your child sees’.”

However, the decision to extend her bail was taken out of Mr Wedger’s hands, despite his protestations.

Connelly was previously released from prison in 2013 but recalled just two years later after selling nude pictures of herself online.



Then, despite a mountain of controversy, the decision was made to free Connelly again in 2022 and she was made subject to 20 licence conditions – but was once again locked up again in August last year for a further breach.

Yesterday’s report agreed Connelly still presents “a high risk of serious harm to children, the public and known adults”.

Experts found she would prioritise her own sexual needs over that of anyone in her care and could even seek out her surviving adult children once her licence terms end.

Due to the nature of her sentence, she would only have to serve two years on licence if she was to be released from prison again.

A Parole Board statement said: “Parole Board decisions are solely focused on what risk a prisoner could represent to the public.

“Parole reviews are always undertaken thoroughly and with extreme care. Protecting the public is our number one priority.”

Justice Secretary Alex Norris must now review the panel’s decision and decide whether to approve or reject the transfer to open prison.

Asked if he believes she can ever be rehabilitated, Mr Wedger said: “My opinion on meeting her – she will come across as plausible, respectable but she’s a liar. She’s a deep rooted, manipulative liar.



“She covers her tracks very well… she always did things to her advantage.”

He has his doubts if she can change, having witnessed the moment “the monster in her came out”.

He went on to say: “It’s twisted and sadistic – I don’t think that woman should be allowed near children ever.

“I don’t think that woman should ever be given a second chance.”

He said: “I would say that woman needs to be kept in an environment where there are no children.

“And if that’s prison then it’s prison.”

News.title: TV florist who appeared on hit BBC show killed great-gran, 89, in horror crash at Sainsbury’s car park
News.content:
SMASH TRAGEDY TV florist who appeared on hit BBC show killed great-gran, 89, in horror crash at Sainsbury’s car park







Next

A TV florist who appeared on a hit BBC show killed a great-gran in a horror crash in a Sainsbury’s car park.

Jonathan Moseley, who featured on BBC Two’s The Big Allotment Challenge, smashed into Barbara Matthews, 89, as she did her weekly shop.



The gran, who walked with a stick, suffered a head injury and died at the scene in Dronfield, Derbyshire on June 10 last year.

Moseley claimed he had looked both ways before turning at a junction but did not see Barbara until it was too late.



The 55-year-old pleaded guilty to causing death by careless or inconsiderate driving but avoided a prison term.

He was instead given a three-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, at Derby Crown Court.



Moseley was also disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work.

Barbara’s daughter Tracy, who lives in the US, slammed the sentence, saying: “Our mum lost her life, and while we recognise that no sentence could bring her back, the consequences for the driver feel so small compared with the loss of a life.

“Mum left behind her children and their families, and we have all felt her loss deeply.

“The sentencing guidelines seemed shocking to me but I live in America and the guidelines here just don’t make sense to me.



“It feels that if someone dies it should automatically go to a certain level of serious category but it doesn’t work that way.”

Barbara’s family said she was very well known in the area and set up the first Brownies pack in Dronfield and was involved in Girl Guiding.

They told how she had a large family including five children, eight grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.



The family added: “She often said: ‘I will live to be 100.’ She said it so often that, somewhere along the way, we all rather believed her.

Receiving her royal letter when she reached 100 was something she genuinely looked forward to.”

They added: “Mum was still independent, still walking to the shops, still involved in our lives and still making plans. It is the simple things we miss most.

“She should still be here giving her two pennies’ worth, hearing about the achievements of her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and telling everyone else about them.

“We are grateful for the life we had with her, but if mum had had her way, she’d still have had another 11 years to go.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Moseley appeared on the judging panel as a floral expert on The Big Allotment Challenge.

He has worked with the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) at their major shows including Chelsea and Hampton Court.

News.title: My dad Ian Huntley was evil until the day he died & didn’t deserve to live…his killer did world a favour
News.content:
Next

SOHAM killer Ian Huntley’s daughter today said the man who has admitted killing her father has “done the world a favour”.

Samantha Bryan, 28, of Gateshead, Tyne and Wear, blasted her dead biological father Huntley, responsible for killing schoolgirls Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, as a monster.



Her words came as triple killer Anthony Russell, 44, who bludgeoned Huntley to death with a metal bar was given a second whole life jail term.

Samantha said of her dead father: “We haven’t got the likes of him walking around any more and we’re not wasting money keeping him in prison.



“In no way do I condone the terrible crimes Anthony Russell has also carried out that led to him being in prison.

“I have huge sympathy for his victims, particularly as my own mother is a victim of Huntley, and so my heart is very much with them and I am horrified for what he’s in there for.

“But I do think by killing Huntley he has done the world a favour. He should get a medal for that.

“However, it is also right that he feels the full weight of the law and a harsh sentence because murder is murder.”



Samantha, who never met Huntley, added: “Living was too good for my biological father.

“He was a monster.

“I do believe Huntley would never have changed or been rehabilitated.

“He never fully admitted what he had done. He was evil.”

Anthony Russell, 44, had initially denied intentionally killing Huntley, 52, at the high security Frankland Prison, near Durham, in February, but admitted manslaughter.



But Russell changed his plea on the second day of his trial at Newcastle Crown Court today.

He and Huntley, who killed 10-year-old schoolgirls Holly and Jessica in August 2002, were both on the high security prison’s A-wing, the trial had heard, and there was “tension” between the pair of killers.

At about 09:00am on 26 February, Russell attacked Huntley in the prison’s recycling workshop, repeatedly beating him about the head with a metal bar, the court had heard.



He told prison officers Huntley was an “arrogant” and “cocky” bully who had previously punched him and that he was a “horrible narcissistic person”.

And Samantha’s mother Katie Bryan said Huntley had been a wicked bully all his life – launching a terrifying series of attacks on her when they were together, after meeting her as a 15-year-old schoolgirl.

Katie said: “Seeing Huntley’s face on the news today has brought back to me the full horror of what he did to me, as well as his other victims including Holly and Jessica and others he attacked.

“My thoughts are with her parents.

“Like Samantha, oh god, I definitely feel Huntley’s killer has done the world a favour because now it’s the end.



“We don’t have to see his face any more. We don’t have to be reminded of the crimes he’s committed.”

She admitted she has continued to live in fear that Huntley might one day get parole – and his death freed her of that.

Katie, a carer, said: “I’m relieved that he will never have the chance to see my daughter Samantha.”



Samantha first found out Huntley was her father aged 14, by a fluke.

She was asked to research a school project on crime and when she clicked on Ian Huntley’s name in a search engine in the classroom she recognised a pixelated photo of herself.

She discovered her mother Katie had met him as a 15-year-old schoolgirl and they embarked on a relationship, when she was under the legal age of consent.

Katie said their relationship descended into violence culminating in a sickening act of rape as she got out of a bath, for which she courageously waived her anonymity.

Katie also claims he exerted control over her through fear and bullying, and among a catalogue of domestic abuse, he made her eat cat food when she burned his dinner, cut off her hair so other men wouldn’t admire her and in a final act of violence pushed her down the stairs when she was pregnant with Samantha.



That was the catalyst for her to leave him as she feared for her unborn baby.

Her family did report Huntley to police at the time but he claimed he was shielding Katie who had run away from home – which was a lie.

Years later Huntley went on to kill Holly and Jessica and the disappearance and murders of the girls in Soham, Cambridgeshire, sparked one of the largest hunts in British criminal history.

Their bodies were found after two weeks, leading to a manhunt for their killer, which ended with the arrest of former school caretaker Huntley, who had hung around TV crews covering the murder, even giving interviews.



He was found guilty in December 2003.

Katie said: “Huntley was always a bully whose violence and gaslighting nearly broke me as a teenager.

“If I didn’t have my family he would have broken me.

“And it is clear by Russell’s words that Huntley was still a bully.



“Further proof that he had not changed and it was not possible to rehabilitate someone who had committed such terrible crimes.

“I have such mixed feelings like Samantha, because as a victim, Russell is a monster too.

“I also don’t condone his crimes in any way, shape or form, but he has done everybody a favour.

“But the full weight of the law still needs to come down on him.”

When she turned 18, Samantha wrote to her father asking to meet him – because she wanted him to give an account of his crimes – which he never did.



Samantha said: “When Huntley first wrote to me, he hinted that one day he might tell me the truth, but then whined about his life.

“I knew then he would never give the answers that I wanted.

“I think to be rehabilitated you have to be accountable for what you have done.

“That was never going to happen.

“I feel he was trying to manipulate and put a barrier between me and my mum and make me question what she had told me.



“It was sickening.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Katie added: “As a family this closes the door on the darkest chapter of our lives – we don’t have to see Huntley’s face on the TV any more or even think about him.

“But we can never forget what he did.”

News.title: Everyone can see the polar bear but what YOU spot first in this Christmas illusion reveals your true personality
News.content:
Next

THE festive season is upon us and nothing sparks Christmas joy like a game played amongst friends and family.

So why not try your hand at deciphering this illusion – and see what it reveals about your personality.

Upon first glance, this snowy scene may appear to be a mix of at least five separate animals, each one smaller than the last.



However, the animal your eyes are drawn to first can, in fact, reveal key aspects of your character and nature – using the Myers-Briggs personality test.



Polar bear

If you spotted the polar bear first, you may value tranquility, privacy and consistency.

You can be considered a reliable person to those around you, and are loyal regardless of the circumstances.

Donkey

Meanwhile, those who found the donkey first may be considered strong-minded individuals.

Although you have no issue with voicing your opinions, you are also considered a kind and loving person, willing to offer guidance and advice to those around you.

Reindeer

Reindeer-centered individuals can be seen as knowledgeable and resilient, although they find comfort in community.

Sticking close to a pack is important to those who saw the reindeer first – animals which are known for their intellect, playfulness and curiosity.

Turkey

If you saw the turkey above all other animals, you are likely to be generous with those around you – without asking for favours in return.



You may use these traits to strengthen the relationships in your life and pay close attention to their needs and desires.

Robin

Although small in size and stature, those who spotted the robin first are likely to be practical problem solvers.

Those with this trait may be ambitious towards achieving their goals but are still considered empathetic and appreciative of the simple things in life.

Squirrel

Both energetic and self-confident, if you spotted a squirrel first then it is likely you are never scared of new situations.

Whether this means taking on a new challenge, meeting new people or finding a different path in life – you tackle each day with confidence and enthusiasm.



Partridge

On the opposite end of the spectrum, those who see the partridge first tend to be quiet and reserved in situations that are outside of their comfort zone.

However, you value your close friends and family, and can be considered a fiercely loyal character.

Turtle Dove

Lastly, if you saw a dove, it means you are likely to be a considerate, calm and people-centered individual.

Your laid-back nature means you are capable of getting along with almost anyone – but also means you may be conflict avoidant.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Myers-Briggs Type personality test sorts people into 16 types based on how they perceive the world – or in this case, which image they spot first.



The test uses four parameters to classify personalities, which is Extraversion or Introversion, Sensing or Intuition, Thinking or Feeling, and Judging or Perceiving.

News.title: Hunt for five ‘mole people’ spotted climbing out of sewer with headlamps & shovels before escaping in getaway car
News.content:
PIPE DREAM Hunt for five ‘mole people’ spotted climbing out of sewer with headlamps & shovels before escaping in getaway car







Next

POLICE are hunting five people spotted crawling out of a sewer last week in the latest suspected sighting of Manhattan’s “mole people”.

The subterranean crew emerged from the manhole wearing headlamps and holding shovels before they fled in a getaway car.



Photos released by the New York Police Department (NYPD) appear to show one woman and four men climbing up from the sewers.

The explorers then jumped into a red sedan with a female getaway driver behind the wheel, before they disappeared into the night.



There have been no arrests so far after police were alerted to the mysterious sighting at around 5am last Wednesday.

It marks the latest in a series of suspicious sewer activity throughout New York City in recent months that has sparked wild conspiracy theories.

Cops said another group were spotted sneaking out of a manhole on Manhattan’s Upper East side just days earlier, the New York Post reports.

Baffled residents have feared everything from bank raids to sabotage plots.



But investigators believe the bizarre sewer excursions may have a far less sinister explanation – hunting for precious goods.

In September a duo of suspected “mole people” were arrested in the city.

Kevin Rodrigues, 26, and Samuel Reveron, 25, were charged with conspiracy and trespassing after emerging from the sewers.

Their expedition found them underneath a hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had been staying, cops said.

Reveron allegedly told police: “We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value.”



They have both pleaded not guilty and have since been released from custody, court records show.

New York cops have reported a number of cases where people have been spotted diving into the sewer system to look for valuable items.

It was unclear if Reveron and Rodriguez are connected to any of the previous cases caught on surveillance footage.



In August, CCTV footage showed one suspect exiting a manhole in Queens in the early hours of the day.

The same month, cops said they were probing three people wearing overalls and headlamps coming out of a manhole near Penn Station.

Sources told the New York Post that an NYPD Emergency Services Unit sweep and a city environmental investigation found no signs of criminal activity.

Instead, authorities suspect the men were scavenging through the sewer network hunting for valuables accidentally lost down drains.

In Gravesend, shocking footage showed a man lifting a manhole cover from McDonald Avenue before placing it on the curb.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Moments later, a man carrying a flashlight climbed out of the sewer – followed by six others in a scene compared to a circus clown car.

Some appeared to be wearing waders and boots before stripping off their filthy clothing on the pavement and loading belongings into three waiting cars.

News.title: Daughters of dry cleaning tycoon, 88, in inheritance row after he left £3m fortune to woman, 69, he met in supermarket
News.content:
DIRTY LAUNDRY Daughters of dry cleaning tycoon, 88, in inheritance row after he left £3m fortune to woman, 69, he met in supermarket







Next

THE family of a dry cleaning tycoon are locked in a bitter inheritance fight over his £3m will – after he left his fortune to a woman he met in a supermarket.

Entrepreneur Ali Djemal, who died in 2022, left his entire estate to Hacer Gun, who he met while shopping when she was 52 and he was 75.



Djemal’s daughters say Hacer exerted “undue influence” on their father and have gone to court in a bid to have his decision to leave his entire state to her overturned.

Half sisters Saniye and Mary Djemal are challenging their dad’s last will on grounds that he lacked full mental capacity and that Hacer alienated the pair from him.



Lawyers for the sisters say Ali’s bank account was “decimated” by payments to Hacer’s family, who tried to distance him from his family by changing his number and “blocking his children from his telephone”.

Hacer, now 69, said she started helping around Ali’s London home, but that their relationship “deepened” and they became romantically involved, leading Ali to change his will in 2018 and leave her his estate.

But Saniye and Mary say Hacer was only their father’s “carer”.

Ali died in 2022 and left Hacer everything, on the condition that “she satisfies the needs of my daughter, Mary, for all her life”.



Saniye and Mary Djemal were left outraged by the terms, claiming that despite the caveat it provided no protection for his “adored” younger daughter Mary and nothing at all for Saniye.

The two sisters want Judge Alan Johns KC to overrule the 2018 will and reinstate one from 1992, which left three properties in now upmarket Swinton Street, Kings Cross, to his three children in equal shares.

Ali’s third child, the sisters’ brother, Murat Soyer, who lives in Cyprus, is playing no active part in the case.

Susan Bayliss, for Saniye and Mary, said the two sisters also take issue with claims that Hacer was ever romantically involved with their dad, telling the court: “Hacer Gun is the deceased’s former carer.

Hacer’s lawyers say Ali’s will reflected his true feelings, insisting that for his last 12 years they were a couple, “that they enjoyed a happy and romantic relationship” and that he made clear he’d be “dead without her”.



London’s High Court heard that Hacer says she initially helped around Ali’s house in Grays Inn Road, central London, after the pair met in a supermarket, as well as helping care for his disabled then partner.

But their relationship blossomed, claimed her barrister, Ollie Murrell, and by 2010 the pair were romantically involved, with Hacer visiting him six times per week and later also helping out in his dry cleaning business.

Lawyers said that due to her alleged “coercive control” over Ali, “it may be inferred” that the will was “procured by the undue influence” of Hacer at a time when he was mentally frail and vulnerable.

Overall, her conduct made his children “extremely concerned about Ali’s wellbeing,” Ms Bayliss told the judge.

“They observed that he was frail and became easily confused and they took action about their concerns, contacting his GP about his mental decline – and subsequently the police and social services when they could not contact him personally.



“They were extremely concerned about the influence of Ms Gun over the deceased because they had witnessed her involve herself in his business and finances, and isolate him from his family.

“They contend that, by 2016-2017, her influence over Ali was such that he was entirely dependent on her and she assumed more or less complete control over him.”

As well as isolating their dad, the sisters’ barrister claimed Hacer was behind a series of transactions which ended up depleting £500,000 from Ali’s coffers, which she said her clients deem “suspicious”.

This half million pound splurge included £270,000 transferred to Hacer’s son in August 2017, other smaller cash injections to her and her family, and £107,929 lavished on Amazon bills.

Denying that Hacer “decimated” Ali’s bank accounts, Mr Murrell added: “By 2015 the deceased had come to view Hacer and her family as his own and his relations with his own family had begun to break down.



“The deceased was, therefore, doing nothing unusual in gifting money, driving lessons and other items of relatively significant value to (her children) in the usual course of love and affection.”

Ali had “routinely” asked Hacer to make purchases on his behalf, and much of the whopping Amazon bill was incurred during Covid when online shopping was the norm, it was argued.

And far from Hacer alienating his family, it was Ali himself who wanted to keep them at arms’ length due to ongoing conflicts with Saniye – one of which involved a running dispute over a dead relative’s will.

“His decision to distance himself from – in particular Saniye and her son – is readily explicable,” Mr Murrell told the judge.

“Quite aside from some orchestrated campaign by Ms Gun to isolate Ali from his family, he had very good reason to reduce and break off contact.



“Firstly, there were Saniye’s and Mary’s actions on 16 November 2016 when they contacted Ali’s GP to make allegations of poor memory and health.

“There is no doubt this marked a serious fracture in Ali’s relationship with Saniye, and Hacer says it is one which never healed,” the barrister continued, adding that Ali felt he was being “manipulated”.

On top of this, Ali was “already embroiled” in money disputes with Saniye and her son, the barrister pointed out.

But the sisters’ barrister, attacking the 2018 will, said its terms contradicted Ali’s “expressed lifetime intentions and conduct – to provide for his blood family”.

And although his relationship with Saniye had hit a “rocky patch” in 2016, providing for his family was always on his mind.



Quizzed by the sisters’ barrister in the witness box, Hacer described Ali as a “strict and authoritarian person” who made his own decisions about whether to see his close family.

Saniye and Mary say their dad was forgetful and “apt to be confused” in his final years, and “susceptible to Hacer’s influence”, but in her evidence she insisted that Ali was still clear-minded and capable of taking business decisions up until the final months of his life.

“He didn’t suffer from any forgetfulness whatsoever,” she told the court.

Hacer, who denied “pushing” Ali away from his family and said they had offered Mary a room once they moved to Enfield, also disputed that the younger sibling’s phone calls were blocked from his phone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ali’s net estate has been valued at up to £3m.



The trial continues.

News.title: Wild double life of professor’s mistress revealed as ‘real-life Fatal Attraction affair’ sparks bombshell legal battle
News.content:
Next

THE “real-life Fatal Attraction” mistress at the heart of a bitter legal battle with her former lover is also a Britney Spears-inspired singer.

Annie Kerman, 36, is accused of launching a vicious harassment campaign against Columbia University professor Wouter Dessein, 52, after he refused to end his marriage for her.



The allegations filed in a lawsuit on Tuesday sparked a bombshell feud, with Kerman firing back her own suit accusing Dessein of sexual assault.

Now wild details of Kerman’s alleged aliases have emerged – including as a classically trained “new queen of rock”, the Daily Mail reports.



Kerman has a number of online accounts under the name Abi Lorrel – which is mentioned in Dessein’s lawsuit, according to the outlet.

In one profile, she describes herself as a former opera star who won an MTV music award as a teen in Belarus.



She also claims to be a “Chernobyl survivor” while her website says she was mentored by singer Gladys Knight and rapper Sticky Fingaz.

A lengthy biography states: “Abi’s career took off rapidly, finding fame in Belarus and parts of Russia.



“With a foundation in music theory, she became a classically trained opera singer, composer, and arranger.

“By the age of sixteen, she won MTV’s Best New Artist award in Europe.”

Kerman is not listed as a winner or nominee in this category for the MTV Europe awards or regional awards for 2001-2008.

“Today, Abi Lorrel is on the cusp of releasing collaborations with legends like Gladys Knight, KRS-One, and many more,” the website continues.

Kerman’s websites also claim she has played at venues called the New York Stadium and the Borgata Center in Philadelphia.



But there are no records of stadiums by these names in these cities, the outlet reports.

Kerman posted a YouTube video called “Don’t Ban TikTok” in 2024, when Congress was considering banning the social media site over ties to China.

In the clip she can be seen writhing around in a Barbie sweatshirt and Louis Vuitton-print sunglasses.



Details of Kerman’s alleged alter egos surfaced after her former lover referenced her aliases in his lawsuit filed on Tuesday in New York’s Westchester County.

The lawsuit from Dessein branded Kerman an “intelligent, manipulative woman who has an Ivy League education and a penchant for vengeance.”

He went on to describe her “calculated, months-long campaign to destroy” his life as a “real-life” version of the 1987 thriller Fatal Attraction.

According to Dessein’s filing, the pair met for their first date in 2024 where Kerman introduced herself as Veronica, lied about being 28 and said she came from Lithuania.

She claims none of those details were true.



The relationship reportedly grew increasingly serious, with the professor allegedly paying towards Kerman’s rent, travel and other living expenses from May 2025.

But he claimed trouble erupted when Dessein decided to save his marriage to Zhihong Zhang rather than build a future with his mistress.

His lawsuit alleged Kerman began demanding £4,500 a month before he confessed the affair to his wife on January 17.

Four days later, Dessein allegedly ended the relationship during a video call.

He claims she told him: “It’s gonna be ugly for you. Very ugly. Very … the worst possible thing you can think of.”



Dessein and his wife are seeking damages including more than £91,800 in legal fees, £6,800 for mental health treatment, and £34,200 in lost tuition payments for their child.

According to Kerman’s lawsuit, Dessein sexually assaulted her, ignoring her objections and continuing after she had made clear she did not want sex.

Her lawsuit claims the alleged assault triggered a severe psychological crisis that resulted in her hospitalisation.

She is seeking unspecified damages for sexual battery, assault and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Dessein has vehemently denied the accusations.

News.title: Jilted bride who went ahead with wedding despite groom no-show marries 'forever man'
News.content:
Jilted bride who went ahead with wedding despite groom no-show marries 'forever man'

Kayley Stead, 30, from Swansea, went ahead with her £12,000 wedding celebrations after being left at the altar - now she's tied the knot with former university friend Richard Perrott.

Jilted bride who carried on with her wedding gets married after finding love again

A bride who celebrated her £12,000 wedding alone after her fiancé failed to turn up has finally married her “forever man” more than four years later.

‌



‌



Kayley Stead, 30, tied the knot with former university friend Richard Perrott, 31, on November 13 in front of 156 guests at a Grade II listed Georgian home in Fairyhill, Swansea.

‌



Richard proposed to Kayley on the university campus where they first met while studying acting more than a decade ago.

‌



Kayley was left devastated in September 2022 when her former fiancé failed to show up on what was supposed to be their wedding day.

Rather than cancel the celebrations, Kayley spent the day posing for photographs and celebrating with family and friends.

The insurance team manager from Swansea reunited with Richard in February 2024. The couple spent more than a year in a long-distance relationship before he moved from Manchester to be with her.

‌



View 7 Images (Image: Neil Jones Photography / SWNS)

Speaking before her second wedding, Kayley said: "I'd say Richard has been involved but he's very much more of a yes or no man rather than putting things together on spreadsheets.

‌



"That's my job. It's been completely different this time around. I learnt a lot from the first one.

"When I think about another wedding, there is always that little devil on my shoulder reminding me that I trusted someone before and they let me down.

‌



View 7 Images Kayley and Richard Perrott tied the knot in front of 156 guests. (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

"But Richard is different. Not only do I trust him, I trust his family too. It feels like it’s always meant to be. I can just be myself and be honest - no class difference and just complete honesty.

‌



"The one thing I didn't get to last time was I didn't step into the ceremony room. That's one thing I'm excited about but also nervous.

"I keep on saying 'fingers crossed he's going to show up'. I do believe he'll be there but you never know."

‌



View 7 Images (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

The pair moved in together in March, with Kayley unaware Richard, a commercial insurance broker, was already secretly planning a proposal.

‌



Kayley said: "He took me back to our university campus and suggested we go for food afterwards.

"We stopped to look at the view and he was acting really strangely. I remember thinking, ‘What is he doing? He’s seen all this before.’

‌



"Then he said, ‘Back where it all began’ - I joked and said, ‘Is this where it’s going to end? "He said he had a confession to make and told me he hadn’t actually booked any food. I was horrified because I was so hungry - but then he got down on one knee."

View 7 Images Richard moved from Manchester to Swansea to be with Kayley. (Image: Kayley Stead / SWNS)

‌



The couple were surrounded by their nearest and dearest, with 11 bridesmaids and 13 groomsmen. "The majority of the bridesmaids are the bridesmaids I had before," Kayley said.

"It's nice to have a full circle moment with the girls who stood by me last time.

‌



"I think the ceremony is what I'm looking forward to most and enjoying that, it's the moment I've always dreamed of happening."

Kayley said the pair are both keen foodies and focused on the catering rather than other details "like the flowers and all that".

‌



View 7 Images (Image: Neil Jones Photography / SWNS)

Guests were treated to pancakes, hot chocolate and a make-your-own s'mores stand at the wedding reception, with a saxophonist providing entertainment after a string quartet accompanied Kayley down the aisle.

‌



For her big day, Kayley opted for a custom-made gown by designer April Banbury, describing the experience of finding her wedding dress as “different” to her first.

"A woman who runs a boutique called The Dress & I invited me to come to her venue and I didn't expect to find a dress at all," she said.

‌



View 7 Images (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

"My body is different, I'm different and I wanted a different dress to the first one because I'm a different person.

Article continues below

"The first dress I tried on I absolutely loved but it wasn't completely perfect, because I wanted something that celebrated me.

"Luckily the designer April Banbury was willing to change the skirt to make it bespoke so it's a completely unique dress, one of a kind."

News.title: Martin Lewis' MSE says £10 item could save money on energy bills
News.content:
Martin Lewis' MSE says £10 item could save money on energy bills

Many households are having to choose between heating and eating

Martin Lewis shares his thoughts after 26% increase in energy price cap

Money Saving Expert (MSE) has useful advice that could help ordinary UK households as they prepare for energy bills to shoot up. People can check what setting their radiators are on and fit a valve for around £10. MSE, which was founded by Martin Lewis, says that "energy costs are in turmoil right now due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East", with many struggling to pay.

‌



‌



The updated advice, posted on November 24, came a day before it was announced the Ofgem price cap on energy bills was set to soar by 26%. Today (November 25), regulator Ofgem explained that from January 1 to March 31 2027, energy prices will go up by 26% for a typical household that uses electricity and gas and pays by Direct Debit.

‌



The energy regulator reminded households that the UK government had also announced that around 20 million households will receive £100 towards their energy bill from January. The UK government has also announced plans to remove standing charges from gas bills in 2027 or as soon as possible afterwards.

‌



£10 purchase could save on energy bills

View 2 Images Martin Lewis has urged people to speak to their energy provider if they are worried (Image: ITV)

In its cost-cutting tip, MSE explained that thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) are a good source of "extra control" which you can use to set the temperature of each individual room - other than where your main thermostat is. Once the room temperature exceeds the level set on the radiator valve, the valve stops hot water from flowing through that radiator.

The boiler can still heat other rooms, but it will use less energy overall. MSE explains: "Installing them and using them with your thermostat allows you to control the temperature room by room, and could save on energy bills, but there will of course be an initial cost for the valves, which cost about £10 plus installation costs.

‌



"Most thermostatic radiator valves have a frost prevention setting – usually a snowflake symbol. So when the valve is fully turned off, it'll still let a small amount of hot water through to prevent pipes from freezing. If your radiators don't have TRVs, be careful not to turn them off completely, as this could result in burst pipes in very cold weather."

You could save £40 a year

To help with these soaring costs at such an expensive time of the year, MSE further recommends turning down radiators in unused rooms so you’re not heating empty spaces. It notes that Smart Energy GB says setting radiator valves to the midway point in rooms you don’t use could save about £40 a year.

‌



However, it warns: "In some homes, colder rooms could lead to more condensation, which can increase the risk of mould. Also, be aware that fridges and freezers generally can't function properly if room temperatures drop too low (typically below 10C)."

Start this daily habit now

View 2 Images Martin Lewis spoke to Good Morning Britain viewers following the news of the energy price cap (Image: ITV)

‌



If you commute to the office, try to turn the radiator dials down before 9am, when many start work, so you’re not heating your bedroom or living room once you’ve left for the day. Even if you work from home, it’s a useful habit.

If your desk is in your bedroom, consider wearing an extra layer to stay comfortable while keeping the thermostat set slightly lower to save money. Heating the person may be better than heating the home if you are struggling, Mr Lewis says.

‌



Should you paint your radiator black?

Is this a myth, or does it work? Well, according to MSE, don't bother. It says: "Some also say that painting your radiators black can help them heat rooms more efficiently, but as far as the Energy Saving Trust is concerned, this is a waste of time and money (and paint)."

News.title: Pharmacist says anyone taking blood pressure meds should avoid 2p item
News.content:
Pharmacist says anyone taking blood pressure meds should avoid 2p item

Never assume something is automatically okay without seeking medical advice

View 2 Images Ramipril is prescribed to around six million people in the UK alone (Image: Trevor Williams)

People taking certain blood pressure medication have been warned to avoid a common pill that could cause kidney issues when mixed together. People should be aware of the red-flag symptoms that something is wrong after taking ibuprofen, pharmacists say.

‌



‌



Ibuprofen is a painkiller for headaches, toothache and back pain that is readily available in most stores and supermarkets, such as Asda, Morrisons and Aldi for as little as 2p a pill. Pharmacists are warning it can be risky to mix it with some blood pressure tablets like ramipril, lisinopril, losartan and candesartan without first getting advice.

‌



Experts say ibuprofen reduces blood flow to the kidneys by blocking chemical messengers called prostaglandins, which normally help keep kidney blood vessels open and support filtration. A sudden drop in kidney function can happen over hours or days, especially if blood flow is already strained.

‌



Pharmacist Raj Patel, known online as the Straight Talking Pharmacist, says people should treat buying ibuprofen as a 'mini medicines check'. This is because the interaction risk depends on your full list of prescriptions and what you’ve picked up yourself from supermarkets or online.

Before buying ibuprofen, the medicine expert advises telling a pharmacist the names and strengths of all medicines you take, including low-dose aspirin, supplements and anything bought elsewhere. A photo of your repeat prescription list can help, but it’s also important to mention what you’ve actually taken recently, not just what’s on the list.

‌



One common misconception is that taking ibuprofen with food makes it “safer”. Mr Patel says food may reduce stomach irritation, but it does not eliminate kidney or blood pressure interactions.

He also warns people not to assume that because one combination has been mentioned as acceptable, all similar combinations are safe. For example, he says that 75mg of aspirin can be taken with ramipril, but that does not mean adding ibuprofen to regular low-dose aspirin is automatically suitable.

‌



Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as a Preferred Source in your Google search settings

View 2 Images Be sure to seek medical advice before assuming something simple is safe (stock)

‌



If ibuprofen is prescribed, Mr Patel suggests asking your doctor whether you need blood tests to check kidney function and potassium levels. A normal older result doesn’t guarantee safety during a new illness.

Taking one dose does not automatically mean you have done any major harm to your body. It is, however, worth noting the product, strength, amount, and time, then checking with a pharmacist before taking more.

Article continues below

Mr Patel urges people to watch for red flags of possible kidney injury such as much less urine, new swelling, unusual confusion or drowsiness. It is important to seek urgent help via an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111. For life-threatening symptoms, call 999.

News.title: Budget airline with popular UK flights warns situation is 'criticial'
News.content:
Budget airline with popular UK flights warns situation is 'criticial'

Norse Atlantic, an Oslo-based long-haul budget airline that operates routes from London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok, Cape Town and Phuket, is in discussions about a potential takeover

View 2 Images Norse Atlantic's bosses are in short-term financing talks

Norse Atlantic's financial situation is "critical," with the airline's future in serious doubt. The long-haul budget carrier, which operates from London Gatwick, may have to cancel its remaining flights if its financial situation isn't resolved, potentially affecting thousands of customers.

‌



‌



The Oslo-based airline currently operates routes from London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok, Cape Town and Phuket, although in recent months some flight routes have been scrapped, including both US routes from the UK to New York and Los Angeles.

‌



Norse has also gotten rid of staff, scrapping 75 jobs earlier this year. In July, the airline launched a formal process for a potential sale or merger, the Independent reported. Bosses said it was in talks with airlines about leasing some Boeing 787 aircraft to manage soaring fuel costs.

‌



The Norwegian company is now in talks to secure short-term financing, it said in a statement.

View 2 Images Norse Atlantic operates routes from London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok, Cape Town and Phuket (Image: Norse Atlantic Airways)

“Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover,” the company said.

‌



“In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short-term financing; however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution. Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”

The long-haul budget carrier operates a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. It also runs charter flights to serve P&O Cruises ships in the Caribbean during the winter, while leasing two aircraft to Pakistan International Airlines.

‌



The announcement on Wednesday morning caused Norse shares to plummet. They dropped more than 53 per cent in early Oslo trading to a new all-time low.

The US and Israeli bomb campaign in Iran, and the subsequent closure of the Straight of Hormuz, has caused fuel prices across the world to rocket. The carrier does not hedge its jet fuel needs, leading it to be hit hard by the spike in prices.

‌



Norse Atlantic is not the only airline to encounter issues this year.

The UK's newest airline, launched by a millionaire influencer with plans to fly the world's largest passenger aircraft on transatlantic routes, was placed in compulsory liquidation earlier this month.

‌



James Asquith's Global Airlines was set up in 2021. The founder of Airbnb rival platform Holiday Swap said the airline would be like no other, operating a fleet of A380s across the Atlantic Ocean with a 'Gamer Class' of video gaming pods.

While attention grabbing, the challenge of launching a new airline seems to have proved too great, with Global Airlines placed into compulsory liquidation following a High Court winding-up order.

‌



The order was made by the Insolvency and Companies Court on 4 November 2026 and subsequently published in The London Gazette on 12 November. The company now faces the formal process of compulsory liquidation, UK Aviation News reports.

The company initially outlined ambitions to establish a fleet of four aircraft, with proposed flights from the UK to destinations in North America and beyond.

News.title: 'I'm an NHS doctor – here are the flu season products I don't bother with'
News.content:
'I'm an NHS doctor – here are the flu season products I don't bother with'

An NHS GP shared the products in the pharmacy that she would never pick up if she had a cold or the flu and revealed the remedies she thinks are far more effective

View 3 Images Sometimes, at-home remedies are more effective than ones you can find on the pharmacy shelves (Stock Image) (Image: Getty)

Cold and flu season is officially upon us, and it feels almost impossible to avoid mingling with people at this time of year. From work Christmas parties to socialising with friends at festive markets, once someone in the group chat says they've started to develop cold symptoms, you'll likely grab all the over-the-counter remedies you can carry from your local pharmacy.

‌



‌



However, one NHS doctor has said these remedies may be entirely futile and that you may be wasting your money. Dr Mandy, a GP, warned that many over-the-counter remedies are "either overpriced paracetamol, boiled sweets or ingredients your gut destroys before they even get to work".

‌



Dr Mandy shared what she personally wouldn't bother with if you're unfortunate enough to catch a cold or the flu during the winter months and beyond - but also recommended things she would try.

‌



Cough syrups don't tend to work...

She said that cough syrups "do very little" and often contain high levels of sugar. She said there's "very limited evidence" behind them, and that's why they "don't recommend them on the NHS".

Content cannot be displayed without consent

But physical defence sprays can...

If you sense that you're getting unwell, if you use a physical defence spray, Dr Mandy shared it can "physically flush out the virus particles and stop them from multiplying". She also recommended saline spray, which is "drug-free" if you'd prefer.

‌



Over-the-counter cold and flu remedies often aren't great...

View 3 Images Sometimes, at-home remedies are better (Stock Image)

Dr Mandy shared that over-the-counter cold and flu remedies are often ineffective, thanks to components like phenylephrine being "broken down in your gut before it can do any decongesting".

‌



But you can make your own that's far more effective...

She recommends a concoction of two paracetamol, honey, and lemon instead, as it will "soothe the throat" and hopefully make you feel better. She did note it's not in a "convenient sachet," but there aren't too many ingredients to procure for this.

Ditch the big name brands...

When it comes to paracetamol and ibuprofen, she said that you can save yourself some serious money by putting the big-name brands back on the shelf.

‌



And buy generic instead...

Dr Mandy said that getting supermarket or pharmacy-brand tablets will save you a lot of money, and that they "work identically".

Mineral supplements may not be the best idea...

It may feel convenient to drop a tablet into a glass of water, watch it fizz, and then drink it down quickly, hoping that the vitamin C in it does the trick.

‌



But Dr Mandy said that "once the cold has settled in, high-dose vitamin C actually has very little benefit". She also warned that "your body can only absorb so much, and the rest ends up in your wee".

One vitamin she did recommend taking during the winter months, regardless, however, is vitamin D.

‌



But if you want to get vitamin C naturally...

View 3 Images Peppers and kiwis are much better (Image: Getty)

Dr Mandy said there are many things "better than a fizzy tablet," including golden kiwis and red peppers. She said: "You're better off getting it from whole foods so you can get the amazing polyphenols, nutrients and gut-busting fibre, too!"

‌



Ditch the boiled sweets...

"Expensive boiled sweets that don't fight inflammation or numb pain, or taste that nice," need to be ditched, according to Dr Mandy.

She said you should "look for medicated lozenges" if you want to get any, explaining that from these boiled sweets, "relief comes from making your mouth water, which you could get by sucking on a mint".

‌



Gargle salt water instead...

Dr Mandy said it's good to dissolve half a teaspoon of salt in warm water and gargle it. Yes, it might not taste that pleasant, but it's worth it. Just be sure to not swallow it.

"The salt draws out fluid to reduce swelling and cleanse the throat. Use it as often as you like, or two to three times a day," she recommended.

‌



And if you try Sudafed...

She recommended you go for the behind-the-counter version, because it contains pseudoephedrine, "which actually survives digestion".

Final advice...

Dr Mandy wrote: "Most winter bugs just need time, fluids and rest. Skip past the fancy packaging, stick to proven basics, and if your symptoms aren’t shifting or you’re worried, we’re always here to help".

If you're struggling with any illness, contact your GP. In an emergency, dial 999.
