News.title: Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn
News.content:
British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.

It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' (Natsal, external) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.

Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.

But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.

Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.

News.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
News.content:
The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by European ambassadors later on Wednesday.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Alignment with higher EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles would increase their price in the UK, at a time when they have become increasingly popular.

It also raises the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on cars made in the UK.

News.title: Hundreds complain about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive'
News.content:
Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "aggressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else".

"I think women who speak their mind and are forthright, that's 'aggressive', whereas a man who speaks his mind and is forthright is a 'strong man'," she said, but added that "I totally get that there's more" when race is involved.

Odudu responded: "I do definitely see your point and agree with it, but those words stick as well. Those words can stick for us. The moment passes for you and it doesn't pass for me."

"But hopefully it has?" Frostrup asked.

Odudu replied: "Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have been there."

Signs of friction resurfaced when Frostrup told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well".

Odudu replied that "of course" she had accepted her apology, before Frostrup accepted that "it's really important to me to understand why it's triggering".

Odudu added: "It's good you asked, but it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women."

"Good to know," Frostrup concluded.

An ITV statement said: "The production monitors everyone in camp 24/7 and if at any time we feel someone has overstepped the line by using inappropriate language or displaying unacceptable behaviour, we would take steps to intervene and speak to everyone involved.

"The duty of care for our contestants is of the utmost importance to us. We take the welfare of the celebrities very seriously and have measures in place to ensure they are supported at every stage of the process: before, during and after filming."

News.title: Why has China sent the first Pakistani astronaut to space?
News.content:
China has sent a Pakistani astronaut along with two Chinese astronauts onto its Shenzhou-24 mission, marking the first time a foreign national has set foot aboard the Tiangong space station.

The landmark moment for 40-year-old air force pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali highlights China's desire for its space station to become an international research facility.

The mission is expected to last for several days before returning to Earth.

Read more here.

News.title: Boy, 3, died after choking in nursery, inquest hears
News.content:
A three-year-old boy died after choking at a Greater Manchester nursery earlier this month, an inquest heard.

Thiago Wall died on 5 November after becoming critically ill at Cosy Toes Nursery, in Middleton, on 2 November.

An inquest at Rochdale Coroner's Court heard on Wednesday that Thiago had choked on a bowl of food and died three days later at the Royal Manchester Children's Hospital. A CT scan later confirmed the toddler had suffered a brain injury.

The nursery - and three other nurseries owned by Cosy Toes LTD - remain closed.

The inquest heard the toddler had a hypoxic brain injury, which can be a result of decreased oxygen supply to the brain.

An investigation by Greater Manchester Police continues.

News.title: Festive market cancels bookings after backlash over misleading AI images
News.content:
The organisers of a Christmas market have cancelled all bookings and promised to refund stallholders following a backlash to AI-generated promotional materials.

David Rowland, who produced the images for Kernow Christmas Market in Pool, Cornwall, said claims they did not match reality were a "lesson learned".

Images showed rows of stalls beneath Christmas decorations, fairy lights and festive displays for the event last weekend. But photographs taken by visitors showed a mostly empty hall with only a handful of traders, little Christmas decoration and buckets on the floor collecting water from a leaking roof.

Rowlands Attractions said it was "gutted" things "didn't go as planned".

It said: "The criticism we have faced and the words that have been seen on social media and across the news make us look at the world slightly differently.

"Kindness and compassion goes out of the window so easily to knock something that people don't care to understand the full story of."

News.title: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
News.content:
Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

The prime minister has ordered an independent panel modelled on the Hillsborough disaster investigation to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.

Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness" as he vowed to set up a "gold standard" investigation.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.

He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.

"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."

News.title: Influencers hit back at criticism of Downing Street videos
News.content:
Social media influencers have hit back at criticism of content filmed at an event in Downing Street with Andy Burnham, which critics said "demeaned" Number 10.

Max Balegde, who posted a TikTok video of himself miming to explicit lyrics outside the front door of the PM's official residence, apologised if any offence had been caused.

But he blamed "revolting right wing people" for stirring up controversy about it.

Government minister Bridget Phillipson said Balegde's now deleted TikTok video had been "totally unacceptable" but she said the prime minister was right to try to "reach people where they are" by engaging with influencers.

About 60 content creators were invited to a Downing Street reception last month, with videos from the event subsequently emerging online.

In one video, Max Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the Number 10 door, a symbol of the UK's power and authority, had been "degraded".

She said the PM "should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the use of the Downing Street door in videos was "puerile" and "demeaning" but he would also engage with content creators if he was PM.

Responding to the criticism in an Instagram post, Balegde said: "My content is always meant to be silly, fun, and light-hearted.

"If anybody was offended by that video, I sincerely apologise."

But he said "nobody was offended for weeks until revolting right-wing people tried to put this disgusting narrative on it".

"And if anybody then looks at the video and is offended, I get that. So hence why I took it down because I think that is disgusting."

News.title: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game
News.content:
Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (Â£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

News.title: Racism, misogyny and homophobia remain in Met force, report finds
News.content:
A new report has found institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia still exist in the Metropolitan Police, three years after a damning review that called for significant changes.

The landmark review by Dr Gillian Fairfield examined how much the UK's biggest police force has changed since Baroness Louise Casey's scathing review in 2023, external. It found the Met had failed to make good progress in any area flagged as needing improvement.

Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he accepted the Fairfield Review's findings.

London's mayor said much of the report came as "no surprise", and accused the Met and Sir Mark of "institutional defensiveness" that had downplayed the seriousness of previous reports.

Sir Mark said he had been "very clear" since he started the job that prejudices including racism, misogyny and homophobia "have got to be ruthlessly confronted".

But Lord Khan told BBC London he was "impatient for change" and that too often the Met used the phrase operational independence to "deny scrutiny, to deny accountability and to deny transparency".

"There are examples where successive independent victims, commissioners, have made recommendations and given advice to the police which has been ignored," he added.

"It's really important for this to be an opportunity to reset the relationship between the police service and those whose job it is to support them and hold them to account."

Among other criticisms, the Fairfield Review found the Met continued to struggle to acknowledge racism as a structural problem "rather than something people can be trained out of".

It added: "None of these behaviours have changed sufficiently. Neither has the Met's institutional defensiveness."

Fairfield said she was struck by the fact that after a number of strategic briefings with the Met, no senior leader had used the word "racism" and she felt the force was too defensive in its approach.

News.title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
News.content:
The UK government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent.

Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public "to share their experiences and inform this process".

The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned.

The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct.

The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened.

Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims".

Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA.

Writing in the Guardian,, external Burnham said: "NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women."

He added he would "keep working to make sure NDAs can't be used to silence others, including freelancers employees and fans who experience abuse".

The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year.

Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo."

The Close the Consent Gap campaign is proposing that 16-year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson said there is a question about what is considered "appropriate" for 16 and 17-year-olds.

She said: "I think some of the cases that we've seen where you have a huge age difference and often where you've got a much older adult man, who is in a position of authority, having a relationship with a 16 or 17-year-old makes me feel deeply uncomfortable."

She added: "I think we do need to look at that, but it's complex, we want to look at all of the options and we'll be setting out more and making sure survivors, women's groups and others are involved in that so we can get this right."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "some common sense" about staggering the age of consent but questioned whether a new law could be enforced.

She also said it was "very confusing" to see Labour ministers talk about staggering the age of consent for sexual relations while at the same time lowering the voting age to 16.

Scotland's justice secretary Neil Gray earlier this month said the Scottish government would "consider carefully any evidence-based proposals intended to strengthen protections for young people" when asked about a staggered approach.

He also said there were "no current plans" to change the general position of the age of consent being 16.

A complication with changing the age of consent in Scotland is how it would affect marriage law which allows people to marry or enter a civil partnership at 16. The legal age of marriage in England and Wales is 18.

Some countries around the world have a staggered age of consent. In Canada, external the age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years-old but a 14 or 15-year-old can consent to sexual activity as long as the partner is less than five years older.

News.title: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about 'search for justice'
News.content:
Nuclear test veterans and their relatives have reacted to the prime minister's announcement of an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

Andy Burham said a panel will assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s on troops, adding that the process will be treated with the "utmost seriousness".

The BBC heard reaction from veterans and their families as part of Newsnight's 'Nuclear Test Veterans: The Newsnight Special'.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

You can watch the full Newsnight special on BBC Two or on BBC iPlayer.

News.title: 'I'm proud of it': Killer confesses after murdering Ian Huntley
News.content:
A triple murderer who beat the notorious child-killer Ian Huntley to death in prison has been given a second whole life jail term.

Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly bludgeoned Huntley, 52, with a metal bar at the high security Frankland Prison near Durham in February, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

In footage released by the Crown Prosecution Service, Russell confesses to planning to kill Huntley and says: "I'm proud of it."

Russell, who was jailed for life with no chance of parole in March 2022 for raping and murdering a pregnant woman and killing a mother and son in the West Midlands, admitted Huntley's murder on the second day of his trial.

Sentencing him for what prosecutors called a "cold-blooded" and planned attack, Mr Justice Hilliard KC said Russell would never be freed from prison or eligible for parole.

Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Watch: Delia Smith says data centre will be bad for county
News.content:
Television cook and author Delia Smith has warned a new data centre in Norfolk would do nothing for the local community.

Campaigners fear the Â£1.2bn proposed centre at Keswick, on the edge of Norwich, will create noise pollution and have a negative impact on nearby Marston Marsh.

Smith, honorary life president and former majority shareholder of Norwich City FC, said "it's going to be bad", while TV presenter Jake Humphrey added the countryside was "not for sale".

Developer Norwich Apex said an ecological impact assessment concluded no effect on the reserve was expected.

Follow Norfolk news on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, Instagram, external and X, external.

News.title: As GLP-1 use grows, patients and doctors rethink Thanksgiving dinner
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For many people, Thanksgiving can feel like a competitive eating event. But for Kim Dillard Davis, one of millions of American adults who take prescribed weight loss medications known as GLP-1s, it is a day like any other.

The 54-year-old Raleigh, North Carolina-based digital creator and wellness coach has lost around 80 pounds since 2023 using GLP-1s. Thanksgiving on a GLP-1 means she doesn't participate in the part of the holiday associated with indulgence.

“I can’t sit down and eat the amount of calories that I once could. I’ll still be able to sample everything, but I just can’t overdo it,” said Dillard Davis, who said she plans to be on the drug for life so long as her insurance is covering it.

More and more Americans are using GLP-1s, and as the medications become more popular, they could be changing some Americans’ approach to food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving, altering how they eat, what they enjoy about food and scrambling some social interactions surrounding food.

The jump in popularity comes as President Donald Trump's second administration has made expanding access to GLP-1s part of its health policy, arguing that the drugs, if made more affordable, could help combat rising obesity rates and other related chronic illnesses, eventually lowering broader healthcare costs.

While GLP-1s will likely cause major shifts in ways that are hard to predict, Ashley Gearhardt, a psychology professor at the University of Michigan, suggests the over-indulgence associated with the holiday could diminish over time.

“I anticipate that flavors and tastes that have been culturally linked with Thanksgiving will continue to be important. There just may be fewer turkey comas at the end of the day," she said.

Navigating the holiday while taking GLP-1s

Some people who use GLP-1s feel full faster and stay full longer, meaning they tend to eat smaller portions. The drugs have been reported to change how people think about food, reducing cravings and emotional eating but also diminishing the sensory pleasure people get from food. Some users also avoid eating rich or heavy foods, because the drugs can cause nausea or bloating.

Doctors say people who are just starting their weight loss journey this year with the drugs should be particularly mindful of potential side effects.

“Thanksgiving doesn’t have to be off-limits,” said John Horlander, a Louisville, Kentucky, gastroenterologist. “The key is moderation, smaller portions, avoiding excessive fatty foods, staying hydrated and recognizing warning signs.

"A little prevention can go a long way toward keeping someone out of the emergency room over the holiday.”

The Trump administration has framed its steps toward increasing access to and bringing down costs for GLP-1s as “a historic opportunity to reverse the obesity epidemic.” More than 100 million American adults are obese, according to the latest Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data.

In 2025, Trump, a Republican, signed a deal with drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to expand coverage and reduce prices for the popular weight loss drugs Zepbound and Wegovy.

And coverage of the drugs for obesity was expanded to Medicare patients this year when the federal government began offering a selection of the brand name medications to certain Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries for $50 a month through a new trial called Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. The program is scheduled to sunset after Dec. 31, 2027.

A June analysis by healthcare research nonprofit KFF found that 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries could be eligible for the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, based on claims data from 2023. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services does not provide projections of how many people will start taking GLP-1s as a result of the Trump administration’s actions. The agency wants to expand access to GLP-1 treatments, said a spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak publicly and talked to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Those policy changes come as the share of people on GLP-1 medications for weight loss has risen in the past few years — 11% of U.S. adults said they currently take the drugs for weight loss purposes, according to a Gallup poll conducted in May and June 2026. The poll found that 15% of Americans report having used the medicine for weight loss, an increase of 9 percentage points from two years ago.

The social dynamics of eating

That means Americans, even if they aren't taking the drugs, could find more people on the medication who are sitting across from them at the Thanksgiving table. That could change how people talk about eating.

Gearhardt said that dinner guests should be mindful about not pushing loved ones to eat or commenting on appearances.

“We all have a tendency to kind of monitor and police each other’s eating behavior," said Gearhardt, who studies food marketing and how addictive processes shape eating behaviors and mental health.

Commenting on how little or how much someone is eating “usually isn’t a great relationship strengthener,” she said. GLP-1 users might be especially sensitive, she said, because Thanksgiving can evoke feelings of grief over losing the intense reward sensation of highly processed foods.

Dillard Davis advised family members not to ask, “Is that all you’re going to eat?”

“Leave that phrase off the table. We’ve spent our whole lives overeating. Let us eat small portions and be happy,” she said.

Babak Orandi, an obesity medicine specialist at NYU Langone Health, said, “There’s a social aspect of eating, especially around the holidays. We don’t want to lose that.”

Patients, Orandi said, should focus “a little bit less on weight loss and a little bit more on weight loss maintenance” during the holidays, so as to not lose the enjoyment of eating.

For Dillard Davis, Thanksgiving has changed in other ways. Because of the reduced appetite brought on by the medication and to avoid large quantities of leftovers at home, her family has spent the last four years celebrating Thanksgiving at restaurants.

But as someone who has been on a weight loss journey since she was 8 years old, she has learned to accept the changes.

“We still have to eat," she said. "Just don’t worry about it so much.”

News.title: Mandatory knife licences risk burdening responsible sellers, retailers warn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Mandatory licences for retailers to sell knives risk burdening responsible shopkeepers and could push more sales online, industry groups have warned.

Retailers are calling for a “proportionate” scheme that targets the products and sellers most closely linked to harm.

The Home Office set out plans for a UK-wide scheme which means all businesses and individuals selling knives and bladed articles will need to pay a fee for a licence which is expected to last three years.

This means that selling cutlery could fall under the licensing scheme.

The plan is intended to cut down on knife crime by tackling rogue operators who supply dangerous knives or sell to children.

The British Independent Retailers Association (Bira), which works with more than 6,000 independent retailers in the UK, said it supports efforts to reduce knife crime by selling bladed items responsibly.

Bira chief executive Andrew Goodacre said: “The vast majority of shop owners share our views and take their responsibilities very seriously.

“It is, however, disappointing to see plans for a licensing scheme that will apply to shop owners.

“The Government itself recognises that the problem lies with rogue and unregulated online sellers, and that is where enforcement should be concentrated, rather than adding cost and bureaucracy for responsible shops.”

Mr Goodacre warned that the scheme may not effectively tackle the issue of online sales of knives.

“Some shop owners may decide to stop selling bladed items as a result of this licensing, pushing more sales online and into a retail space that is already proving difficult to regulate,” he said.

The British Retail Consortium (BRC), which fed into the Home Office’s consultation about the scheme, also called for licensing to be targeted.

Lucy Whing, crime policy adviser for the BRC, said: “Retailers support an evidence-led approach to knife licensing that meaningfully tackles knife crime and improves public safety.

“Licensing should be proportionate and risk-based, targeting the products and sellers most closely linked to harm without placing unnecessary burdens on responsible retailers.”

Details about the fee that sellers will pay to hold a licence have not yet been set but it is intended to cover the full cost of administering the system.

The Government is set to work with retailers, law enforcement and groups including heritage collectors to finalise how the licensing scheme will operate.

News.title: Bayern Munich insist Jamal Musiala’s health is ‘top priority’ following criticism
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bayern Munich have insisted that Jamal Musiala’s health remains their "top priority" following a "constructive meeting" with representatives of the 23-year-old midfielder.

Earlier this year, the player collapsed on two occasions within four days during pre-season fixtures. It was subsequently disclosed that he was suffering from absence seizures linked to a form of "neurological dysfunction".

The German club faced scrutiny over their handling of the matter after public remarks from senior figures. Honorary president Uli Hoeness questioned if Musiala would "regain the performance level he once had", suggesting his 2025 contract might no longer match his potential on-pitch contributions.

Similar doubts were voiced by member of the supervisor board Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who proposed renegotiating the agreement, while chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen questioned the deal, should Musiala struggle to recover his peak conditioning.

These comments drew criticism from global players’ union FIFPRO, which voiced concern over repeated public remarks challenging the player's contract, saying that "a club of Bayern’s standing should know better".

open image in gallery Musiala has been with Bayern since he was 17-years-old ( Getty )

Responding on Wednesday after Tuesday's discussions, Bayern sought to clarify their position in a joint update with Musiala's agency, 11WINS.

The club stated: "Yesterday, Tuesday, FC Bayern Munich held a constructive meeting with Jamal Musiala’s management. The player’s health is the top priority for both parties. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throughout his recovery.

"Following numerous rumours over the past few days, FC Bayern and 11WINS, the agency representing Jamal Musiala, would like to clarify the following: Jamal Musiala was first examined for symptoms resembling absence seizures on 22 April 2025. This examination took place in consultation with FC Bayern and its medical department, immediately after the neurological symptoms first appeared.

"FC Bayern and Jamal Musiala’s management have agreed to continue their discussions in a spirit of partnership and confidentiality."

On the pitch, Musiala returned as a substitute during last Friday's 1-1 draw against Cologne, marking his first outing since September after recovering from a hamstring injury. He has also been selected in Bayern's squad to play Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.

News.title: Trump-era deportation saga comes to close with Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaving US voluntarily
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump’s administration has reached an agreement to let Kilmar Abrego Garcia leave the U.S. voluntarily, ending a nearly two-year legal battle over the fate of a Salvadoran immigrant whose story has been at the center of the president’s mass deportation campaign.

He boarded a commercial flight to Spain on Tuesday night.

Abrego Garcia’s case has been a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s efforts to rapidly arrest and deport tens of thousands of people from the country despite legal safeguards and humanitarian protections that the president has also eroded since returning to the White House.

The administration has spent the last year trying to deport Abrego Garcia a second time — including to Liberia — after the government unlawfully deported him to a brutal prison in his home country, triggering the high-profile legal battle for his return.

“After a protracted fight, Abrego Garcia, on his terms, boarded a flight tonight to Spain,” his legal team said in a statement Tuesday. “We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department. He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”

open image in gallery The Trump administration has reached an agreement to allow Kilmar Abrego Garcia to leave the US voluntarily after a months-long legal saga that has been a lightning rod for the president’s anti-immigration agenda ( Reuters )

The Independent has requested comment from the Department of Homeland Security.

Abrego Garcia, 31, has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years after fleeing gang violence in El Salvador and entering the U.S. illegally as a teenager. An immigration judge blocked the government from deporting him to his home country in 2019.

But last year, federal agents abruptly deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison where he says he endured torture and “severe” abuse for several weeks before he was transferred to a separate jail.

Government officials admitted in court that his removal was due to an “error,” and several federal judges and a unanimous Supreme Court ordered the administration to “facilitate” his return.

The government spent weeks battling those orders while White House officials launched a barrage of public attacks against him and declared that he would never again step foot in the country.

He was returned to the U.S. last June — only to face allegations that he illegally moved other immigrants across the country. He pleaded not guilty.

A federal judge later dismissed the criminal case against him after finding that the administration unlawfully targeted him as part of a smear campaign.

“Objective evidence” has shown that federal prosecutors only brought charges against Abrego Garcia after he won his lawsuit challenging his arrest and removal, the judge ruled.

open image in gallery Abrego Garcia’s wrongful removal from the US to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador — and ICE’s attempts to re-detain and deport him a second time — launched high-profile legal battles at the center of the Trump administration’s attempts to rapidly deport thousands of immigrants ( Getty )

The administration has, at the same time, tried to deport him to at least five different countries, including four in Africa, and refused to let him leave the country for Costa Rica.

In a memo issued in March, ICE’s then-acting director Todd Lyons argued that sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”

In April, the administration “analyzed and eliminated all other options” from the table and settled on Liberia as “a final country of removal,” despite his own attempts to voluntarily remove himself to Costa Rica.

Government lawyers argued in court documents that the U.S. has expended significant political capital and entered “high-stakes” and “extensive negotiations” to send him to Liberia.

open image in gallery Abrego Garcia was abruptly deported to El Salvador’s brutal CECOT prison in March 2025 despite a court order that blocked his removal from the US to the country he fled, what government attorneys called an ‘error’ that sparked a 20-month legal battle for his freedom ( Getty )

But the judge overseeing his deportation case had blocked Immigration and Customs Enforcement from re-deporting or detaining him, noting earlier this year that the government has made “one empty threat after another to remove him to countries in Africa with no real chance of success.”

Both sides were scheduled to discuss his case at a hearing in October, but U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis abruptly ended the hearing after she met privately with attorneys in her chambers.

Judge Xinis issued an order in the case on November 20 but it remains sealed.

Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who traveled to El Salvador in an attempt to secure Abrego Garcia’s release from prisons there, said his constituent is now “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

“While the Trump administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said in a statement Tuesday night.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution,” he added. “This is a victory for due process and our Constitution.”

News.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national mistakenly deported from the US, arrives in Spain
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Ábrego García was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” His departure to Spain follows months of legal wrangling as he battled the administration’s drive to deport him to Africa.

Ábrego García reached Madrid on Wednesday morning.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn’t receive any incentives and won’t be allowed back into the U.S.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” about Ábrego García’s departure, listing a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.

Ábrego García's deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually.

Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by U.S. Congress, the administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

He was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by DHS officials.

News.title: Tube strikes this week: What you need to know about Thursday’s walkout and future dates
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Passengers are being warned of tube strikes affecting the whole network this Thursday, with more dates to follow in the lead-up to Christmas.

The Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) announced eight sets of 24-hour strikes starting in November, ending in February 2027 over plans for a voluntary four-day week for drivers.

The first walkout will take place on Thursday, 26 November, and is expected to cause disruption across all Tube lines.

The RMT suspended planned strikes in March and May this year after progress in talks, but strike action is scheduled t go ahead after last-ditch negotiations failed this week between the union and Transport for London (TfL).

The Tube drivers’ strikes land on some of the busiest days of the year, including the last weekend before Christmas Day.

Here’s everything we know so far about the strike dates.

When are the tube strikes?

Some Tube drivers plan to strike on certain dates from November 2026 to February 2027, affecting the whole network.

The 24-hour strikes will run from midday on the first day to midday the following day.

November 2026

12pm Thursday 26 to 11.59am Friday 27 November 2026

December 2026

12pm Thursday 17 to 11.59am Friday 18 December 2026

12pm Saturday 19 to 11.59am Sunday 20 December 2026

January 2027

12pm Monday 4 to 11.59am Tuesday 5 January 2027

12pm Wednesday 6 to 11.59am Thursday 7 January 2027

February 2027

12pm Wednesday 17 to 11.59am Thursday 18 February 2027

12pm Tuesday 23 to 11.59am Wednesday 24 February 2027

12pm Thursday 25 to 11.59am Friday 26 February 2027

Will some trains still be running?

TfL says that during the strike, trains will run on most Tube lines, but disruption is expected across the network.

On the first strike day, services are likely to run as normal until 10am, but will then start to be reduced.

From 12pm, it is expected there will be disruption on all lines, with no service on the Waterloo & City line from midday.

No service is expected on the Circle and Piccadilly lines all day.

After 9pm, TfL says no Tube services are expected to run.

As the strike runs into its second day, services are expected to resume from around 7am, but there will still be disruption across all lines, as well as no service expected on the Circle, Piccadilly and Waterloo & City lines.

From midday, as the 24-hour strike comes to an end, disruption will continue across the Tube network as services recover.

TfL expects normal services to resume from 6pm on the second day.

Which lines are affected during the driver’s strike?

There will likely be some disruption across all Tube lines.

The Elizabeth line, DLR, London Overground, buses and trams will be running as normal during the strikes but will be busier than usual.

What advice is being given to travellers?

Passengers are being told to plan ahead and check the live train timetables during the strikes.

TfL added that passengers should allow more time than usual to complete their journey.

Why are strikes taking place?

RMT has announced strike dates in retaliation over plans to impose new working arrangements, including a voluntary four-day week, which the union says would mean drivers face spending more time driving trains, longer duties, earlier starts and later finishes.

The union has also raised concerns that the proposals would pave the way for hundreds of job cuts, with initial rosters published for the Bakerloo line indicating significant reductions in staffing.

“London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers’ working conditions as a voluntary four-day week,” RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said.

“But there is nothing voluntary about a scheme that forces drivers to give up existing protections whether they work four days or five, and threatens those who refuse with displacement from their depots.

He added: “RMT is not opposed to a genuine four-day working week that benefits our members, but we will not accept it being used as a vehicle for job cuts, intensified working and the erosion of terms and conditions.”

Aslef, Britain's trade union for train drivers, said the switch to a four-day week would give train drivers an extra 35 days off a year.

“We are surprised that the RMT has, once again, decided to take strike action to try to prevent Underground drivers moving to a four-day week on a voluntary basis,” Finn Brennan, Aslef’s full-time organiser on London Underground, said.

He added: “The voluntary four-day week gives Tube train drivers an extra 35 days off every year with rosters based on a 34-hour week in return for some changes to working conditions and moving to electronic, rather than paper-based, systems for booking on for duty.

“We are in discussions with Transport for London about how the final details of this will work in practice.

“Management have agreed that anyone who wants to keep working a five-day week will be able to do so without suffering any detriment, and we will be holding them to that.

“A strike designed to stop people having the choice of a shorter working week and more time off is a strange choice to make.”

Nick Dent, director of customer operations for London Underground, managed by TfL, said: “We have engaged with our trade unions for months about our proposal for a new four-day working week.

“As a result of that engagement, drivers can now choose to remain on a five-day week with a guarantee of remaining at the same depot.

“This will give our colleagues a real, meaningful choice on their working pattern without having to change where they work.

“This will also mean less time at work for Tube drivers, while delivering a more efficient, reliable Tube service for our customers.

“Given that we have provided this new option after their feedback, we urge the RMT to put this proposal to their members.”

News.title: Wendy’s hit with lawsuit over ‘inflated’ menu prices
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A California man is suing burger giant Wendy’s over allegations the chain schemed to artificially inflate prices.

Plaintiff Andy Garcia accuses the company of using a pricing scheme to drive up the cost of food between 2016 and 2022. The proposed class-action lawsuit claims Wendy’s collected sensitive data from franchisee locations to co-ordinate prices and reduce competition.

​“By delegating pricing decisions to a common decision-maker, it eliminates critical price competition that drives costs down for consumers,” Garcia’s attorney, Blake Hunter Yagman, told CBS News.

“This is even more important with respect to food prices, which have never been higher - and Wendy’s owes its customers to compete on the merits for better service, more innovative products and better pricing.”

Wendy’s maintains that independent restaurants set their own prices.

open image in gallery A California man has filed a lawsuit against Wendy's, alleging that the firm centrally set prices at franchise locations ( Getty )

The document says that it seeks redress for all Americans who bought items from Wendy’s from January 1, 2022, until the time of filing.

Arguing Americans have long relied on the burger chain as an affordable option for feeding their families, the lawsuit claims the chain carried out an “abuse of that reliance and the use of it to extract supracompetitive profits from Wendy’s customer base.”

​Wendy’s is named in the lawsuit alongside the NCR Voyix Corporation, which provides the fast-food company with a point-of-sale system called Aloha POS. The system has been used since 2016, according to Garcia.

​The filing cites the NCR Voyix website, which states that the Aloha POS system allows brands to “update menus and pricing quickly across locations with centralized menu and pricing management.”

​“Wendy’s uses all of this confidential information to control pricing between its franchisees - who should be competing independently,” Garcia’s filing reads.

open image in gallery The lawsuit claims that centrally setting product prices eliminates competition between franchisees ( AFP/Getty )

Attorney Allen Neumark has also disputed suggestions by Wendy’s that franchisees control their own prices.

“Wendy's tells its investors that franchisees set their own prices,” Neumark told Reuters. “But this is false. And when businesses that should be competing stop competing on price, consumers pay more.”

​According to Garcia, the activity is a violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act - which is meant to preserve free competition - and means that prices at Wendy’s restaurants are “artificially higher than they otherwise would have but for the Defendant’s illegal conduct.”

​Garcia is asking the court to declare the alleged activity to be a violation of the Sherman Act. He is also seeking legal fees and treble damages for those who purchased a Wendy’s product after January 1, 2022.

​The Independent has contacted Wendy’s and NCR Voyix for comment.

The lawsuit comes weeks after McDonald’s was sued for allegedly using an AI tool to set prices at its franchises. The filing, reviewed by Reuters, claims that algorithms have been trained on nonpublic data and have led to customers paying higher prices.

McDonald’s has denied the allegations.

News.title: Raheem Sterling avoids jail after Lamborghini nitrous oxide crash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has avoided jail after admitting to dangerous driving in his Lamborghini while inhaling from a balloon on a busy motorway during rush hour, before crashing into a metal gate.

The 31-year-old showed no emotion as he was sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court for dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide on May 28.

He was also handed a 24-month driving ban and ordered to undertake 100 hours of unpaid work.

A motorist who contacted police expressed that he was “shocked” by what he saw, while another witness noted she had "genuine concerns the driver might kill someone", previous court proceedings heard.

Body-worn video recorded during Sterling’s arrest at 9.15am showed him inside the crashed vehicle holding two gas canisters on his lap, with an officer saying: "You can put that down, mate."

open image in gallery Sterling was found with multiple cannisters of nitrous oxide ( Crown Prosecution Service )

Sterling pleaded guilty in September to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously across the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road in Surrey.

He further admitted to possessing six canisters of class C drug nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, alongside a charge of failing to provide a specimen.

During the September hearing at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court, prosecutor Simon Jones informed the court that multiple emergency calls were made between 7.45am and 8.52am regarding the erratic driving of a black sports car.

Witness Christopher Jennings alerted police at 7.49am after travelling beside Sterling’s vehicle on the M25, with Mr Jones noting "he was shocked by what he saw", adding that "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".

Fiona Jennings, driving along the southbound M3 at roughly 8.45am, described the black Lamborghini’s driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes", the court heard.

"She had genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," Mr Jones said.

She initially believed an airbag had been deployed before realising it was an inflated white balloon with its neck in the driver's mouth.

Dashcam footage provided by the Crown Prosecution Service showed the car changing lanes repeatedly before striking a concrete barrier on the right side and driving onwards.

Sterling exited junction 4a of the M3, completed a loop via the A327, and lost control shortly after passing a roundabout.

open image in gallery Camera footage shows the winger swerving across all three lanes ( Crown Prosecution Service )

The vehicle veered off the road and "must have collided with either the sign or metal gate", causing "substantial" damage to the car and all four wheels, rendering it inoperable, the hearing was told.

After officers brought Sterling to Basingstoke police investigation centre, he told custody personnel "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", according to Mr Jones.

While he completed an impairment test, Sterling requested legal counsel before deciding whether to supply a blood sample, Mr Jones said.

In the police sergeant’s view, "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer".

When interviewed later alongside his solicitor, Sterling admitted he had been driving but gave no comment regarding his manner of driving.

Defending, Jason Bartfeld KC acknowledged it was a "top category case" owing to prolonged driving and "at times" severe impairment over brief intervals.

However, the defence disputed that vehicle damage was severe and highlighted "confusion" surrounding the failure to supply a specimen.

open image in gallery Raheem Sterling being detained by police ( Crown Prosecution Service )

Sterling scored 20 goals across 82 England appearances, helping the national side reach the 2018 World Cup semi-finals and the Euro 2020 final.

Born in Kingston, Jamaica, Sterling transferred to Manchester City from Liverpool in 2015, winning four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the 2019 FA Cup. He joined Chelsea in 2022 before spending the 2024-25 season on loan at Arsenal.

Following his departure from Stamford Bridge, Sterling moved to Dutch side Feyenoord on a short-term contract lasting until the end of the season. He is currently without a club.

Sterling received an MBE in the 2021 Queen’s Birthday Honours for services to racial equality in sport, following years of leading anti-racism initiatives and speaking out against discrimination. The honour came amid public debate surrounding fans who booed players taking the knee prior to matches.

News.title: Mick Harford: ‘My prostate cancer diagnosis was a shock. As a footballer, I’d felt bulletproof’
News.content:
However, an MRI scan and a PSMA PET scan at UCLH, where I had been referred, showed only a little bit of growth on my prostate, and I was told I would be fine. But, while I was symptomless at the time, within around eight months I was getting up three or four times in the night to go to the toilet, and then feeling the urge to go back again only two minutes later. I instinctively knew something was wrong.

Upon my return to UCLH in December, I was told my PSA was now “very high”, at around 48 ng/mL – far more elevated than the 4.5 ng/mL considered healthy for my age group. Advanced prostate cancer was then confirmed with a biopsy. The first person I told was my son, William, in a phone call from the car at the hospital. It was horrible – it was not just me who would suffer, but my family too. I also needed to tell Luton Town, who were amazing and gave me as much time off work as I needed from my role as assistant manager.

Facing the opponent

My brilliant oncology team immediately had a plan for me. They got me on a course of hormone therapy medications called Enzalutamide and Zoladex, in preparation for me to begin radiation treatment from mid-August. I had 49 sessions over the space of about eight weeks, and it was daunting each time I travelled into London on the train from my home in Harpenden to go underground to the hospital’s Radiotherapy Department.

But I got through it, even with a bit of collateral damage. While my ongoing symptoms are not a pleasant conversation, it’s an important one, because it has affected my life in so many ways. My sleep is disrupted because I still need to get up multiple times during the night to go to the toilet so I can avoid an accident in bed. I also have to wear a nappy every day in case of leakage, and need to be careful when I’m out to ensure I’m close to a toilet.

I’m still on a hormone therapy called Triptorelin to block my testosterone, which feeds the cancer, and takes the form of an injection every six months. As a result, I’m going through the “male menopause”, which is not very nice and can cause tiredness, sleep issues and brain fog. It has given me lots of sympathy for women of my generation.

However, as I approach six years since my diagnosis, I’ve tried to stay proactive as much as possible. The discipline and drive instilled in me as a footballer have come in handy. To be a successful player, you need to stick to a routine. In the same way that I worked hard to ensure my teammates and coaches respected me on the pitch, so I’ve adhered to what all the doctors have advised – including trying to be diligent in terms of lifestyle.

News.title: Underperforming Manchester City are an accident waiting to happen
News.content:
Enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win. On Tuesday, however, they ended up being taunted by Rasmus Hojlund on another evening that raised more questions than answers.

It is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit. Worryingly, their reliable source of goals, Erling Haaland, had his quietest game of the season. It required Rayan Cherki to rescue a point against Napoli.

Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season. Defeat would put them nine points off the pace, with Maresca still trying to find his best combination of players to pick.

Club captain Rúben Dias was on the bench here and Josko Gvardiol was left out of the draw against Fulham at the weekend, which also ended as a draw rather than a morale-boosting win to get City out of their slump.

News.title: Arsenal get the best and worst of Gyokeres on frustrating night for Arteta
News.content:
Mikel Arteta may prefer to imagine his Arsenal team as a remorseless winning machine, although on nights such as these they can still demonstrate a familiar unreliability when it comes to the main purpose of it all.

There were 30 shots over the night from the English champions, only four of which were on target, and in the end their winner never came. Even in the 95th minute, Arteta’s players were still conspiring to foul it up. This Champions League game might have been decided in Arsenal’s favour within 20 minutes. By half-time it should have been a formality. Yet, as chance after chance slipped away, there was always a possibility this would end differently.

The leaders of the Bundesliga were traumatised at times by the ferocity of the Arsenal press, and there were times when Borussia Dortmund will likely have no idea how they survived. Even so, they did just that and, liberated in the second half, Maximilian Beier scored an improbable equaliser in his team’s best period. There were still 40 minutes for Arsenal to put this one to bed and they found many ways not to do so.

It was notable that the man who put Arsenal ahead in the ninth minute with a right-footed thump from space on the edge of the Dortmund box was the same striker who would miss the best chance to win it. That is the Viktor Gyökeres dilemma. In the space of a single game he can look like a potential match-winner and also the last man his manager would wish to see arriving on the end of a perfect Martin Odegaard cross.

So it proved after 75 minutes when Gyökeres thrust himself at an Odegaard ball into the box that just needed guiding inside a post, yet planted it decisively wide of the mark. On the touchline Arteta tried very hard to hide his despair and failed to do so.

News.title: Emery unhappy with ‘unfair’ referee but Aston Villa are toothless
News.content:
Aston Villa supporters have happy memories of Istanbul after May’s Europa League final, and they return to face Galatasaray this evening in a fixture which could forecast their Champions League prospects.

It has been par for the course for Unai Emery’s team in Europe so far, with victories over Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking and a defeat at Barcelona aligning with the form book.

Nine points from 12 leaves them inside the top eight at the halfway stage of the league phase, but tougher challenges are ahead with PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come after tonight’s game.

Since a statement victory over Manchester City, it has been a frustrating time for Villa either side of the international break. They were dumped out of the League Cup by Bournemouth, were second-best in a home draw with Fulham, threw away a pair of two-goal leads at Old Trafford, and were held by Sunderland at the weekend.

Though Villa put six past Galatasaray’s city rivals Fenerbahce at Villa Park, away games against Turkish opposition can be different beasts, as Liverpool discovered in the last round of Champions League matches.

Galatasaray’s two major attacking threats, Victor Osimhen and Rafael Leão, are both absent with injuries. Davinson Sanchez and Lucas Torreira are former Premier League players in their squad. Galatasaray have won two of four Champions League games, losing to Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon, but they are top of the Turkish Super Lig.

Villa will be without right-back Matty Cash owing to a concussion sustained during the international break with Poland, but will hope to have Victor Lindelof available again after he missed the Sunderland draw with illness.

Emery’s team were unable to train at Rams Park yesterday in order to give a troublesome pitch maximum recovery time after emergency renovation work.

“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery said. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is important, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Anthropic falls below stock market listing price
News.content:
Anthropic’s shares dropped below their initial public offering price for the first time, sealing a dramatic reversal of fortunes for the AI giant following its blockbuster stock market debut last week.

The Claude chatbot maker saw its shares fall more than 8pc from their $83 offer price to stand at around $76 as investors appeared to grow sceptical of its valuation.

The slide on the Nasdaq exchange was set to wipe over $200bn from the company’s market value.

Anthropic raised more than $81bn in the biggest IPO on record, with its valuation surging to $2tn as the shares peaked at around $115.

But the company bucked Monday’s huge rally following Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia with the shares slipping from Friday’s close.

Wall Street resumed its slide on Tuesday as underlying fears over the AI trade appear to have outweighed the impact of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 was down as much as 3pc, with the benchmark S&P 500 around 1.2 pc lower.

In London, the FTSE 100 closed slightly lower, down 0.1pc, unable to sustain gains made in global markets on Monday.

The ability of AI companies to generate sufficient returns on their massive investment has proved more important than Nvidia’s boardroom drama, according to Goldman Sachs analysts.

Sharon Bell told Bloomberg: “The AI trade really depends on whether companies can make a return on the capex they spend.

“If the answer is yes, then the tech sector should do well over time and if the answer is no, it won’t do so well.”

Ms Bell argued that the management changes at Nvidia would not “make a huge difference either way”.

Glenn Yin at online trading platform ACCM told the Reuters Global Markets Forum: “By the end of ​the day, these businesses need to make enough money to justify investors’ expectations.

“‌My point is: Jensen’s return does not solve this. So, the sentiment is more emotional than sensible, in my opinion.”

Major chipmakers saw their stocks sink on Tuesday as general AI-related optimism faded.

Nvidia, the world’s largest chipmaker, saw its stock fall more than 7pc, while the Philadelphia semiconductor index, which tracks the major US manufacturers of chips, fell 8pc.

Microchip maker AMD’s share price was down as much as 10pc, while shares in Broadcom were down around 3pc.

The dollar eased back from its highest level in almost two years after Jensen ​Huang’s return to Nvidia revived the AI rally and fuelled expectations of more interest rate rises.

The President’s intervention, however, is a “slippery slope”, according to a top Republican senator.

Dave McCormick, the former boss of hedge fund Bridgewater, told Bloomberg: “I am worried about the precedent of the executive branch getting involved in real ownership deals with companies but also in board governance and making these decisions.

“This is a precedent that I don’t think we want to replicate or reinforce.”

Mr McCormick will be one of the politicians grilling the Nvidia boss next week when he testifies before the Senate Banking Committee.

Todd Blanche, the US Attorney General, has labelled Nvidia “a good corporate citizen” despite questions over whether Jensen Huang’s alleged affair could have threatened national security.

Mr Blanche added that if Nvidia was the target of a criminal investigation, “that wouldn’t be the message”.

News.title: Meningitis outbreak triggers epidemic alert in Gaza
News.content:
Cases of meningitis have risen dramatically in Gaza and have triggered an epidemic alert, the territory’s health ministry has said.

At least 272 cases were recorded across the enclave in October, more than eight times the usual monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases, Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior health ministry official, told a press conference on Tuesday.

Children under one year old account for 71 per cent of cases, with newborns alone accounting for 13 per cent, World Health Organization (WHO) spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said in a separate briefing.

Dr Ghoneim added that 15 Palestinians had died of meningitis since the start of the year, and that the spread of the disease through the strip threatened the lives of thousands of people, mostly children.

It is thought that most cases are being driven by enterovirus – the leading cause of viral meningitis – which is shed through faeces and can spread rapidly between people in unsanitary environments.

All six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza are currently out of operation, meaning an estimated 150,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage flows into the environment every day, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

News.title: Trapped Ebola health workers rescued after three days of fighting in Congo
News.content:
Ebola health workers have been rescued after being trapped by fighting for more than three days, in clashes further hampering efforts to curb the virus in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, head of the World Health Organization, said staff had been evacuated from a hospital in Akwe, Ituri province, “under very challenging circumstances”.

The health chief had earlier pleaded for peace, and warned staff had “been sheltering for their lives in a maternity ward of the facility for over 24 hours”.

Staff were caught in a crossfire between the Congolese army, and the People’s Revolutionary Convention (CRP) group led by former International Criminal Court (ICC) convict, Thomas Lubanga, French RFI radio reported.

Local media reported heavy clashes between the army and the CRP in Ituri in recent days. At least 10 people were killed and a stream of refugees fled to the provincial capital, Bunia.

As security worsened, the WHO said it had relocated health teams from Mongbwalu.

News.title: Welsh slogger blasts England to crushing win over Australia
News.content:
It will take more than a few lusty blows to become the cricketing Don in these parts, but an extraordinary display of six-hitting from Aneurin Donald, ably supported by Phil Salt, helped England and Wales to a stunning eight-wicket victory over Australia.

Donald and Salt, the Welsh-born opening pair, put on 151 to help chase down Australia’s 184 with 41 balls to spare. David Gower famously flew a pre-war Tiger Moth between the floodlights, about 200 feet above the ground, on England’s only previous visit to this ground in 1991. It was a good thing he was doing no such thing tonight, with balls flying everywhere off Donald’s blade. He hit nine sixes, one shy of Salt’s England T20 record, in his 85 from 32 balls, before being caught on the fence with the game as good as won.

Donald, who turns 30 next month, has taken the slow road to the big stage. As a teenager, he smashed 234 off 136 balls for Glamorgan against Derbyshire in the County Championship at Colwyn Bay, but at 21 left for Hampshire. Two serious ACL injuries derailed his career, and he moved to Derbyshire in 2023, where he has turned into a formidable T20 opener.

“I am pretty decent at slogging and not too good at batting, so I will keep swinging as hard as I can,” he reflected afterwards. “Luckily there might be a career in it now, not a few years ago.”

Sports.title: Ex-England star Raheem Sterling AVOIDS jail after being caught in Lambo with laughing gas canisters and deflated balloon
Sports.content:
Next

RAHEEM Sterling has avoided jail after he was caught in his Lambo with laughing gas canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap.

The ex-England star, 31, had been swerving in and out of lanes on a busy motorway as terrified drivers were forced to keep their distance.



Sterling was seen by motorists on the M25 at 7.45am with a large canister in his hand and a balloon in his mouth.

The former Liverpool, Man City and Chelsea winger later crashed his £270,000 Lamborghini before being arrested.



Police bodycam footage showed Sterling sat in his passenger seat with gas canisters on his lap and a deflated balloon.

A cop then tells him “you can put that down” as the star moves the paraphernalia.

The officer then asks Sterling to get out the car and tell him who was driving at the time of the crash.

When the footballer, who is currently without a club, does not respond, the cop continues: “So you refuse to answer, okay.”

Sterling has now avoided a jail term after he admitted dangerous driving on the M25, M3 and A327, possessing laughing gas and failing to provide a specimen.

He was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months and banned from driving for 24 months.



Sterling will also have to complete 100 hours of unpaid work and pay a £187 victim surcharge plus prosecution costs of £85 by December 16.

District Judge Kirsty Allman said he “voluntarily engaged with addiction services” and checked into a rehab centre in June for 12 days after the crash.

She added: “The evidence before me demonstrates genuine engagement and meaningful progress.”



The court heard Sterling was first spotted driving erratically at 1.10am that morning – eight hours before his arrest – at a McDonald’s in Hayes.

Motorists then dialled 999 after seeing his black luxury 4×4 swerving across the M3 in Hampshire just before 9am on May 28.

They described how the star quickly and repeatedly swerved between lanes without indicating, accelerated and braked suddenly.

At one point the Lambo nearly smashed into the central reservation on the M25, the court was told.

Defence barrister Jason Bartfeld KC told the court that the only damage caused in the incident was to Sterling’s car – and that not one of the eight airbags had deployed.



In mitigation, he also told how the star’s achievements as a footballer are “extremely well known” but said what is perhaps “slightly less well known” is his charity work.

The lawyer said this year marks the fifth year anniversary of the Raheem Sterling Foundation, which “supports youth education projects” and carries out community work including combatting knife crime and poverty.



Mr Bartfield said Sterling has tarnished his own reputation but he is more concerned by “the unfortunate side consequences it’s had for his family, particularly his children who have had to deal with a certain degree of unpleasantness”.

The lawyer added Sterling wants to put this behind him, move forward and “resume his role as very much a role model” for those who have followed his career and engaged with him and his organisations.

Sterling, who has 82 caps for England, was just 15 when he was signed by Liverpool from the QPR academy in 2010.

He became a fans’ favourite at Anfield before a contract dispute saw him move to Manchester City in 2015.



Sterling enjoyed huge success at the club – winning four Premier League titles, five Carabao Cups and an FA Cup.

But in July 2022, the winger moved from City to Chelsea in a deal worth £50million.

He was eventually ordered to train separately to the first-team group after then-manager Enzo Maresca decided he was surplus to requirements.

A loan deal to Arsenal followed, but did not work out, so in February he joined Dutch club Feyenoord.

The former boss of the Romanian national team becomes the 26th head coach in 15 years under controversial Hornets owner Gino Pozzo.



Alessio Dionisi became the latest Vicarage Road casualty on Sunday when he was axed after just 18 games.

Edward Still lasted just 15 matches before him, with Tom Cleverley the most recent boss – five hires ago – to surpass 20 games in the hot seat.



Iordanescu told club website: “I am very proud and happy to be at this football club.

Sports.title: Lincoln City SACK managers Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw with ex-Man Utd ace, 40, appointed to interim coaching team

LINCOLN CITY have sacked joint-managers Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw after five defeats on the spin.

The Imps were consigned to a 4-0 loss by fellow Championship strugglers Charlton on Tuesday.



And club chiefs decided to wield the axe less than 24 hours after Lincoln saw their horror run of form continue.

They fell to within three points of the Championship’s relegation zone following the thrashing at the Valley.



Lincoln chairman Ron Fowler and chief executive Liam Scully felt Cohen and Shaw, both 39, needed to be relieved of their duties to stop a slide back into League One.

A statement from the pair read: “We have worked incredibly hard to reach the Championship and will do everything in our power to retain our status in this division.

“We know how much this football club means to our supporters and are humbled by the level of support we’ve had home and away so far this season.”

Shaun Pearson has been placed in interim charge ahead of Lincoln’s showdown with high-flying Wolves on Saturday.

Former Manchester United defender Paul McShane, 40, and David Preece have also been named on the coaching team ahead of a permanent appointment being made.

Cohen and Shaw were handed the managerial reins just weeks after Lincoln bagged the League One title last season.

They were picked as the leading candidates following Michael Skubala’s decision to quit when Championship rivals Bristol City came calling.

But the duo only oversaw four domestic wins during their 17 matches at the helm.

Lincoln’s most recent win came against Burnley last month, which led to the Clarets sacking Nicky Hayen.

And the Imps have gone on to concede 11 goals in their losses to Birmingham, Watford, QPR, Wrexham and Charlton since that three-point haul.

Rock bottom Derby are the only side with a worse goal difference than the Sincil Bank strugglers.

Sports.title: Ken Fagerberg dead aged 37: Swedish footie star and father of three tragically passes away
Sports.content:
Next

KEN FAGERBERG has tragically died at the age of 37.

The Swedish footballer’s passing was confirmed by his parents.



Fagerberg starred for the likes of FC Midtjylland, AC Horsens, and Viborg FF during his career.

He was found dead in his home in Tórshavn in the Faroe Islands on Thursday, with his cause of death not yet clear.



Fagerberg made his breakthrough at Orgryte as a prolific striker in the second tier of Swedish football.

The father of three scored 12 goals in 22 matches before he made his transfer to Danish giants Midtjylland in 2008.

The striker also played six times for the Sweden U19s.

He ended his playing career in the Faroe Islands, having featured for local clubs 07 Vestur and TB Tvøroyri.

He settled in the North Atlantic islands and continued to live there after playing and started working as a coach.

Father Goran told local media: “He was the kindest man in the world and had a heart of gold.



“He was very talented. He could have gone further if he had just put in a bit more effort.”

Fagerberg had given a similar account of his playing career during an appearance on a podcast four years ago.

He said: “I squandered my talent throughout my entire career. I lived a very destructive life, involving the persistent abuse of drugs and alcohol.



“It started back when I was playing in Sweden, and I brought that lifestyle with me to Denmark.

“I kept the wrong kind of company. If I hadn’t had football, things would have ended up much worse.”

Midtjylland released a statement after learning of the news of Fagerberg’s death.

It read: “It is with great sadness that we have received the news that our former player Ken Fagerberg has passed away, at just 37 years old.

“Our thoughts are with Ken’s family, friends and loved ones. Rest in peace, Ken.”
