The company claims a duty-free exemption, and final liability is unconfirmed. A House joint committee is reviewing three years of its corporate income tax payments.

Environmental and community grievances add to the pressure. A May 2022 cyanide spill from the tailings facility was linked to fish deaths near Jikandor, Marvoe Creek and the Mafa River. The EPA says corrective measures, including tailings dam reinforcement, have since been implemented. In July 2025, residents of Ngojah Town petitioned the Supreme Court over alleged illegal land seizure and contamination. These remain allegations, not court findings.

That record bears directly on MIDA, because the new deal would flood large areas for reservoirs. Reeves notes that Annex A covers at least 446.42 square kilometers, while only US$50 million is set aside for compensation.

The company also has supporters on the ground. Residents of the Matamo Corridor in Grand Cape Mount recently commended BMMC for its development initiatives. Their statement cited education, youth empowerment, healthcare and jobs.

WHAT NOBODY HAS ANSWERED

Several basic questions remain unanswered. The government statement does not say how much extra revenue is involved or how it differs from the company’s existing obligations. Nor does it say how the new plants would fit with the planned 150 MW SP2 dam, which the World Bank Group pledged US$300 million toward in 2023. The price Liberians will pay for the electricity has not been disclosed, and lawmakers will want to know what happens to the financing if gold prices fall.

BMMC has not publicly answered the specific charges raised by Reeves, Fahnbulleh or others.

A MIDDLE ROAD

Almost none of the deal’s critics are saying Liberia should walk away from building power plants and roads. What they reject is the agreement in its current form.

Their proposals have a lot in common. Reeves wants five conditions met before ratification: publish the full deal and independently verify its prices; cap total exposure and guarantee minimum cash payments to the Treasury; tie payments to certified, usable infrastructure; give the Auditor General full access to cost records; and make community and jobs commitments binding.

Fahnbulleh suggests splitting the program. A small, fully specified first phase covering biomass, transmission and a road would go ahead on corrected terms. Each dam would need its own feasibility study, an open tender with development-bank financing, and a separate ratification vote. In his framing, the MIDA would become “the benchmark to beat” rather than the only option.

Splitting the program could keep the projects that would deliver early benefits, such as the biomass plant and the transmission lines the government already wants within two years, while giving the far more expensive dams the scrutiny they need.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Timing matters. Fahnbulleh warns that once the agreement is ratified, its terms would be protected by Article 25 of the Constitution and the deal’s stabilization clause, so any problems have to be fixed before then.

Liberia needs the power and the roads. Higher gold prices have given it real bargaining power. The question for lawmakers is whether this agreement makes the most of that moment for Liberians, or ties up decades of the country’s gold income on terms few people have been able to read in full.

World.title: Liberia Ratifies Four Intellectual Property Treaties as Senate Concurs with House
World.content:
–As legislative actions advance Liberia’s efforts to build a robust intellectual property ecosystem and support economic transformation

The Liberian Senate has concurred with the House of Representatives to ratify four regional and international intellectual property (IP) treaties, marking a significant step toward strengthening the country’s legal framework for protecting innovation, creativity, agricultural development and traditional knowledge.

The four instruments are the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO) Kampala Protocol on Voluntary Registration of Copyright and Related Rights; the ARIPO Arusha Protocol for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants; the International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV Convention); and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge.



The Senate’s decision follows the House’s earlier approval of the instruments, which formed part of eight IP treaties and protocols submitted by His Excellency Joseph Nyumah Boakai, Sr., to the 55th Legislature for ratification.

The remaining four instruments, including the UNESCO 2003 Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage, the 2005 Convention on the Diversity of Cultural Expressions, the WIPO Copyright Treaty and the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty, are expected to receive legislative consideration in the coming months.

The development aligns with President Boakai’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, particularly Pillar One, Economic Transformation, which prioritizes building a robust national intellectual property ecosystem.

Welcoming the legislative actions, the Director General of the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO), Hon. Garmai Koboi, described the concurrence as an important advancement in Liberia’s efforts to position intellectual property as an instrument of economic development. According to Hon. Koboi, these instruments will provide additional legal frameworks to help unlock the economic value of Liberia’s agricultural resources, creative industries, indigenous knowledge and innovations.



“These agreements represent an important investment in Liberia’s economic future. They provide opportunities to strengthen the protection of creative works, encourage the development of improved plant varieties, safeguard knowledge associated with our genetic resources and create a more predictable environment for innovation and investment,” Hon. Koboi noted.

Hon. Koboi further noted that, for Liberia, this means building a system in which its creators, researchers, farmers, entrepreneurs and businesses can better protect, develop and derive economic value from their intellectual contributions and resources.

The legislative action, according to LIPO, brings Liberia closer to an internationally aligned intellectual property system capable of supporting innovation, strengthening economic competitiveness and expanding opportunities for sustainable development.

Meanwhile, LIPO also expressed its appreciation to President Boakai, Sr., for his leadership and to the Honorable Members of the House of Representatives and the Liberian Senate for their support in advancing the ratification of the four intellectual property instruments.

World.title: Liberia: Sheriff Fights Personal Prosecution as LACC Defends Gbarpolu Yellow Machines Indictment
World.content:
GBARPOLU COUNTY – The legal battle surrounding the controversial procurement of earth-moving equipment for Gbarpolu County has intensified, with Omaru Sheriff, General Manager of City Lion Incorporated, seeking to have his name removed from an amended corruption indictment in his individual capacity.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Sheriff’s attempt to separate himself from the criminal proceedings, however, is facing opposition from the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC), which argues that his position as head of the company does not shield him from personal criminal liability for transactions prosecutors allege facilitated tax evasion and the misuse of public resources.



The dispute unfolded Monday, November 23, at the 16th Judicial Circuit Court in Gbarpolu County, where Sheriffs’s legal team argued that City Lion Incorporated, rather than its general manager personally, should answer for alleged contractual violations arising from the procurement of the county’s yellow machines.

The defense, in a motion filed November 20, maintained that City Lion is a legally incorporated entity with a separate legal personality and should therefore bear responsibility for transactions conducted in its corporate capacity.

But the LACC, represented by Cllr. Jimmy Saah Bombo of the Central Law Offices, rejected the argument, insisting that the allegations against Sheriff go beyond his position as a corporate officer and include conduct allegedly undertaken in his personal capacity.

The court has reserved ruling on the motion until Wednesday, November 26, leaving Sheriff facing the possibility of remaining an individual defendant alongside City Lion and several current and former county officials.



Sheriff Invokes Corporate Legal Protection

In his motion, Sheriff argued that City Lion Incorporated was the contracting party in the transactions under investigation and should therefore be held responsible for any alleged contractual breaches.

The defense cited paragraph nine of the amended indictment, which states that on October 30, 2023, Gbarpolu County entered into three separate sales contracts with City Lion, represented by Sheriff, for the procurement of one bulldozer, one excavator and one motor grader equipped with a ripper.

Paragraph 11 of the indictment further identifies three payments totaling LRD80,750,000 made to City Lion for the equipment.

According to the defense, the payments were made to the corporation, not Sheriff personally. It also argued that the indictment acknowledges the existence of the machinery at the Freeport of Monrovia following information supplied by the vendor.

Sheriff’s lawyer, Cllr. T. Sensee Sewah, contended that the prosecution had failed to sufficiently distinguish between alleged corporate contractual defaults and criminal conduct personally attributable to his client.

To support the argument, the defense relied on Section 2.5 of Liberia’s Associations Law, which recognizes the separate legal personality of incorporated entities and their capacity to sue and be sued in their own names.

The defense also cited Section 14.3 of the Criminal Procedure Law, arguing that an indictment must contain a clear and definite statement of the essential facts constituting the alleged offenses.

Citing John K. Perkins v. Republic of Liberia, 23 LLR 352 (1974), the defense maintained that identifying Sheriff as a corporate officer and associating him with the transactions does not, by itself, establish individual criminal responsibility.

The motion therefore requested that Sheriff be removed from the amended indictment as an individual defendant while allowing the prosecution against City Lion Incorporated to continue.

LACC Rejects Sheriff’s Argument

Opposing the motion, Cllr. Bombo argued that the defense was attempting to revisit an issue the court had already considered and decided.

He invoked the doctrines of res judicata and collateral estoppel, arguing that Sheriff had previously filed a similar application seeking to be removed from the proceedings and that the court rejected it.

According to Bombo, entertaining another motion seeking substantially the same relief could undermine the court’s earlier decision.

The prosecution also challenged the defense’s reliance on misjoinder, arguing that the doctrine, as presented by the defense, applies to civil proceedings and cannot be used in the manner proposed to remove an accused person from a criminal indictment.

More importantly, Bombo argued that City Lion’s separate incorporation does not automatically absolve its general manager of criminal responsibility for actions he allegedly undertook personally.

He specifically cited an alleged US$6,400 payment involving Sheriff and Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah.

According to the prosecution, the alleged transaction was not simply a payment made by City Lion as a corporate entity. Bombo argued that Sheriff personally made the payment in connection with the inclusion of two additional earth-moving machines beyond the three covered by the county’s duty-free arrangement.

The LACC contends that the alleged payment could expose Sheriff to individual criminal liability if the prosecution establishes that it was intended to facilitate the avoidance of legitimate government revenue.

The allegations have not been established in court and remain subject to proof at trial.

Five Machines, Three Contracts and the US$6,400 Question

Beyond the legal arguments, the proceedings have brought renewed attention to questions surrounding the number of machines involved in the procurement arrangement and the handling of their customs clearance.

The amended indictment identifies three machines covered by the October 30, 2023 contracts: a bulldozer, an excavator and a motor grader with a ripper.

However, the controversy also involves references to five earth-moving machines, raising questions about the additional two machines and whether they were properly covered by the duty-free privileges granted for the county’s equipment.

In a submission to the LACC, Superintendent Zinnah provided an account of how the machinery reportedly became entangled in port charges, customs clearance and an auction process at the Freeport of Monrovia.

According to his submission, the three machines procured for the county arrived at the port on May 6 and May 23, 2024.

Zinnah alleged that City Lion failed to clear the equipment within the required period, resulting in the machines remaining at the port for more than 90 days and eventually being declared abandoned.

The National Port Authority reportedly issued a public auction notice on October 22, 2024, as part of the process involving the equipment.

In a letter dated October 5, 2024, City Lion reportedly informed the county that the NPA had agreed to release the three machines in the county’s favor.

Zinnah’s account further stated that the county eventually took possession of the three machines after they were offloaded and assembled at the port.

However, the clearance process remains central to the LACC’s allegations.

The prosecution contends that the additional two machines were not covered by the duty-free privileges granted for the three machines intended for Gbarpolu County.

Bombo argued that the alleged US$6,400 payment involving Sheriff and the Superintendent was connected to the handling of those additional machines and could have facilitated the avoidance of customs duties.

In his submission, Zinnah said Brown’s Trucking Handling Services Enterprise was engaged to offload, assemble and load the machines onto transport vehicles at a cost of US$7,500.

He alleged that City Lion paid US$6,400 in two installments: US$2,500 to Randall Clarence and US$3,900 to Lucia Massaquoi.

The submission further stated that the company failed to pay the remaining US$1,100, which Zinnah claimed he personally paid to the service provider.

However, Bombo presented a separate allegation to the court, arguing that the LACC considers the alleged US$6,400 payment involving Sheriff and the Superintendent a critical component of its case.

The prosecution maintains that the money was allegedly paid directly to the Superintendent rather than to the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), potentially depriving the government of legitimate tax revenue.

The circumstances surrounding the payment, including its purpose, recipients and connection to the additional machinery, will require proof during the proceedings.

Duty-Free Documents Under Scrutiny

Questions have also emerged about the documentation used to secure duty-free privileges for the equipment.

In his submission to the LACC, Zinnah alleged that an approved duty-free letter from the Ministry of Internal Affairs contained inaccurate information, including the inclusion of two additional machines on the bill of lading.

He questioned whether the additional machinery was improperly included in the documentation to avoid payment of government taxes.

The submission also raised questions about City Lion’s subsequent position concerning customs duties and whether the relevant documents were consistent with claims that duties had been paid.

Communications involving City Lion’s clearing broker, Amadu S. Mulbah, were also referenced.

In a communication dated November 22, 2024, Mulbah reportedly raised concerns about the handling of the machinery and the county’s involvement in the clearance process.

These issues have placed the transactions involving City Lion, the county administration, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the National Port Authority and the Liberia Revenue Authority under scrutiny.

At the center of the investigation is whether the duty-free privileges were properly obtained and applied, whether additional machinery was improperly included in the documentation and whether individuals involved in the transactions facilitated the alleged loss of government revenue.

Six Defendants Face Multiple Charges

Sheriff is among six defendants named in the amended indictment.

They include current Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah; former Superintendent J. Keyah Saah; former Fiscal Superintendent Anthony Yorkor; former Chairperson of the Gbarpolu Project Management Committee Robert Benda; Sheriff; and City Lion Incorporated as a corporate defendant.

The charges include economic sabotage, fraud against the Internal Revenue of Liberia, misuse of public money, property or records, theft or illegal disbursement and expenditure of public money, illegal compensation for assistance in government matters, theft of property, criminal facilitation, criminal conspiracy, violations of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission and Public Financial Management laws, criminal solicitation and tax evasion.

The charges place both public officials and a private contractor under scrutiny over the procurement, financing, clearance and delivery of the county’s earth-moving equipment.

For the prosecution, the case is not limited to whether City Lion fulfilled its contractual obligations. It also concerns whether individuals involved in the transactions allegedly facilitated the misuse of public resources or deprived the government of legitimate revenue.

The LACC will ultimately have to establish the specific conduct and responsibilities of each defendant through evidence rather than rely solely on their official positions or association with the procurement arrangement.

Court Decision Pending

Following arguments from both sides, Judge Zuballah A. Kizeku reserved ruling on Sheriff’s motion until Wednesday, November 26, according to the proceedings.

The decision will determine whether Sheriff remains personally listed as a defendant alongside City Lion Incorporated or whether the court grants his request to remove him in his individual capacity.

Even if the court grants the motion, questions surrounding the alleged US$6,400 transaction, the duty-free documentation and the handling of the machinery would remain relevant to the broader proceedings against the other defendants and the corporate entity.

For Gbarpolu residents, the controversy extends beyond Sheriff’s attempt to separate himself from the indictment. It raises broader questions about the management of public funds, the protection of government revenue and the accountability of public officials and private contractors involved in public procurement.

Ultimately, the case will test the distinction between corporate responsibility and individual criminal liability, while placing the procurement and handling of the county’s yellow machines under judicial scrutiny.

World.title: Liberia: Green Guard Eco Solutions Earns Waste Collectors’ Praise for Improving Efficiency and Transforming Waste Management Operations
World.content:
Montserrado County– A Liberian waste management company, Green Guard Eco Solutions, is receiving commendation from independent waste collectors for improving waste disposal operations at its facility outside Dixville, with operators reporting reduced waiting times, faster offloading of garbage and increased opportunities to expand their businesses.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

The improvements are providing relief to waste collection companies that previously struggled with long queues and accumulated garbage at the Stockton Creek disposal facility, sometimes spending several hours and, on some occasions, an entire day waiting to dispose of waste collected from households and businesses.



For operators whose businesses depend on regular waste collection and disposal, the improved efficiency is translating into more working hours, additional collection trips and the potential to serve more customers.

In interviews on Monday, November 23, 2026, Prince Freeman, Chief Driver of Zero Waste, and Dennis Cheyou, Supervisor of CleanPath Waste Solutions, praised the changes at the facility, describing the current operations as an improvement over the delays they previously experienced.

Freeman said he has witnessed a noticeable difference in the pace of waste disposal, explaining that the situation was previously challenging for independent collectors who had to wait for extended periods before they could offload their garbage.

“Everywhere was a lot of dirt. It used to take us some time. We would sit out there for about two to three hours waiting. Sometimes, it takes us the whole day because we cannot leave without dumping the dirt,” Freeman said.



According to him, the delays affected the ability of waste collectors to return to their assigned communities and continue collecting garbage from customers.

However, he said operations have improved, allowing drivers to dispose of waste more quickly and make additional trips.

“But now we are dumping the dirt with speed. We are speeding with our work, and this is helping us come back fast and do more trips,” he said.

For Freeman, the improvement is not simply about spending less time at the disposal site. It also creates opportunities for waste collection businesses to increase their earnings by serving more customers.

“Now that it is clear, it means we can grow our business and bring more waste. I think my business will be growing,” he added.

He expressed hope that the management would sustain the improvements, noting that consistent performance was important to the businesses that rely on the facility.

Freeman said he was encouraged by the changes but hoped the company would maintain its current pace of operations instead of allowing the facility to return to the conditions that previously caused delays.

He also emphasized the importance of time in the waste collection business, explaining that customers depend on collectors to remove household waste regularly.

A similar endorsement came from Dennis Cheyou, Supervisor of CleanPath Waste Solutions, who also commended the improvements at the disposal facility.

Cheyou said he was pleased with the efforts being made by the municipal authorities and the company managing the facility. “I would highly applaud them because they are trying their best,” he said.

CleanPath Waste Solutions operates directly within communities, collecting household waste from residents and transporting it to the disposal facility.

Cheyou’s comments reflect the importance of efficient disposal services to independent waste collection operators, whose daily operations depend on the ability to transport and offload garbage without unnecessary delays.

The commendations from the two operators provide an indication of how improvements at the disposal facility can benefit businesses beyond the company responsible for managing it.

When waste collectors spend less time waiting to dispose of garbage, they can return to communities sooner, complete additional trips and attend to more customers.

A Liberian Company’s Broader Environmental Ambition

The improvements in waste disposal operations form part of the broader ambitions of Green Guard Eco Solutions, a Liberian company seeking to transform the country’s waste management sector through investments in environmental protection, renewable energy and resource recovery.

In an earlier report published in January 2026, Green Guard outlined its ambition to position Liberia as a regional hub for waste-to-energy innovation, climate mitigation and sustainable livelihoods through a partnership with Philippines-based Alterna Verde Cooperation.

The partnership is designed to combine Green Guard’s local waste management operations with Alterna Verde’s technical expertise in waste processing and anaerobic digestion technology.

Green Guard broke ground on its facility outside Dixville on May 5, 2024, as part of its plan to establish an integrated waste management and resource recovery system.

The company also secured a 10-year renewable agreement with the Paynesville City Corporation (PCC), designating Green Guard as the primary entity responsible for solid waste collection. The arrangement extends beyond conventional garbage disposal to include waste-to-energy initiatives and revenue-sharing arrangements.

One of the project’s major objectives is to convert waste into cleaner energy, particularly cooking gas, as an alternative to charcoal, which remains widely used by Liberian households.

For decades, charcoal production has contributed to deforestation, while smoke from charcoal use has exposed households to harmful air pollutants associated with respiratory illnesses.

Green Guard has said its proposed clean cooking gas will be packaged in high-density polyethylene (HDPE) containers designed to make handling safer and the product more accessible and affordable.

The company has also outlined a reforestation commitment as part of its environmental compliance measures.

According to the company, it plans to plant more than 1,000 trees in an area where the applicable requirement would call for approximately 250 trees.

“Every acre you clear, you need to replant 50 trees. The place we are clearing is not more than five acres. Instead of 250, we are doing over 1,000, meaning we are doing more. We are sending more oxygen into the environment,” the company stated.

Philippines Partnership Targets Renewable Energy Production

Through its partnership with Alterna Verde Cooperation, Green Guard is pursuing a waste-to-energy model intended to transform organic waste into methane and subsequently electricity.

Alterna Verde Chief Executive Officer Dr. Nervy Santiago has described the initiative as an opportunity to apply decades of experience in anaerobic digestion technology to Liberia’s waste management challenges.

The proposed development covers approximately 30 acres and is designed around four major components.

These include a lined landfill intended to protect groundwater from contamination, an anaerobic baffled reactor (ABR) to break down organic waste and produce methane, a phytoremediation system to absorb heavy metals from contaminated liquid waste, and a power station designed to convert methane into electricity.

The project also incorporates the use of citronella and vetiver grasses as part of its environmental management strategy.

Citronella grass is expected to help absorb heavy metals from leachate, the contaminated liquid generated when water passes through waste materials.

The process could also support the production of citronella oil, a commercially valuable product with international demand.

The approach is expected to provide environmental and economic benefits by addressing waste contamination while creating opportunities for additional revenue generation.

Plans to Expand Waste Collection Beyond Montserrado

To support the proposed facility’s capacity, Green Guard has outlined plans to collect waste from several communities and cities beyond its immediate operational area.

The company’s targeted collection areas include Montserrado County, Kakata, Buchanan and Harbel, particularly Unification Town.

The expansion is expected to provide the facility with sufficient waste to support its broader waste processing and energy production ambitions.

If successfully implemented, the initiative could create opportunities in renewable energy production, environmental protection, clean cooking fuel distribution and employment across the waste management value chain.

The company’s ambition also extends to establishing Liberia as a regional player in waste-to-energy innovation, with the potential to demonstrate how waste can be converted from an environmental burden into an economic resource.

For the independent waste collectors already using the facility, however, the immediate benefits are reflected in their daily operations.

Freeman’s account of reduced waiting times and the opportunity to complete more collection trips, alongside Cheyou’s commendation of the company’s efforts, suggests that improvements in waste disposal services can have a direct impact on businesses operating within Liberia’s sanitation sector.

Their experiences also underscore the importance of maintaining efficient waste management operations as Green Guard advances its broader plans for renewable energy production, environmental sustainability and regional leadership.

World.title: Liberia’s Rubber Economy Gets Local Industrial Boost as BNB Opens US$ Multi-Million Processing Factory
World.content:
Monrovia-Liberia’s ambition to move beyond exporting raw agricultural commodities and build a stronger domestic industrial economy has received a boost with the commissioning of BNB Rubber Factory Incorporated, a 100 percent Liberian-owned processing facility, expected to strengthen the country’s rubber value chain and expand local participation in one of its most important agricultural sectors.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Located in the Morris Farm Community, Todee District, Montserrado County, the multi-million-dollar investment is designed to process locally produced natural rubber into Technically Specified Rubber, TSR, particularly TSR 10 and TSR 20, products used by international rubber and manufacturing industries.



With an installed processing capacity of four metric tons per hour, equivalent to approximately 100 metric tons daily, the facility represents an important step toward retaining more economic value within Liberia, reducing dependence on the exportation of relatively unprocessed commodities and creating opportunities for domestic industrial development.

The factory’s commissioning on November 24, comes nearly a century after Liberia entered the modern commercial rubber industry through its landmark 1926 agreement with Firestone, presenting what government officials described as an opportunity for Liberians to take greater ownership of the economic possibilities surrounding the country’s natural resources.

Representing President Joseph Nyuma Boakai at the ceremony, Agriculture Minister Alexander Nuetah said the investment was strategic, not merely because of its ownership structure but because it reflects the kind of domestic entrepreneurship needed to transform Liberia’s agricultural economy.

The Minister recalled that the President considers rubber the lifeblood of Liberia’s economy, emphasizing the historical and economic importance of the commodity.



However, he argued that despite Liberia’s early entry into commercial rubber production and its historical position in the industry, the country has failed to achieve the level of production, industrial development and domestic ownership necessary to maximize the sector’s potential.

From Raw Commodity Export to Domestic Value Addition

For decades, Liberia’s rubber economy has largely depended on producing and exporting natural rubber, with much of the additional industrial value generated outside the country.

BNB’s establishment seeks to change that pattern by introducing domestic processing capacity that will transform raw rubber sourced from Liberian farmers and suppliers into standardized industrial products for international markets.

According to the company’s Chief Executive Officer, Sylvanus B. Broh, Sr, the investment emerged from the experience of Broko Enterprising Corporation, established in Tappita, Nimba County, in 2018.

The company initially operated in the rubber trade, purchasing, aggregating, and exporting natural cup lump rubber while working with farmers, brokers, suppliers, and other participants in the value chain.

That experience, the CEO explained, exposed the limitations of an economy that produces agricultural commodities but captures relatively little of the value generated through processing and manufacturing.

The realization led to the establishment of BNB Rubber Factory, with a vision of positioning Liberia as a competitive center for rubber processing and eventually finished rubber manufacturing.

The CEO said the factory’s production process begins with receiving, weighing, inspecting, and sorting raw rubber before it undergoes washing, shredding, cleaning, dewatering, and controlled drying.

The material is subsequently compressed into standardized bales, tested through laboratory quality-control procedures, and prepared for packaging and shipment.

He disclosed that the company sources its raw materials from smallholder farmers, brokers, cooperatives, and aggregators across Liberia.

The company has also established business relationships with buyers in Austria, Malaysia, Singapore, China, and Europe, according to the CEO.

The international market connections could provide an opportunity for Liberian-produced rubber to enter broader industrial supply chains while allowing the country to retain a greater portion of the value generated from its agricultural resources.

New Competition Could Reshape the Rubber Industry

Beyond its contribution to local processing, BNB’s entry could introduce a new competitive dimension into Liberia’s rubber industry, where large foreign-owned concessions and established companies have historically occupied prominent positions.

Minister Nuetah challenged Liberians to move beyond depending on foreign investors and begin taking advantage of opportunities in sectors where the country possesses natural resources and comparative advantages.

He cited Côte d’Ivoire as an example of how domestic participation can contribute to the development of a competitive rubber industry, noting that locally owned small and medium-sized enterprises have played important roles in its expansion.

The Minister presented figured showing that Liberia exported approximately 41,000 metric tons of rubber in 1961, compared with about 88 metric tons from Côte d’Ivoire during the same period.

By 2024, he said, Côte d’Ivoire’s rubber exports had increased to approximately 1.6 million metric tons, while Liberia exported about 118,000 metric tons.

The comparison, according to the Minister, illustrates the extent to which Liberia has lost ground despite its historical advantage in commercial rubber production.

He attributed part of the problem to the country’s limited domestic investment and failure to expand production and processing opportunities.

BNB’s emergence, could therefore encourage competition not only among rubber processors but also across the broader value chain.

With another processing outlet available, farmers, cooperatives, brokers, and aggregators could have additional opportunities to market their products. Increased competition among buyers could also encourage improved purchasing arrangements, more responsive services, and potentially better farm-gate prices.

For existing operators, the entry of a Liberian-owned processor could create additional pressure to improve efficiency, strengthen relationships with farmers, and consider investments in domestic value addition.

However, the extent of these benefits will depend on BNB’s ability to sustain production, maintain competitive purchasing prices, and establish a reliable nationwide supply network.

Policy Environment and the Push for Local Investment

The factory’s establishment also reflects the relationship between government policy and private-sector investment.

Minister Nuetah recalled that the government inherited an executive order restricting the exportation of unprocessed rubber, a policy environment that presented challenges for traditional participants in the rubber trade while creating incentives for investment in domestic processing.

He praised BNB’s leadership for recognizing the potential business opportunity in local value addition rather than viewing the policy change exclusively as a disadvantage.

The investment demonstrates how government policies can potentially encourage domestic industrialization when supported by private capital and entrepreneurial initiative.

However, the long-term success of such policies will depend on consistency, transparency and the government’s ability to create an enabling environment for businesses, including access to financing, reliable electricity, transportation infrastructure and efficient regulatory services.

For Liberian-owned enterprises to compete effectively with established international companies, policy restrictions alone will not be sufficient.

They must be accompanied by practical measures that reduce production costs and strengthen the competitiveness of local industries.

A New Market for Smallholder Farmers

Perhaps the most important development implication of BNB’s investment lies in its potential relationship with smallholder rubber farmers.

Liberia’s rubber economy depends not only on large plantations but also on thousands of farmers whose livelihoods are tied to the production and sale of natural rubber.

By sourcing raw materials from smallholder farmers, brokers, cooperatives, and aggregators, BNB could provide an additional commercial outlet for producers who often depend on established purchasing networks.

The factory’s demand for raw materials could help strengthen the connection between agricultural production and industrial processing.

If properly implemented, this relationship could stimulate local economic activities, improve market access, and encourage farmers to increase production in response to more dependable demand.

It could also create opportunities for cooperatives and aggregators to formalize their operations and become more active participants in the industrial supply chain.

Nevertheless, the company will need to demonstrate that its operations translate into tangible benefits for farmers through fair purchasing arrangements, timely payments, and sustained demand.

The number of farmers expected to supply the factory, the annual quantity of rubber it intends to purchase, and its proposed farm-gate pricing arrangements will be important indicators of its actual impact on rural livelihoods.

From Processing to Manufacturing, The Bigger Vision

While the immediate operation focused on producing technically specified rubber for international buyers, BNB’s leadership has outlined a longer-term ambition to move into finished rubber manufacturing.

Such a transition could represent a more substantial transformation of Liberia’s industrial economy.

Instead of exporting processed rubber for further manufacturing abroad, the country could eventually develop domestic industries producing rubber-based goods for local consumption and international markets.

This could expand employment opportunities beyond agricultural production and primary processing, while creating demand for technicians, engineers, laboratory personnel, logistics workers, and other skilled professionals.

Mr. Broh said the company’s journey from concept to commissioning took less than two years.

The facility was acquired in January 2025, construction began in April 2025, equipment installation commenced in January 2026, and was completed in July 2026.

Trial operations were conducted between September and October before the official launch.

The timeline, according to Broh, reflects its commitment to establishing a domestic industrial operation capable of supporting Liberia’s agricultural transformation.

Measuring Investment Beyond the Launch

For Liberia, BNB’s commissioning represents more than the opening of another commercial facility. It raised concerns about local ownership, agricultural productivity, industrial employment, and the country’s ability to capture greater economic benefits from its natural resources.

The investment also offers an opportunity to test whether Liberian entrepreneurs can successfully enter an industry traditionally dominated by foreign capital and compete through processing, technology, quality assurance, and international market access.

But the ultimate measure of its developmental contribution will not be the commissioning ceremony or installed production capacity.

It will be determined by the number of Liberians employed, the volume of rubber purchased from local farmers, the consistency of production, the competitiveness of its products and the extent to which its operations stimulate additional investment in the agricultural and manufacturing sectors.

For the Boakai administration, the emergence of BNB presents an opportunity to demonstrate that policies promoting local value addition can translate into tangible economic development.

For Liberia’s rubber farmers and entrepreneurs, it offers the prospect of a more diversified market and greater domestic participation in the industry’s future.

Nearly 100 years after the country entered the modern commercial rubber industry, BNB’s establishment presents a renewed opportunity to shift the conversation from simply producing and exporting rubber to processing, manufacturing and building an industrial economy in which Liberians have a greater stake.

World.title: Split Jury Verdict in 13-Year-Old Rape Case Sparks Fresh Debate Over Liberia’s Jury System
World.content:
Monrovia-A split jury verdict in a rape case involving a 13-year-old girl has reignited debate over the effectiveness and integrity of Liberia’s jury system, after eight jurors reportedly voted to acquit a defendant who had sought to withdraw his initial plea of not guilty and enter a guilty plea midway through the trial.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

The verdict, which resulted in a hung jury and a mistrial, has prompted the Ministry of Justice’s Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Crimes Unit to question the jury’s handling of the case and announce plans to pursue legal redress.



The case, Republic of Liberia versus Patrick Weefur, was heard at Criminal Court ‘E’ at the Temple of Justice, presided over by Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh.

Speaking in an interview following the jury’s decision, the Director of the Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Crimes Unit at the Ministry of Justice, Cllr. Isaac L. George, described the outcome as troubling, arguing that the defendant’s attempted change of plea should have seriously influenced the direction of the proceedings.

According to the prosecution, the defendant initially pleaded not guilty to the rape charge but later sought to withdraw that plea and enter a guilty plea after the government had presented five witnesses, including the alleged victim.

The development occurred after the defense had presented its first witness, with the defendant expected to subsequently take the witness stand in his own defense.



However, rather than testify, Weefur reportedly informed the court of his decision to accept criminal responsibility and waive his right to testify.

Cllr. George said the prosecution was particularly concerned that the defendant’s attempted admission of guilt was followed by a jury decision that produced eight votes for acquittal and four for conviction.

“We are disappointed by the conduct of the jurors, the eight jurors,” Cllr. George said, questioning how the panel could return a not-guilty majority when the defendant had reportedly indicated his willingness to accept responsibility for the crime.

He argued that the jury’s decision raised serious questions about the administration of criminal justice, particularly in cases involving sexual violence against children.

Disputed Guilty Plea

The prosecution’s account indicated that Weefur’s decision to change his plea came after the government had presented its evidence, and the court had rejected a defense motion for acquittal.

Cllr. George explained that following the prosecution’s presentation of approximately five witnesses, the defense filed a motion for acquittal, which Judge Wesseh denied, directing the defense to proceed with its case.

The defense subsequently presented witnesses before the defendant decided to abandon his earlier not-guilty plea.

But the judge declined to accept the guilty plea, exercising the discretion provided under Chapter 16.4 of Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law, according to the prosecution’s account.

The court nevertheless allowed the defendant to waive his right to testify.

Cllr. George maintained that once the defendant expressed his willingness to plead guilty, the court should have moved toward determining the case rather than allowing the jury process to continue.

He argued that the defendant’s attempted admission of criminal responsibility, combined with the evidence already presented, should have informed the court’s subsequent handling of the matter.

However, the legal distinction between an attempted guilty plea and a formally accepted plea remains central to understanding the controversy.

A guilty plea that has not been accepted by the court does not automatically amount to a conviction.

The court’s decision to reject the proposed plea meant that the case remained subject to the applicable trial procedure.

Prosecution Highlights Key Testimony

The prosecution also identified the testimony of one of its witnesses as a significant development in the trial.

According to Cllr. George, the witness, testified that she knew the 13-year-old girl and had previously seen her interacting with the defendant at her shop.

The witness reportedly recalled an incident in January when the defendant allegedly approached the child and asked whether she knew about “man business.”

The witness said she subsequently cautioned the defendant against asking children such questions.

Cllr. George described the testimony as a turning point in the prosecution’s case, arguing that it challenged the defendant’s earlier position that he did not know the child and had never interacted with her.

He suggested that the testimony contributed to the defendant’s decision to seek a change of plea after the prosecution had presented its evidence.

The prosecution further maintained that the alleged victim testified about her experience before the court.

However, the jury’s divided decision meant that the prosecution failed to secure the required unanimous verdict for conviction.

Calls for Jury System Review

Beyond the immediate case, the verdict has opened a broader conversation about the role, independence, and accountability of jurors in Liberia’s criminal justice system.

Cllr. George called for an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the jury’s deliberations, expressing suspicion about the decision of the eight jurors who voted to acquit.

He, however, provided no evidence of bribery or improper influence, and the split verdict alone does not establish misconduct by any juror.

The prosecution director argued that jurors are expected to determine cases based on the evidence and applicable law rather than personal sympathy, emotions, or external considerations.

He also questioned the composition of some contemporary jury panels, noting that jurors increasingly come from government ministries, agencies, and academic institutions.

According to him, the educational and professional backgrounds of jurors should translate into a stronger appreciation of their responsibilities in dispensing justice.

His comments come amid continuing discussions about judicial accountability and the effectiveness of Liberia’s jury system.

Cllr. George also referenced concerns attributed to Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay about the need to examine the country’s jury-trial framework.

“I think there is a need for us to look at the jury system seriously,” he said, warning that unresolved weaknesses could undermine public confidence in the justice system.

He questioned whether Liberia should continue relying on the existing jury arrangement without addressing the challenges associated with jury deliberations and verdicts.

Government Plans Legal Redress

Despite the mistrial, the Ministry of Justice says the case is not over.

Cllr. George disclosed that the prosecution intends to return to court through the appropriate legal procedure to seek a new trial.

He said the government intends to pursue the matter immediately, while also pushing for an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the jury’s decision.

The proposed legal action could provide another opportunity for the prosecution to present its case and seek a determination of the allegations against Weefur.

The controversy, however, raised a fundamental concern about the relationship between a defendant’s right to a fair trial, the court’s authority to accept or reject a guilty plea, and the jury’s constitutional responsibility to determine disputed facts.

While the prosecution considers the outcome a miscarriage of justice, the jury’s decision must also be assessed within the legal framework governing criminal trials.

Ultimately, the case has placed Liberia’s jury system under renewed scrutiny, particularly over whether existing safeguards are sufficient to ensure that justice is administered fairly, independently, and without undue influence.

For the 13-year-old alleged survivor, the hung verdict means that the legal process remained unresolved, with the government now preparing another legal move.

World.title: Matambo cautions water and sanitation officials
World.content:
The Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation has directed all Provincial Water Supply and Sanitation to prioritise giving the service to villages without boreholes or piped water schemes in the 2027 work plans, in order to accelerate access to clean and safe water.

The ministry says every province should identify underserved communities and develop practical interventions that will ensure no village is left behind in the provision of water supply services.

Speaking during the ministry’s 2027 Planning Meeting in Chilanga district today, Minister of Water Development and Sanitation Elisha Matambo said every village must have access to clean and safe water.

Mr Matambo said provincial officers should prepare village-level water access plans indicating communities requiring intervention, proposed solutions, estimated costs and implementation timelines.

He noted that depending on population, settlement patterns, groundwater potential and technical feasibility, interventions should include borehole development or piped water schemes.

Mr Matambo said the ministry’s ambition should go beyond constructing water infrastructure to ensuring that facilities remain functional, while providing reliable services.

He added that water security is essential for agricultural production, irrigation, livestock development, industrialisation, tourism, job creation and improved rural livelihoods.

Meanwhile, UNICEF Country Representative Dr Saja Abdullah said adequate funding for the operation and maintenance of water infrastructure is critical to ensuring sustainable service delivery.

Dr Abdullah said the government, development partners and the private sector should align resources towards Zambia’s water, sanitation and hygiene ambitions, adding that UNICEF is ready to provide technical assistance to strengthen the sector.

She further said the cholera outbreak has highlighted the need for urgent response to go hand in hand with prevention, preparedness and resilience.

Dr Abdullah said climate resilience should also be central to the 2027 plans, particularly with a strong El Niño projected for the 2026/2027 season, requiring drought preparedness and continuity of essential water and sanitation services.

She reaffirmed UNICEF’s commitment to supporting the government through technical expertise, evidence and partnerships to ensure equitable access to sustainable water and sanitation services, particularly for vulnerable children and communities.

World.title: ZIPRC calls for the integration of PR into strategic decision-making
World.content:
The President of the Zambia Institute of Public Relations and Communication (ZIPRC), Patricia Luhanga, has called for the integration of public relations and communication practitioners into strategic decision-making, policy formulation, and implementation processes, saying this is critical for Zambia to achieve its national development aspirations under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Ms Luhanga said communication should no longer be viewed as a peripheral institutional function confined to issuing press statements and managing media relations but rather should be recognized as a strategic tool for stakeholder engagement, building public trust, managing risks, and advancing national development.

She emphasised that public relations professionals must be involved from the initial stages of programme development through implementation, monitoring and evaluation to ensure that institutional decisions reflect stakeholder interests and contribute to sustainable outcomes.

“We should be right where this agenda is being developed, where the implementation is happening, where the monitoring and evaluation is going on,” she said.

Ms Luhanga said this when she featured on ZANIS tv programme “The Deep Dive.”

She stressed that public relations practitioners play a critical role in identifying key stakeholders, assessing their influence, anticipating potential risks, and advising institutions on how their programmes and policies are likely to be received by the public.

Ms Luhanga said this enables organisations to address concerns at an early stage and prevent challenges that could undermine development initiatives.

She stressed the need for communication practitioners to work closely with experts in various fields rather than attempting to replace their technical expertise.

Ms Luhanga said such collaboration is essential for effectively supporting productive sectors such as mining, energy, agriculture, and tourism.

“Our responsibility is to translate complex technical information into language that stakeholders could understand while identifying the appropriate experts to communicate specialized issues,” she said.

Meanwhile, Ms Luhanga disclosed that ZIPRC is strengthening collaboration with government, private sector institutions, universities, and other stakeholders to promote professional standards and ensure that qualified practitioners are considered for communication positions.

She also urged institutions to strengthen their capacity to address emerging challenges related to artificial intelligence, misinformation, disinformation, and crisis communication.

Ms Luhanga said organizations should develop comprehensive communication, social media, and artificial intelligence policies to effectively navigate the evolving information landscape.

She also urged organizations to strengthen their capacity to combat misinformation and disinformation through real-time monitoring, the development of appropriate policies, and collaboration with fact-checking and verification platforms such as Zambia’s I Verify.

Ms Luhanga called on institutions to integrate communication and stakeholder engagement into their strategic plans, emphasizing that the impact of public relations should be measured through levels of public awareness, stakeholder participation, and trust, rather than media coverage alone.

She, however, bemoaned limited funding for communication departments, describing it as a major challenge affecting the effective execution of communication strategies. She urged practitioners to demonstrate their value through practical initiatives, strategic partnerships, and measurable results that contribute to organizational objectives.

The ZIPRC President also highlighted Zambia’s participation at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja, which provided opportunities for international recognition, knowledge exchange and partnerships with other countries, including Nigeria.

Ms Luhanga said going forward ZIPRC wants communication professionals to play a bigger role in advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

And She welcomed the introduction of Principal Public Relations Officer positions in government ministries and revealed that some ministries had approached the institute for experts to support the agenda’s communication strategy.

World.title: NAC calls for equitable access to HIV services
World.content:
National HIV/AIDS Council North-Western Provincial AIDS Advisor, Hillary Sakala, has called for concerted efforts to address inequalities that continue to limit access to HIV prevention, testing and treatment services.

Mr Sakala says the availability of effective HIV services does not automatically mean that everyone who needs them can access them.

Speaking ahead of the World Aids Day Commemoration on December 1, Mr Sakala said stigma and discrimination, gender disparities, declining funding and the limited inclusion of vulnerable communities continue to undermine progress in HIV response.

He said this year’s theme, “ending AIDS starts with access,” highlights the need to make HIV services readily available, affordable, confidential and closer to the communities that need them.

Mr Sakala has identified adolescent girls and young women, adolescent boys and young men, pregnant and breastfeeding women, children, men, mobile and cross-border populations, key populations and persons with disabilities as groups that require targeted HIV services.

Mr Sakala has also raised concern over the reported mother-to-child HIV transmission rate of 6.12 percent, which is above the elimination threshold, and the decline in Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PREP) coverage between 2024 and 2025.

He added that expanding access to new prevention options, including long-acting injectable prep, oral prep and condoms, is important in strengthening HIV prevention.

Mr Sakala further called for increased domestic financing to sustain HIV programmes as external funding declines, urging government, the private sector, cooperating partners and citizens to support initiatives such as the Zambia HIV Trust Fund.

‘‘Local authorities, district HIV and AIDS Committees and District Health Offices also have a critical role to play in translating national HIV commitments into practical services and budgeted actions at community level,’’ he said.

The AIDS Advisor said ensuring access to HIV prevention, testing, treatment, care and support services is essential to Zambia’s goal of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

‘‘As a Province, preparations for the 2026 World AIDS Day scheduled for Tuesday, December 01, have reached an advanced stage and I am calling upon the general public to take advantage of this day and turn up in large numbers to access free HIV testing and syphilis among other services,’’ he added.

World.title: Pedestrian dies in Nakonde ‎RTA
World.content:
A 35 year old pedestrian has died after being hit by a truck laden with bags of flour along the Nakonde-Mbala road in Nakonde district, Muchinga Province.

‎

‎Muchinga Province Police Commanding Officer, Lubinda Mayamba has confirmed the accident and identified the deceased as Gerad Simpanda of Chileshe village in Chief Nsokolo’s area, Senga Hill district.

‎

‎ Mr Mayamba said the fatal road traffic accident occurred yesterday, Monday, November 23, 2026, around 23:10 hours at Nakakola village, approximately 20 kilometres west of Nakonde Central Business Centre.

‎

‎”According to Nakonde Traffic Police, the accident involved a Sino Howo truck and trailer, registration number AIH 3811 and AIH 3812ZM respectively, a property of Goodmorning Star Company of Lusaka,” he said.

‎

‎He disclosed this development in a press statement made available to the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS) today.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba further said the truck, laden with an undisclosed number of bags of flour, was being driven from east to west by 41 year old Blackson Besa of Kasama district.

‎

‎The Commanding Officer stated that preliminary investigations indicate that Besa was attempting to avoid hitting a stationary vehicle when he lost control of the vehicle due to excessive speed and veered off the road to the right side, striking Simpanda the now deceased who was walking off the road in the same direction before the said truck overturned.

‎

‎”Simpanda sustained multiple body injuries and was pronounced dead upon arrival at Nakonde Urban Clinic. His body has since been deposited into the Nakonde Urban clinic mortuary awaiting a postmortem examination,” he said.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba pointed out that the truck driver sustained nose bleeding and general body pains and is currently admitted at Nakonde district hospital where he is receiving medical treatment.

‎

‎He adds that a 26 year old passenger Bernard Mumba who was on board suffered a cut on his lower lip, a bruised right knee and general body pains and was treated as an outpatient at the same hospital.

‎

‎The Commanding Officer further said the truck involved in the accident sustained a damaged cabin and is still at the accident scene awaiting towing to the police station for physical inspection by the Road Transport and Safety Agency (RTSA) as police investigations continue.

World.title: East records 9 cholera cases
World.content:
Eastern Province has recorded nine cholera cases, affecting Chipata and Kasenengwa districts.

Speaking at a press briefing in Chipata today on behalf of Eastern Province Permanent Secretary Paul Thole, Chipata District Commissioner Elidah Mwanza has noted that as of today, November 24, 2026, a total of nine cases have been reported with four confirmed cases.

She says out of the nine reported cases, three are from Chipata while six are from Kasenengwa.

The District Commissioner says all patients are linked to attending the funeral of an eighty-year-old relative who died on November 18, 2026, and was buried on November 21, 2026, in Kazimule area.

Meanwhile, the Provincial Health Office says it has heightened the outbreak response activities.

Eastern Province Public Health Specialist Bernard Chimungu says members of the public especially those in Chipata and Kasenengwa districts have been urged to follow preventive measures to stop the spread of the disease.

World.title: Muchinga Minister happy with ECE hub construction project
World.content:
Muchinga Province Minister, Jairo Simbeye, has commended the local contractor engaged to construct an Early Childhood Education (ECE) Center in Kampumbu area of Isoka District for putting up quality work.

‎

‎Mr Simbeye says the contractor, who was engaged under the labour based model, has met all the benchmarks of timely delivery, quality works and the right cost.

‎

‎He explains that although the project was done by the community, the work is up to the required standard.

‎

‎” I think it has been done very well. Like the President always says quality, timely delivery and worth the money. This is what has been done here,” he says.

‎

‎ZANIS reports that the Provincial Minister was speaking after inspecting the Kampumbu ECE hub school in Isoka.

‎

‎Mr Simbeye has also challenged other firms engaged to implement projects under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to emulate the contractor and deliver quality works.

‎

‎He noted that there are a number of projects that contractors are currently undertaking in Muchinga and across the country and emphasised the need to observe quality.

‎

‎”Let every contractor have this mindset of giving the right infrastructure to the people. If you’re given a contract, come and learn from here. For me I think I’m so impressed,” he said.

‎

Mr Simbeye also praised the government through the Zambia Enhancing Early Learning (ZEEL) project for providing learners in the rural district with such a standard facility.

‎

‎He stated that the facility will give learners in this rural part of Isoka the best start in life.

‎

‎”To have such educational facilities is a plus, it shows that we are heading in the right direction. Our learners will be in the right environment, with running water, electricity, having furniture in the school, having right offices, everything well suited, Play Park. For me I think it’s an enticing thing that every child would want to be here,” he said

‎

‎And Kampumbu Primary School Headteacher, where the hub has been constructed, Robert Kaluba, disclosed that the project is at about 98 percent completion.

‎

‎Mr Kaluba said the project is only remaining with the installation of doors, and other fittings.

‎

‎He has expressed hope that the facility will be opened to the public at the start of the new academic year in 2027.

‎

‎Mr Kaluba has also thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for launching the ECE schools under ZEEL across the country.

‎

‎”We are so grateful to the President for having brought the 222 hubs countrywide which were commissioned in Mansa back then,” he said.

‎

‎An ECE Teacher at Kampumbu Primary School, Katepa Tembo, said the facility will provide adequate space for learners in both level one and two.

‎

‎Ms Tembo said the school is facing serious challenges as it was given only a classroom to accommodate the two ECE levels.

“So with the help of this hub, it’s an advantage to us because it is a one by two classroom block. Meaning the ECE level one have their own class and the ECE level two also have their own class.

“The space is very big as you can see even with the play park. The learners will be enjoying themselves when they want to develop their motor skills,” she said,

Kampumbu Primary School currently has about 121 ECE learners.

World.title: MINISTER OF EDUCATION URGES YOUNG PEOPLE TO BE INNOVATIVE
World.content:
Minister of Education Harry Kamboni has urged graduating pupils to embrace hard work and use their education to contribute to national development.

Mr Kamboni said Zambia needs innovative young people capable of turning its natural resources into economic opportunities.

Speaking during a graduation ceremony at International Maarif Schools, Mr Kamboni said education should not end with academic qualifications but must equip learners with the knowledge and skills to identify challenges and develop solutions.

He urged the graduates to think about their future ambitions and identify how their education could help address Zambia’s development needs.

The Minister said the country was endowed with natural resources, including copper, but needed educated and innovative citizens who could explore opportunities beyond traditional employment.

He encouraged the graduates to pursue practical knowledge and skills that could help them create opportunities and contribute to the country’s economic growth.

The minister cautioned parents against allowing social media and television to take over their children’s lives, stressing the importance of parental supervision and engagement.

He urged the graduates to remain disciplined, focused and proud of their cultural identity as they pursue opportunities beyond school.

Speaking earlier, Turkish Ambassador to Zambia Hüseyin Barbaros Dicle urged graduates to embrace innovation, remain open to learning and use their education to strengthen relations between Zambia and Turkey.

Mr Dicle said the graduates had an opportunity to become a bridge between the two countries through education, cultural understanding and cooperation.

The Turkish Ambassador said the partnership between Zambia and Turkey in education was helping to build lasting connections between the two nations.

He expressed appreciation to the Minister for attending the ceremony, describing his presence as a demonstration of the value attached to cooperation between the two countries.

Mr Dicle said Turkey was committed to strengthening its relationship with Zambia, particularly in education and other areas of mutual interest.

“You do not need to have everything figured out today, and you do not need to succeed at everything you try,” he said.

He also challenged them to prepare for emerging technological developments, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), which he identified as one of the major challenges and opportunities they would encounter.

Mr Dicle said their experience at International Maarif Schools placed them in a unique position to promote friendship between Zambia and Turkey.

The Board of Trustees of International Maarif Schools Selim Cerrah said the graduates had a responsibility to apply the knowledge acquired at school towards addressing challenges and supporting national development.

Meanwhile International Maarif school out-going head girl Dora Takondwa acknowledged the support and leadership of the school during their schooling.

World.title: Police in Muchinga opens inquiry on Police DIG attack
World.content:
Police in Muchinga Province has opened an inquiry into an incident of malicious damage to property following a violent mob attack at Muwele area in Chiundaponde Chiefdom of Lavushimanda District.

‎

‎Muchinga Province Police Commissioner, Lubinda Mayamba, says the incident occurred on November 24, 2026, at approximately 15:00 hours, when a mob allegedly damaged a police vehicle and two tents at Muwele Police Post.

‎

‎ Mr Mayamba explained that the incident happened when Deputy Inspector General of Police, Fred Hamaamba, and his entourage visited Muwele Police Post to inspect a site earmarked for the construction of government structures.

‎

‎He said upon arrival, the police delegation found a large crowd gathered at Muwele Primary School, which was reportedly expecting the Deputy Inspector General to be accompanied by the area Member of Parliament, District Commissioner and Chief Chiundaponde.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba narrated that the community had gathered in anticipation of receiving clarification over misinformation circulating in the area suggesting that government will impose a five-year fishing ban.

‎

‎He stated that the misinformation had caused discontent among community members who depend on fishing for their livelihood.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba said after Mr Hamaamba clarified that his visit is unrelated to the alleged fishing ban and that the other expected leaders are not part of his entourage, the crowd allegedly became violent.

‎

‎He indicated that the mob reportedly believed that the Zambia Police Service was working in collaboration with Bangweulu Wetlands Management to introduce the alleged five-year fishing ban.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba said the crowd subsequently pelted stones at the Deputy Inspector General of Police and his entourage, while some members vandalised tents and looted food rations belonging to officers deployed at Muwele Police Post.

‎

‎He stated that the police officers were compelled to discharge firearms and use tear gas canisters to disperse the crowd and restore order, thereby facilitating the safe evacuation of Mr Hamaamba and other officers.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba said no casualties were recorded during the incident, adding that all officers’ luggage and equipment had been secured and accounted for.

‎

‎He further disclosed that the damaged property included the rear windscreen of a white Toyota Hilux registration number 2865B and two green tents, whose value is yet to be established.

‎

‎Mr Mayamba said all officers have since been accommodated at Chiundaponde Village as they await further instructions from higher authorities.

World.title: Botswana Speaker elected SADC PF president
World.content:
Ezulwini, Eswatini BOTSWANA’s – Speaker of the National Assembly, Dithapelo Keorapetse, has been unanimously elected president of the SADC Parliamentary Forum, pledging to bring the institution closer to the region’s people and help turn the legal foundation for a SADC Parliament into a functioning institution.

Accepting the two-year mandate at the forum’s 59th plenary assembly, Keorapetse said he was “deeply honoured” by the confidence placed in him and accepted the role with “a deep sense of duty”.

He paid tribute to outgoing president Siteny Thierry Randrianasoloniaiko, thanking him for his “steady stewardship, dedication, and the strong foundation” he leaves behind.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: War veterans hit back at Mahiya over Chiwenga’s ‘Pasi  nezvigananda’ slogan
World.content:
A WAR veterans pressure group has taken a swipe at Zanu PF Mashonaland West provincial coordinating committee member Douglas Mahiya for dismissing Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga’s “Pasi neZvigandanga” slogan, accusing him of defending politically connected economic elites benefiting from state capture.

In a statement responding to recent remarks by Mahiya and Zanu PF spokesperson Christopher Mutsvangwa, the pressure group said the two had departed from the ideological foundations and economic emancipation objectives of Zimbabwe’s liberation struggle.

Mahiya reportedly dismissed the “Pasi neZvigandanga” slogan, popularised by Chiwenga, arguing that it vilified an emerging indigenous middle class which he described as indispensable to Zimbabwe’s economic development.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Zim Women fall to Ireland in Super Six thriller
World.content:
ZIMBABWE Women suffered a heartbreaking three-wicket defeat to Ireland Women in their Super Six clash at the Seven Districts Ground in AJMAN, United Arab Emirates, this Sunday despite a brilliant all-round performance from Nyasha Gwanzura.

Batting first, Zimbabwe posted 120 for nine in their 20 overs.Gwanzura was the star with the bat, smashing 38 off just 30 balls, including four fours and a six, to give Zimbabwe a flying start after they had raced to 62 for two at the halfway stage of their innings.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.content:
THE mining sector is a solid pillar of Zimbabwe’s economy and a key driver in realising Vision 2030 and the National Development Strategy 2 (NDS2).

Mining cooperation also constitutes an important dimension of China-Zimbabwe relations, going far beyond capital investment and mineral trade. It embodies a genuine partnership rooted in shared prosperity, skills transfer and a sincere commitment to local communities.
