World.title: Army set to detonate a cache of lead explosives, sending toxic plume across Iowa
World.content:
The Army is set to detonate a stockpile of unstable lead azide explosives in southeast Iowa on Wednesday morning, a plan officials insist is the safest option even though the blast is likely to deposit toxic dust for miles.

The detonation is scheduled for 9 a.m. CT at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Army officials say that 68 drums of deteriorating, toxic lead azide — about 9,700 pounds — have undergone a process of “recrystallization,” putting them at risk of a spontaneous explosion.

Barrels of lead azide at the plant in Middletown. Obtained by NBC News

The Army has called for evacuations in Middletown and a 5-mile zone to the southwest of the ammunition plant.

Soldiers went door to door Tuesday afternoon to notify residents that they should evacuate. The Federal Emergency Management Agency is providing short-term hotel lodging to those in the evacuation zone through Friday.

Based on Wednesday’s expected weather conditions, Army projections indicate the cloud of lead dust could travel some 100 miles southwest and cross into northeastern Missouri.

The plan has prompted widespread fear and anger among local residents, many of whom say they did not receive enough warning about the detonation. People in the potential path of the plume have scrambled to change Thanksgiving plans, tape windows, cover gardens and buy cleaning supplies.

Jill Holler, who has a family farm about 20 miles west of Middletown, said she spent Sunday night rushing to take soil samples for future comparisons of lead concentrations.

“I was down in the dark getting the soil samples, and it’s just frustrating,” she said.

Windows are covered to reduce the chance of shattering at a home near the plant in Middletown. Scott Olson / Getty

Lead is a potent neurotoxin and no amount of exposure is safe. It poses the biggest health threat to children. Exposure is associated with learning disabilities, reproductive health problems, mental health issues and increased risk of hearing loss, among other effects.

Once deposited on surface or in soil, lead particles can remain there forever unless physically removed.

Army officials maintain that it is safer to detonate the chemicals in a controlled manner, with mitigation measures in place, than risk a surprise blast.

“I take the Army’s warning seriously that the choice is between a planned detonation and an uncontrolled explosion,” outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said in a statement Tuesday. She has declared a disaster emergency for three counties expected to be affected.

“I believe, based on the information I’ve been given, that the danger is immediate, and I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” Reynolds said.

Middletown on the edge of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Scott Olson / Getty

Army officials have said they are employing a range of mitigation strategies in an attempt to keep as much lead dust as possible within the ammunition plant.

That includes two stories of “HESCO” barriers — modular, collapsible structures filled with sand — built around the blast site, with a plan to spray water as the detonation occurs to catch small particles. Officials said aqueous foam blocks, gel blocks and two “water walls” made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks each will also help absorb the blast.

According to emergency permitting documents submitted to the Environmental Protection Agency, the Army expects the blast to leave a crater about 38 feet wide and 5 feet deep.

The Army said in a release Tuesday that after the detonation, environmental monitoring teams plan to follow the plume’s path “to collect soil, surface-water, and surface-wipe samples to verify lead levels against baseline models and guide any localized cleanup.”

If any residential properties are found to exceed a certain threshold of lead contamination — 200 parts per million — the Army said, “remediation teams will remove affected soil, clean surfaces, and restore the property at complete government expense.”

It has offered few specifics, however, about how or when such testing will be conducted — or the process or timeline for any government-led remediation work.

Andrew Whelton, a professor of civil, environmental and ecological engineering at Purdue University in Indiana, said that even the documents in the Army’s emergency permit do not describe those plans in detail.

“Based on the document I reviewed, there is no plan for applying an evidence-based approach to determine if people’s homes, schools, and businesses are safe after the detonation,” he said.

Peter Thorne, a pulmonary toxicologist and environmental health specialist with the University of Iowa’s College of Public Health, said scientists will work to conduct independent monitoring of the plume of lead dust.

“We have monitoring equipment out there that’s going to tell us the extent of lead that’s became airborne and moved with the wind,” he said. “Our models will be able to tell us how much lead is depositing on soil and on playground equipment and so forth. And from that, we can make some estimates of what what the degree of of danger is associated with this exposure.”

He questioned how these explosives were allowed to become so dangerous over time. The nation’s stockpile of lead azide — once used to make bomb triggers but phased out about 15 years ago — was moved to the ammunition plant in 2009, officials have said.

“Why wasn’t this dealt with long ago when they could have chemically degraded and the lead azide would no longer be a hazard?” he said. “It should have been dealt with in the past, and now of it’s become a crisis with very few good options left.”

World.title: Trump says pardon is always an option for Huang, and that invoking the Fifth isn’t necessary
World.content:
President Donald Trump said that while pardoning Jensen Huang for any potential criminal activity remains an option, he doesn’t think that will be needed for the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO.

“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump told the New York Post in an interview published Tuesday night.

Asked about Huang’s scheduled appearances next week on Capitol Hill, Trump said, “I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people.”

“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” the president said.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on Trump’s comments. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated he would have told Trump if Huang had been involved in any criminal activity.

“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.

In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are preparing to grill Huang over their national security concerns.

A spokesperson for the Republican-led House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement “changes nothing” and that there “are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers.”

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are expected to sit for transcribed interviews next Tuesday and Wednesday before the House Select Committee on China, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Huang, who has not been charged with a crime, resigned from his post as CEO of the chip giant following reports that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. In a Nov. 8 memo to Nvidia’s staff, he said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Trump worked behind the scenes over the weekend to get Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. That move has been met with bipartisan backlash.

Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., on Monday raised concerns over Nvidia’s quick reversal to rehire Huang after indicating it wouldn’t.

“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts wrote in a post on X.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., wrote that with Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang, “the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”

Cramer and Ricketts are both members of the Senate Banking Committee, where Huang is scheduled to testify in public Dec. 3.

In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social post that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Similarly, Nvidia’s board said it reached the decision to reinstate Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

World.title: Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia staff, saying he went ‘too far’ and is in therapy
World.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around.

No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world.

According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source.

Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8.

Jensen Huang outside the Hart Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C. in July. Finn Gomez / Getty

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee.

Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled.

The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”

World.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves the U.S. for Spain ‘a free man’ after deportation battle
World.content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has left the United States for Spain, ending a closely watched and controversial deportation battle that became a symbol for the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Abrego Garcia had been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.

He was spotted Tuesday night boarding a commercial flight at Washington Dulles International Airport bound for Madrid.

In a statement Tuesday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said Abrego Garcia was “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

Abrego Garcia, wearing a dark hooded jacket, was seen at the airport with his wife and brother, as well as lawyer Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and representatives from immigrant rights group We Are CASA (Central American Solidarity and Assistance).

Sandoval-Moshenberg said his client was leaving the country his way, on a commercial flight to Madrid, instead of the way the administration wanted, “in shackles,” as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainee headed on a government plane to the West African country of Liberia.

The attorney suggested Abrego would return to the United States to open arms and the reunification of his family here following the end of Donald Trump’s presidential term.

“Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen and the father of a U.S. citizen child,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

He added, “Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice.”

The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis late Tuesday hailed Abrego’s departure as a win.

“The El Salvadoran man chose to self-deport to Spain — a country that has been wrecked by open border policies. Good riddance,” she said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin used similar language, calling this a matter of self-deportation, and characterized his presence in the United States as focused on an alleged life of crime.

“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported,” he said. “Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans.”

The Washington Post reported earlier in the day that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the United States under an agreement with U.S. authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings.

Court records in Maryland have yet to reflect such an order. There has been a handful of sealed filings in his civil case against the administration over the past several weeks, however.

The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the United States for years, is married to an American and has a child with her.

He had lived and worked in Maryland for years under the regular supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from gang members.

Guards lead a man identified by his wife as Kilmar Abrego Garcia through the Terrorism Confinement Center in Tecoluca, El Salvador, in 2025. U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland via AP

He was deported there anyway in 2025 and sent to the CECOT megaprison. Activists have decried alleged abuses there and described inmates being packed into cells with no time outdoors.

Prison officials allowed Abrego Garcia a brief outside meeting with Van Hollen, who told reporters that Abrego Garcia had “experienced trauma” after an “illegal abduction.”

He was returned to the U.S., where ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an “administrative error.”

Not long after his return to U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a 2022 traffic stop for alleged speeding in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers.

Abrego Garcia told Tennessee Highway Patrol troopers he was taking the group of nine to a construction job. Authorities there did not pursue charges. A federal judge dismissed the 2025 Department of Justice case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed.

The administration continued to pursue Abrego’s removal, and he was fighting that in a lawsuit that was ongoing prior to today’s news.

Abrego Garcia has been fighting deportation to Liberia, as proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. He wanted to go to Costa Rica, according to court records.

Trump and immigration officials alleged Abrego Garcia was an MS-13 gang member, something he denied.

In 2019 records from a loitering case in which he was picked up in a Home Depot parking lot, authorities in Prince George’s County said that Abrego appeared to be an MS-13 member.

They said they made that conclusion based on his clothing (including a Chicago Bulls hat) and tattoos, as well as a proven confidential informant. Abrego Garcia was not formally arrested that day, police said, and they did not have contact with him again. Abrego Garcia’s lawyers later called the evidence of his gang membership “hearsay.”

U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who presided over the Tennessee smuggling case, warned top Trump administration officials to stop making statements about Abrego Garcia that were “exaggerated if not simply inaccurate” and could influence a potential jury.

World.title: 2 men charged with burglary after break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate’s country home
World.content:
LONDON — Two men have been charged in connection with a burglary at the royal family’s Sandringham estate, British police said Wednesday, after a reported break-in at the country home of Prince William and Princess Kate.

The pair were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site, the local police force said in a statement.

Officers were called just before 6 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET) on Monday “to reports of suspicious activity at a property,” Norfolk Police force said.

“Police and specialist resources attended and two men were arrested nearby on suspicion of burglary and trespass and taken into custody for questioning,” the statement added.

A police officer near Anmer Hall in Norfolk, England, on Tuesday. Martin Pope / Getty

The two men, named by police as Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, have now been charged. They remain in custody and are due to appear in court in the eastern city of Norwich on Wednesday morning, the statement said.

The Sun newspaper first reported Tuesday that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, one of the residences used by the heir to the British throne and his wife. The property, gifted to the couple by the late Queen Elizabeth II as a wedding present, is nestled in the heart of the royals’ sprawling estate.

In an earlier statement, police said the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident.

Separately, a royal source told NBC News that the couple and their three children, George, Charlotte and Louis, were not there at the time.

Britain's Prince William and Princess Kate with their children, Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince of Wales, in London in 2025. Chris Jackson / AFP via Getty

The couple and their children have often enjoyed weekend breaks and holidays at the royal estate in eastern England. While they weren’t present at the time of the burglary, the incident is a significant security breach for the royals.

The break in “of course, raises huge concerns,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said Wednesday. “This is the home of our future king and queen.”

“Nobody wants to feel as though their home, their private space is being violated,” she said. “They do have a great deal of security in place and so they’ll be looking at why that has lapsed.”

Security arrangements “are naturally cloaked in secrecy because they don’t want to let people know too much about what’s happening,” she added.

“Essentially, it’s a bit like an onion. They have multiple layers of security,” she said, adding that when they were on the estate “they also have their armed police protection officers who ensure that nobody can get close to them.”

Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom country house built in the early 1800s, entered the royals’ extensive property portfolio when it was bought in 1898 by Queen Victoria’s son, who would later become King Edward VII.

The prince and princess of Wales’ main home is Forest Lodge in Windsor, a small town around 30 miles west of London. The couple said they moved there for a “fresh start” in 2025 after the death of the late queen and Kate’s cancer diagnosis.

There have been several previous high profile security breaches involving the royal family.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. King Charles and Queen Camilla weren’t at the property at the time.

But perhaps the most famous break in came in 1982, when a man called Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the queen’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes talking with the intruder before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.

The latest incursion came days before the release of a new documentary about Kate’s cancer diagnosis and remission, called “Heal.”

Set to air on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on Peacock from Dec. 1., the highly personal film will see her share her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

“It changes your body, it changes you physically, but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you,” Kate says in a clip released ahead of Sunday’s air date

“It is often through pain that we realize there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that,” she adds.

World.title: Fort Hood mass shooter makes legal move to stop Pentagon’s firing squad execution
World.content:
The former Army officer whose scheduled military execution by firing squad provoked outrage over an initial proposal to livestream his death is planning to file a constitutional challenge that could halt his December execution, his lawyers said Tuesday.

Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that claimed 13 lives, filed a motion for a stay of execution so he can submit what’s known as a habeas corpus petition, which requires the government to justify a person’s detainment.

“There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss,” Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. “But the gravity of that loss does not change the government’s obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system. Mr. Hasan, like every person facing an irreversible punishment, must have a chance to pursue federal review of his case.”

Hasan, 56, had officially exhausted his military justice appeals, opening the door to President Donald Trump in October approving his death sentence and the Army setting an execution date.

Hasan’s request was filed in civilian court, which is another process available to military prisoners. Military experts told NBC News the legal maneuver to file a habeas corpus petition would all but assure Hasan’s case will be tied up in a lengthy review process that could effectively stall his pending execution to well beyond the end of Trump’s term. At that point, they say, Trump’s successor may avoid setting another execution date.

The motion was filed on behalf of Hasan by the ACLU of Kansas. Pentagon and Army officials could not immediately be reached for comment.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth first raised the prospect of livestreaming Hasan’s execution, telling a conservative news outlet that he would ensure “people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

But John Baker, the federal public defender for the Western District of North Carolina whose capital habeas unit is assisting Hasan, said the case deserves further review by a federal court.

“The President, the Secretary of Defense, and others have turned Mr. Hasan’s case into a political spectacle,” Baker said in a statement. “Our government cannot be permitted to execute Mr. Hasan until his death sentence has received full and fair review, which the Constitution safeguards through our federal courts.”

Mourners at a memorial service for the thirteen victims of the shooting rampage at Fort Hood in 2009. Joe Raedle / Getty

Few details were made available about how a firing squad execution could unfold, although Army officials said it would occur at 1 p.m. Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — around the time the attack occurred at the military base. During the shooting, Hasan was injured by responding officers and paralyzed and now requires a wheelchair.

Within days of Hegseth’s announcement, Trump said he would ultimately decide whether Hasan’s death could potentially be watched by millions of people online. He subsequently said in a Truth Social post that while livestreaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent,” there are other people who “would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad,” the president said, “but this event will not be streamed.”

Hegseth’s announcement had set off immediate backlash from a bipartisan group of lawmakers, human rights organizations and religious leaders, many of whom said a livestreamed execution would be “medieval” and “barbaric,” echoing public killings conducted by the most brutal totalitarian regimes and terror states and harkening back to the nation’s dark period of public lynchings and racism.

In the U.S., the last large-scale gathering for a lawfully public execution occurred in 1936 in Kentucky, where a Black man convicted of raping a white woman was hanged in front of thousands, according to news reports.

Opponents of livestreaming Hasan’s execution also warned it could be used as propaganda by jihadist militants, while playing into the desires of Hasan, an American-born Muslim who had become radicalized.

“I’m paraplegic and could be in jail for the rest of my life,” Hasan told a mental health panel following the shooting spree. “However, if I died by lethal injection, I would still be a martyr.”

The U.S. military has not put a service member to death by firing squad since 1945 and last executed a service member in 1961, by hanging. Both were conducted privately.

Currently, four people, including Hasan, are on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

World.title: Black Friday deals are already here, and I’m tracking the best ones live: Walmart, Apple, PlayStation and more

Black Friday 2026 is only three days away, but brands aren’t waiting to offer deals, so you shouldn’t wait to shop. In fact, the longer you do, the more likely it is for something on your wish list to sell out. Start browsing sales at Amazon, Walmart, Home Depot, Apple, PlayStation, Alo, Hoka, Nintendo and more as soon as possible — at this point, you can be pretty confident that live discounts are as good as they’re going to get.

I’ve covered major sales events as a reporter and on-air correspondent for NBC Selected since 2020. I’ve been tracking prices for weeks and combing through thousands of discounts to find the best Black Friday deals actually worth buying. Each one I recommend below is highly rated and 20 percent off or more. When possible, I also ran deals through price trackers like CamelCamelCamel to make sure they’re at their lowest price in at least three months — I even found seven that are currently at their lowest price ever. I’m updating this live today, November 24, with my expert-approved picks, so save this link and check back in often.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

Best Black Friday Deals Overall

Hoka’s Arahi sneakers are one of our favorite pairs, and since the brand recently released the ninth edition, the previous one is currently on sale. Hoka made minimal changes between the models, so it’s worth buying the Arahi 8 if you need a solid walking or running shoe. It has a built-in stability system that helps prevent overpronation, and a moderate layer of soft cushioning to absorb shock and keep your feet comfortable. The sneakers come in regular and wide styles, and men’s and women’s sizes.

The most life-changing product I’ve used in 2026 is a robot vacuum and mop like this one. It picks up dirt, hair and crumbs while scrubbing floors to leave them sparkling — and the best part is that you don’t have to lift a finger. When the robot is done cleaning, it returns to its charging base and empties itself into the dustbag. It maps your home to detect where carpets, hard floors and obstacles are, and connects to an app that lets you set schedules and routines, as well as adjust settings.

Batteries are an essential you always need to have at home, so you may as well buy them on sale, especially before the holidays — in my family, they’re always in high demand to power remotes, lights and toys. This pack comes with 48 total: 24 AA and 24 AAA. The batteries hold their power for up to 10 years in storage and they’re leak-resistant for up to two years, according to the brand.

You can use Audible through the app on your mobile device or tablet, online through your computer or through your Kindle e-reader.

World.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. and arrives in Spain
World.content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, left the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, his team and the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.

Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid early Wednesday morning, alongside his wife, an American citizen, and his lawyer, a representative for the family told CBS News.

CBS News was first to report Abrego Garcia's plans earlier Tuesday.

Abrego Garcia, whose case became an early flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration's deportation crackdown, was flying to Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday night, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity to talk about an arrangement that has not been disclosed publicly.

The exact nature of his arrangements and the conditions of his departure from the U.S. were not immediately clear. The federal judge in Maryland overseeing his civil legal case issued an order Friday that remains sealed.

In a statement, Abrego Garcia said he's leaving the U.S. "happy" and "with his freedom."

"In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible," Abrego Garcia said.

Abrego Garcia traveled out of the U.S. with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez, his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg and representatives from We Are CASA, the U.S. advocacy group that has been helping him and his family.

Trump administration officials touted Abrego Garcia's departure.

"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said. He reiterated the Trump administration's allegation that Abrego Garcia belongs to a gang — which his legal team has denied — and said he now "cannot terrorize innocent Americans."

In a social media post late Tuesday night, the Department of Homeland Security wrote: "To be clear: Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives. He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States."

The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country's CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the United States last year to face criminal charges.

Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal.

But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, DHS said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa.

Abrego Garcia's departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly cancelled. The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued.

But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis' orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia's "prompt removal." The Justice Department said in March that the government was "ready, willing, and able" to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa.

Abrego Garcia's case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an "error." Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT.

But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs.

In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.

The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and in May, a federal judge in Tennessee dismissed the criminal charges on the grounds that his prosecution was vindictive.

The Justice Department has appealed that decision, and arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit are scheduled for February.

World.title: Leaked data shows 490,000 Russian forces have died in Ukraine war
World.content:
More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News. Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.

A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.

The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000.

In May, the head of the United Kingdom's communications and cyber spy agency also put the number of Russian military deaths during the war at about 500,000, citing Western intelligence.

"Putin is going backwards on the battlefield, with new intelligence showing that almost half a million Russian soldiers have been killed since the conflict began," Anne Keast-Butler, the director of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), said at the time.

Soldiers carry the coffin of 20-year-old Russian serviceman Nikita Avrov during his funeral at a church in Luga, south of St. Petersburg, April 11, 2022, after his death during the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine. AFP/Getty

The Kremlin has not publicly revealed the Russian death toll from the war. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said for the first time in February that his country's losses stood at 55,000. That figure has not been independently corroborated, however, and the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank estimated as many as 150,000 Ukrainian fatalities up to June 2026.

The BBC also reported that the leaked data shows 65% of 18- to 24-year-olds in Russia who died in 2025 were casualties of the war. For Russians aged 25-34 last year, the number was 59%, making the war the main cause of death for young Russian adults last year, according to the data.

When asked about the various reports surfacing from the data leak, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday: "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the Defense Ministry of the Russian Federation."

"I suggest not to pay attention to any other data," he said.

World.title: Trump owned millions in Nvidia stock as he pressed for Jensen Huang's reinstatement
World.content:
President Trump holds tens of millions of Nvidia shares, giving him a personal stake in the company's stock market roller coaster ride over the past two weeks, financial disclosure documents show.

Mr. Trump stood to lose large sums with CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt departure, and stood to profit handsomely after he successfully pressed the chip developer's board to reinstate Huang. Nvidia stock surged more than 30% when Huang returned to the company on Monday, reversing a weekslong slide.

Huang resigned two weeks ago over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China, and another alleged affair with a subordinate. Mr. Trump said Monday he personally spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced them" to rehire Huang, offering an "assurance" that there was no national security threat.

Mr. Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock in his investment accounts as of the end of 2025, according to financial disclosures filed with the Office of Government Ethics. He bought or sold the company's stock in more than 100 transactions that were worth between $27 million and nearly $98 million between January 2025 and September 2026.

The value of the president's Nvidia shares increased anywhere from $1.3 million to $14.8 million on Monday, before paring back some of those gains when Nvidia's share price ticked down Tuesday. The range is so large because it isn't clear how many shares of Nvidia the president currently owns, but it can be roughly estimated based on his sales and purchases this year.

"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions," a White House spokesman told CBS News Tuesday, adding that his investments mirror indexes like the Schwab 1000. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."

In addition to the president, several of his appointees to positions in the State, Commerce and Treasury departments as well as the IRS reported millions in Nvidia stock in their investment portfolios. Many have since sold their holdings.

Forbes estimates Mr. Trump's net worth at more than $6 billion, making Nvidia a small part of his total wealth. And Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable public companies, at more than $3.7 trillion, so many investors hold shares in the tech giant.

Still, some ethics experts questioned Mr. Trump's large stake in Nvidia, especially after he intervened to boost the company's fortunes.

"This goes beyond a conflict of interest," said Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "He is squarely, explicitly using his power as president to benefit himself financially. He has prioritized his finances over the security of the nation."

Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit government watchdog, told CBS News that Mr. Trump's "continued ownership of stock in this company is the clearest example of how the president's personal financial interest makes everything he does suspect."

Mr. Trump's personal investments have drawn controversy in the past, including his stakes in publicly traded energy companies, firms that have business with the government and his family's cryptocurrency firm. He has denied any conflict of interest.

Some critics called for legal reforms to prohibit the president and members of Congress from buying and selling stocks while they hold office. Elected officials are generally allowed to trade individual stocks, though lawmakers from both parties have called for the practice to be banned.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and former chief ethics attorney for the White House between 2005 and 2007, said he has long argued for changes to the federal conflict of interest law that prohibits government employees from participating in matters that result in their personal enrichment while in office. That current law does not apply to the president, vice president or members of Congress, he said.

"We need a prohibition on this right away," he said, adding that the new Congress may take up the cause in January.

Painter called Mr. Trump's intervention with the Nvidia board "a huge conflict of interest" and overreach of government power.

"It's not the job of the government to call up and say who the CEO of a company should be," he told CBS News.

The president has defended his decision to intervene, saying on CNBC that "we have to protect our geniuses" and arguing that Nvidia — as the world's leading designer of advanced chips — plays a key role in maintaining the U.S.' lead over China in AI technology.

Mr. Trump has also frequently pointed to the performance of the stock market as a barometer of his success as president. Shortly after Huang was reinstated, Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal the "response from the market has been very positive," and "that really shows the decision was right."

Beyond Mr. Trump, numerous political appointees held Nvidia stock. Some divested themselves of their holdings after they were appointed to government positions, federal filings show.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin owned between $250,000 and $500,000 in Nvidia stock in March 2026, and sold $500,000 to $1 million in shares of the tech company in June of this year, his financial disclosures show.

"As Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin acts to ensure full compliance with all ethics and conflict of interest rules," said a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

In the Commerce Department, where Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing scrutiny over whether he has done enough to crack down on highly sensitive AI chip sales to China, a number of senior advisers last year reported selling large positions in Nvidia.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm that was previously run by Lutnick and is now controlled by his sons, reported holding roughly 1 million shares of Nvidia for its clients as of Sept. 30, worth around $228 million at the time. Those shares were worth just over $150 million at Tuesday's price. None of Lutnick's personal financial disclosures filed by the federal government mention Nvidia holdings or transactions.

In the State Department, some of Mr. Trump's diplomatic appointees had Nvidia holdings.

Charles Kushner, the U.S. ambassador to France and father of Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, reported Nvidia holdings totaling between $1.5 million and $6 million, according to public disclosures filed January 2025.

U.S. Ambassador to Costa Rica Melinda Hildebrand reported Nvidia holdings between $5 million and $25 million, her April 2025 disclosures show. The Texas billionaire, who was a major Trump campaign fundraiser, sold the stock in November of that same year, filings show.

Warren Stephens, another major Trump donor and ambassador to the United Kingdom, reported Nvidia holdings between $750,000 and $1.5 million, according to his January 2025 disclosures. He sold those shares in July and August 2025, a few months after he was sworn in as ambassador.

In the Treasury Department, Under Secretary for International Affairs Erin Browne held Nvidia shares totaling between $250,000 and $500,000, her disclosures from January show. Browne sold the stock before her confirmation in August of this year, filings show.

Todd Newnam, who was appointed chief financial officer of the IRS in January, holds between $115,000 and $250,000 in Nvidia stock, according to his financial disclosure, filed in April of last year. Newnam, a former CEO of a tech company, was part of the Department of Government Efficiency team that sought to streamline government spending and cut the federal workforce.

"All OGE (Office of Government Ethics) 278 filers are required to disclose any equity positions they hold and are advised of their recusal obligations in accordance with the ethics rules," an IRS spokesperson said Tuesday, referring to the financial disclosure required by members of the executive branch of the federal government.

Many other officials could be indirectly exposed to Nvidia stock if they invested in mutual funds or similar assets. For example, Vice President JD Vance reported $1 million to $5 million in a fund that tracks the S&P 500 — and Nvidia is one of that index's largest components.

World.title: Security forces storm scene, end Colombia supermarket siege
World.content:
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held hostage had been rescued and one captor killed.

Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to have been held by armed men.

"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a video posted on social media.

A Colombian Army soldier is seen in the Exito Supermarket after security forces stormed the building to free hostages held by gunmen in Cartagena, Colombia, in the early hours of Nov. 25, 2026. AFP via Getty Images

Shortly after midnight, a police helicopter hovered low over the shopping center as security forces massed outside the supermarket, AFP reporters saw.

Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.

Ten of the roughly 30 people initially held had been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.

Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Exito supermarket as security forces secured the building.

De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and a sidearm while brandishing a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a roaring success.

"We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively," he said, lauding the operation as "absolutely flawless."

The president said one hostage-taker had been killed.

Cartagena's mayor said all the hostages were "safe and sound" and would reunite with their families before undergoing medical checks.

Hostage takers were "caught off guard"

The siege gripped Cartagena, one of Colombia's main tourist draws — a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship visits.

Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.

"My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told AFP earlier in the standoff. "He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.

Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared on social media appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear carrying long guns alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.

Police officers at the entrance to a supermarket where a hostage-taking incident was in progress in Colombia's northern city of Cartagena on Nov. 24, 2026. Xinhua via Getty Images

De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups.

"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping -- no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.

Authorities said the siege began after an attempted armored vehicle robbery at the shopping center.

According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly $2 million, two armored vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles northeast of Cartagena.

AFP couldn't independently verify those reports.

The Rafael Nunez airport in Cartagena resumed landings after a brief suspension of about 45 minutes so the armed forces could use one of its runways in connection with the incident. the Reuters news agency reported.

The siege unfolded on the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas and a series of attacks across the country.

Despite the deal that ended the region's largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organizations still fight for control of parts of the country.

Late Monday, authorities blamed a dissident FARC faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

Separately, the presidency said a "terrorist attack" on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several southwestern departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

World.title: NATO allies anxious as war spreads beyond Ukraine, Russia borders
World.content:
Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.

Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.

Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning."

"I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."

A "need for stability in our near areas"

Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.

A photo provided by the Finnish Border Guard shows efforts to extinguish a fire on board the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, Nov. 22, 2026. The ship, under U.S. sanctions for transporting illicit weapons, was attacked by Ukraine using sea drones. Finnish Border Guard/Handout/Reuters

The Sparta II cargo vessel, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, has been under U.S. sanctions since 2022 for illicit transportation of military hardware. Russian authorities confirmed that it had been towed back to a Russian port on Tuesday.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani spoke Tuesday with his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiha, meanwhile, in a phone call to express Italy's concern over another Ukrainian attack carried out over the weekend, this one off the coast of Libya.

Zelenskyy lauded Ukrainian forces on Monday for that attack, which sank a Russian warship and damaged another U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, the MV Angara, off the North African nation's Mediterranean coast, where Russia has a naval base.

"The minister emphasized to his Ukrainian counterpart how crucial it is for Italy to keep working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading into the Mediterranean," Italy's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday in a readout of the ministers' call.

A screengrab from video obtained by Reuters shows the sanctioned Russian cargo ship MV Angara being struck by Ukrainian sea drones off Libya, Nov. 22, 2026. Volodymyr Zelenskyy via Telegram/Reuters

Zelenskyy framed the strikes on the Russian ships as legitimate defensive actions in response to Russia's ongoing deadly missile and drone strikes, which it launches from land, sea and air.

"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."

The Russian Foreign Ministry this week accused Estonia, another NATO ally, of being "on the verge of triggering open war" after the small Baltic country announced it would close its land border with Russia starting Dec. 1.

Estonia accused Russian intelligence agencies last week of a plot to infiltrate and sabotage the domestic defense company Threod Systems.

"Any attempt to threaten Estonia's security, sow fear, or act hostilely against us will be met with a decisive response," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement last week. "By closing the border crossings, we are sending a clear message to the Kremlin: Russia's hostile actions come at a cost. The more aggressively Russia behaves, the narrower its room for manoeuvre becomes."

The Estonian move came only a couple of weeks after Poland's prime minister said a large-scale security operation launched along the Polish-Russian border may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation by Russian operatives.

"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do"

While NATO members' concern over the spread of the war has been more clearly iterated in recent weeks, Ben Hodges, a former top commander of the U.S. Army in Europe, told CBS News on Tuesday that, in his opinion, all of Ukraine's actions constitute a legitimate defense in the face of Russia's aggression.

"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do to disrupt Russian oil/gas exports and other international activities to degrade Russia's ability to sustain its war effort," Hodges said. "This is also an important signal to anyone who would willingly support Russia's shadow fleet."

Moscow uses its so-called shadow fleet — hundreds of dubiously registered tankers — to evade international sanctions on its oil sales, keeping money flowing in to power its war machine.

Hodges told CBS News that Kyiv has likely calculated the risks involved in attacking Russian vessels in neutral waters.

"The risk is that Russia will attempt to use these as an excuse for its attacks against the Ukrainian economy and civilian infrastructure," he told CBS News. "But Ukraine knows this and anticipates it."

"Most European countries also already understand this and will not be moved by it," he added.

CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean said, meanwhile, that Ukraine's "successful effort to expand the map of its war with Russia is bound to cause tension with partners, both in Washington and in NATO countries who feel their security is threatened by Ukranian operations near their territory. But Ukraine can no longer rely on Washington's support, which negates the leverage Washington once had over Kyiv's decision-making."

While European support for Kyiv is "more robust," MacLean added, "the Ukrainians — with some justice — feel as though they are fighting a war on behalf of many of NATO's eastern members, and so feel like they have some running room to impose pain on Russia, even in ways that its NATO partners might sometimes find uncomfortable."

World.title: Prince William and Kate's country home broken into, 2 arrested
World.content:
Two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of William and Catherine, the Prince and Princess of Wales, U.K. police said.

Police responded to reports of "suspicious activity" at Anmer Hall on King Charles III's Sandringham estate in eastern England Monday at about 6 p.m., Norfolk police said. William and Catherine and the rest of their family weren't present at the time, the police said.

The police said Wednesday that Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They were due in court later Wednesday.

]Police dogs, drones and a helicopter were used to search the property and make the arrests, officials said.

Kensington Palace told CBS News it wouldn't comment on security matters.

Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from Queen Elizabeth II. It is used as a country residence on weekends. William and his family spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, which they have described as their "forever home."

The reported break-in came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street.

Catherine recently opened up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

"Heal" follows the 44-year-old royal as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

World.title: Army to detonate unstable lead explosives at Iowa plant today
World.content:
The U.S. Army is set to detonate a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning, following community outcry and a legal fight that delayed the operation by several days.

Five tons of unstable explosive material, containing the highly sensitive compound lead azide, will be blown up in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 9 a.m. local time. Middletown is a small community of about 350 people, located four hours west of Chicago by car.

The plant houses about 68 barrels or roughly 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the explosives degraded over about 20 years in storage, giving way to a process called recrystallization that made the material more susceptible to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.

Barrels that contain lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. U.S. Army

The Army has pushed to carry out the controlled detonation because of the public safety risks associated with the cache possibly blowing up on its own. But environmental groups and local residents attempted to block its plans, fearing the health and agricultural consequences of a toxic plume of lead dust that could disperse across the region after the blast.

The plume was expected to spread over parts of southeastern Iowa and northeastern Missouri, potentially threatening homes, playgrounds, farmlands and other spaces. Maps released Tuesday by the Army noted that the dust cloud could travel as far as 100 miles, but the most potent effects would likely be felt within 30 square miles of the munitions plant.

Legal challenge questioned detonation

The detonation was postponed last week after environmental groups filed a lawsuit challenging the emergency permit the EPA had granted the Army to authorize it. The groups argued the agency had not provided residents of the area with adequate notice of its plans or evidence showing the detonation was the best course of action from a health and safety perspective.

But the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals' initial ruling blocking the detonation was lifted Monday. The court acknowledged "the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation," but ultimately found the risk of an uncontrolled explosion more harmful.

The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 23, 2026. AP Photo/Laura Bargfeld

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said at a Tuesday news conference that plans would move forward as falling temperatures caused the explosives to become more and more volatile, increasing the chances of a spontaneous explosion. Telle said the weather forecast Wednesday is "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."

President Trump had said earlier this week that the Army would not move ahead with the detonation without the court's affirmative ruling and the approval of Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. However, Sand was not required to weigh in and hasn't officially taken office.

World.title: Paperwork, not work, causing enrollees to lose Medicaid in Nebraska
World.content:
When Nebraska chose to implement Medicaid work requirements eight months before it was called for under President Trump's sweeping 2025 budget law, many health policy analysts panned the decision. They worried people would lose coverage because of system glitches.

Many also watched the Cornhusker State's experience to see whether it would offer lessons to the more than three dozen other states that would follow it in 2027.

On Nov. 13, the Trump administration gave states the option of taking extra time to get ready.

They'll have until July 2027, rather than January, to begin dropping coverage for people who don't meet the work requirements. States have until Dec. 11 to decide whether they will still fully implement the requirements on Jan. 1 and begin dropping those who don't comply or start refusing new coverage to people who aren't working.

Congressional Democrats, who often criticized Medicaid work requirements on the campaign trail and have sided with states in urging a reprieve from the January deadline, claimed victory.

"The Trump-Vance Administration finally admitted what Democrats have said from the very beginning: Republicans' chaotic maze of red tape requirements jeopardize the health care of millions of Americans," Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) said in a statement.

Democrats' massive election victories in November will give them control of both chambers of Congress next year. Top Democrats said they'll prioritize legislation to stop the Medicaid work requirements before they're fully enforced.

The basics

Not everyone in Medicaid must comply with the new requirements. They will apply only to low-income adults who were made eligible for the program in 43 states, along with Washington, D.C., that chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act or through a special waiver from the federal government. Most enrollees are already working, surveys show, so to comply, they will only have to provide proof of their employment to their states.

But that may not be as simple as it sounds, depending on how well states notify Medicaid beneficiaries of the requirement and how easy they make it to submit paperwork. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the new rules would increase the number of uninsured U.S. adults by 5.3 million by 2034.

The rules require work, volunteering, or school attendance for at least 80 hours a month. There are several exemptions, including for people who care for young children or those with disabling medical conditions, a category called "medically frail."

It all adds up to about 20 million people subject to work Medicaid requirements, including about 70,000 in Nebraska.

On May 1, Nebraska became the first state to implement the work requirements. After it began dropping people from coverage in August, 7% of Nebraska Medicaid enrollees who were subject to the requirements when renewing their coverage, or 533 adults, were disenrolled because of the new rules, according to the latest state data.

Nebraska's Medicaid agency was able to verify that 8 in 10 enrollees met the new rules using various state and federal databases. Those people didn't have to deal with requests for more information, interim state Medicaid director Jeremy Brunssen told KFF Health News.

About 14% of new Medicaid applicants subject to the new rules, or 557 people, had been denied because of the work requirements since they were implemented.

But the state data also shows some troubling issues.

For example, 92% of cases in which existing enrollees lost coverage were due to procedural or paperwork issues rather than state determinations that they did not meet the new work rules.

Brunssen attributes that high percentage to the state having to verify the numerous ways people can meet the new requirements or exemptions. "It's not as simple as typical eligibility enrollment that you can meet via income and household size," he said.

Many enrollees lost coverage because they did not respond to the state's outreach. Those enrollees may have deemed themselves ineligible or were unsure how to respond, Brunssen said.

The rate of procedural denials is much higher than in prior years, according to data analyzed by KFF. Critics fear it means people who may still qualify are losing coverage.

"This is definitely a red-flag warning," said Amy Behnke, CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska, a trade group representing federally funded community health centers. "The high proportion of procedural denials is troubling."

Navigating the new requirements

Cheri Stollar, 48, of Lincoln, Nebraska, received her Medicaid renewal notice in the mail in early November and was confused about which documents to submit to the state to prove she works as a mental health therapist. She also didn't understand why she had less than a week to respond. She said she tried to call the state Medicaid agency but could not get through. Her renewal has since been completed.

"I want to make sure I send in everything they need," said Stollar, who lives in a three-bedroom mobile home with three of her four children. She has been on Medicaid for two years and credits the coverage for enabling her to afford medications for depression, sleep, and an ulcer.

She said the new law will make it harder for people like her to get and stay covered, which will make it harder to stay healthy — and get and keep a job.

Behnke said enrollees calling the state Medicaid agency for help have been put on hold for up to two hours. The assistance line operates only on weekdays, during daytime hours, making it difficult for people who work to call. State Medicaid officials say they are working to add more staff to reduce wait times.

One challenge in evaluating Nebraska's implementation is that the state, as of mid-November, had released data only through August.

State officials said this summer that they would post an online dashboard with various performance metrics to improve public transparency. That hasn't happened yet.

"We have seen a lot of negative effects so far," said Sarah Maresh, program director at Nebraska Appleseed, a nonprofit social justice advocacy group. "Every person that goes without coverage is a problem."

She worries that people are being deterred from applying to Medicaid because of the policy.

Brunssen, the interim Medicaid director, defended his state's performance.

"We are experiencing what we expected," he said in an October interview at a National Association of Medicaid Directors conference in Maryland. "The vast majority of people newly applying, or for those going through redetermination, are getting coverage or retaining coverage."

Yet, Brunssen noted, it's still early. Fewer than 25% of Medicaid enrollees subject to the work requirement have had to prove they meet the new rules to retain coverage. The rest won't be completed until next summer, he said.

The state's Department of Health and Human Services, which operates its Medicaid program, has used various methods to inform enrollees about the new rules, such as letters, emails, texts, and messages in an online portal, Brunssen said.

"Most Medicaid enrollees know about the new rules," he said, attributing awareness to community partners and managed-care companies that helped get the word out.

"I feel like we've done everything in our power to communicate what was coming," he said.

Brunssen noted the state has taken advantage of a federal option to let enrollees self-attest that they meet exemptions. All declarations must be truthful, or enrollees could face perjury charges.

Self-attestation is as easy as checking a box on an online form. No supporting documents are required. That's made it easier for people to comply, Brunssen said.

The state has also exempted people living in three counties with high unemployment rates and in two counties declared federal disaster areas because of weather events, he said.

"Our goal is to make sure people who are eligible get or retain coverage," Brunssen said.

Some enrollees say the state could do more to make the process easier.

Chalandria James, 37, of Omaha was worried about whether she still had Medicaid coverage after she tried to renew in July but did not hear back from the state, despite repeated calls. Unsure of her coverage status, she canceled a doctor's appointment to check her blood pressure. It took until September, and a multi-hour visit to the state agency office, for her to find out she still had Medicaid and was exempt from the work requirement because she had a child under 14 years old.

"It was nerve-racking not knowing," said James, a community health worker and doula.

In Nebraska, about 37% of enrollees met the work requirement while 61% qualified for an exemption — with the most common reasons being medical frailty or caregiving.

Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families, said Nebraska's experience shows the work rules do little to promote work, since most who can are already working. "This policy punishes low-income people by subjecting them to serious, often insurmountable, hurdles," she said.

Even with data showing the large majority of enrollees working or meeting an exemption, Brunssen said the new requirements still are a good idea. "Part of being a good, healthy person does involve engagement with the community," he said, "and we think there is value in the work we are doing in this space."

Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? Click here to contact KFF Health News.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
World.content:
Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor

Emily Feng/NPR

As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.

Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.

Sponsor Message

A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.

World.title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
World.content:
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap

toggle caption i ㅤ/J Studios/Getty Images

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. 

Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?

Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.

Sponsor Message

That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.

To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?

Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.

If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.

There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.

What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?

New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.

Sponsor Message

But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.

These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?

Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions. These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.

For example, at the checkout page of a website or an app, there might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.

The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.

toggle caption i J Studios/Getty Images

What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?

Expand what I call "the new-thing gap." That's the time and distance between you encountering a new thing and you acquiring it.

If you've got one-click checkout with a certain company, maybe delete the app from your phone or remove your credit card information from that app.

Another easy tactic is to drop something in your cart and leave it there for 24 hours. Researchers have found that when you delay a purchase, interest in that thing will start to decline.

What happens when you use all these tactics and still feel like buying something new?

The main thing is to make intentional choices. The goal here is not to say no to all new things.

Now that I know my brain is programmed to find new things, I bring my attention to that whenever I feel drawn to something new. Is this something I want, or am I being influenced?

You can get really good at saying no to the wrong type of new things, better at saying yes to the right type of new things.

You say because we're programmed to want new things, we can be quick to set old things aside. So is it possible to get joy from old things?

Research has found that if we force ourselves to revisit old things, we may find there's untapped enjoyment in those old things.

Sponsor Message

In one study, researchers had people go through a museum exhibit. At the end, they asked participants how much they thought they would enjoy going through the exhibit again. People predicted they would get less enjoyment from the repeated experience.
