But when the researchers forced them to go through it again, the participants said, "Actually, we enjoyed that just as much, if not more, the second time." They discovered details they missed the first time around or just liked seeing everything again.

How do we apply this lesson in our own life?

Reexperience old things. Books, movies, board games, your neighborhood. Go to that restaurant down the street that you love. Travel to that city that you've been to before.

What's great is you can relieve yourself of this obligation to always be spending money, time and attention on new things. You can fight against this bias that we have for novel experiences and find there's joy and excitement hiding in plain sight.

World.title: A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years
World.content:
A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

The Ariston Cafe along Route 66 in Litchfield, Ill., has been a favorite for more than 90 years. Just past the front door, underneath the vintage neon signs that read "Ariston" and "Budweiser," is a diner staple: a glass case, full of sweet temptations. It took one of the Ariston's owners, Will Law, nearly a full minute to reel off all 12 of the day's choices.

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

"There's a peach crisp bread pudding with the vanilla bourbon sauce," he said. "Then, of course, a traditional cheesecake with or without cherries, and we have a chocolate delight, a lemon delight, a coconut delight."

Sponsor Message

They were all delightful to look at and the kind of classic American comfort desserts that you might crave while you're road-tripping on America's most famous highway. All of them — like everything else served at the Ariston — are still made in-house.

Litchfield isn't the most natural stop on Route 66; it's a sleepy town about an hour outside St. Louis. But the Ariston Cafe, which sits just across the road from the charming Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center, has become an institution in its own right with its wooden chairs and cozy decor.

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

Travelers still flock to the Ariston, thanks to the internet and social media. The waitstaff says many visitors come in already knowing exactly what they intend to order based on what they've read and seen online.

Right by the front door there's a guest book for diners next to a basket of reading glasses to make reading and signing easier. Within just a few days, the Ariston has welcomed patrons from Australia, South Korea, Nicaragua and Germany, among other nations. And they come from all over the U.S. too.

Bob Dickson celebrated his 75th birthday with his wife, Ann, by traveling Route 66.

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

"I said to her, 'I would love to go out west to Los Angeles and bring Highway 66 all the way back to where we live,'" he said. "So we did that. We took 31 days, stopped every place you can imagine on and off the highway. We had a great time, an absolutely great time talking to people and just seeing the sights."

Sponsor Message

On this day's visit, they are just a couple of hours away from their home in Quincy, Ill., and they've stopped for a last celebratory lunch on their big trip. The menu offers so many choices, from patty melts to turkey clubs to pork chops and stuffed shrimp. They said this restaurant, with its throwback vibes and sprawling menu, encapsulates the spirit of their whole road trip.

"It was really adventurous and old fashioned and very joyful," Ann Dickson said.

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

Opinions run hot about what exactly is the oldest eatery along Route 66, but the Ariston Cafe claims to be the oldest continually operating restaurant on the highway.

Nick Adam is one of the Ariston's former owners. His father, Pete, founded it as a candy shop in 1924. Adam says his father was very young when he arrived in this country.

"He left when he was 10 to come to the United States," Adam explained. "He went back to Greece when he was 12, and then he came back to this country."

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

Pete Adam seems to have had big ambitions even back then: The shop's name, Ariston, means "the best" in Greek. In 1935, he moved it to its present location on Route 66. Then Nick and his wife, Demi, ran the restaurant for decades.

From first dates to engagements, Demi Adam said the Ariston Cafe has been a fundamental part of this community for decades.

"To be honest," she said, "there's nothing else like this around."

Eight years ago, when the Adams were ready to retire, they sold the restaurant to Will Law and his partners. Law said the Ariston's position as a place locals and visitors alike choose for the big moments in their lives remains unchanged.

toggle caption i Neeta Satam for NPR

"I can't tell you how many wedding proposals have happened in those booths," he said. "We have a couple from Iowa that will come back every year for their anniversary just to have dinner. I see a 50th anniversary at least once a week, if not 60, 65. How cool is that? And they want to share that with you."

Sponsor Message

In 2006, the Ariston Cafe was put on the National Register of Historic Places. It's another lasting reminder of what this restaurant that steps back in time can mean to visitors in the present.

World.title: In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
World.content:
In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis

toggle caption i Haven Daley/AP

This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.

But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.

Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.

In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.

Sponsor Message

Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.

As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.

A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.

On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.

Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.

"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."

Sponsor Message

The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.

In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.

It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.

"It's forced a race to the bottom," said Beau Whitney, the founder and chief economist at Whitney Economics. "What this is resulting in is great prices for the consumer, they're spending less and getting the same or more, so that's good for them on an affordability perspective. But it's hurting operators."

Though the industry has seen a slight rebound this year — an increase of about 5% in sales for the same period last year, Whitney's team found — forecasts for the end of 2026 and the outlook for 2027 remain relatively modest.

The biggest reason for this, Whitney said, is customer behavior.

Through the beginning of the 2020s, Whitney said, consumers would typically come into a dispensary with a set amount to spend. Their cannabis budget. If they got a discount, Whitney said, they'd add additional products into their carts to hit their budget.

But that began to change in 2024, as inflation rose and the cost of essentials, like gas, ballooned.

"Behavior changed literally overnight," Whitney said. "What they're doing is they're taking the discounts — and there's a lot of them now — and they're using that money to buy gas and buy groceries. So they're adjusting the amount that they purchase based on what's going on in their own personal economy."

Sponsor Message

The discount model, he said, has also forced prices down. With legal retailers competing for a pool of customers that has not seen rapid growth in years, discounts help draw people into stores. But they've also created a culture where customers expect them, several cannabis store owners said.

It's why doing well on a week like this one, as customers flood in for Green Wednesday deals, is essential for shop owners like The Forest's Christina Betancourt Johnson.

On Monday, the Baltimore store was stocked — with edibles and pre-rolls and other cannabis products, but also stacks of snacks for customers waiting in longer-than-usual lines, branded giveaways and samples of gummies to try (no weed in those).

A steady flow of customers wandered in. Some for their usual supplies, others for a little holiday shopping.

Employee Thomas Bourne loaded a vape into a paper bag for one of the dispensary's regular customers. That seemed a little light for the holiday, he observed, teasingly.

"Gotta come back for your cousin walk essentials, man," Bourne said. "'Tis the week."

The customer smiled, nodding. He'd be back.

World.title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
World.content:
China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining

toggle caption i Ng Han Guan/AP

BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.

The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.

Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.

A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.

Sponsor Message

The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.

"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."

The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.

"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."

Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.

Sponsor Message

The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.

Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

World.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. voluntarily for Spain
World.content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. voluntarily for Spain

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant who became a symbol of the pitfalls of President Trump's mass deportation campaign, has voluntarily left the U.S. after a legal battle that spanned nearly two years.

Abrego Garcia, who was arrested in 2025, mistakenly deported to El Salvador, and then brought back to the U.S., left for Spain on Tuesday, according to his lawyers and Trump administration officials.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, said he "left the United States a free man."

"The government wanted to deport him in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia. Instead, he departed on a commercial aircraft, to a country that he chose, and able to move freely around the world," Sandoval-Moshenberg told NPR.

Sponsor Message

He called the move "a temporary departure" and said that Abrego Garcia - who has a wife and a child, both of whom are U.S. citizens - has many options to return to the U.S.

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," he added.

Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia will choose where "to settle in the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration."

Another lawyer for Abrego Garcia, Sean Hecker, confirmed Spain as his destination.

U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who played a leading role in championing Abrego Garcia's case, released a statement saying he "is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man, unharmed and with dignity."

Trump administration hails Abrego Garcia's 'self-deportation'

Abrego Garcia's case became a flashpoint for Trump's mass deportation campaign. It raised serious questions about due process, third country deportations and to what extent this administration is sending people to countries where they may face threats.

Before Tuesday's move, Abrego Garcia and the Trump administration had been at an impasse about where he should go.

Sponsor Message

Abrego Garcia said he'd be willing to move to Costa Rica if the government allowed it. According to his attorneys, Costa Rica offered him refugee status. But the administration did not support that plan and instead sought to deport him to Liberia. That attempt was ultimately blocked by the courts.

The Trump administration hailed Abrego Garcia's departure late Tuesday.

"We are DELIGHTED to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Department of Homeland Security wrote on X. He accused Abrego Garcia of being a gang member and a human trafficker, without evidence.

The legal battle

Abrego Garcia has been living in the U.S. for over a decade. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to his home country of El Salvador, after he made the argument that he would be tortured or persecuted there.

In 2025, immigration officers arrested Abrego Garcia and sent him to a notorious Salvadoran prison, where he claimed he suffered from beatings and sleep deprivation.

Later, immigration officials said that Abrego Garcia was deported by mistake, due to an administrative error. He was brought back to the U.S. in June 2025. Upon arriving in the U.S. he was charged with human smuggling. The allegations were based on bodycam footage from 2022, which showed Tennessee police pulling over Abrego Garcia with several other men inside his SUV. Prosecutors claim that Abrego Garcia was a human trafficker, helping immigrants move from Houston to Maryland. He denies the allegations and his lawyers argue that the government's criminal case was retaliation after his wrongful deportation received national attention. A judge in the case ultimately dismissed the charges.

World.title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
World.content:
Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco

toggle caption i Youssef Loulidi/AP

More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.

Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.

Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.

CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.

Sponsor Message

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.

The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."

Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Morocco raises concerns over CAS process

Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.

In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

Sponsor Message

The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.

Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."

CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.

Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.

Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."

Trouble on the field and in the stands

Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.

The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.

Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.

The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.

Sponsor Message

Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.

Soccer's laws versus regulations

Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.

The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.

In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."

The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.

The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.

Soccer fans in Senegal celebrate a win

"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.

Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.

"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.

Sponsor Message

"At the end of the day Morocco and Senegal are brothers," Sidibé added, referring to the countries' long shared close ties built on religion, trade and culture.

Sidi Sylla, a philosophy student at Dakar's main university, said the court's ruling was "not just a win for Senegal but for football in general."

Historic decision

CAS rulings have stripped many athletes of Olympic medals for doping, but it's rare to overturn the result of a major soccer competition.

CAS refused to change the results of the 2019 Asian Cup, dismissing an appeal that the star striker on winning team Qatar shouldn't have been eligible for the tournament.

A lengthy legal battle over the same year's African Champions League final also ended with the original winner, Esperance of Tunisia, taking the title after its opponent Wydad from Morocco refused to play on.

One notable CAS ruling on a team sport title came at the Winter Olympics in 2022. A doping case involving then-15-year-old Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva ended up with her disqualification, and the Russian team being dropped from gold to bronze in the team event.

World.title: These deer walk 300 miles a year. The race is on to save their migration
World.content:
These deer walk 300 miles a year. The race is on to save their migration

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

On a spring morning, a mule deer and her fawn follow a well-worn trail through the Wyoming sagebrush. They're on a 150-mile journey, one of the longest land migrations in the lower 48 states.

Like many other migrations in the U.S., the mule deer's epic journey is hidden in plain sight. Mule deer move in small groups instead of large herds, following pathways likely used for millennia. They're part of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in western Wyoming, a place where elk, deer and pronghorn antelope still have the space to move across vast landscapes.

They migrate with careful seasonal choreography, timed to reach the best feeding grounds in summer and avoid the harshest winter weather. Still, as the climate gets hotter, that timing is being tested.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Droughts are getting more intense in the Western U.S., limiting the food supplies for deer. Their migrations are also being constricted by development, forcing them to navigate a complex maze of fences, roads and subdivisions. Research shows mule deer may be able to adapt to increasingly unpredictable seasons, but development is limiting that ability.

Wyoming is working to keep migration routes from being severed. It's one of the few states that has protected migratory corridors for wildlife, restricting development in the most crucial paths. Landowners and conservation groups are also permanently preserving open lands and working ranches.

The question is whether that work can keep pace with growth. Wyoming's migratory wildlife are on the decline. The state's mule deer population was more than 500,000 in 1990. It's now half of that number .

"The history of wildlife migration is one of loss – we've lost migrations around the world," says Matt Kauffman, wildlife biologist with the U.S. Geological Survey and the University of Wyoming. "We are in this little race to map the migrations and figure out what tools we need to keep those landscapes open, as the American West continues to change."

Loading...

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

On the path of mule deer

In the foothills outside Pinedale, Wyoming, Kauffman and research associate Ashley Townsend make their way through the sagebrush, scanning for a radio signal. They pick one up – a beep, beep, beep – from a mule deer with a tracking collar, which the team put on months earlier.

"This was a fawn, a nine-month-old fawn that we caught on winter range," Kauffman says, scanning the horizon.

This year, Kauffman and his colleagues tracked the spring migrations of about 100 mule deer with GPS collars. It's part of the Wyoming Migration Initiative , a multi-year project run by the University of Wyoming, that has revealed migration routes in unprecedented detail. The deer make far more arduous journeys than once thought, crossing highways, rushing streams and ice-covered lakes. One mule deer set a record, migrating more than 240 miles one way.

Kauffman says for mule deer, the need to migrate is hard-wired. This herd these deer are part of spends summers in the mountains south of Grand Teton National Park, where the food supply is ample. But deep snow in the winter makes it impossible to stay, so the deer migrate south to Wyoming's Red Desert. There, the deer have very little to eat.

Ryan Kellman/NPR

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

"These animals are basically coming out of, if not starving, losing fat all winter," he says. "They come into it with a lot of fat and they're burning those fat stores all through winter. At the end, animals are always in their worst shape."

Sponsor Message

In the spring, the deer set off to find food, but long-distance migration comes with risks, like for the fawn Kauffman has been tracking. The signal from the tracking collar shows it hasn't been moving, a sign that the fawn may have died.

After homing in on the tracking signal for about 10 minutes, the team finds the collar on the ground, next to a few bones left by scavengers.

"She probably started migrating a few weeks ago from the desert, but yeah, she didn't make it," Kauffman says.

Loading...

In years with harsh conditions, thousands of deer can die in Wyoming, which was seen in 2022-23, when a severe winter brought cold temperatures and heavy snowfall. Drought can also take a heavy toll on the population. The best insurance deer have against tough years is to build up fat reserves by eating as much as possible.

"The fatter animals survive the harsh winters better," Kauffman says. "The fatter animals survive the dry summers better. Fat is really the currency of life and of reproduction."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Surfing the green wave

In their quest to bulk up, migration can give deer an edge, because underfoot is the best possible food – the young plants and grasses that emerge after the snow melts.

These tender shoots are protein-rich and have little fiber, so they're easy for deer to digest.

"It's like this sort of spring salad mix," Kauffman says. "We like the spring salad mix because it's nutritious. It's sort of sweet, easy. And that's the same thing that mule deer like."

Loading...

The land begins to green up at lower elevations and, over weeks, spreads to higher elevations where the snow melts later. The deer follow this progression of green closely to eat the best food, what Kauffman says is known as "surfing the green wave."

"I like to say they're choreographing their movements," he says. "If you're ahead of the wave, you move less quickly and let the wave catch you. And if they're behind the wave, they move more quickly to catch it."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Some years, following this spring green-up is trickier for deer. Kauffman says in drought years, the green wave doesn't last as long, or it can be spotty, making it hard to find. Droughts in the Western U.S. are getting more intense as the climate gets hotter.

Kauffman says mule deer have the flexibility to adapt to shifting green waves, even as climate change makes them less predictable. But another challenge may be holding them back.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

An obstacle course of development

"So this is a bottleneck, because just over that ridge are the subdivisions," Kauffman says, pointing to where newer homes were recently built in Pinedale. The bottleneck is a narrow strip of land where 5,000 mule deer must pass between buildings and fences.

Sponsor Message

Throughout their migration, deer navigate a maze of development. There's evidence that some routes in Wyoming have been used by wildlife for thousands of years , which were well-known by Native American tribes. As European settlers moved in, roads and fences crisscrossed the landscape and growing communities constricted the paths. Mule deer are often wary of human infrastructure, which changes their behavior during migration .

"They hold up and then eventually race through the developed portion," Kauffman says. That hesitation can make it harder to stay with the spring green-up, something his team observed when they tracked a group of mule deer approaching a natural gas development.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

"They held up at the edge of the gas field, and then the green wave passed them by," he says. "And then eventually they sped through the development but were basically mismatched with the green wave after that point."

Kauffman says development makes mule deer less flexible at a time when a changing climate requires them to be more flexible.

"We need to just make their migrations less difficult," he says. "We need to remove obstacles so that they have the best chance to match their seasonal movements with whatever climate change comes at them with."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Protecting ranchland from development

To keep migration routes open, Wyoming is working with landowners like rancher Maggie Miller.

"I've never seen a winter, spring like this, never ever," she says, walking near her ranchland outside of Pinedale. The snow has already melted during an extremely warm spring. "I have never been up here with bare ground in April."

Miller has run Grindstone Cattle Company for 27 years, which has been in her husband's family since the 1800s. She's watched as small towns like Pinedale have grown and expanded over the years. So, she started looking for ways to preserve her land.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

"I don't ever feel that I own this or I own that," she says. "I feel it belongs to the wildlife and it's just one of those last special places."

Sponsor Message

She protected some of her land from future development with a conservation easement . Along with a nearby ranch, Miller sold the land's development rights to the Wyoming Stock Growers Land Trust, a restriction that prevents development if the 19,000 acres are ever sold.

Miller also started thinking about the miles of fenceline that cross her property, which can slow down wildlife or can even be deadly. Deer can get caught and entangled in the barbed wire.

Loading...

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

"The deer and the antelope run into a lot of different kinds of fences – they're traps," she says. "So we've been replacing all our ancient fences with wildlife-friendly fences."

The fence changes are simple – the bottom wire is smooth, not barbed, so animals like pronghorn antelope can go under safely. The top wires are spaced closer together, so when deer jump over, their legs are less likely to get caught. Miller says the biggest challenge in converting her fences is the cost – around $25,000 a mile. She and other landowners had the costs offset by a state and federal program to address fences within migration areas. So far, more than 900 miles of fence have been converted.

"Obviously, you have to have a landowner that is willing and interested in doing it, but we have so much interest and demand now for this," says Jill Randall, big game migration coordinator with the Wyoming Game and Fish Department. "We're lucky in Wyoming that we still have so much functional, connected landscape. We're working our tails off to try to keep what we have."

Loading...

Keeping migration lands open

Wyoming has also protected migratory routes, something few other Western states have done. So far, the state has four designated migratory corridors , which provide the land with varying levels of protection.

In the most crucial areas, the bottlenecks with little space left for wildlife, development isn't permitted. In areas where deer have more space, development is allowed, in consultation with wildlife officials. The rules don't apply on private property, however.

"We want to make sure to not encroach on private landowner rights," Randall says. "So, the work that happens on private lands, of which there is a lot, is voluntary and based on whatever that individual landowner wants to do."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

The question is whether Wyoming's migration policies can keep up with the rapid pace of development. Some of the biggest battles have been over oil and gas projects in Wyoming. Conservation groups recently sued the Trump administration to overturn a recent oil and gas lease sale near migratory corridors.

Sponsor Message

"I think we're reaching a crisis point with some of these migrations that's driven by development," says Arthur Middleton, professor of wildlife management at UC Berkeley, who works on wildlife migration in Wyoming. "You can see why we lose these long-distance migrants first. They're acutely vulnerable, by virtue of the scale of the land they have to cover."

Scientific research has revealed where these vital pathways are, Middleton says. Now, it's a matter of scaling up the work to protect them.

"We have the landowners that want to participate," Middleton says. "The work is happening. It's just getting outpaced by development and fences and traffic and all of that. So we need the resources to accelerate the work that everybody wants to do."

World.title: From 'Super' to 'Godzilla' to 'Mega': Just how monstrous is this year's El Niño?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Godzilla has battled giant moths and three-headed dragons. But even the king of the kaiju might have trouble keeping up with this year's El Niño.

First came "Super El Niño." Then "Godzilla El Niño." Now there's a new monster in town: "Mega El Niño." At this rate, King Ghidorah may be next.

But has this year's El Niño really been upgraded?

"As far as I can tell there's no reason to invent a new category above 'very strong' that we have right now," said Emily Becker, a research associate professor of atmospheric sciences at the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School.

But David Phillips, a climatologist emeritus with Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), was more enthusiastic, given the unprecedented nature of this El Niño.

"Maybe 'Godzilla' is not strong enough for it."

A NASA visualization compares Pacific Ocean surface temperatures in 2025 and 2026, showing the dramatic warming associated with El Niño. Red indicates warmer-than-average water, while blue shows cooler-than-average temperatures. The maps use satellite-derived data averaged over seven days to highlight broader temperature patterns. (NASA/JPL)

What's behind the 'mega' headlines?

El Niño is a climate phenomenon that occurs when unusually warm water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific alters atmospheric circulation patterns, changing the weather around the world, according to ECCC.

Scientists measure the strength of an El Niño by averaging the sea surface temperature over three months in a large section of the Pacific Ocean, as opposed to measuring extreme temperatures in localized areas.

The latest name gained attention after U.S. meteorologist Ryan Maue posted a map on X on Sunday showing what he said were sea surface temperatures as much as 10 C above normal near Peru and the Galápagos Islands.

"This is now a Mega El Niño," he wrote.

+10°C sea surface temperature anomaly near Galapagos 🐢and off coast of Peru. This is now a Mega El Niño. https://t.co/xfavOfY16L —RyanWeather

But the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s analysis doesn't show temperatures that high at the ocean's surface, said Michelle L'Heureux, its El Niño team lead and a physical scientist with the U.S. National Weather Service.

Instead, it shows temperature anomalies of roughly 4 C to 6 C in the eastern Pacific, she said.

NOAA hasn't changed its terminology for classifying El Niño events, said meteorologist Erica Cei, a National Weather Service spokesperson.

The agency's Climate Prediction Center simply classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong.

NOAA's Nov. 12 update reported extremely high sea surface temperatures in parts of the eastern Pacific. However, isolated temperature readings do not necessarily reflect the overall intensity of an El Niño.

Instead, NOAA uses the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) to measure average sea surface temperature anomalies in the central tropical Pacific over a three-month period, while accounting for warming across other tropical oceans. By that measure, this year's El Niño has reached NOAA's highest classification: very strong.

"This event is running on par with our previous very strong events," Becker said, referring to the El Niños of 1997-'98 and 2015-'16.

While "mega El Niño" is not an official category, the term has appeared in the scientific literature. A 2023 peer-reviewed study used it to describe the very strong El Niño events of 1982-'83, 1997-'98 and 2015-'16.

WATCH | A 'super' El Niño could bring record heat, floods and droughts: I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before | Duration 3:17 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a 'super' El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this 'super' El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

Is this El Niño really exceptional?

There is no question this is an unusually powerful event.

NOAA's Nov. 12 forecast gave it roughly a 60 per cent chance of surpassing the strength of previous El Niños dating back to 1950.

But that remains a forecast, not a record already broken.

Mandy Freund, a climate science lecturer at the University of Melbourne who has written about "Godzilla El Niño," said some ocean temperatures recorded near South America are unprecedented.

She also defended the dramatic terminology.

"I believe if the language serves the purpose of raising awareness of a dangerous situation, that’s acceptable," she said in an email to CBC News.

But Freund said making bold predictions before forecasts become reliable could undermine public confidence.

Becker also cautioned against assuming that an exceptionally strong El Niño will always bring extreme weather: "We don't necessarily expect to see extreme impacts from an extreme El Niño."

A skier walks down a patchy ski slope at Whistler, B.C., in December 2023. A powerful El Niño is expected to bring warmer-than-normal temperatures to much of Canada this winter, potentially affecting snowfall and conditions at ski resorts. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

What could a very strong El Niño mean for Canada?

Western and central Canada typically experience a milder winter during El Niño years, but impacts can be quite variable.

ECCC's Nov. 1 seasonal forecast also suggests that much of Eastern Canada could experience above-normal temperatures this winter.

Phillips said the current season could be compared with the very mild winter Canada experienced in 2023-'24. But even with very strong El Niño conditions, cold spells and snowstorms are possible.

An area of great uncertainty this winter is the polar vortex, a large circulation of winds in the upper atmosphere over the Arctic. When it is disrupted and weakens, cold Arctic air can push down into Canada and the United States.

Phillips compared this coming winter to a clash straight out of a Hollywood blockbuster: "It's the Godzilla El Niño meeting the frigid polar vortex," he said.

The lack of winter snow and moisture could increase the risk of spring drought and lead to an earlier start to the wildfire season, Phillips said.

WATCH | A giant underwater wave linked to El Niño raises concerns about climate change's impact: The Kelvin wave along B.C. may be 'strongest El Niño we've ever seen’ | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 2:54 A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is moving up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells among scientists about how climate change is magnifying the impacts of the naturally occurring phenomenon.

Is climate change making El Niños more powerful?

It is still unclear whether human-caused climate change is making powerful El Niños more frequent or intense.

Canada's Changing Climate Report 2026 finds, with medium confidence, that year-to-year climate fluctuations associated with El Niño have been larger since 1950 than in the previous century, but expresses low confidence that the change is due to human activity. This is because El Niño itself is highly variable, making it difficult to separate natural fluctuations from the effects of climate change.

There is no evidence to suggest that exceptionally powerful El Niños are increasing in frequency, Becker said.

However, global warming can make the effects of a strong El Niño even worse because warmer air holds more moisture and can cause more rainfall in regions that are already wet during an El Niño year.

Phillips called the combination of a powerful El Niño and a warming planet a "double whammy."

So while there is no official classification for a "mega" El Niño, the El Niño monster is out there somewhere.

World.title: Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Four computer programmers who did contract work for the British Columbia government were likely North Korean operatives, CBC's the fifth estate has learned.

Between 2023 and 2025, the four were hired to work on the province’s business registry platform.

As part of a contract worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the province with software developers, an IT staffing firm based in B.C.’s Lower Mainland facilitated the hiring of a man calling himself Kevin Zhang.

"Kevin's resume was ideal for the situation that I was dealing with," said the owner of the staffing firm. He spoke with the fifth estate on the condition that he and his company not be named. He said due to the nature of remote hiring, he was completely unaware he hired likely North Koreans.

Over the last year, the fifth estate has been investigating North Korean IT workers and how they, like Zhang, have been able to infiltrate Canadian businesses and government.

"With Zhang, he's pretty known," said Michael Barnhart, a former U.S. Army intelligence officer who investigates North Korea for the private sector.

"I had tracked him before. There's a couple crypto companies that had tracked him before. A couple of other just different industries that had been tracking him. And everyone had a different piece of the puzzle."

The photo from Kevin Zhang’s website, left, does not match that of the passports saved to his GitHub account, right. (kzdev420/GitHub)

Alongside the confirmation of experts like Barnhart, the fifth estate found multiple online clues that point toward North Korean IT worker tradecraft:

In an online profile Zhang used to do work for the B.C. government, he stored two fake Chinese passports. The place of birth for the holder is the Chinese province of Liaoning, which directly borders North Korea. The U.S. Department of the Treasury has previously sanctioned companies operating IT worker cells in Liaoning.

Watch the full documentary, "For Hire: North Korea's IT Army" from the fifth estate on YouTube , CBC Gem or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

The names on the passports appear to have been modified, with neither matching the name on the bottom stripe of the document.

A resumé-style website for Zhang contained a headshot that did not match the photo on the passports.

"This is the same guy that also goes by Kevin Chang, too," Barnhart said. "Sometimes he’ll only go by that.

"Chang, Ching or Zhang, just different variations of the beginning or ending name."

As time went on, the B.C. government hired three more remote developers via the same IT staffing firm. The owner of the firm told the fifth estate that each was recommended by Zhang, who said they were former colleagues.

The owner said the B.C. government made the ultimate decision to hire them and would have conducted a 30-minute interview focused on competency.

The fifth estate reached out to multiple people and entities within the B.C. government, but received no response or was told that because of the provincial election, which concluded Oct. 24, the government would not be able to provide a response.

In response to a freedom of information request, the fifth estate was told that the ministry where Zhang worked could not locate an employee by that name, despite having been provided the account details that logged his specific contributions to a ministry software project.

Red flags

Beyond the fake Chinese passports and differing headshots, an investigation of Zhang and his colleagues conducted by the fifth estate revealed numerous other oddities.

For instance, a resumé for Zhang found online, which listed the B.C. government as a prior employer, stated his address was "Main St. E, North Bay, ON," with the street number absent.

In email correspondence provided to the fifth estate by the B.C. staffing firm, Zhang and the other developers can be seen repeatedly changing their banking information.

"In retrospect, there's a highly unusual situation to have somebody change their bank, change their company," the B.C. staffing firm’s owner said. "I think in the years that I've been doing this, right, this happened once before, twice before."

This is a red flag, according to cybersecurity expert Barnhart.

"I’ve had the same bank account at my employer for decades. I’ve never told my company to change it, ever. If I have, it would have been once. If I’d have done it twice, that would have been like: 'What are you doing?’"

At one point last year, Zhang asked to be paid to the bank account for a company called Dev Dragon Inc. Corporate records show Dev Dragon , now defunct, was registered by a James Zhang at a derelict building in Dawson City, Yukon.

The registered address for DevDragon Inc. was a long-abandoned bank building in Dawson City, Yukon. (CBC)

One of the other remote workers, Brandon Galli, had a similarly confusing digital footprint. On the account connected to his position working on B.C. government code, Galli’s profile photo is of an Asian man. However, his closely linked personal website provides a photo of a Caucasian man.

In an email obtained by the fifth estate, Galli asked for his pay to go to the account of an Ontario company called Luk Castle Investments, registered to a home in Markham by a man named Kenny Luk.

According to his LinkedIn, Luk did computer programming jobs for a number of Canadian banks before starting a software development consultancy.

When the fifth estate contacted Luk to ask about Brendan Galli and the money paid to him, he said that "Luk Castle Investments does not participate in media inquiries or respond to unsolicited questions regarding its business activities. Neither I nor anyone associated with the company will be providing comment on this matter."

It is a common practice for North Korean IT workers to use a real person’s identity to commit their fraud. (GitHub/Brandongalli.io)

The fifth estate tracked down the real Brandon Galli in New Jersey. When told that someone using his identity had worked for the B.C. government, he said his identity might have been stolen.

But pressed further, he admitted he gave his identity to someone he was working with online. He said this person continues to use his identity without his permission, causing him a host of problems.

"It was before the pandemic. We were working together on upwork and freelancing platforms and I was receiving small payouts for a short time while I was in college just to pay for food," Galli told the fifth estate in a WhatsApp message.

Barnhart has seen this same pattern play out before.

"You'll see them targeting college students a lot that might need some money," he said.

"Where it's like: 'Hey, I don't want anything from you, I just need — can I use your LinkedIn profile? Can I use your driver's licence to try to get this job one time?’ And then once you [let them use it] one time, they have it forever."

World.title: Can AI chatbots really help shoppers find the best deals?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians are increasingly turning to AI to help hunt down Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals, but as CBC’s Philippe de Montigny explains, the chatbots might be missing some of the best bargains.

With Black Friday deals popping up everywhere, Monique Welter used ChatGPT to set up a daily alert to find a Garmin Instinct 3 smartwatch for less than $400.

"I was pretty shocked with the last deal it sent me because, even before Black Friday, it was 30 per cent off," she said. "Usually, famous brands don't need to go that deep in discounts."

The chatbot referred her to Sail, a Canadian outdoor equipment retailer she hadn’t even considered, which was selling the watch for $350.

Monique Welter regularly uses AI chatbots Claude and ChatGPT for wardrobe recommendations and to find Black Friday deals. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)

As the holiday shopping season ramps up, more Canadians are turning to AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Muse to help them pick a gift at a good price point. A Deloitte survey of more than 1,000 Canadians found that 39 per cent of respondents were planning to use AI to help them shop ahead of the holidays this year, including to find deals — up from 25 per cent the year before.

"We're really seeing a lot of price comparison work being done through AI chatbots, comparing between retailers, tracking the best price of a specific item across a range of retailers, and also looking for promo codes," Calgary-based retail consultant Jeff Doucette said.

But whether those bots are turning up the best prices is another question.

"It's not actually looking [through] the whole internet. It's looking for stuff that is available to AI," Montreal shopper Étienne Parent points out. "Amazon, for example, prevents bots from looking through it."

As shoppers change the way they search, buyers and businesses worry smaller shops — and potentially better deals — might be missing from their recommendations.

But AI firms and retail experts say there are ways for businesses to make sure they show up, and for consumers to find the product they're looking for.

How products get picked up by AI

Doucette says some of the best deals out there might never be picked up by chatbots.

Search engine optimization has long been a strategy for retailers, but now they're optimizing for AI search. If the shops with the best deals haven't done the work to make their websites visible to bots, retailers and consumers might both lose out.

"If you're not cited in the AI search engines, then you're not alive in the selection of choices from a consumer perspective," said Doucette, the founder and general manager of shopper research company Field Agent Canada.

Amazon released its own AI-powered assistant Alexa for Shopping earlier this month — but the e-commerce giant also quietly blocked rival AI bots from accessing information on its site. CBC News reached out to Amazon for comment, but the company did not respond.

Retail expert Jeff Doucette says consumers often use AI chatbots to compare prices and Black Friday sales across retailers, while also looking for promotional codes. (Ryan McLeod/CBC)

A recent analysis from AI research company Vaer AI and commissioned by point-of-sale and e-commerce platform Lightspeed found that AI recommendations from a number of chatbots favoured large retailers over smaller, local ones about 90 per cent of the time when relying on its own training data, and roughly half the time when live web search was enabled.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, told CBC News in an email that items from small businesses can show up next to options from bigger chains.

"As an example, our partnership with Shopify also helps shoppers discover products from its merchants, including small businesses, and sends shoppers directly to those stores when they click through," spokesperson Taya Christianson said.

Google, which operates Gemini, says its AI tools pull information from websites and businesses of all sizes, tapping into more than 60 billion products, including descriptions, special promotions and inventory levels.

"So if you're a retailer who is keeping your product feed in the Merchant Centre refreshed, you certainly will have the opportunity to show up," said Jamie Gargatsougias, head of retail at Google Canada.

Anthropic (which operates Claude) and Meta (Muse) did not respond to a request for comment from CBC News.

'People shop over a billion times a day and discovery on Google is applicable to businesses of all sizes,' Google Canada's head of retail Jamie Gargatsougias told CBC News. (Claude Beaudoin/CBC)

Retailers like Aldo have started to change their websites to adapt to the new ways shoppers are looking for products with AI.

The shoemaker's chief information officer, Matthieu Houle, says search used to be simple — shoppers would type in keywords, like the colour and style of shoes they were looking for, and sift through options from there.

With AI, shoppers are having a conversation with a chatbot instead.

"Now the consumers are asking more, 'Hey … I'm going to a holiday party at the office. This is what I'm gonna wear. Can you recommend me a shoe?'" Houle said.

On Aldo's end, that means providing more description about a product, as well as context about where someone might wear a pair of shoes or what to match them with, to make sure they show up in AI results.

Those changes, plus Aldo's use of Shopify's tools, which help agents and chatbots discover products, make Houle confident that Aldo is showing up in AI search. But he's not convinced by the technology’s deal-finding power just yet.

"Is [AI] a deal-hunting machine? Not in my experience so far," Houle said.

Aldo's chief information officer Matthieu Houle says AI is not quite a 'deal-hunting machine' yet. (Charles Contant/CBC)

How to find the product you want

Several retailers have launched AI-powered shopping assistants to help consumers navigate their websites.

Walmart recently launched its "Sparky" agent in Canada. Loblaw integrated its PC Express grocery delivery service with ChatGPT. Canadian Tire offers the "CeeTee" assistant to guide customers through tire comparisons, recommendations and store inventory checks.

Earlier this month, Google, in partnership with retailers including Lululemon, Shoppers Drug Mart and Simons, rolled out a new tool that lets users buy things with an AI chatbot , practically replacing the online checkout process.

Santo Ligotti, vice-president of marketing at the Retail Council of Canada, says consumers should revise their AI prompts — and the links they provide to the chatbot — to make sure they’re finding the right product at the right price. He says AI sometimes draws upon inaccurate information, fake reviews and outdated pricing.

"I think it's important to be clear about … what it is that you're asking for and making sure that you're reviewing that information," he said.

That’s something Monique Welter did when searching for a discounted smartwatch.

"I did in the beginning get a few alerts that, when I opened the link, weren't exactly the price it was saying it was," said the Toronto resident, who also uses AI to help with wardrobe recommendations.

Ligotti suggests also asking chatbots if there has been a trend of users returning the product. To state the obvious: The cheapest item may not necessarily be of the best quality.

While AI search results may not be perfect, many shoppers say chatbots save them "a lot of time" by cutting through all the Black Friday and Cyber Monday noise.

"Instead of going to five different websites, AI will do it for me in, like, three seconds," said Marc-Antoine Laporte, an avid online shopper based in Rimouski, Que.

As the old saying goes: Time is money.

World.title: Pentagon prepared to 'up the ante' in defence dispute with Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The war of words between the Pentagon and the Canadian government escalated on Tuesday as a senior U.S. defence official warned of further unspecified measures if Canada doesn't focus its military investments on protecting the continent.

The remarks were made in a background briefing given to Canadian journalists and approved for release by the U.S. Department of War.

The senior official described how they have been taking a very deliberate, graduated approach to get the attention of the Canadian government, starting with the suspension of the Permanent Joint Board on Defense (PJBD) last spring.

"That sent a message but has not solved the problem," said the Department of War official.

"We're postured to up the ante when we need to. If Canada cannot credibly turn its defence spending pledges into investments important for North American defence, we'll have no choice but to start looking at more significant mitigation measures."

The official did not spell out what those measures might look like, but suggested there's a sense of urgency.

"Prudence demands the department explore how we protect the United States in a situation where we cannot rely on Canada to prioritize military optimization and meet its obligations in a meaningful time frame," the official said.

"Canada has dismissed a lot of our concerns, including in NORAD, for many years. So, we want to communicate in a credible but also intelligent way that the current situation is not acceptable."

Mounting pressure

The pressure began building over the weekend with a leaked report in The Washington Post that said the U.S. military now had restrictions for interacting with Canadians. On Monday, the Pentagon publicly released a fact sheet that said Canada is not a credible defence partner and pointed to subpar Canadian military readiness statistics.

"Canadian political leadership continues to pursue unfocused global commitments, resulting in personnel and platform overextension, deferred modernizations for key equipment and low readiness rates," said the fact sheet.

"Ottawa's prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer."

The fact sheet accused Canada of not being able to meet its NORAD and NATO commitments.

In the background remarks, the senior U.S. official went further, saying when it comes to delivering to allies "the gap between rhetoric and reality in Ottawa is the widest in all of NATO."

The official pointed to Germany as a model ally that quickly turned around its defence spending and is on track to deliver.

The official also said there are a group of European countries that are on track to meet NATO's five per cent of gross domestic product defence spending target by the end of the decade — five years ahead of the timeline agreed to by allies last year.

"Canada has an extraordinarily long way to go," the senior official said. "We are encouraged by the modest progress thus far, but we need to see much more credibility in terms of spending commitments."

Going into cabinet on Tuesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty was peppered with questions about the Pentagon's fact sheet.

WATCH | McGuinty on Pentagon's criticisms: McGuinty 'can't divine' thinking behind Pentagon's criticisms, says co-operation with U.S. continues | Duration closed caption 1:26 After the Pentagon released a 'fact sheet' publicly criticized Canada's defence spending and military readiness, Defence Minister David McGuinty says military cooperation between the two countries is business as usual.

"Canada's a sovereign nation. I'll be very direct: We don't report to the United States," said McGuinty.

He pointed to the recent federal budget, which laid out a defence spending path to four per cent of GDP by 2030.

In its fact sheet on Monday, the Pentagon said Canada needs to be more specific about how it's going to meet the five per cent target.

The federal budget was vague on spending beyond 2030 and both McGuinty and Prime Minister Mark Carney said much will depend on NATO's planned review of the goal in 2029.

Kerry Buck, Canada's former NATO ambassador, said there's obviously more at play in the Pentagon's complaints than defence spending.

She acknowledged the U.S. concerns about Canada's military readiness and its effect on NORAD, but said decades of underinvestment will not be rectified overnight.

The fact that Carney is pulling Canada closer to Europe and has made buying military equipment from suppliers other than the United States a priority seems to be the subtext of some of the arguments she's seeing.

WATCH | More about the Pentagon's 'fact sheet': Pentagon releases 'fact sheet' criticizing Canada's military, defence spending | Duration closed caption 1:38 The Pentagon publicly released a 'fact sheet' criticizing Canada's defence spending and military readiness, saying the country isn't meeting its obligations to NORAD or NATO.

"Maybe the U.S. complaints aren't really about what we're doing at NATO," said Buck. "Maybe the U.S. complaints are about what our focus is and the fact that we're diversifying away from an overreliance on the U.S. military, including buying American."

Steve Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University, also acknowledged military readiness is a problem in Canada, but he sees U.S. domestic politics at play.

"This is about [U.S. Secretary of War] Pete Hegseth," said Saideman. "He's trying to do something he thinks of as being manly … bullying allies as opposed to actually getting his own house in order."

In Washington, Hegseth is facing intense congressional scrutiny and recently survived a bipartisan effort to impeach him.

That pressure is only expected to increase as Democrats take both the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in the new year.

World.title: Yes, COVID cases are on the rise again. And yes, experts say, it's still a very good idea to get vaccinated
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The COVID-19 vaccine is probably not in your mind the way it was when the global pandemic was in full swing.

But given this year's influenza season is off to an early start — and that respiratory viruses could already be causing school and work absences in your household — you may be wondering if it's time to think about getting an updated shot.

Here's what you need to know.

How common is COVID right now?

The Canadian respiratory virus surveillance report on COVID-19 shows that for the week of Nov. 14, the most recent for which data is available, there were 2,170 laboratory confirmed cases.

The number is rising from previous weeks, but that level is still considered low.

However, infectious disease specialists say there's plenty of reason to get the vaccine to reduce risk of severe infection either for yourself or someone around you who may be at higher risk.

"Some people think COVID is gone and forgotten, and it absolutely isn't," said Dr. Isaac Bogoch, a professor at the University of Toronto. "It's still a very dangerous pathogen, especially for people over the age of 80."

McMaster University professor Dawn Bowdish, who researches respiratory diseases, notes that in 2024, COVID-19 was still among the top 10 causes of death in Canada, "which I think a lot of people are surprised by."

WATCH | Large-scale review backs efficacy of mRNA vaccines: MRNA vaccines much safer than getting COVID-19: review | Duration closed caption 1:53 MRNA vaccines are effective and safer than getting COVID-19, according to a large-scale review published in The Lancet, which looked at all clinical trials, real-world data, research and case reports from 2020 to 2025.

Where are outbreaks happening?

According to the respiratory virus surveillance report, 61 confirmed outbreaks of COVID-19 were reported by participating provinces and territories for the week of Nov. 14.

The majority were in congregate settings like acute care (52 per cent) and long-term care facilities (33 per cent).

Who should get the COVID-19 vaccine this fall?

Canada's National Advisory Committee on Immunization (NACI) strongly recommends the vaccine for anyone who is at increased risk of exposure to the SARS-CoV-2 virus or who is vulnerable to severe COVID-19 disease.

That includes everyone over the age of 65 and those living in long-term care or in other congregate settings like retirement homes.

NACI also strongly recommends vaccination for those over the age of six months who have underlying health conditions that put them at higher risk of severe infection, as well as health-care workers and others employed in community settings.

Those who are pregnant, or who are from First Nations, Inuit, Métis and other equity-denied communities are also at higher risk of severe infection and should get the vaccine.

Lynora Saxinger, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, says people sometimes underestimate their own vulnerability to severe COVID-19 infection, thinking of only the very elderly and ill as at-risk.

"But it honestly could just be someone in the community who's on cardiac medications and is 66 years old," she said.

WATCH | Long COVID patients in B.C. raise fears over treatment access: Long COVID patients could see delays, cutbacks with changes to B.C.’s virtual care access | Duration closed caption 2:43 More than 300,000 British Columbians live with long COVID, with many relying on virtual appointments to access the care they need. But with changes coming to the Medical Services Plan, a long COVID clinic is warning this could result in extended wait times and cutbacks to vital programs. The CBC’s Ruby Cornish reports.

Can I get the vaccine if I'm not in one of those groups?

Yes. NACI says vaccines may be offered to other individuals aged six months or older based on individual risk assessment or preference.

Even if you remove the most severe outcomes from the equation, COVID disrupts schools and health-care systems, says Bowdish, "so we have the power to reduce those."

Saxinger says people in frequent contact with higher-risk people should consider getting the vaccine.

A COVID-19 infection could fly under your radar as a minor cold, but it could have "really terrible consequences" when you visit, for example, a grandparent or someone undergoing chemotherapy, Saxinger said — an important consideration heading into the holiday season.

Another thing to ask yourself is how long it's been since your last COVID-19 vaccine.

"If your last booster was in 2022 … it's a good idea to get a repeat vaccination this season," says Saxinger.

Some provincial health ministries, including those in Quebec and Alberta , no longer make COVID-19 vaccines universally available for free, something Bowdish describes as "a huge equity issue."

WATCH | Confusion in Alberta over vaccine distribution: Having a hard time getting the COVID-19 shot? | Duration closed caption 2:52 Alberta pharmacists are reporting delays, confusion and missing orders related to the province's distribution of COVID-19 vaccines. Pharmacists say they must cancel appointments and close bookings due to unpredictable vaccine supply. The Alberta government says there is no vaccine shortage in the province. We are joined by Edmonton-area pharmacist Fayaz Rajabali. He is the President of the Alberta Pharmacists' Association.

What will the vaccine do for me?

While the vaccine will vastly reduce your risk of getting a severe case of COVID-19, or of infecting someone else, it won't reduce your risk of catching the virus in the first place, in the way the first COVID-19 vaccines did, says Bogoch.

When the virus was brand new and the global population had no immunity whatsoever, those first vaccines were game-changers that did "a remarkable job in reducing the risk of infection," he said.

But as the different variants emerged, "the vaccines' ability to reduce the risk of infection was curtailed."

"So, really, the vaccines are there to mitigate the risks of severe infections, such as hospitalization and death," Bogoch said.

Does it matter which vaccine I get?

Right now there are two mRNA-based vaccines available in Canada — from Moderna and Pfizer — and a protein-based vaccine from Novavax.

Supply may vary based on how much of each vaccine a provincial or territorial health ministry has chosen to order. Links to appointment information for each jurisdiction can be found on this federal government hub, or you can ask your local pharmacy about which vaccines are available near you.

But Bowdish says all three vaccines have met rigorous safety standards, so there's no reason to shop around.

"The best vaccine is the one that's in your arm," she said.

However, some people may be more comfortable sticking with a vaccine they've previously had — and if that brings them back for routine immunization, that's a good thing, says Bogoch.

On the flip side, if people have been put off by flu-like symptoms they've experienced after having an mRNA vaccine, they may prefer to try Novavax instead, says Bowdish.

WATCH | Health Canada approves combo vaccine: Health Canada approves Moderna's new mRNA shots for flu, flu-COVID combo | Duration closed caption 1:59 Health Canada has approved two new Moderna mRNA vaccines — one for flu, the other for both flu and COVID-19. So far they're only approved for those 50 and older.

What about that combo vaccine?

You may have heard about a shot that combines influenza and COVID-19 vaccines.

Health Canada approved Moderna's combination mRNA vaccine earlier this month , but the company told The Canadian Press it won't reach pharmacies in time for this respiratory virus season.

Saxinger says anything that makes it easier to get immunized against respiratory viruses is a plus.

"I myself usually get [flu and COVID vaccines] at the same time, and having one sore arm instead of two seems like a bonus."

World.title: Dancing with the Stars Season 35 Finale: Who Won the Mirrorball?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Warning: Spoilers ahead

Dancing with the Stars has crowned its winner.

Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech and his pro partner Daniella Karagach won Season 35 of the reality TV dance competition, taking home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

But it was an unexpected moment during the final freestyle that turned an already powerful performance by the winning pair into an unforgettable one, prompting a standing ovation and bringing the room to tears.

Midway through the pair's performance, Frech's prosthetic leg came off. The track athlete didn't miss a beat, continuing the choreography before putting it back on, and carrying on.

Frech and Karagach were in tears as their names were announced and Season 34 winners Robert Irwin and Witney Carson handed over the trophy.

"This is the most special moment of my life," Frech told the audience as his fellow cast members hoisted him into the air and confetti rained down.

'I'm just so freaking grateful," Karagach added.

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach won Season 35 of Dancing with the Stars, taking home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy. (Eric McCandless/Disney)

For Tuesday's finale, five pairs remained: Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn and pro dancer Pasha Pashkov, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood and pro dancer Rylie Arnold, Frech, reality star Maura Higgins and dance partner Mark Ballas and actor Tatyana Ali and dancer Jan Ravnik.

The jam-packed, three-hour finale saw each couple take to the floor for three dances and the entire cast return for dazzling interludes.

The show pairs professional ballroom dancers with celebrity partners, with viewers voting alongside the judges to decide the winner.

First up was the judges' choice, where a judge assigned each finalist a specific dance style and song. Then came the instant dance, where couples found out their style and song just moments before. And the freestyle, where anything goes — think of it as their Superbowl halftime show, their pop star moment.

For their freestyle, Frech and Karagach danced to Linkin Park's Numb, paying tribute to people with disabilities, drawing on the Paralympian's own experiences. The two danced alongside an ensemble of dancers in wheelchairs.

Frech began the routine without his prosthetic leg before disappearing behind a wall to put it on and rejoin Karagach on the dance floor.

WATCH | Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach’s finale freestyle :

But when Frech's prosthetic came off on the dance floor, he rallied and quickly put it back on. The pair finished with Karagach balancing on his prosthetic as Frech held a bedazzled one in the air, earning a standing ovation and some of the loudest applause of the night.

"If one person with a disability feels more confident and holds their head up high because of this show then ive done my job." he said, before scoring perfect 10s.

The judges were moved.

Derek Hough called Frech "incredible," saying the performance would have a "ripple effect far beyond this show" and praising how he rose to the moment.

Bruno Tonioli declared him "a national treasure," describing the routine as a "powerful, beautiful, life-affirming statement."

And Carrie Ann Inaba, made sure Karagach got her flowers too, saying, "Dani, we need to salute you" for creating a "whole new vocabulary for dance."

Frech and Karagach scored perfect 10s throughout the night—in both the judge's salsa choice to Danza Kuduro by Don Omar and surprise tango to Levels by Avicii.

Here's how the other finalists finished, and a look back at their final performances.

Runner-up: Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov

WATCH | Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov’s finle freestyle:

Score: 90/90

Judges' choice: Quickstep to Sing, Sing, Sing by Louis Prima

Instant dance: Cha-cha to Sabrina Carpenter's Tears

Freestyle: A routine to Madonna's Music and Like a Prayer, a song Glenn skated to at the Olympics. It featured an acrobatic silk ribbon routine, aerials and a dance floor ensemble featuring Team USA’s Madison Chock and Evan Bates.

Third place: Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold

WATCH | Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold’s finale freestyle:

Score: 82/90

Judges' choice: Viennese Waltz to Willing and Able by Noah Kahan.

Instant: Cha-cha to Buttons, The Pussycat Dolls

Freestyle: A Tom Holland-styled, Lip Sync Battle-inspired performance to Gene Kelly's Singin’ in the Rain and Rihanna's Umbrella. Yes they actually danced in the rain and yes he ripped off his shirt to reveal a corset.

Fourth place: Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik

WATCH | Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik’s finale freestyle:

Score: 82/90

Judges' choice: Salsa to Jamaican (Bam Bam) by Hugel & Solto

Instant : Jive to Land of 1000 Dances, Wilson Pickett
