World.title: CIA and US intelligence office suffer intrusion exposing unclassified information
World.content:
CIA and US intelligence office suffer intrusion exposing unclassified information

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 01:08 UTC Full article

The CIA headquarters seal in Langley, Virginia

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a computer intrusion that exposed unclassified information from an open-source intelligence analysis system, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Unlike the system outages of recent weeks, attributed to technical failures, this is a security breach.

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a computer intrusion that exposed unclassified information from an open-source intelligence analysis system, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Unlike the system outages of recent weeks, attributed to technical failures, this is a security breach.

The intrusion affected a network analysts use to draw intelligence from public, unclassified material such as social media, satellite imagery and commercial databases, according to US officials and people familiar with the incident cited by the newspaper and by Reuters. It is unclear what information was compromised or how the intrusion occurred, and data from other federal agencies was probably also exposed. Those responsible have not been identified.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there had been “no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems”. The CIA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The incident adds to a series of security breaches at federal bodies: according to Reuters, one has recently been reported at the Department of Agriculture and two at the FBI, one of them at its National Crime Information Center, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been affected by cyber incidents.

It also coincides with a string of technology failures that authorities attributed to technical causes: the global Microsoft outage on November 12; the nationwide ground stop of all US flights for about four and a half hours on November 13, which the government blamed on outdated telecommunications equipment; and the outage of the National Security Agency's classified internal network on November 17, which the agency attributed to routine maintenance.

According to Uruguay's El País, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that the failures are linked or that the country is under a systemic attack.

World.title: Argentina enters technical recession after two quarters of contraction, the first since 2024
World.content:
Argentina enters technical recession after two quarters of contraction, the first since 2024

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 00:55 UTC Full article

Argentina's economy has entered a technical recession for the first time since 2024

Argentina's economy has entered a technical recession, with two consecutive quarters of contraction, for the first time since the first half of 2024. GDP fell 0.6% in the second quarter, and INDEC's monthly activity indicator points to a contraction of about 1.8% between July and September.

Argentina's economy has entered a technical recession, with two consecutive quarters of contraction, for the first time since the first half of 2024. Gross domestic product fell 0.6% in the second quarter, and the monthly activity indicator of the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC) points to a contraction of about 1.8% between July and September.

In September, activity rose 1.1% from August but fell 1.2% year on year, according to INDEC. In the first nine months of the year it has grown by just 1%, and in September it stood 2.4% below December. The institute revised July upwards, from a 2.8% fall to 2.5%, and August, from growth of 0.1% to 0.4%.

Ten of the fifteen sectors posted year-on-year falls in September. Industry fell 1.8%, commerce 2.2% and financial intermediation 11.5%, the largest negative contribution, while mining grew 11.1% and construction 3.5%. According to the consultancy ACM, agriculture and mining account for almost all of this year's growth.

Weak employment and incomes are holding back a recovery in consumption. According to calculations by the consultancy Ficonomics based on official data, 274,300 registered private-sector salaried jobs were lost between November 2023 and August 2026, a fall of 4.3%, more than half of them in industry and construction. Juan Manuel Franco, chief economist at SBS, notes that registered private real wages remain 2.3% below November 2023. Industry used 60.1% of its installed capacity in September, against 67.9% in the same month of 2023.

Analysts expect the economy may exit recession in the fourth quarter, although without a strong recovery. ACM calculates that if activity holds at September's level, the final quarter would grow 0.9%. The consultancy LCG expects a positive close but forecasts growth of at most 0.7% in 2026 and about 1.5% in 2027. “We do not expect a radical change in the short-term dynamic, but some months of growth that allow the last quarter to close positive,” it said. ACM forecasts growth of close to 1% this year and SBS around 0.6%, while Ficonomics does not rule out another quarterly fall.

Analysts warn of an additional risk: that the need to contain pressure on the exchange rate could force interest rates higher, making credit more expensive just when consumption and investment need it to recover. Country risk reached its highest level in a year in early November.

World.title: In Beijing, Ebrard pushes for more Mexican exports to China
World.content:
Remaining in China after last week’s close of the APEC summit, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard took advantage of the 11th Mexico-China High-Level Group Meeting to arrange for a working group to be formed to address Mexico’s gaping trade deficit with the Asian giant.

Ebrard met with his Chinese counterpart, Commerce Minister Wentao Wang, in Beijing — a 2,000-kilometer flight from Shenzhen, the site of the APEC summit — to urge the establishment of new mechanisms to boost Mexican exports to China.

Resultados de la reunión del Grupo de Alto Nivel México-China https://t.co/YUgHILOlH0 — Marcelo Ebrard C. (@m_ebrard) November 23, 2026

He emphasized the need to change the “persistent and growing” trade imbalance between Mexico and China. While China is projected to export more than uS $130 billion worth of goods to Mexico this year, Mexico will likely export only around $10 billion to China.

The hope is that the new bilateral working group will create the necessary protocols to allow the export of certain Mexican products, such as avocados, lemons, beef, pork, sorghum and processed seafood, some of which have been in the works for a decade.

“Our ability to export more to China depends on the authorization of all these protocols, so that the balance between imports and exports improves in Mexico’s favor,” Ebrard said. “That is fair and reasonable.”

Several Mexican companies are prepared to export their products if a favorable business environment can be established. For example, the Mexican state-owned company Exportadora de Sal (Salt Exporter) hopes to increase its market share in China, having provided a proposal to supply up to 10 million tonnes of salt over four years.

After attending the APEC meeting, President Sheinbaum stressed that deepening trade ties with China would not impede Mexico’s bilateral relationship with the United States.

“The economic integration between Mexico and the U.S. is very significant,” Sheinbaum said during a press conference. “What we want is greater cooperation with China on various issues, from scientific research to tourism, and everything related to this collaboration.”

At the same time, Sheinbaum ruled out for now the negotiation of a free-trade agreement with China.

With reports from La Jornada, Líder Empresarial and El Financiero

World.title: Nescafé coffee producers protest in southern Mexico over low pay
World.content:
Coffee producers from the Costa, Sierra and Frontera regions of Chiapas – Mexico’s largest coffee-producing state – marched on Monday to protest against the low prices that the multinational food company Nestlé pays them to produce coffee beans for Nescafé.

The demonstration moved through the main streets of Tapachula and concluded with a rally in front of the municipal government building.

Protestan #Productores de #Café contra la empresa #Nestlé.

En #Tapachula cerca de 400 #Cafeticultores se manifiestan frente al palacio municipal contra la empresa global #NESCAFÉ exigiendo mejores precios al producto que le venden.

Les están comprando por debajo del precio de producción. #Chiapas — Gabriela Coutiño (@GabyCoutino) November 23, 2026

“We harvest the coffee, tend to it all year round, and we get paid 43 pesos (US $2.20) per kilogram. That same coffee sells for 580 pesos ($29) in the supermarket,” the protesters pointed out.

The farmers are demanding a fair price of at least 60 pesos ($3) per kg.

Meanwhile, farmer Eduardo Camarena told the newspaper La Jornada that the discontent extends throughout at least twenty municipalities and that the issue affects 165,000 families.

He noted that the gap between the price Nestlé pays farmers and the coffee’s retail price does not result in higher earnings for producers.

Camarena added that although farmers have held talks with the company, Nestlé has refused to adjust prices in response to the cost increases producers have faced. Moreover, he accused the company of centralizing the coffee market in the border region.

Protesters requested the intervention of the Chiapas state government to facilitate negotiations with Nestlé to agree on what they consider a fair price for their coffee.

“The cost of production, plus a decent profit for the producer — that is what we are asking for; it’s only fair,” he stressed.

Figures from the Agriculture and Rural Development Ministry (Sader) revealed that in Mexico, approximately 701,735 hectares across 10 states are dedicated to growing coffee beans, with national production expected to exceed one million tonnes by the end of 2026.

Production is spearheaded by Chiapas, with a contribution of 392,000 tonnes of beans per year, followed by Veracruz, with 256,000 and Puebla, with 225,000.

With reports from La Jornada and Diario de Chiapas

World.title: Mexico attracts record US $43.1B in FDI through September, but new investment plunges 42%
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico received a record-high US $43.09 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first nine months of 2026, a 5.3% year-on-year increase, the federal Economy Ministry (SE) reported Tuesday.

The figure exceeds the total FDI Mexico attracted in 2025 — $40.87 billion — but new investment declined 42.1% compared to the January-September period of last year.

The SE said in a press release that the FDI result “reflects the strength of the country’s macroeconomic and institutional foundations, as well as the momentum of Plan México, and reaffirms Mexico’s status as one of the world’s most attractive destinations for foreign investment.”

FDI in Mexico has increased in recent years amid the nearshoring trend, although some analysts argue that the country has yet to fully capitalize on the opportunity.

The Economy Ministry highlighted that Mexico was the world’s sixth-largest recipient of FDI in the first half of 2026, behind the United States, China, the Netherlands, Brazil and the Czech Republic, according to OECD data.

Mexico received $23.591 billion in FDI in the first quarter of 2026 and an additional $11.377 billion in the second quarter to bring the six-month total to $34.968 billion. The third quarter total was $8.122 billion.

The lion’s share of FDI came from the reinvestment of profits

According to the SE, foreign companies already operating in Mexico reinvested $34.975 billion in profits between January and September. Thus, 81.2% of Mexico’s FDI total came from the reinvestment of profits.

The dollar total increased 26% year over year to reach a record high, reflecting “foreign investors’ confidence in continuing to bet on our country over the medium and long term,” according to the SE.

The second-largest share of FDI came from the transfer of funds between companies within the same corporate group. Those transfers totaled $4.315 billion between January and September, representing 10% of the FDI total.

The dollar value of transfers between companies declined 34.6% compared to the same period of last year.

Finally, new investment in Mexico accounted for 8.8% of the FDI total in the first nine months of the year, down from a 16% share in the same period of last year. New FDI totaled $3.8 billion, down 42.1% from $6.563 billion in the first nine months of 2025.

The SE didn’t mention the year-over-year decline in overall new investment, but highlighted that new investment in Mexico’s manufacturing sector increased 58.8% to reach $1.124 billion.

The ministry reported that new foreign investment in the transport equipment sector, which includes automotive, aerospace and train production, surged 999.3% annually, while new FDI in the computer/electronic components sector increased 605.2%.

“This reflects the strength of domestic production chains and foreign investors’ confidence in Mexico as a high value-added manufacturing hub,” the SE said.

The think tank México ¿Cómo Vamos? has set a target for Mexico to attract $10 billion annually in new foreign investment. With cumulative new investment at just $3.8 billion through the first three quarters of the year, the think tank gives Mexico a yellow light — the middle rating in its three-color economic traffic-light system.

Over three-quarters of FDI came from just 5 countries

In the first nine months of 2026, the United States retained its position as the leading source of FDI in Mexico. U.S. companies invested $19.334 billion in Mexico in the period, accounting for 44.9% of the total.

The next largest sources of FDI in Mexico were:

Spain: $6.208 billion (14.4% of the FDI total between January and September)

Germany: $2.895 billion (6.7%)

The United Kingdom: $2.586 billion (6%)

Canada: $2.447 billion (5.7%)

The five top sources of FDI in Mexico accounted for 77.7% of total foreign direct investment in the country in the first nine months of the year. The SE also highlighted that 50.5% of FDI came from the United States and Canada, reflecting what it described as “the deep integration of North American value chains.”

The SE data indicates that 22.3% of FDI in Mexico between January and September came from countries outside the top five investors. Chinese investment in Mexico has increased in recent years, but the East Asian nation was not among the top 10 investors in the country in the first half of the year. The SE didn’t report an investment total for China in the first nine months of 2026.

Mexico City was easily the top FDI recipient

The SE reported that Mexico City — where many large foreign companies have offices — remained the leading destination for FDI in the first nine months of 2026. The capital received $19.602 billion during the period, accounting for 45.5% of total FDI.

The next biggest recipients of FDI were:

Nuevo León: $4.431 billion (10.3% of the FDI total)

Jalisco: $2.707 billion (6.3%)

Baja California: $2.362 billion (5.5%)

Puebla: $1.753 billion (4.1%)

The five top recipients of FDI in Mexico received 71.7% of total foreign direct investment in the country in the first nine months of the year.

Twenty-seven states shared the remaining 28.3% in FDI, which totaled $12.236 billion.

Almost 45% of FDI went to Mexico’s manufacturing sector

Mexico’s large manufacturing industry was the top recipient of FDI between January and September, receiving $19.231 billion, representing 44.6% of the total. FDI in the manufacturing sector increased 26.6% compared to the same period of last year.

The SE reported that the increase in FDI in the manufacturing industry was mainly driven by higher investment in the production of computer/communications equipment and electronic components ($1.814 billion); beverages and tobacco ($1.804 billion); food ($1.309 billion); and chemicals ($1.271 billion).

Mexico’s exports of computer equipment, including AI servers, have surged this year, fueled by growing demand amid the AI boom in the United States.

The financial services and insurance sector was the second-largest recipient of FDI, after manufacturing. The sector received $10.635 billion in FDI between January and September, representing 24.7% of the total. Foreign investment in the financial services and insurance sector grew 3.7% year over year.

The next largest recipients of FDI in the first nine months of 2026 were:

The transport, postal services and storage sector: $3.099 billion (7.2% of the FDI total). Foreign investment in this sector increased 59.3% year over year.

The construction sector: $2.481 billion (5.8%)

The temporary accommodation sector: $1.826 billion (4.2%)

The remaining 13.5% of FDI totaling $5.818 billion went to other sectors of Mexico’s economy.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: It’s official! Mexico will co-host the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup
World.content:
As expected, Mexico will serve as co-host of the FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2031, an assignment that the Claudia Sheinbaum administration said “reaffirms Mexico’s organizational capacity and its position as a great host of international sporting events.”

“After the international exposure and excellent image that Mexico offered to the world as host of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, this new designation confirms that our country has the infrastructure, experience, human talent and organizational capacity to host competitions of global scope,” the government said in a press release.

¡EL SUEÑO DE JUGAR UN MUNDIAL EN CASA SERÁ UNA REALIDAD!🥹🇲🇽 Las futbolistas mexicanas no ocultaron su emoción después de la confirmación de México como anfitrión de la Copa Mundial Femenina de 2031. Una noticia que ilusiona a las nuevas generaciones y representa una oportunidad histórica para seguir impulsando el futbol femenil en nuestro país. — Claro Sports (@ClaroSports) November 23, 2026

As the lone proposal for the 2031 “Mundial,” the joint Mexico-U.S.-Costa Rica-Jamaica bid was approved by FIFA on Monday. The four North American nations will play host to a newly expanded 48-team tournament, up from the 32 participants in next year’s Cup in Brazil.

This will be the first time Mexico stages the Women’s World Cup and national soccer federation officials are lobbying to have a significant presence, offering to host the final, the opening match and the tournament draw.

In the men’s World Cup (which Mexico co-hosted alongside the United States and Canada), Mexico hosted the inaugural match (and only 13 of 104 total games), while the final and the draw were held in the United States.

Presently, there are no binding commitments from host cities or stadiums. FIFA’s bid evaluation report listed four primary Mexican host cities — Mexico City, Guadalajara, Monterrey and Torreón (Coahuila) — while Mexican officials proposed additional candidate cities.

FIFA announced that 42 stadiums across the four countries have signed Memorandums of Understanding, demonstrating “each stakeholder’s motivation to participate in the organization of the tournament.”

Mexico’s National Commission for Physical Culture and Sport described the hosting opportunity as “a platform to inspire new generations, expand opportunities for participation, and demonstrate that Mexican girls and young women can find in sport a path to develop, compete and achieve their dreams.”

Looking beyond the tournament, the government said it hopes “to leverage its legacy so that women’s soccer reaches more schools, neighborhoods and communities; so that more and more girls have access to decent and safe sports spaces, and so that talent finds opportunities to develop.”

With reports from Record, El Universal, The Athletic, ESPN and Milenio

World.title: Nearly half of Mexican firms report that US tariffs impact their cost structure
World.content:
U.S. tariffs have had an impact on the cost structure of 45% of companies in Mexico, a global survey conducted by HSBC revealed, with most businesses (68%) believing that the resulting high costs will continue through the next few years.

According to the survey, conducted among 500 companies in Mexico, tariff costs affected expenses more than supplier issues (40%) and raw material prices (38%).

Which of the following have impacted your cost base over the past 6 months?

Nevertheless, 90% of Mexican business owners plan to expand their international business in the next two years. Such optimism about bilateral trade despite the tariffs has actually strengthened since last year’s HSBC survey, when 86% of Mexican businesses foresaw a rise in the international exchange of goods,

Maximiliano Rossi, regional director of Global Trade Solutions at HSBC Mexico and Latin America, told Imagen Radio that the survey’s offsetting findings (tariff impact and trade expansion) are notable, particularly in light of “the uncertainty surrounding [U.S.-Mexico trade] negotiations and the issue of tariffs.”

Rossi said companies established in Mexico have “modified operating processes and supply networks to mitigate the financial impact of trade barriers and maintain competitiveness in international markets.”

In this regard, global trade has begun to abandon the indiscriminate opening and outsourcing scheme toward Asia of the 1980s and 1990s and regional blocs are now playing a more important role.

As such, 83% of companies indicated that the changes made to respond to trade uncertainty and disruptions have been effective.

Survey respondents confirmed that the changes are reshaping suppliers, energy security, inventory and production footprints. “With further action planned, the redesign of trade networks remains an ongoing process rather than a one-off response to disruption,” the HSBC report says.

Rossi went further, saying that “supply chains are adapting, and Mexico has a unique, unparalleled situation.”

AI adoption as tariff adaptation

Furthermore, as businesses “expand internationally through the transformation of supply chains, the adoption of digital channels and the use of digital intelligence (AI) tools” are becoming increasingly important.

Of note, the HSBC survey found that AI adoption is accelerating faster than AI oversight.

While 85% have already deployed AI in at least one trade-related function, 76% have implemented fewer than five of the 10 AI safeguards assessed in the survey.

In other findings, 73% said changes made to their supply chains have improved their cash flow and working capital, and 49% of firms said they have optimized their trade networks.

With reports from Expansión and Imagen Radio

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: All-ages activities for family visits to Vallarta
World.content:
Living on the Nayarit coast on Banderas Bay for more than 11 years, with family and friends who like to visit often, we’re always on the lookout for events and activities everyone would enjoy — from kids to grandparents. As high season kicks off in Puerto Vallarta and more families and friends are coming together, here are some of our favorite all-ages activities, plus what’s on our list to check out.

Make your own chocolate

Did you know the chocolate you love today has its origins in Mexico? The Mokaya in Chiapas were the first to turn cacao into chocolate, circa 1900 B.C. Subsequent civilizations such as the Olmecs, Maya and Mexica (also known as the Aztecs) further expanded the production and uses of cacao, from fermented drinks to currency.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mente Cacao (@mentecacao)

As a national heritage food, today cacao is used and celebrated all over Mexico, from spicy moles and sweet treats to hot beverages and ceremonies. For a chocoholic like me, Mexico is the place to be.

My parents are also chocolate lovers, so when they visited last year, we booked a chocolate-making workshop at ChocoMuseo in downtown Vallarta. Our workshop leader was knowledgeable and entertaining, sharing the history of chocolate in Mexico and teaching us the intricacies of chocolate making. We came away with more than a dozen uniquely flavored chocolates apiece, which we made from scratch starting with grinding cacao beans.

ChocoMuseo is one of several local chocolate shops and cultivators that offer chocolate-making workshops in Vallarta, including Xocodiva, Mente Cacao in Nuevo Vallarta (which makes the best chocolate ice cream I’ve ever tasted, and I’ve eaten a lot of chocolate ice cream in my 54 years) and Planeta Cacao.

Explore nature without breaking a sweat

Banderas Bay and the rivers and mountains that surround it are brimming with beautiful, bold and curious wildlife, from brightly colored macaws and noisy chachalacas to lumbering crocodiles and iguanas the size of large dogs. The area is also home to unique plant life and pollinators that are becoming harder to see as development encroaches on their native habitats.

But you don’t have to hike through the jungle to view nature’s treasures, thanks to gardens and sanctuaries that make getting up close and personal with local wildlife and plants possible and the experience more accessible for all ages. These include the Vallarta Botanical Gardens (which also has a lovely restaurant), Santuario de Guacamayas (a conservation center for the Mexican green macaws) and El Cora Crocodile Sanctuary in Nuevo Vallarta. Or just take a walk alongside the Marina Golf Course and you’ll likely happen upon a few crocodiles wading or lounging at the ponds’ edges, or giant iguanas sunbathing in the middle of the afternoon.

And of course, el rey of the bay — humpback whales — start making their appearance in December when ocean temperatures cool down. The official start of whale-watching season this year is Dec. 8, and several outfitters can take the family out for a viewing trip, a must-do for anyone coming to Vallarta this time of year.

Go see a show

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Movie Picnic | Cine al aire libre (@moviepicnic)

Vallarta has tons of entertainment options, from outdoor movies to musical revues and simple community theater to high-production shows. Most are open to all ages (for some shows, children under 18 must be accompanied by an adult) and cater to a variety of tastes and budgets.

From Nov. 12 to May 27, Puerto de Luna Hotel hosts Movie + Picnic outdoor cinema in its garden area with family-friendly movies on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays. This week (Nov. 26-28), the movies are “Top Gun: Maverick,” “Billy Elliot” and “Klaus.” Also, now through Dec. 6, Teatro Sin Borders, the only English-language theater in Vallarta, is presenting the crime comedy “Laughs in Spanish.” If your family speaks Spanish, Cerka, a community theater in Nuevo Vallarta, has performances throughout the year (as well as acting and singing classes).

For those looking for something extra spectacular, LUDÕ, an underwater acrobatics show from Cirque du Soleil at VidantaWorld, is bound to take your breath away (and make you wonder how the acrobats hold their breath so long!). The amphitheater where the production takes place is equally impressive. Audiences sit inside a 360-degree aquarium where acrobats perform on stage and in the water behind the aquarium walls. The show recently received the Thea Award for Outstanding Achievement from the Themed Entertainment Association. This one’s on our list to check out as a possible holiday gift for the family.

Make your own art

Visiting Mexico will definitely inspire your inner artist. If your family likes to create, Puerto Vallarta has many artist spaces and classes throughout the year. A few include the Artist Hour at the Living Room Bookstore and Cafe in the Marina, where local artists teach classes such as painting, ceramics and more on Thursday afternoons. Also, Arte Vallarta Museo in the Romantic Zone and The Annex Studio and Gallery, a community art space near Playa Camarones, offer classes in printing, painting, ceramics, mosaic, folk art, weaving and more.

What are your favorite family-friendly activities and events in Vallarta? Drop your recommendations in the comments section below.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: Inflation rises to nearly 4% in first half of November
World.content:
Annual headline inflation in Mexico ticked up to 3.96% in the first half of November, the highest rate since early May, fueled in part by a 20% year-over-year surge in fruit and vegetable prices.

Reported by the national statistics agency INEGI on Tuesday, the headline rate came in slightly above the 3.92% median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters.

It is 0.21 percentage points higher than the 3.75% reading for October. The last time Mexico’s annual headline rate was higher was in the first half of May, at 4.11%.

The annual headline rate has now risen in five consecutive quincenas (15-day-periods) between the first half of September and the first half of November. It appears likely that headline inflation will rise for a fourth consecutive month in November after declining every month between April and July.

INEGI also reported on Tuesday that Mexico’s annual core inflation rate — which excludes volatile food and energy prices — was 3.68% in the first half of November, down from 3.80% across October. That was lower than the 3.88% forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters. The annual core rate — which is watched closely by economists and policymakers — was the lowest since the first quincena of March.

INEGI also reported that consumer prices increased 0.54% in the first half of November compared to the second half of October.

The publication of the latest inflation data comes almost three weeks after the Bank of Mexico board voted in favor of lowering the central bank’s benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%. Three of five board members voted in favor of the cut, despite recent increases in Mexico’s headline inflation rate. The board is expected to vote in favor of maintaining the central bank’s key rate at 6.25% at its final monetary policy meeting for 2026 on Dec. 17.

The Bank of Mexico targets an annual headline rate of 3%, with a tolerance range of 2%-4%.

Inflation data in detail

INEGI’s data shows that fruit and vegetable prices were 20.05% higher in the first half of November than a year earlier. Those prices are sensitive to adverse weather conditions, which can disrupt production and reduce supply.

Compared to the second half of October, prices for green tomatoes surged 39.31% in the first half of November, while regular tomatoes were 28.95% more expensive and poblano chiles were 26.97% dearer.

Annual inflation rates in the first half of November for other categories monitored by INEGI were as follows.

4.66% for processed food, beverages and tobacco

1.86% for non-food goods.

4.17% for services.

3.53% for energy, including electricity and gasoline.

Meat prices fell 2.15% on a year-over-year basis. Annual inflation for agricultural products (fruit, vegetables and meat) was 6.65% in the first half of November.

With reports from La Jornada and Reuters

World.title: Aeroméxico now offers 7-day Mexico City stopovers as tourism to the capital surges
World.content:
Mexico City’s government wants travelers who change planes in the capital to stay a while.

The city’s Tourism Ministry and the airline Aeroméxico announced on Nov. 18 a “stopover” program that lets connecting passengers stay more than 24 hours and up to seven days before continuing to their final destination. Travelers can take advantage of the offer from both the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA), and can use it on the outbound trip, the return or both.

The goal, according to a press release, is to lengthen visits and increase tourist spending. The program is meant to showcase the capital’s culture, food, entertainment, hotels, attractions and shopping.

“In Mexico City, there are 3,000 activities per day, so a stopover is a wonderful way for visitors and tourists to easily extend their stay,” said Tourism Minister Alejandra Frausto Guerrero during the program’s announcement.

For Aeroméxico, it’s a chance to make use of its main hub and strengthen the capital’s role as a gateway for domestic and international travelers.

Jennie Shrem Serur, director general of the city’s Tourism Promotion Institute, said the agency is working with the airline on a broader strategy that includes developing experiences, routes and tours to be offered through Aeroméxico’s platform. The aim, she said, is for travelers to see the capital as a reason to pause, not merely a stop on the way elsewhere.

The program applies in every market where Aeroméxico operates, as long as the itinerary connects in Mexico City. It is offered in all cabins and fare classes, with costs, conditions and baggage allowances varying by fare. When scheduling a flight online, select the option for “stopover;” round-trip flights will permit travelers to make two stopovers in Mexico City: one on their way out and one on the way back.

World.title: Jamaica’s Central Bank Eyes Farm Loan Relief
World.content:
The plan is early and unfinished, and the governor says it is no substitute for interest rates. It shows how a central bank fighting food-driven inflation is looking beyond its policy rate.

A National Commercial Bank branch in Montego Bay, Jamaica, photographed in 2015 (Photo: Balou46, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Economy: Jamaica

Jamaica’s central bank is studying a plan to make it cheaper for banks to lend to farmers who build for drought and hurricanes, Governor Brian Langrin said on Monday 23 November 2026 at the bank’s quarterly press briefing in Kingston. Under the idea, the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) would halve the risk weight on such loans, the share of a loan that a bank must back with its own capital.

The BOJ’s Monetary Policy Committee, its rate-setting panel, met on 16 and 17 November and voted unanimously on Wednesday 18 November 2026 to raise the policy rate by 50 basis points, or half a percentage point, to 6.50%, effective 19 November, the bank said in its press release. It was the second rise of that size in two months, after the 28 September decision that lifted the rate from 5.5% to 6.0%.

What. The bank is exploring halving the capital banks must hold against climate-resilient farm loans.

As of 25 November 2026, 12:00 GMT

The plan is early and unfinished, and the governor says it is no substitute for interest rates. It shows how a central bank fighting food-driven inflation is looking beyond its policy rate.

The policy rate is what the BOJ pays deposit-taking institutions on their current-account balances at the central bank. The November release warned that inflation could stay above target until late 2027, “a more persistent breach than previously communicated”.

A park by the waterfront in downtown Kingston, Jamaica’s capital. File photo, 2007. (Photo: Tillon Aniel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Statistical Institute of Jamaica (STATIN), the national statistics office, put headline inflation at 8.2% in October 2026, against 8.6% in September and 2.9% in October 2025. That was the fifth month above the bank’s 4% to 6% target band, while core inflation, a narrower measure, stood at 5.4%, against 5.3% in September and 3.7% a year earlier.

The BOJ projects inflation above target over most of the next four quarters, peaking in the quarter ending March 2027 and returning to the band by late 2027. It expects a temporary dip into the band in December 2026 from base effects, a statistical quirk after the price jump that followed Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

The release names imported inflation from commodity prices, linked to the Middle East conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war, and government reconstruction spending as drivers. It also cites above-seasonal food inflation from a worsening El Niño, a weather pattern that disrupts rainfall, and second-round effects on processed food and services, meaning knock-on price rises.

At the 23 November briefing, Langrin said the bank is exploring a framework to halve the regulatory risk weight on bank loans for qualifying climate-resilient agriculture. In practice a weight of 100% would fall to 50%.

A lower weight means banks hold less capital against those loans. Langrin gave examples of eligible projects: solar-powered drip irrigation, water storage, hurricane-resilient greenhouses, cold and dry storage, farm roads, drainage and post-harvest infrastructure.

The assets must be physical, independently verified and show a clear resilience element, and credit checks would not be relaxed, he said. Banks historically lend against real estate and vehicles, so he said: “They have to lend against cash flow.”

The BOJ is looking at technology that lets banks assess small business cash flows with the borrower’s permission. Langrin also set a test for the lenders themselves: “We will have to watch: Do they in fact pass on these incentives to climate-resilient agricultural production?”

The governor was blunt about the limits, saying the initiative is not a short-term fix and that monetary policy stays the main tool. “Interest rates cannot prevent a drought, restore damaged crops, or repair a disrupted food supply chain,” he said.

According to the bank, food is roughly one third of Jamaica’s consumer price index, and BOJ research over 25 years found that global food-price shocks had a larger and more persistent effect on domestic inflation than comparable oil and alumina price moves. Langrin said much of the food-price impulse comes from imported food.

On local supply he said: “We would love for the industry to be able to supply the demand, especially from the tourism sector, but it simply cannot do so on a sustainable basis.” Hotels that serve US visitors depend on that food supply, which is why the tourism link matters beyond Jamaica.

The BOJ itself says the plan is at an early stage: no framework is agreed, and it remains subject to internal assessment, legal review and approvals. The bank has not held detailed talks with the banks, only alerted them, and it offered a symposium of banks, farm stakeholders and government agencies, with no date set for it or the framework.

The next rate decision falls on Friday 18 December 2026, according to the BOJ’s announcement schedule. Langrin said the bank will monitor whether lenders pass the capital relief on to farm borrowers.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Bank of Jamaica considering?

It is exploring whether banks could hold less capital against loans for climate-resilient farming. No framework has been agreed.

Will this lower food prices soon?

The governor says it is not a short-term fix. Interest rates remain the main tool against inflation.

Why should US readers care?

Langrin named tourism as the sector that local farms cannot yet supply reliably. Hotels that serve US visitors therefore depend on that food supply.

World.title: Brazil Barred Trump Aide Darren Beattie
World.content:
Beattie attacked a Brazilian Supreme Court justice in public, and in March 2026 Brasília revoked his visa when he sought to visit a jailed former president. His story shows how one adviser’s travel plans turned into a diplomatic incident.

Profile: Brazil

Darren Beattie, the Trump administration adviser whom Brazil barred from entering the country in March 2026, has left the US State Department. The department confirmed his exit on Tuesday 24 November 2026 and gave no reason.

Beattie attacked a Brazilian Supreme Court justice in public, and in March 2026 Brasília revoked his visa when he sought to visit a jailed former president. His story shows how one adviser’s travel plans turned into a diplomatic incident.

Beattie served as the department’s senior adviser for Brazil policy, a title the department confirmed in February 2026. His appointment came while Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil’s former president, was in prison for a coup attempt.

Beattie has taught at Duke University in North Carolina, and in Trump’s first term he worked as a policy aide and speechwriter. He left the White House in August 2018 after a news investigation, and reports at the time said he was fired.

File photo: the Supreme Federal Court building in Brasília, where Justice Alexandre de Moraes of the Supreme Federal Court sits.

That investigation reported that in 2016 he had spoken at the H.L. Mencken Club conference, a gathering of right-wing intellectuals that, according to the reporting, also drew white nationalists.

Beattie said at the time that he had said nothing objectionable and stood by his remarks. In July 2025 the board of the US Institute of Peace, a federally funded peace-research body, named him acting president while he kept his State Department post.

He had earlier founded the right-wing website Revolver News, and before the Brazil job he was acting Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy and Public Affairs. Beattie has publicly described Justice Alexandre de Moraes of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court as the architect of a censorship and persecution complex aimed at Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters.

Moraes oversaw the trial in which Bolsonaro, the former president, was sentenced to 27 years and 3 months for a coup attempt. On Wednesday 30 July 2025 the US Treasury’s sanctions office, OFAC, put Moraes under Global Magnitsky sanctions, a US programme aimed at alleged human-rights abusers.

OFAC removed him from its sanctions list on Friday 12 December 2025. In March 2026 Bolsonaro’s defence team asked for Beattie to visit him at the Papudinha, the Brasília facility where he is jailed.

Moraes first authorised the visit and then asked Itamaraty, Brazil’s foreign ministry, about the trip. Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira told Moraes in a letter that Beattie’s visa request mentioned only a Brazil-US critical-minerals forum.

On Thursday 12 March Moraes reversed his order, saying the visit was not on the agenda Brazil had been told about. Vieira warned that a visit by a foreign official to a former president in an election year could amount to “undue interference” (“indevida ingerência”), in our translation from his Portuguese.

On Friday 13 March Itamaraty confirmed it had revoked the visa because of the “omission and falsification of relevant information regarding the reason for the visit”, in our translation. The same day President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, speaking in Rio de Janeiro, said in our translation: “That American guy who said he would come here to visit Jair Bolsonaro was banned from visiting, and I banned him from coming to Brazil until the visas of my health minister, which are blocked, are released.”

The health minister is Alexandre Padilha, a member of Lula’s cabinet. Lula tied his ban to the visa of his health minister, while Itamaraty gave a different reason: omission and falsification in the visa application.

Brasília therefore gave two public reasons for keeping him out. We found no public statement from Beattie on the visa decision, though that does not prove there is none.

The Brazilian account, from Vieira, Itamaraty, Lula and Moraes, is therefore the only version on the record that we found. The episode shows how a quarrel over a court case reached routine diplomacy, because an American adviser was barred from the country he was appointed to handle.

The State Department has not said who will handle Brazil now. His exit comes about a month after Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator and Jair Bolsonaro’s son, lost the presidential runoff to Lula on Sunday 25 October 2026.

No official explanation links the two events, and we do not claim a connection. The State Department has not said whether Beattie resigned or was dismissed.

Whether Lula’s entry ban still stands is unclear, and no dated next step has been announced.

Who is Darren Beattie?

He is a right-wing political aide who worked on Brazil policy at the State Department. He publicly attacked a Brazilian Supreme Court justice.

Why did Brazil bar him?

Brazil’s foreign ministry said he misrepresented the purpose of his trip when applying for a visa. The president also said the ban would last until Washington released the blocked visas of Brazil’s health minister.

Does his exit change US policy?

The department has announced no change. What happens next depends on whom it names for Brazil.

World.title: Costa Rica Bank Warns Fuel Could Lift Prices
World.content:
Inflation is still low, but the central bank is watching how a costly oil shock travels into transport and production costs.

File photo, 2023. The Banco Central de Costa Rica building in San José, with the bank's name on the facade. (Photo: MyCatIsAChonk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Economy: Costa Rica

Costa Rica’s central bank warned on 30 October 2026 that dearer imported fuel could spread through the economy and lift prices faster than it expected a month earlier. Its Monetary Policy Report now sees inflation near 2.7% in the second half of 2027, a higher path than in July.

The warning matters beyond San José because Costa Rica is a US free-trade partner and a destination for many American travellers. Fuel and transport costs touch visitors’ bills and the running costs of companies in its free-trade zones.

Key Facts Who. Róger Madrigal, president of Costa Rica’s central bank, the Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR).

What. The bank projects inflation near 2.7% in late 2027, higher than its July forecast.

Numbers. Annual consumer price inflation reached 0.55% in October 2026, up from 0.34% in September.

As of. 25 November 2026.

Inflation is still low, but the central bank is watching how a costly oil shock travels into transport and production costs.

Costa Rica’s prices have been unusually calm. The bank’s monthly economic report of 29 October 2026 put annual inflation in September at 0.3% (0.34% in the exact figure of INEC, the national statistics institute), back in positive territory after 16 consecutive months of falling prices and still below its 3.0% target.

INEC put October inflation at 0.55%, with fuel and transport fares pushing it higher. Both readings sit below the bank’s tolerance range of 2% to 4%.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The same monthly report said fuel prices rose 10.5% year on year because of higher international oil prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. Separately, its Monetary Policy Report says the higher inflation path is explained mainly by dearer hydrocarbons.

Downtown San José. File photo. Photo: Mariordo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

The bank also tracks the 3-2-1 crack spread, the margin refiners earn turning crude oil into petrol and diesel. It averaged US$66.7 per barrel in the first nine days of October, against US$66.4 the month before, because of scarce global refining capacity and geopolitical risk.

In its Monetary Policy Report, approved by its board on 28 October, the bank said the spread peaked near US$75 in August. That compares with about US$20 before the conflict and a 2022 peak of US$65, while the US retail price of diesel stood above US$6 per gallon, against about US$4 before.

Presenting the report on 30 October 2026, Madrigal said, in our translation from Spanish, that “the famous second-round effects are the ones we have to be very careful about”. He explained that such effects occur when an initial price shock, such as dearer oil, spreads through the economy via higher costs.

He said the effects are felt mainly in the transport division of the consumer price index, which covers fuels, public transport and vehicles. He added that fuel prices are rising faster than crude oil because of refining margins.

The board kept the policy rate, known as the TPM, at 3.0% at its September meeting, unchanged since July. The rate is the bank’s main lever on borrowing costs.

At the pump, Aresep, the public-services regulator, approved an extraordinary fuel rise of up to ¢89 per litre (about US$0.20) at the end of October 2026. Regular petrol went from ¢719 (about US$1.61) to ¢808 (about US$1.81) per litre, converted at the central bank’s reference selling rate of about ¢446 per US$ on 25 November.

Recope, the state oil import company, argues that it has little room to move prices. It imports finished fuels, so it creates no local refining margin, and it said in October that its operations are about 5% of the final pump price.

It is not known how large the second-round effect will be or how long oil prices stay high. Both answers will shape whether the bank has to raise rates.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a second-round effect?

It is the spread of an initial price shock, such as dearer oil, through the economy via higher costs. The bank says transport and production costs are where it bites most.

Will Costa Rica raise interest rates?

The bank has held its policy rate at 3.0% since July and has announced no change. Madrigal has named second-round effects as the development to watch.

Why should US travellers and companies care?

Fuel and transport costs touch visitors’ costs in Costa Rica, a destination for many American travellers. Firms in the free-trade zones face the same cost pressure.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Approves US Extradition
World.content:
A Costa Rican court has cleared the way for a football club’s former president to face US cocaine charges, but the ruling can still be appealed and does not mean an immediate handover.

The Courts of Justice building of San José's First Judicial Circuit, pictured in 2010. File photo that does not show the court handling this case. Photo: Antonio Solera / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

Security: Costa Rica

A court in Costa Rica has approved the extradition of Wilder Eusse Osorio, 51, the former president of a top-flight football club, so that he can face cocaine trafficking charges in a US federal court in Texas. The Judicial Branch, the Costa Rican court system, said on Tuesday 24 November 2026 that the ruling was issued the day before.

The ruling is number 542-2026, issued at 2:30 p.m. on Monday 23 November 2026 in case 26-000092-016-PE by the Tribunal Penal del III Circuito Judicial de San José, which sits in Pavas. The Judicial Branch said on Tuesday 24 November that the ruling had been notified to all parties, which opens a window of three working days to appeal.

The court granted what is called passive extradition, in which a foreign state asks Costa Rica to hand over a person for trial there. In this case the United States wants Eusse tried in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Texas.

According to the Judicial Branch, the court rejected two arguments from Eusse’s defence. The first was that the statute of limitations, the legal time limit for bringing charges, had run out.

The second was that the May 2025 reform of article 32 of the constitution was being applied retroactively, meaning to acts that came before it. That reform allows Costa Rica to extradite its own nationals for international drug trafficking and terrorism.

Santiago Arguedas, a Costa Rican criminal lawyer, said on 24 November that the United States must give formal guarantees through diplomatic channels. Guarantees, in this setting, are promises that the requesting country makes to the country handing the person over.

Several points are still open. The defence has not said whether it will appeal, and no date for a handover has been announced.

Eusse’s plea has not been published. He is presumed innocent, and the charges are allegations that a court has yet to test.

The next fixed date is Friday 27 November 2026, when the appeal deadline passes. The Judicial Branch has not said what happens after that date.

Not yet. The ruling can still be appealed, and no handover date has been announced.

World.title: Colombia Says Air Strike Killed Five Rebels
World.content:
The government calls it a heavy blow to a rebel front accused of killings, extortion and child recruitment, but the toll rests on official figures that no independent body has confirmed.

Security: Colombia

Colombia’s presidency said on Sunday 22 November 2026 that an air strike killed five members of the National Liberation Army (ELN), a rebel group. The government dates the operation to Saturday 21 November and places it near Dagua, on the road linking Cali with the Pacific port of Buenaventura.

The ELN has fought the Colombian state for decades, and the strike hit its Luis Carlos Cárdenas Arbeláez front in La Elsa, a rural district of Dagua in Valle del Cauca department. The people most exposed are those who live and work along the road corridor that carries trucks to Colombia’s main Pacific port.

Key Facts Who. President De La Espriella says forces hit the ELN’s Luis Carlos Cárdenas Arbeláez front.

What. Five rebels killed in Operation Neptuno, an air strike the presidency dates to Saturday 21 November 2026.

Where. La Elsa, a rural district of Dagua, Valle del Cauca, on the Cali to Buenaventura corridor.

Power Index. Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. 25 November 2026.

The government calls it a heavy blow to a rebel front accused of killings, extortion and child recruitment, but the toll rests on official figures that no independent body has confirmed.

The strike follows earlier bombings of ELN camps in Cauca, the department next to Valle del Cauca, including one in October in which the government counted ten ELN members dead. President Abelardo De La Espriella, who took office on 7 August 2026, has made air strikes a regular tool against armed groups.

He presented the results of Operation Neptuno in a presidency statement dated 22 November, as a joint action of the armed forces and the National Police. He said the five dead make up 25% of the front’s members and strike the armed and security wing of a leader of the front, alias ‘Bertha’.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The state offers a reward of up to 787 million Colombian pesos (about US$225,000 at roughly 3,500 pesos per US$ in late November 2026) for ‘Bertha’. The presidency attributes to the front 68 selective killings, 72 cases of child recruitment, 55 extortions, 18 forced displacements and 10 attacks.

The presidency also accuses the front of burning six cargo trucks on the road from Loboguerrero to the Pacific port of Buenaventura and of harming 300 families in Dagua. Forces seized six rifles, one handgun, 41 magazines, 1,300 cartridges and 14 explosive devices, along with other war and supply items.

President Abelardo De La Espriella, who announced the results of the operation. (File photo)

Late on Thursday 19 November the president wrote on the social network X that Colombia’s Air Force had carried out a bombing against a narco-terrorist target in Valle del Cauca, and that he would give details the next day. Colombian accounts differ on whether the strike came on the night of 18 to 19 November or on 21 November, and the presidency says 21 November.

“The threat persists, but we are not going to yield,” De La Espriella said, in words from the presidency’s account translated from Spanish. He said there is “no truce against narco-terrorism” and that the actions weaken the group’s command and finances, curb its expansion in the Pacific region and protect the corridor between Buenaventura and Cali.

Valle del Cauca’s governor, Dilian Francisca Toro, said on 22 November, in words translated from Spanish, that the blow “shows the importance of coordinated State action to recover territorial control.” She called every action that hits criminals “an act of sovereignty and a breather for our people”, and said regions have long fought armed groups “with isolated efforts”.

Toro asked for a sustained security policy for the Pacific municipalities. Dagua’s mayor, Karol Villarejo, said her priority is protecting families and children, and that security is the job of the armed forces.

A second presidency release of 22 November says Neptuno is the tenth strategic bombing against armed groups since De La Espriella took office. Its balance to 19 November counts 1,455 “affectations”, the government’s term for blows against armed groups, with 1,037 captured, 158 killed in operations and 260 surrenders.

Against the ELN alone the government counts 357 affectations, 291 captured and 51 killed. These are government figures and have not been independently verified.

The president said the strike follows the earlier ‘neutralisation’ of alias ‘Marcos Pacífico’, whom he described as military chief of the ELN’s Southwestern War Front. The presidency statement gives no detail on that earlier case.

The presidency has not published the names or ranks of the five dead, and it has not said whether any civilians were affected. It has also not said whether ‘Bertha’ was in the area.

Those most exposed are the families of Dagua and the truck drivers on the road to Buenaventura, which the president says the strike protects. The government has made air strikes a regular tool, and no next step or date has been published.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Colombia’s government say it hit?

It says Operation Neptuno struck an ELN front in Dagua, in Valle del Cauca. The toll comes from the government, and we found no ELN statement.

Why does the Dagua road matter?

It links Cali with Buenaventura, Colombia’s main Pacific port. Attacks on it affect local families and the trucks that use it.

Is the toll independently confirmed?

No. The figures come from the presidency, and no independent body or ELN account has confirmed them.

World.title: Bolivia Bank Aims to Double Dollar Reserves
World.content:
The goal is bold for a bank whose dollar holdings are still small, and it rests on a proposal to turn part of its gold into cash.

Photo: Pavel Špindler / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

Economy: Bolivia

Bolivia’s central bank said on Tuesday 24 November 2026 that it wants to double or triple its foreign-currency reserves in 2027. For anyone who travels to or does business in Bolivia, the goal matters because the country has faced a dollar shortage for years and now lets its currency float.

Bolivia’s reserves stood at about US$15,100 million at the end of 2014, according to the central bank’s data, and have fallen sharply since. Espinoza said foreign currency stood at only about US$50 million a year ago, when the current government took office.

The bank said on 24 November that its foreign-currency reserves reached US$855 million on 30 October 2026. Its latest figures put them at US$726 million on 13 November, when total reserves, mostly gold, were US$3,831 million.

That is a fall of about US$129 million in two weeks. The bank’s data showed in January that foreign-currency reserves rose by US$650 million between November and December 2025 thanks to external loan disbursements.

To lift the total, Espinoza proposed converting part of the country’s gold into dollars. Bolivian law requires at least 22 tonnes of gold in the reserves, and he proposed freeing half of that, worth about US$1.5 billion by his own estimate.

He said the money should strengthen exchange-rate policy and not pay for fuel or current spending. The exact reserve target will come with the bank’s annual monetary programme for 2027, its yearly plan for money and credit, whose date has not been confirmed.

Since late June 2026 the bank has run a flexible exchange rate, after years in which the official rate was fixed at Bs 6.96 per US$ (bolivianos, Bolivia’s currency). The parallel street rate reached about Bs 20 per US$ in May and June, which Espinoza called “the real exchange rate that the population had”.

The dollar traded at Bs 11.78 per US$ on Tuesday 24 November 2026 and has not exceeded Bs 12 since 5 November. Espinoza said the bank will step in if it sees sudden moves.

The central bank said US$1,366 million owed to depositors, frozen under withdrawal limits known as the “corralito”, still has to be returned, down from more than US$2,100 million when the current government took office. Most of that money is owed to private entities and companies, while new dollar deposits and operations are unrestricted.

For Americans who travel to or do business in Bolivia, the result is a floating exchange rate in a country where dollars are still scarce. How easily they can change money will depend on whether the bank can build its reserves.

The open question is how much of the climb will last, since the balance dipped in the first half of November. The next checkpoints are the 2027 monetary programme, date not confirmed, and the bank’s next reserve figures.

What does Bolivia’s central bank want to do?

It wants its dollar and other foreign-currency holdings to be far higher next year, so that banks and savers feel secure. The exact target is still to come.

Why does the gold matter?

Gold is the largest part of the reserves, so converting some of it would lift dollar holdings without new loans. The idea touches the legal minimum Bolivia sets for gold holdings.

What does this mean for travellers and business visitors?

They face a floating exchange rate in a country where dollars are still scarce. The bank says it will step in if the rate moves suddenly.

World.title: Argentine Judge Backs Fentanyl Lab Tests
World.content:
An Argentine judge has ruled that the tests linking contaminated hospital fentanyl to patient deaths stand, rejecting the main defendant’s bid to void them.

Justice: Argentina

A federal judge in Argentina has refused to throw out the laboratory tests that tie bacteria in contaminated hospital fentanyl to patient deaths, according to a ruling disclosed on Wednesday 25 November 2026. Judge Ernesto Kreplak of Federal Criminal and Correctional Court No. 3 in La Plata, the provincial capital near Buenos Aires, rejected the main defendant’s request to annul the sterility tests, though the exact signing date has not been confirmed.

This is pharmaceutical fentanyl, a hospital anaesthetic and painkiller, and not the street drug Americans know from the opioid crisis. The case involves at least 90 deaths, and it turns on whether the state’s own evidence can survive a challenge in court.

Key Facts Who. Judge Ernesto Kreplak rejected Ariel García Furfaro’s request to void the fentanyl sterility tests.

What. Ruling disclosed Wednesday 25 November 2026 in La Plata; appeals pending, no trial date set.

An Argentine judge has ruled that the tests linking contaminated hospital fentanyl to patient deaths stand, rejecting the main defendant’s bid to void them.

The case file, numbered FLP 17371/2025, began on Thursday 8 May 2025, when ANMAT, Argentina’s national drug regulator, issued an alert on lot 31202 and banned it after the first deaths at the Hospital Italiano de La Plata. Regulators then inspected the laboratories on Monday 12 May 2025 and took samples, the judge noted in his ruling.

The tests at issue covered lots 31201, 31202, 31244 and 31245 of fentanyl made by HLB Pharma, and were run by INAME, the national medicines institute, and the private laboratory Gobbi Novag S.A. Later genetic sequencing by the ANLIS Malbrán Institute, the national reference laboratory for infectious disease, linked bacteria found in the product to bacteria found in victims.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

La Plata Cathedral; the city’s federal court is handling the case (photo: David Alsina, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The main defendant, Ariel Fernando García, known as García Furfaro, owns HLB Pharma and Ramallo, and his lawyer Gastón Matías Marano asked the court to void the tests. Marano argued that the sterility test was an expert opinion needing prior notice to the parties under articles 253 and 258 of the national Code of Criminal Procedure.

He also said Gobbi Novag was a “commercial enemy” of Ramallo and HLB Pharma, and that INAME depends on the Health Ministry, which was a plaintiff at the start of the case. Other co-defendants joined the request, among them Wilson Pons, José Antonio Maiorano, María Victoria García, Javier Tchukrán and Rocío Garay.

Kreplak rejected the request and also refused the alternative plea to repeat the sterility study of the ampoules. He wrote that his court did not order the tests, which INAME and ANMAT staff carried out using health policing powers “en un contexto de suma urgencia a nivel nacional” (in a context of extreme urgency nationwide).

The judge said the defence challenged the positive results only after almost a year and a half of investigation. He said he ruled in line with the opinion of the La Plata Federal Prosecution Unit.

Kreplak described the challenge as one that, “con argumentos formalistas y en última instancia falaces, pretende echar un manto de duda” (with formalistic and ultimately false arguments, tries to cast a veil of doubt) over a point he called “abrumadoramente probado” (overwhelmingly proven). That point is the contamination of lots 31202 and 31244.

Prosecutor María Laura Roteta, head of that unit, had filed a 43-page opinion in early November 2026 asking the judge to reject all the defence challenges. She called the defence premise “falsa” (false) and said the tests ran “mientras se encontraba en curso una crisis sanitaria sin precedentes” (during an unprecedented health crisis).

The ruling says 15 defendants and 90 deaths are under investigation, while earlier court counts reached 111 deaths. The toll is therefore still being fixed, and on Thursday 25 September 2025 Kreplak charged the lab-linked defendants as co-authors of adulterating medicines resulting in at least 20 deaths.

ANMAT cancelled the operating licences of HLB Pharma and Ramallo in a decision, Disposición 1848/2026, published in the Boletín Oficial, the official gazette, on Friday 10 April 2026. All the accused remain defendants until a court convicts, and the ruling keeps the central scientific evidence in the case.

Defence appeals against the earlier indictments are pending before the Federal Chamber of La Plata, an appeals court that has not said when it will rule. After that the judge can send the case to oral trial, but no date has been set.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the judge decide?

He refused to annul the tests or to repeat them, so the evidence linking bacteria in the product to the victims stays in the case.

Is this the street drug?

No. It is a hospital anaesthetic and painkiller made by a pharmaceutical laboratory, which is why the regulator’s role is central.

What happens next?

The Federal Chamber of La Plata must decide the defence appeals, after which the judge can send the case to oral trial. No date has been set for either step.

World.title: Argentina’s Peso Feels 2027 Vote Pressure
World.content:
A year before Argentines choose a president, their bonds, their peso and their parallel dollar are already trading on the election.

File photo. The headquarters of the Banco Central de la República Argentina, Buenos Aires, September 2012. Photo: Diana2803, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Markets: Argentina

Argentina’s bond and currency markets are pricing the presidential election of October 2027 a year early. On Tuesday 24 November 2026, country risk, the extra yield investors demand on Argentine dollar bonds over US Treasuries, closed at 1,094 basis points, the highest level of the year.

The national statistics institute INDEC said on 12 November that consumer prices rose 2.2% in October, a pace the peso’s fall over the past month has now exceeded.

The CCL works by buying a bond in pesos and selling it abroad for dollars. On Tuesday 24 November it closed near 1,800 pesos per dollar, against a gap of about 8% on 11 November.

Argentina holds the first round of its presidential election on Sunday 24 October 2027, the fourth Sunday of October under Article 53 of the National Electoral Code. A government bill would suspend the PASO, the compulsory open primaries held before the general election, for 2027, and the Senate’s constitutional affairs committee signed its report on 18 November.

Economy Minister Luis “Toto” Caputo told a Sociedad Rural Argentina event, a farming-sector association, on 6 November: “What some people fear is that President Milei will not be there.” Javier Milei, in office since December 2023, is the president he meant.

On Monday 16 November, in a radio interview, Caputo said of that fear: “I think that fear is exaggerated.” Finance Secretary Federico Furiase said on 22 October that “sooner rather than later” the market would price in that Milei will “win walking”, Argentine slang for winning without effort, and that he expects no big swings in the dollar in 2027.

Caputo and Furiase call the fear overdone, yet country risk and the CCL gap both widened over the same weeks. The central bank has not said whether it will let the peso move faster, and nobody has shown whether the gap is temporary.

The central bank’s gross international reserves stood at US$49.44 billion on Thursday 19 November, according to the central bank’s own series. That gross figure counts everything the bank holds before subtracting what it owes.

For US investors, Argentine dollar bonds and American depositary receipts, the US-traded shares of firms such as the oil company YPF and the lender Galicia, now carry election risk a year ahead of the vote. For US travellers, the spread between the two dollar rates shows why spending power depends on which rate applies.

INDEC publishes November consumer prices in mid-December, date not confirmed, the next test of whether prices run ahead of the peso. The full Senate is expected to take up the PASO suspension on Thursday 26 November, a date not yet confirmed, and the first round follows on Sunday 24 October 2027.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction-market prices are real-money bets, not polls. On Polymarket, a prediction-market exchange, traders had put US$1,638,880 into the Argentina Presidential Election Winner market by 05:59 ET on Wednesday 25 November 2026.

They priced Milei at 45.5%, Axel Kicillof, the governor of Buenos Aires province from the Peronist movement, Argentina’s largest political tradition, at 29.5%, and Sergio Massa, a former economy minister, at 14.3%. Prices move with the news, so these figures are a snapshot of the morning of 25 November.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does a vote in 2027 move markets now?

Investors price what they expect for policy and the peso, and the government and the market disagree about the outcome. The moves show that disagreement, not a forecast.

What does the CCL dollar tell a reader?

It shows how much more a dollar costs outside the official market. A wider gap means dollars are dearer through that legal route.

Does the government expect trouble?

Economy Minister Caputo calls the fear exaggerated, and Finance Secretary Furiase does not expect big dollar swings next year. Markets are pricing a different view.
