World.title: Las Terrazas Resort offers free night, resort credit and couples massage as new flights to Belize are announced
World.content:
Las Terrazas Resort offers free night, resort credit and couples massage as new flights to Belize are announced

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Las Terrazas Resort on Ambergris Caye is promoting three guest offers, as new airline service continues to expand access to Belize.

The resort’s first offer gives guests a fifth night free when they stay four nights. It is valid through December 15, 2026.

The second offer provides a US$100 resort credit per room, per stay, for bookings of four consecutive nights or more.

The third offer includes one complimentary 60 minute couples massage for guests who book three consecutive nights or more.

The offers come as the Belize Tourism Board announced today that BermudAir will add San Antonio, Texas, to its Belize schedule for summer 2027.

The airline will serve Belize from six US gateways next summer: Fort Lauderdale, St. Pete Clearwater, Raleigh Durham, Orlando Sanford, San Antonio and Boston. The San Antonio flights will operate twice weekly from May 20 through September 6.

BermudAir launched its Fort Lauderdale service on October 26, with four more routes scheduled to begin in December 2026.

Tourism Minister Anthony Mahler said every new service creates more opportunities for travellers to visit Belize and brings added value to the tourism industry.

Summer 2027 flights went on sale today at flybermudair.com.

Details on the Las Terrazas Resort offers are available at lasterrazasresort.com/offers.

World.title: Man’s Best Friend, Brother’s Worst Enemy: Brothers reconcile in court after drunken fight and threats of death over ‘smelly’ dog named Snow
World.content:
Man’s Best Friend, Brother’s Worst Enemy: Brothers reconcile in court after drunken fight and threats of death over ‘smelly’ dog named Snow

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A drunken dispute between two brothers over a black dog named Snow that allegedly escalated into a death threat involving a machete ended peacefully in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court after the younger sibling chose forgiveness over prosecution.

Walter Sheran, 65, walked free after charges of aggravated assault with a machete and threat of death against his younger brother, Kert Sheran, were withdrawn before the Chief Magistrate.

Also present at court was none other than Snow, the four-legged subject of the entire controversy, who accompanied his owner but was not permitted inside the courtroom to give his side of the story.

The incident occurred during the early morning hours of September 23, 2026, at the brothers’ family home following a night of drinking.

According to Kert, the argument started when Walter questioned why Snow was inside the house and called Snow “stinky” and “smelly.”

Kert took offense to his brother’s remarks, and the confrontation allegedly escalated when Walter grabbed a machete and threatened to chop off his younger brother’s head.

Police were called to intervene, and both brothers were initially detained. Walter was subsequently charged.

In court on Tuesday, Kert admitted that both brothers were heavily intoxicated at the time and told the Chief Magistrate that he had forgiven his older brother and wanted no further court action.

Meanwhile, Snow, who reportedly accompanies Kert wherever he goes, waited patiently outside the courthouse. Kert had initially attached the dog’s leash to his belt buckle but secured it to a bench under a tent and asked a security guard to watch over his beloved companion while he went inside to testify.

Kert spent less than five minutes in court.

The charges were subsequently withdrawn, and the brothers were seen leaving the courthouse together, having put their differences aside.

Speaking to Breaking Belize News outside the courtroom, Kert referenced the biblical story of Cain and Abel, explaining that he did not want their family dispute to end in tragedy.

“No time to fight and war against your family. It’s time for peace and make love,” Kert said.

Snow was also present during the interview but declined to comment on the allegations concerning his personal hygiene.

World.title: International News: Decades of gains against AIDS at risk as global HIV funding dries up
World.content:
International News: Decades of gains against AIDS at risk as global HIV funding dries up

By Zoila Palma: Decades of progress in the fight against HIV and AIDS could be reversed as funding shortages threaten access to life-saving treatment, prevention programmes and community health services, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) has warned.

Although advances in medicine have transformed HIV from what was once considered a death sentence into a manageable health condition, the agency says a US$4.3 billion funding gap in low- and middle-income countries is putting those achievements at risk. Currently, approximately 32.1 million of the 40 million people living with HIV worldwide are receiving treatment.

HIV prevention programmes have been among the hardest hit by funding cuts. UNAIDS reported that approximately 446,000 fewer people accessed pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in 2025 compared to the previous year. PrEP use also declined among key populations, including sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender people, and gay men and other men who have sex with men. Global condom distribution fell from three billion to 2.7 billion between 2024 and 2025, while voluntary medical male circumcision procedures declined by 53 percent across priority countries.

UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima warned that weakening prevention services could lead to more infections, increased treatment costs and preventable deaths. She also highlighted the impact of funding cuts on community organizations, many of which provide essential support to vulnerable populations. One study found that more than three-quarters of surveyed civil society organizations experienced service disruptions, while over 80 percent were operating at less than half their capacity by the end of 2025. Byanyima stressed that these organizations are often the only trusted connection between healthcare systems and people most at risk of HIV.

The funding crisis is particularly challenging for countries heavily dependent on international assistance to finance their HIV programmes.

According to UNAIDS, external resources account for as much as 98 percent of HIV funding in Nigeria, 94 percent in Mozambique and 80 percent in Uganda.

International donors also finance all reported HIV prevention spending in Eritrea and Zambia. Meanwhile, mounting national debt and limited government health budgets are making it increasingly difficult for these countries to compensate for reductions in international support.

UNAIDS warned that the full consequences of the 2025 funding cuts may not yet be visible, but disruptions to testing, prevention and treatment services could eventually result in rising infections and AIDS-related deaths.

Warning signs include fewer people being tested or starting treatment, weakening laboratory services and reduced support for patients. Testing for advanced HIV disease declined by 35 percent across six countries between 2024 and 2025. Advanced HIV disease affected approximately 3.4 million people worldwide in 2025, with about one in eight dying within a year, highlighting the importance of early diagnosis and access to specialized care.

Despite the challenges, UNAIDS maintains that ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 remains achievable.

World.title: International News: Shein to pay US$100 million settlement over misleading consumer practices
World.content:
International News: Shein to pay US$100 million settlement over misleading consumer practices

By Zoila Palma: Chinese fast-fashion retailer Shein has agreed to pay US$100 million to settle allegations by the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) that it misled consumers about shipping times, product reviews and the origin of cotton used in some of its products.

The settlement was outlined in court documents filed on Tuesday and will also require the company to make changes to its consumer protection and business practices, Reuters report.

According to the FTC, Shein advertised fast shipping despite knowing that some customers received their orders days or even months late, while others never received their packages. The agency also accused the retailer of filtering out negative product reviews, including complaints about defective items and products that caused skin staining. Under the settlement, Shein must stop misrepresenting shipping times and preventing customers from posting negative reviews. The settlement funds will be used to reimburse affected consumers.

The FTC also raised concerns about the company’s sustainability and supply chain claims. Shein had marketed certain products under its “evoluSHEIN” label, suggesting they came from suppliers with above-average social responsibility audit scores. However, the agency said the company could not provide independent audits to support those claims.

Regulators also questioned Shein’s statements about the origin of cotton used in products sold in the United States, citing testing that was often inaccurate or inconclusive.

Shein said it had not admitted liability and disagreed with some of the FTC’s allegations, but agreed to strengthen its consumer practices and compliance efforts.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture and Food and Agriculture Organization provide coconut pest management training to farmers and students
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture and Food and Agriculture Organization provide coconut pest management training to farmers and students

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), in partnership with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), has conducted a series of specialized training sessions aimed at strengthening Belize’s coconut industry through improved pest and disease management.

The workshops were held across northern and central Belize to help protect coconut production from major phytosanitary threats and promote sustainable agricultural practices.

The training sessions form part of FAO’s global initiative, One Country One Priority Product (OCOP), which is being spearheaded in Belize by the Ministry of Agriculture. In the Corozal District, 27 coconut farmers benefited from a two-day workshop held on October 27 and 28.

The initiative was also extended to academic institutions, reaching more than 50 students at the University of Belize on November 5 and Centro Escolar México Junior College on November 17 and 18.

Participants received practical training on identifying major pests and diseases affecting coconut production, as well as sustainable methods for controlling and managing them. Students also participated in hands-on field and laboratory exercises, allowing them to identify different coconut pests and pathogens while developing a better understanding of plant health and agricultural sciences.

The initiative aims to strengthen the technical capacity of both farmers and future agricultural professionals to protect Belize’s coconut resources.

World.title: Corozal Agriculture Department hosts training on thrips management and pest control
World.content:
Corozal Agriculture Department hosts training on thrips management and pest control

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Corozal Agriculture Department conducted a one-day training workshop focused on integrated thrips management and pest control, as part of efforts to strengthen sustainable agricultural practices and protect local crop production.

The training was held in collaboration with FORAGRO Guatemala representative Ingeniero Hector Mejicanos and BELAGRO representative Carlos Medrano, with coordination support from CRESAP officer Uziel Vasquez.

A total of 20 participants, including agriculture extension officers, attended the workshop to strengthen their technical knowledge and understanding of effective thrips management. The training focused on helping participants identify different thrips species, understand their life cycles, and recognize early signs of pest damage in locally grown vegetable crops.

Among the crops discussed were sweet pepper, watermelon and cucumber, which can be affected by thrips infestations. Participants also received guidance on monitoring techniques, cultural practices, resistance management and broader Integrated Pest Management (IPM) strategies aimed at controlling pests while promoting more sustainable farming methods.

The workshop also featured a presentation on FORAGRO’s thrips control program, including the use of the insecticide Seiken, its mode of action, proper application timing and the importance of rotating insecticides to prevent resistance. Participants also explored an interactive display of agricultural products offered by FORAGRO and BELAGRO.

The Corozal Agriculture Department said the initiative aims to equip extension officers and farmers with the knowledge and practical skills needed to accurately identify pest damage, improve pest control practices and protect crop yields.

World.title: International News: Armed men seize supermarket and take at least 25 hostages in Colombia
World.content:
International News: Armed men seize supermarket and take at least 25 hostages in Colombia

By Zoila Palma: At least 25 people were taken hostage after a group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, today triggering a tense standoff with police.

Colombian officials said the incident began when the suspects fled into the supermarket following an unsuccessful attempt to rob an armored truck, AP reports.

President Abelardo de la Espriella described the suspects as common criminals and said they initially held approximately 30 people hostage before releasing at least five elderly women.

Footage circulating on social media showed dozens of people fleeing the Éxito supermarket in the city’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media reported seeing police snipers positioned on nearby buildings.

The incident also disrupted operations at Cartagena’s airport, which temporarily suspended services before announcing that operations were gradually returning to normal.

World.title: PREDATOR!
World.content:
A 58-year-old Trelawny man who in 2022 dragged a 10-year-old girl into his house, raped her, and later falsely claimed that a relative had sent her to him so he could have sex with her, has been sentenced to 17 years behind bars after he pleaded guilty to the act. He had snatched the girl while she was on her way to fetch water from a spring.

The man, who already spent 10 years behind bars for incest with his own child, and who was also on the Trelawny police’s Most Wanted List for murder, was sentenced by Supreme Court Judge Justice Judith Pusey in the Portland Circuit Court on November 17 after pleading guilty.

In the matter prosecuted by Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Malike Kellier and Crown Counsel Nyron Wright, the child — who lived next door to the man — left her home one evening in June 2022 for the spring and “took a shortcut through his yard”. The man called out to her to “come here a little bit”. The child said she told him, “No, I am going to fill my water bottle,” at which point he jumped towards her, grabbed her by the arm, pulled her into his house and closed the door.

She said he then proceeded to touch her inappropriately and kiss her all over her face, except on her mouth. According to the child, she pushed him and kicked him, telling him to stop, but he ignored her protests and threw her on a bed while trying to remove her clothing.

She said he had partially penetrated her when a knock on the door by her grandmother, who began calling her name, interrupted him. According to the child, her violator told her not to answer or make a sound or he would “thump” her in her mouth. She obeyed.

The relentless grandmother, however, pushed the door down and entered the house, at which point the man replaced the child’s underwear before attempting to push the grandmother from the house.

He further told the child to continue on her journey, ordered her to “pretend” as if she was not in his house, and further threatened to kill her if she told anyone. The matter was reported to the police that same day. He was arrested a day later and subsequently charged with rape and sexual touching of a child.

During his arrest the man, who initially refused to divulge his name to cops, when cautioned declared, “Officer a di [name withheld] send her over deh fi mi [have sex] with her.”

The man later told probation aftercare officers that his marriage deteriorated after his wife accused him of inappropriate conduct with his daughter — for which he was prosecuted and found guilty. He had lived in the community for just under a year when he struck.

A probation aftercare officer who interviewed the convicted man ahead of his sentencing said he “appeared nervous and had a disposition of unease during his interview at the Horizon Adult Remand and Correctional Centre” and that “he struggled to speak definitively about the circumstances surrounding the offences for which he was charged”. According to the officer, he admitted to touching the child on her private parts and kissing her all over her face but “vehemently denied raping her”.

According to the officer, the man expressed regret about his actions but claimed that he was “unable to resist the advances” of the child who, he claimed, was “touching him in an affectionate way”. The official said when challenged about the child’s “cognitive ability to respond from an informed position, based on her age, he retracted his claim and expressed that he could not validate his actions”.

He further told his interviewer that while he recognised the experience may have been traumatic for the child and would cause her to struggle because of memories of that day, he could not see how it would affect her in other ways. Furthermore, he said while he was aware of the embarrassment his actions would cause to his family, and particularly his estranged spouse, he did not believe what he did would affect the wider community. The man has also been accused by community members of engaging in inappropriate conduct with other minors over the years.

In a report produced for the courts in February of this year, at which point the repeat offender had yet to plead guilty, a probation aftercare officer said if the man decided to take responsibility for his actions, a custodial sentence would be a “suitable means of punishment”.

Residents from the area, in the meantime, further described him as “brazen”, alleging that he was also involved in praedial larceny and was seen taking produce from the farms of others. Furthermore, the residents, who said they did not confront him out of fear for their own safety, described his actions as “troubling” to them while expressing “relief” at his departure from the area.

World.title: Precarious position
World.content:
Jonathan Bernard’s house that sits precariously on the hillside in Spring Mount, above a gaping breakaway.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — Faced with uncertainty about the structural integrity of his house, Spring Mount resident Jonathan Bernard is hoping Government will buy the property, even as uncertainty swirls around if and when repairs will be done to the massive breakaway which threatens the building.

Bernard’s house sits atop a hillside, offering him a bird’s-eye view of the collapsed roadway that has cut off vehicular traffic along the Spring Mount and Springfield corridor since last year’s Hurricane Melissa. There had been reports that the purchase of his house was being considered as part of efforts to fix the issue, and Bernard confirmed that discussions had taken place.

“Them come to me about it. The last time I spoke to them was in August and since then there hasn’t been any contact,” he told the Jamaica Observer during a recent visit to the community.

Bernard explained that the two-bedroom, one-bathroom dwelling had been his home for the past 17 years, but he was willing to sell.

“We had made some arrangements as it relates to that, but they haven’t come forward again,” he explained.

“We’ve tried to reach out to them but we can’t get a positive response as to what is happening,” he lamented.

The proposed purchase has become even more urgent because, just over two weeks ago, he received word that heavy equipment was being used to cut into the land on which his house stands. He said the intention was to create space for vehicles to pass.

“It has made the situation worse because I can’t access the place and is there I have all of my stuff. If I need to change my clothes, anything I need to do, that’s where I go because I don’t live anywhere else,” said a forlorn Bernard.

He told the Observer that after the Category 5 storm there had been some indication of danger as the house appeared to have tilted. However, he was still able to access the property then. Now, portions of the columns holding it up are increasingly being exposed as the surrounding soil continues to loosen.

“It wasn’t in danger but a this that them come do now cause the problem. I had my place, I would sleep there,” he said.

“Them just think that my thing has no value. Them want them road and that is the most important thing to them,” Bernard added.

He explained that he began building the house 17 years ago after landing a job at a call centre.

“Most of the material, a me carry them there, most of the blocks a me carry them up there,” he said.

“It’s not like I have money or whatever, it’s [from doing] a 9-5 I work,” he told the

Observer.

Bernard now farms for a living and he has put together a makeshift shelter while he awaits word on his precariously perched house.

“I have a hut in the bush so this is all I have,” he lamented.

Bernard said he has reached out to political representatives in the area and was told that efforts would be made to assist him.

“The councillor said them going to try build up a place where I can store my things, for now, and then he is going to talk to the member of parliament to see if I can get one of the social house them, something to that sort; but I need somewhere to live now,” he appealed.

Initial indications that nearby land would be bought and the Spring Mount breakaway repaired were dashed after the Government said it would be unwise to spend US$250,000 on a fix that likely would not last more than five years. The focus is now on repairing other routes.

World.title: Curtisay the Bessout turns dubplate job into a bouncy single
World.content:
Curtisay the Bessout .

Emerging dancehall artiste Curtisay was supposed to cut a dubplate and remix a track for Latin pop singer Natalie Q. Instead, the talented rhyme-spitter flipped the script and formulated a whole new song.

The producer, Psycho Pablo, loved the song so much it was released as a separate single, Back it Up Senorita, and he still recorded another verse for Natalie Q.

“All of that happened because of my philosophy of doing more than what is asked. I have a mindset centred on initiative, ownership, and value creation; I always try to go above and beyond,” Curtisay the Bessout said.

Released earlier this month, the song is already putting up impressive streaming numbers.

Curtisay the Bessout is excited about the early feedback. The record reflects the pulse of the streets, built for the dancers, with a Spanish lilt in Psycho Pablo’s instrumental and a chorus that tells you what to do with your waist.

As the sing progresses, the verses get more specific. Curtisay uses his lived experiences in the streets to pen songs about DMs, and the ‘genie wine’ to paint portraits with his music.

“Each line in this song is about someone and a real experience. My babymother, after all, is a dancer,” he said.

The first version was raunchier. Then Curtisay took it to Tuff Gong, where the association with Bob Marley made him think twice about just how far to push it. He dialled back the explicit lyrics and came away thinking the edit made the song easier to take abroad.

The studio changed his approach to the vocal, too. He spent years honing his craft to construct the right sound out of his voice. At Tuff Gong, he could relax and let the lower register do its job.

“All I had to do there was be myself,” he said.

When Curtisay drops into those deep tones he remembers Baby Cham passing his gate in a topless luxury car alongside the Topless Crew.

“Nuff Baby Cham influence is in my style,” he said.

He points to Sean Paul and Shaggy for a different lesson in delivery. Both showed him how far a Jamaican cadence can carry when listeners around the world can follow the words.

On Back It Up Senorita he deejayed with a Spanish touch inspired from the beat. The rest comes from nights out in the dancehall, where selectors, dancers, and the crowd let you know quickly whether a chorus works.

Curtisay has spent enough time in other people’s sessions to appreciate having his own voice out front. He contributed Stay With Me to Jah Cure’s Grammy-nominated album The Cure.

Working with Ahzee on Way You Whine, he recalled going through roughly 20 cuts before settling on lyrics. Curtisay usually likes to walk into the booth and leave with a finished song. Ahzee made him sit with the melodies first, a habit he took back to his own work. Writing for other artistes taught him a tougher lesson about what happens when the paperwork comes around.

These days he demands a substantial advance before taking on that kind of job.

For Back It Up Senorita, Curtisay wrote and performed, Psycho Pablo produced the instrumental, and Ramjam handled the mix.

Once it was time to make the video, Curtisay lined up the dancers, helped organise the shoot, and edited the footage after Driz N8 and Great Devoted Generation filmed it.

The artiste who turned a remix brief into his own single had apparently found a few more ways to make himself useful.

Now comes the litmus test: The walking gauntlet that is the essence of dancehall. He wants to see what dancers like Shelly Belly and others do with the chorus at Boom Sundays.

“I can’t wait to see what the reaction will be inna the dances…It’s going to be epic,” he said.

World.title: ‘TIME TO TALK!’
World.content:
Match officials (from left) Ojay Duhaney, Oshane Nation, Stephanie-Dale Yee-Sing, Okeito Nicholson, and Kemar Gayle receive tokens after officiating the Jamaica Premier League football final between champions Cavalier FC and Mount Pleasant Football Academy on May 19, 2024.

MONTEGO Bay United Chairman Yoni Epstein has called for an urgent meeting involving the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), the Jamaica Football Referees Association (JFRA) and Jamaica Premier League clubs to resolve the dispute over outstanding payments to match officials and get the competition back on track.

Epstein says all parties have a responsibility to find a solution as the continued suspension of games is hurting the sport, its sponsors, supporters and players.

Last Sunday’s Jamaica Premier League games were postponed after referees withdrew their services over outstanding payments. The JFRA and Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) — organisers of the competition — were still uncertain up to yesterday about when the games would resume,

JFRA President Valdin Ledgister told the Jamaica Observer that the association was still awaiting more than $2 million promised by the JFF. Ledgister said that as of 1:45 pm on Tuesday, the outstanding amount had not reached their accounts.

The referees had received approximately $3.2 million from the PFJL but were still awaiting the balance, Ledgister said.

“The referees are not in a position to turn out for the games,” he said, adding that the outstanding money had reportedly been sent since Friday.

Ledgister said the dispute had not affected games in the Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competitions, as the referees were not owed any money for those matches.

“We are not owed anything from the ISSA games, and we have clear communication and arrangements with them,” he said.

PFJL Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill, however, says his organisation had fulfilled its responsibilities and was seeking clarification as to why the referees were still withholding their services.

In a letter to JFF General Secretary Gregory Daley dated November 23, Hill said the PFJL had advanced approximately $3.29 million between November 21 and 23 to the referees’ standard payment account, THE RA Limited, to settle the outstanding claims.

Hill said the payments were made without a formal invoice or the complete supporting documentation normally required, as the PFJL sought to prevent the disruption of the competition.

“The PFJL’s position is that all monies brought to its attention in connection with the current payment dispute have been advanced and settled accordingly, and that no further amounts have been formally established as outstanding in relation to the claims presented,” the letter stated.

Hill also questioned why the referees continued to withhold their services without providing an explanation or a reconciliation of any further amounts being claimed.

The PFJL chief executive said there were no new developments regarding the dispute and that the organisation was still awaiting word on when the next round of games would be played.

“We are yet to hear from the parties involved as to when the next scheduled round of games will be played,” Hill said. “The PFJL has a responsibility to its core stakeholders to protect their investment so we continue to seek a resolution.”

Epstein described the situation as a “real travesty” and says the parties need to put aside their differences and find a solution.

“I understand their concerns, and I think that we are all at fault. At the end of the day, the one thing that is suffering is the football. The sponsors, the supporters, the players trying to progress their careers are all suffering because of this situation,” he said.

Epstein says the clubs, JFF, and referees need to meet within the next 24 hours to understand the concerns and resolve the matter, whether in person or virtually.

“The referees feel disrespected, and as stakeholders we need to understand why, and we need to rectify this. Without them, the game cannot be played,” he said.

Epstein says the dispute is damaging the reputation of the JFF and the Jamaica Premier League while also hurting clubs, referees, players, fans and sponsors.

He is urging all parties to work together to find a solution and have the league back on the field by Sunday.

“There is nothing in life that is insurmountable, but we have to get into a room, and we have to get into a room fast in order to solve this situation to get football back on the field come this Sunday, no questions asked.”

World.title: Fi Wi Land: The fight to save Jamaica’s dying lignum vitae
World.content:
A symbol of Jamaica’s natural beauty and national identity, the lignum vitae holds a special place in the island’s heritage. But despite its significance as Jamaica’s national flower, this treasured species is facing growing threats to its survival, raising concerns about the future of one of the country’s national symbols.

Renowned for its exceptionally hard and durable wood, the lignum vitae has faced years of overexploitation, habitat loss and land degradation, contributing to a decline in its population.

With the species subject to international trade restrictions under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), protecting and restoring its population is an important conservation priority.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, Environmental Officer for Flora at the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), Ashleigh Sanderson, sheds light on the threats facing Jamaica’s national flower and the efforts being made to safeguard its future.

From population surveys revealing concerns about its decline to conservation action plans and environmental protection measures, discover how NEPA is working to preserve the lignum vitae and other threatened plant species across the island.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: From ‘Bulbie’ to ‘Blackman’, the evolution of the Klansman gang
World.content:
The United States has designated the St Catherine-based Klansman gang as a transnational criminal organisation (TCO), a move that will bar purported members of the criminal group from entering the country.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness disclosed the development following a recent meeting with US Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura and members of his delegation, who were visiting Jamaica.

The TCO designation is a formal US government label placed on criminal groups that operate across international borders, and includes major criminal outfits and terrorist organisations such as the Sinaloa Cartel and Hezbollah.

During the 2000s and 2010s, the Klansman gang’s violent turf wars in Spanish Town, resulted in police crackdowns like Operation Kingfish, and the arrests and deaths of reputed figures such as Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett and Tesha Miller.

READ: US designates Jamaica’s Klansman Gang as transnational criminal organisation

ORIGINS OF KLANSMAN

Based in the southeastern parish of St Catherine, west of the capital Kingston, despite the name, the Jamaican gang has no connection to the Ku Klux Klan, an American white supremacist group whose members are called “Klansmen”. Anecdotal tales say the local gang was formed when young men met in a house in Dela Vega City and decided to become one ‘clan’, and set up an extortion racket in the Old Capital of Spanish Town.

The history of the Klansman gang is like a top ten Netflix movie: rival factions, secret burial sites, homicidal bosses.

The recent trials of dozens of members of the gang in Jamaica is shedding light on how criminal groups function on the island. At one time, police said the gang was raking in J$1.8 million weekly from extorting mainly business owners and transport operators. The gang also reportedly made money through targeted killings and weapons trafficking.

The gang’s status and organisation also helped rake in the cash. Its primary means of revenue, according to prosecutors, is extortion. One witness said that extortion payments from a section of the bus park in Spanish Town ranged from $80,000 to $100,000 a day.

One popular loan company, Torpedo, also paid up to $150,000 a month to a splinter faction of the gang, claimed one witness. The witness revealed that another organisation, which he refused to name due to security concerns as it includes “powerful individuals”, paid $200,000 a month.

Fifteen members of the One Don splinter faction of the gang, including leader Andre “Blackman” Bryan, were in March 2023 convicted under Jamaica’s anti-gang legislation. Meanwhile, 25 alleged members of the reputed Tesha Miller faction are now before the Supreme Court answering to 16 offences – including murder and robbery – allegedly committed over the span of five years between August 2017 and November 2022.

According to prosecutors and witnesses in the Klansman trial, the criminal outfit is now firmly a third-generation gang. The testimony of two former gang members stated that the Klansman reportedly had some 400 members within its different factions. The gang also had clearly defined roles, corrupt links with the police, international criminal connections and even allegedly carried out hits ordered by a celebrity musician.

Here are some of the generational figures that have defined the history of the Klansman, a firmly established third generation gang with tentacles in St Catherine, Clarendon and even Manchester.

BEFORE ‘BULBIE’: THE ‘PUPPY STRING’ CHAPTER

Derrick “Puppy String” Eccleston was an early leader of the Klansman, before Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett assumed control.

Eccleston was killed on May 12, 1993. His death marked a change in the gang’s leadership, with Bennett subsequently taking over.

Although some accounts alleged Bennett’s involvement in Eccleston’s killing, that allegation was never proven in court.

BALLAD OF ‘BULBIE’

Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett, the leader of the Klansman gang and Jamaica’s most-wanted man for over a decade, was fatally shot on October 30, 2005, during a joint police-military raid in Clarendon.

Bennett gradually built up a criminal empire through murder and extortion whose assets included 80 motor vehicles and heavy equipment used in construction and hauling industries throughout Jamaica.

Authorities believe he gained leadership through the murder of then leader Eccleston in 1993.

During the early 1990s, Bennett led the gang against their rivals, the One Order Gang, resulting in numerous gangland shootings and other violence in Spanish Town.

READ: From ‘Bubba’ to ‘Thickman’: The ill-fated leadership of the One Order Gang

He later established an elaborate extortion operation targeting local business, particularly taximen, in both the central and south central regions of St Catherine. He would later be connected to criminal activities in Old Harbour and Portmore, St Catherine and May Pen.

He was thought to have briefly fled from authorities in Kingston to Great Britain under a false identity in 2001.

In 2005, security forces under Operation Kingfish cornered the 43-year-old Bennett at a lavish, seven-bedroom hideout he had built in the secluded hillside district of Tanaky (near Rock River), Clarendon.

According to police reports, security forces came under gunfire as they approached the compound in the pre-dawn hours. In the ensuing gun battle, Bennett and his driver, identified only as Nathan, were killed.

Police recovered a .50-caliber Desert Eagle pistol from Bennett, a Ruger pistol from his driver, and a large cache of cash and jewelry. At the time of his death, his wealth—amassed through extortion, construction equipment, and heavy haulage—was estimated at over J$100 million.

News of Bennett’s death triggered immediate violent reprisal across Spanish Town. Gang members mounted roadblocks, burned effigies of then-National Security Minister Dr Peter Phillips, and launched a gun attack on the Spanish Town Police Station, injuring two officers.

Following his elaborate funeral in De La Vega City and burial in Goshen, Clarendon, leadership of the Klansman gang allegedly passed to Tesha Miller, a welder by profession.

THE RISE OF TESHA

Tesha Miller, who grew up in Spanish Town after being born in De la Vega City, gained national attention in 2005 when he was charged with four counts of murder and three counts of shooting, for which he received bail.

Miller however, allegedly absconded to the United States.

He is also known on the streets by the nickname “Rat” (sometimes spelled “Ratt”). He has allegedly also used the alias Marlon Andre Williams (or Marlon Williams) on travel documents during past immigration incidents in The Bahamas and Jamaica.

Authorities linked the organisation under his alleged leadership to widespread extortion networks targeting transport operators, bus terminals, and businesses across Spanish Town and St Catherine.

He became even more notorious, attracting national attention over the June 2008 killing of JUTC chairman Douglas Chambers outside the company’s Spanish Town depot. Sentenced in January 2020 to more than 38 years for being an accessory before and after the fact, Miller had those convictions overturned in March 2026 because of jury-selection errors. The Court of Appeal ordered a retrial.

His history also includes capture and deportation from The Bahamas, where he reportedly travelled under a false identity. He is separately standing trial alongside 24 co-accused on an anti-gang indictment concerning alleged offences across several parishes between 2017 and 2022. Miller maintains his innocence and denies leading a gang.

MILLER HAS A LONG RAP SHEET

On May 3, 2007, after being caught by US officials, he was deported to Jamaica and was slapped with a nine-month prison term for absconding bail.

On March 5, 2008, Miller was fined $100,000 for breaching his curfew order.

On July 7, 2008, a cell phone was allegedly found in Miller’s rectum during a search of his cell at Horizon Remand Centre after the device reportedly rang. Miller strongly refuted the claim.

On November 21, 2008, Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn took the decision not to proceed with a triple-murder case against Miller, as the police were having difficulty locating the sole eyewitness in the matter. He had been charged with the murder of Orane Jackson, Jeffrey Johnson and Nicole Allen who were shot in Braeton, St Catherine, on January 14, 2005.

On March 25, 2009, Miller was back before the court, and was denied bail, as he awaited trial for the murder of Rohan Haughton, who was fatally shot on St John’s Road, Spanish Town in April 2004. The eyewitness in the case was reportedly shot dead in St Elizabeth in August 2008.

After being in custody for almost a year, Miller was found not guilty for the murder of Haughton on June 10, 2009 as the Crown offered no further evidence against him as there was nothing to link him to the offence.

On December 26, 2009, Miller was arrested while at the Boxing Day show, Sting, after he allegedly breached a curfew order imposed by the court.

On May 2010, Miller turned himself in to the police after being listed among 25 men wanted for allegedly being gang members and area leaders.

On June 2010, Miller was detained under a State of Emergency. October 15, 2010, Miller was taken into custody for questioning in relation to an upsurge of shootings and other crimes in the St Catherine North Police Division.

On December 21, 2010, Miller was charged with robbery with aggravation involving a motor car and illegal possession of a firearm. Not long after, his 23-year-old sister Renase James was shot and killed while she was a passenger in a taxi in Spanish Town, St Catherine, in December 2011.

On April 15, 2011, Miller was sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment for robbery with aggravation. He was also sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment for illegal possession of firearm with the sentences to run concurrently.

Miller’s conviction for illegal possession of a firearm and robbery with aggravation was quashed and his sentence set aside on March 22, 2013 by the Court of Appeal.

He left Jamaica for the United States of America in April 2013.

Five months later, he was arrested there and charged with illegal re-entry, having previously been deported, and for having an identification card in another person’s name. Miller was convicted of the offences and sentenced to two years and eight months in prison. He was subsequently deported in March 2016. While Miller was in custody in the US, two of his brothers were shot and killed in 2015.

On August 7, 2016, Miller was listed by the police as a person of interest with claims being he could assist with investigations into several murders recorded in Spanish Town and Portmore, St Catherine.

On April 4, 2017, Miller was deported from The Bahamas after illegally entering the country. Fifteen days later, Miller was fined the $100 maximum fine under the law after he pleaded guilty to making a false declaration to Jamaican immigration officials.

THE RISE OF ‘BLACKMAN’

The One Don gang, led by Andre “Blackman” Bryan, emerged as a breakaway faction of the Klansman following a power struggle with reputed leader Tesha Miller around 2017.

Prosecutors alleged that the faction carried out murders, extortion, arson and firearms offences across St Catherine between 2015 and 2019, particularly in Spanish Town and Jones Avenue.

In March 2023, Chief Justice Bryan Sykes convicted Bryan of leading a criminal organisation and facilitating serious offences in a landmark anti-gang trial. Fifteen of the 33 defendants were convicted. Bryan was subsequently sentenced in October 2023 to 39 years and six months in prison.

Bryan was allegedly once the top hitman for reputed Klansman boss, Tesha Miller. The split dates back to at least 2017, when Bryan appears to have rebelled against Miller and began killing his associates.

Bryan’s ability to operate freely was significantly enhanced in 2016 when both men were on trial for the 2008 murder of senior transport official Douglas Chambers. While prosecutors said Miller ordered the hit and Bryan was the gunman, Miller was sentenced to over 38 years in jail for being an accessory before and after the fact, and Bryan was exonerated. Miller’s conviction was subsequently overturned due to jury selection errors.

Witness testimony has painted Bryan as an incredibly violent individual who laughed upon learning targets had been killed. State witnesses said they were forced to join the gang out of fear for their lives.

During sentencing hearings in late September and early October 2023, Bryan addressed the court and openly acknowledged his leadership role, showing his sense of fearlessness and growing hubris.

World.title: ‘Beaver’ supermoon to illuminate skies on Tuesday
World.content:
The Beaver Supermoon captured by James M from Rainham, Kent, UK, 23 November 2026 at 22:19 local time. (Photo: BBC Sky at Night Magazine)

The first of four supermoons expected between the end of 2026 and the beginning of 2027 will light up the night sky on Tuesday.

A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon’s closest approach to Earth, making it appear larger and brighter than usual.

November’s full moon is traditionally known as the Beaver Moon, as it coincides with the period when beavers are typically busy preparing for winter. It is also known by several other names, including the Digging Moon, Deer Rutting Moon, Whitefish Moon, Frost Moon and Freezing Moon.

Tuesday’s full moon is expected to reach peak illumination at 9:53 am, with the best viewing opportunity anticipated shortly after sunset as it rises in the eastern sky.

Sunset in Jamaica is expected at 5:29 pm.

Skywatchers will also have the opportunity to see the moon alongside a cluster of stars known as the Pleiades, or the Seven Sisters.

The remaining three supermoons are expected on December 24, 2026, and January 22 and February 20, 2027.

World.title: Killer strikes again!
World.content:
A 70-year-old Portland man who was out on parole after serving 24 years for killing, dismembering ,and burning a woman with whom he had a relationship in 1989, has been sent back to prison after he again chopped and killed another woman with whom he claimed to be in a relationship in 2021.

The man, Jasper Jemison, otherwise called Sojie, a farmer of Hopefield District in the parish, had been sentenced to life in prison for the first murder.

On November 17 this year Jemison, who has been before the courts since 2022, pleaded guilty to the July 2021 murder of Cynthia Hinds, also called Tiney, in St Margaret’s Bay.

Supreme Court judge Justice Judith Pusey, who presided over the trial, slapped Jemison with a 25-year sentence at hard labour. He will be eligible for parole after serving 20 years.

The case was prosecuted by Acting Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Malike Kellier and Crown Counsel Nyron Wright.

The court heard that Hinds left her home on the morning of July 22, 2021 for her farm, which was neighbouring Jemison’s, on lands located across from Ken Jones Aerodrome in St Margaret’s Bay. Her partner, after calling her several times on her cellular phone with no success, later that morning went to her farm and found her hut ablaze, but saw no sign of her.

After summoning help, the partner, along with Hinds’ daughter and a police corporal, who was seen along the way, returned to the farm and attempted to put out the blaze. Hinds’ charred body was then found face down with the lower part of the right leg missing.

Investigations led to Jemison being taken into custody after it was discovered that he was the last person to see her alive. Three days later he told cops in a caution statement that he and Hinds were in a quarrel when he chopped her, using her own machete, after she attacked him. He claimed she then fell into a fire in her hut where she had been cooking and was burnt.

Jemison later led the lawmen to his farm where he dug up the machete that he had buried. A day later, in the presence of his attorney, Jemison was charged with murder and arson. When cautioned he said, “Officer, mi neva mean fi kill Tiney, and when mi tell yuh seh mi slap her wid mi cutlass, mi mean fi seh chop.”

When cautioned for the offence of arson, Jemison made no comment.

He later claimed during an interview before sentencing that he had been “experiencing remorse since the incident”, claiming he had shared an intimate relationship with Hinds and described her as a good person who was well regarded by himself and the community.

Vaginal swabs of Hinds’ body revealed semen which matched buccal swabs taken from Jemison, according to the evidence unveiled in the matter.

An assessment of the farmer, who claims to be a Muslim, by the Portland Probation Office said Jemison’s behaviour was of “significant concern, particularly given that he was previously convicted of murder and was afforded the opportunity of clemency through parole”.

In noting concern that the crime was committed while he was on parole for another crime, the parole office said it suggested that his previous experience with the justice system did not “sufficiently deter him from further offending”.

Additional concern was voiced over the fact that Jemison appeared to have withheld information from investigators about his behaviour, as community and family members said before the murder Jemison began “consuming alcohol and displaying behaviours they considered uncharacteristic of him”.

Probation officers further lamented the fact that his age had not acted as a deterrent noting, “Research on recidivism identifies age as an important consideration in understanding patterns of offending… studies have generally establish that offending tends to peak during adolescence and early adulthood before declining as individuals advance in age. However, at the age of 70, Mr Jemison has found himself once again before the court.”

The probation officers also said, “The offender’s actions suggest not only a lack of appreciation for the value of the lives of others but also a resistance to societal norms and values. In addition, his violation of the conditions of his parole order further indicates that community supervision has been ineffective and a custodial sentence is therefore the most appropriate disposition of this matter before this Honourable Court.”

In the murder of then 19-year-old Dorothy Williams for which Jemison was first tried and convicted, he had, for days, told individuals, including the man he accused her of cheating on him with, that she had gone to Kingston and would return shortly.

Ironically, that man was among the people who discovered the body of Jemison’s second victim.

When Jemison confessed to the first murder in February 1989, he told police who had taken him into custody as a person of interest that on January 31 he was going down a steep hill with his cutlass in hand and Williams was behind him. He said she held onto his shoulders and both of them slid down the gully bank at which point she fell onto the cutlass and started to bleed from her neck.

He claimed that he covered her up with a bag and decided not to tell anyone. He told the court at the time that when he returned another day “something had eaten her hands and feet and so he put trash on the body and burnt it”.

He was found guilty in the Port Antonio Circuit Court and sentenced to life. Jemison lost a subsequent appeal in which the court ruled that the burnt body was enough for the jury to infer that he was responsible for Williams’ death and that there was sufficient evidence to rebut the defence of an accident.

World.title: Parliament clears 7 EU budget files for negotiations
World.content:
The European Parliament voted by large majorities to send seven proposals for the EU’s next long-term budget straight into negotiations with the Council, heading off a possible challenge from the far right.

The lawmakers were voting on the proposals for Global Europe, the European Social Fund, Horizon Europe, the Connecting Europe Facility, the European Competitiveness Fund, the asylum and migration program and AgoraEU.

These proposals are now moving to negotiations with the Council of the European Union based on reports adopted by the committees responsible for each file.

World.title: Sánchez to skip EU summit before Spanish election
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will delegate his voting powers to French President Emmanuel Macron as he won’t be able to attend the European Council summit on Thursday and Friday, according to an EU diplomat.

Spain heads to the polls on Sunday, with Sánchez at risk of losing his parliamentary majority. On Thursday evening, he will face conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, far-right leader Santiago Abascal and left-wing alliance chief Ada Colau in the final debate of the campaign.

Sánchez has opted for a liberal leader from another big country, rather than delegating to fellow center-left figures such as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen or Malta’s Robert Abela.

World.title: He’s coming home: Catalan leader Puigdemont plans return to Spain
World.content:
The former Catalan president hinted he’s prepared to lead the independence movement once again.

Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont will return to Barcelona on Dec. 12, ending nearly a decade of self-imposed exile in Belgium.

“I will return to Catalonia without asking for permission and without asking for forgiveness,” Puigdemont said at a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday. The former Catalan president initially fled to Belgium in October 2017 to avoid prosecution over his role in the region’s 2017 unauthorized independence referendum.

Spanish authorities spent years trying to extradite the separatist leader but Belgian judges repeatedly thwarted their efforts. In 2024, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opened the door to his return by securing the passage of a sweeping amnesty for those involved in the independence movement in exchange for crucial support from Puigdemont’s center-right Junts party.

World.title: Von der Leyen: Energy ceasefire would show Putin is serious about peace talks
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addresses members of the European Parliament during a plenary session, in Strasbourg northeastern France, on November 25, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/ AFP via Getty Images

“A strong European team will participate in the next round of talks” on Ukraine, the European Commission chief tells lawmakers.

STRASBOURG — Vladimir Putin’s agreement to a winter energy ceasefire and a Black Sea truce to allow Ukrainian food exports “would show that Russia is serious about negotiations,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday morning.

“As discussed at last week's coalition of the willing meeting, Russia should agree to a winter ceasefire on energy infrastructure, and a truce to ensure the safe passage of food exports through the Black Sea,” she told European lawmakers at a Parliament debate in Strasbourg. Von der Leyen met with the coalition to discuss the European position on Ukraine-Russia peace talks brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump.

She added the Commission was helping strengthen Kyiv's hand at the negotiations by stepping up sanctions and providing cash so as to put pressure on Russia, which persistently bombards cities across Ukraine in an unrelenting military assault.

World.title: Ukraine’s raid in Libya damaged more than a Russian warship
World.content:
From a military perspective the operation was indeed another one of Ukraine’s audacious commando missions. It was reminiscent of the derring-do spirit of Winston Churchill’s “Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare,” better known as the Special Operations Executive, which mounted commando raids along the French coast, causing havoc and raising British wartime morale during WWII .

In fact, the day before, while visiting Kyiv, Britain’s defense secretary Wes Streeting had coincidentally compared Zelenskyy to Britain’s iconic wartime leader.

The comparison was ironic given the circumstances. Despite Churchill’s impatience and determination to take the fight to the enemy, the wartime prime minister was careful to avoid breaching the laws of armed conflict at sea. He didn’t, for example, order British warships to sink the German cruiser Admiral Graf Spee when it was cornered in Montevideo after the Battle of the River Plate. The trapped warship’s captain ultimately decided to scuttle the ship.

But Zelenskyy wasn’t so restrained this week. According to international legal scholars, the attack likely violated international law as well as Libya’s sovereignty. The country’s eastern administration, based in Benghazi, has called on the U.N. to investigate the sinking as well as “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts or military units” in western Libya.

The Libyans would have a good case if they lodged a complaint with the International Court of Justice, said David Letts, a retired Australian naval officer and now director of the military law program at the Australian National University in Canberra. “Unless you’re wanting to mount an argument that Libya is somehow involved in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia and neutrality doesn’t apply, I’m struggling to see how this sinking sits within the law,” Letts said.

Letts is one of the authors of the Newport Manual on the Law of Naval Warfare, a compilation of legislation published and updated by the U.S. Naval War College. He says Ukraine’s Benghazi attack is “quite different when compared to their strikes against Russian vessels in the Black Sea and in Black Sea ports” in disputed and not neutral waters.

World.title: EU Commission failed to deliver cage ban, court finds
World.content:
Animal welfare groups can celebrate a win after bringing the case in 2024, accusing the EU executive of ignoring a European Citizens’ Initiative to ban cages for all farmed animals.

The ruling, while a win for NGOs, has its caveats. The court does not detail by when the Commission must act. What’s more, the EU executive could still avoid taking action if it formally withdraws its promise to phase out cages for these animals.

Following the initiative, which gained almost 1.4 million signatures, the former Commission promised in 2021 to deliver a timeline for banning cages for a list of animals before the end of 2023. When that did not happen, a group of NGOs sued the Commission.

The Commission is obliged to follow through on the promises it made in response to the ECI, regardless of a change in the assembly of commissioners, according to the court.

The NGO leading the case, Compassion in World Farming, said the Commission confirmed in a letter it would not withdraw its promise, according to CIWF Director Debbie Tripley.

The court declined another request from the NGOs for access to internal Commission documents. Still, CIWF said the coalition of animal welfare groups would not appeal the case to the Court of Justice of the EU.

World.title: French justice minister opens probe into prosecutor seen at far-right HQ
World.content:
Gérald Darmanin looks on during a press conference in Paris on Nov. 18, 2026. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images

The prosecutor was discovered at Marine Le Pen’s party headquarters during a police raid, but said he was only there to meet an acquaintance.

PARIS — French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin has ordered an internal investigation to determine why a prosecutor was at Marine Le Pen’s National Rally headquarters when police raided the offices earlier this month.

“We need to clear up a point of ambiguity: Did senior officials provide information to the National Rally, which would obviously be a crime against their office and the high regard they hold for their independence?” Darmanin told France Inter radio on Wednesday.

Christian de Rocquigny, a Paris-based prosecutor, was at the far-right party’s headquarters when police arrived as part of an investigation into allegations that an interior ministry official had leaked confidential judicial information to the National Rally. The official, Hugues Moutouh, has resigned as the senior state representative in the Centre-Val de Loire region and is officially leaving office Wednesday.

World.title: EU Commission warns budget cuts will leave governments worse off
World.content:
His remarks set the scene for tough discussions among leaders on Thursday and Friday. One EU diplomat, granted anonymity to speak freely, said this was likely to be a “bloody” European Council as governments are not ready to compromise on their red lines.

Costa is keen to make progress in negotiations ahead of another summit on the Multiannual Financial Framework starting on Dec. 17. But EU governments are divided over the total size of the budget, with Germany leading a push to shave off further tens of billions from the Commission’s proposal.

“Further substantial cuts are needed to reduce the massive increases compared with the current MFF to a reasonably affordable level,” the German government wrote in an internal note seen by POLITICO.

Berlin also renewed calls to reintroduce discounts on the budget contributions from wealthier countries, known as rebates. “It is a basic prerequisite for any agreement,” it wrote.

But in a more conciliatory move, Germany said it will examine a proposed EU-wide tax on digital giants “with an open mind.”

Serafin dismissed claims that the size of the EU budget is increasing. He argued instead that the proposal on the table is lower than the current seven-year budget that entered into force in 2021 as a share of gross national income.

World.title: From the track to the gallery: Dakar's autumn in the spotlight
World.content:
This November, Dakar hosted two exceptional events: the Youth Olympic Games, which ran until 13 November, and Dak'Art, the Dakar Biennale of contemporary African art, which runs from 19 November to 19 December. The Games were the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent, and the Biennale now brings together artists from across Africa and its diaspora. In this episode, we hear from participants in both events.

Advertising

Dakar, Senegal, hosted the Youth Olympic Games from 31 October to 13 November, a landmark event widely celebrated across the country..

It was the fourth edition of the Games for young athletes, but the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent.

Dancers form the word "Dakar" during the opening ceremony of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games at the Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio on 31 October, 2026. © AFP - SEYLLOU

In this episode, you'll hear from Kirsty Coventry, President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and from RFI English's sports journalist, Paul Myers. Both agree that it was a unique event, and they look ahead to the future of the Games in Africa.

As Senegal sets Youth Games medal record, Olympic hero calls for more investment

After sport, there's art

Then, just a few days after the Games closed, Dakar launched Dak'Art on 19 November. The Biennale runs until Saturday 19 December 2026 and features artists from across the continent and its diaspora.

The theme of this edition is "(Anti)fragility", which, according to the curator and organisers, refers to "the capacity to turn fragile situations into a space for invention and expressive power".

The main venue is the former Law Courts building, now the National Art Gallery.

Cultural exchanges beyond borders as African art gains global interest

"The project emphasises social and community bonds, co-creation, acts of care, and responses that allow the experience of shocks to be transformed into new possibilities," the curator said.

This year's artists include Nu Barreto from Guinea-Bissau, who won one of the main prizes; Ibrahima Cissé and Eva Diallo, both from Senegal; Chemu Ng'ok from Kenya; and Souad Abdelrasoul from Cairo, among many others.

Billboards advertising the Dakar Biennale 2026, the 16th Dakar Biennale of Contemporary African Art, the most important event of its kind on the continent, which showcases the best of African art and its diasporas through hundreds of cultural events combining painting, sculpture, and performance. © Patrick Meinhardt / AFP

Alpha Thiam, Senegal's Minister of Culture, Crafts and Tourism, said these events were "drawing on the philosophy of Senghor" and embracing "modernity without ever forsaking our authenticity".

In his view, the participants show that "contemporary African creation is not merely a superficial construct, but a genuine assertion of sovereignty", allowing Africans to build their future on their own terms.

In this episode, Souad Abdelrasoul, who had just arrived in Dakar for the opening, and her gallery manager, Menna Genedy, of the Misr Gallery in Cairo talked to RFI.

You'll also hear from the Senegalese storyteller, or griot, Bocar Niang, and his associate, the artist and philanthropist Amélie Mourgue d'Algue, of the French charity the Bureau of Invisible Hours (Bureau des heures invisibles).

Dak'Art is also an opportunity for other artists from the region to share their work. Among them is Bocar Niang, a griot, poet and performer, who has set up his own museum in his hometown of Tambacounda. The museum is dedicated to the culture of griots, the travelling musicians and storytellers who keep the tradition of oral history alive in parts of West Africa.

Beyond Senegal

Dakar is also a meeting point for artists from all over Africa, especially in the 'off 'programme.

The book, Made in Sierra Leone — Edition 02, will be unveiled during the fair for instance; it is the expanded second edition of the limited edition book by multidisciplinary artist Sahr Martin Kabba known as Sabanoh, from Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Made in Sierra Leone, Edition 02: by artist Sabanoh © Unx-art

The publication extends his exploration of Sierra Leone’s contemporary visual language through image, design, and cultural memory, as the artist and the curator, Sarah Hachi-Duchene of Unx-art, tell us.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.
