World.title: Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated rights of migrants sent back to Belarus, finds European court
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland, Lithuania and Latvia violated the human rights of migrants from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba who entered their countries illegally from Belarus in 2021 and 2022, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ruled. However, the ECHR did also recognise that states have the right to prevent the entry of migrants who have been “instrumentalised” by Belarus in order to create a crisis on the European Union’s eastern borders. That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation. 📽️ Watch a video explainer on the Grand Chamber cases concerning instrumentalisation of migration. 📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile. In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus. On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus. The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”. This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention. However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”. That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus. In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants. A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence. One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024 For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis. The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus. However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR. The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation. Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025 In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”. At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk. However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention. It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures. ⚖️ Grand Chamber cases ➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections. 🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1 — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026 In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”. He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration. “In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC. Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka. Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją. Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic. — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026 A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards. In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border. Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted. The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration. This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross. World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland in response to last week’s incident in which three Russian missiles struck Polish territory. Shortly after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone that entered from Ukraine. However, although the military was given authorisation to shoot the object down, they did not do so after the drone began to move back into Ukraine. Today, NATO Ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss last week’s violations of Polish airspace. This was a dangerous incident and Russia bears full responsibility. NATO and Allied assets reacted quickly to the airspace violations, and the Supreme Allied Commander… — NATO Spokesperson (@NATOpress) November 23, 2026 On Friday morning last week, three objects struck at different locations in southeast Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine, and on Sunday Poland confirmed that all three were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. The missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before striking the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which were patrolling Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met. However, the pilots were unable to confirm their identity in time due to poor weather conditions. On Monday, an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, took place to discuss the incident. Afterwards, deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski, who represented Poland at the meeting, announced that NATO had agreed to place an AWACS “at Poland’s disposal”. Later, NATO’s spokeswoman, Allison Hart, confirmed that “the Supreme Allied Commander Europe has authorised the forward deployment of a NATO AWACS aircraft” and is also “examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere”. Poland has confirmed that the three objects which struck its territory last Friday were all Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. Preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia https://t.co/4N6k3eBUGN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 23, 2026 “This is a very serious capability that gives us enhanced situational awareness,” said Zalewski, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “This is an immediate NATO response, and we are very happy about it.” “What I heard today is a great demonstration of the alliance’s unity with Poland in the face of Russian attacks,” he added. “It’s safe to say that the Russians have moved up the escalation ladder in their relations with NATO.This means…the need for an appropriate response.” Zalewski emphasised that “we’re not talking about offensive actions in any way, but about the ability to defend against all the attacks Russia is launching against NATO countries”. The aim is “not to escalate, but to…discourage Russia from attacks”. Wiceminister @ZalewskiPawel w Kwaterze Głównej #NATO: Do dyspozycji Polski będzie jeden samolot szybkiego ostrzegania #AWACS. To jest bardzo poważna zdolność, która daje nam pogłębioną świadomość sytuacyjną. I to jest natychmiastowa reakcja NATO. — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 23, 2026 On Monday night, after NATO had made its decision, Poland’s airspace was again violated, this time by a Russian drone that crossed the border from Ukraine. The operational command of Poland’s armed forces announced shortly before midnight that it had continuously tracked the object and granted authorisation to shoot it down. However, after the drone changed course and began to head east, back towards the border, a decision was made to refrain from engaging it, “taking into account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object”, said operational command. W trakcie nocnego ataku Federacji Rosyjskiej na cele w zachodniej części Ukrainy, prowadzonego z wykorzystaniem środków napadu powietrznego, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej przez rosyjski bezzałogowy statek powietrzny. W odpowiedzi na… pic.twitter.com/BhJN7UYg7m — Dowództwo Operacyjne RSZ (@DowOperSZ) November 23, 2026 According to a report by broadcaster RMF, based on unnamed sources, the vehicle was a jet-powered drone that flew 20 km into Poland and remained in Polish airspace for around nine minutes. Speaking to RMF on Tuesday morning, Zalewski said that “it is difficult to imagine that this was an accident; we assume it was an intentional action”. Russia has so far not commented on either its missiles hitting Poland last Friday nor the latest drone incursion. They are the latest in a series of airspace violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. In September 2025, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders in an unprecedented violation that prompted Poland to trigger NATO’s Article 4. The Netherlands will become the latest country to purchase Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defence systems, which have been increasingly in demand following their successful use during Ukraine’s defence against Russia. On Monday, their Polish manufacturer, Mesko, which is part of state-owned defence group PGZ, signed an agreement adding the Netherlands to a list of countries that will buy Pioruns with funds from the European Union’s SAFE mechanism for financing defence spending. 🇵🇱🇳🇱⚡ HOLANDIA DOŁĄCZA DO DRUŻYNY PIORUNA! W @PGZ_MESKO_SA w Skarżysku-Kamiennej podpisano aneks do umowy ramowej, umożliwiający Holandii dołączenie do wspólnych zamówień zestawów PIORUN. ✍️ Dokument podpisali gen. dyw. Artur Kuptel, Szef @AgencjaUzbr, oraz Krzysztof Marwicki… pic.twitter.com/lVH0QgdD0t — Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa🇵🇱 (@PGZ_pl) November 23, 2026 Piorun (meaning “thunderbolt” in Polish) is a shoulder-mounted system that fires air-defence missiles capable of destroying aerial vehicles, such as helicopters, drones and low-flying planes, at short range. In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment that Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems have been successfully used to take down Russian aircraft. Since then, they have been in high demand, with Mesko receiving orders from the United States, Norway, Belgium and Sweden, as well as Ukraine itself. In August this year, Mesko signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.8 billion) agreement to supply further Piorun systems to Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia, with the deal financed through SAFE funds. Precise details were not revealed. However, the agreement was said to involve the supply of “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles, with over 80% of the equipment going to Poland’s own armed forces. Now Mesko has signed an addendum to that deal, adding the Netherlands to the list of countries that are jointly ordering Pioruns. Deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who has overseen Poland’s participation in the SAFE programme, said after attending Monday’s signing ceremony that the Netherlands would not be the last country to join the procurement of Pioruns. “We promised that the list of Mesko’s buyers from all over Europe would grow, and today we have living proof of that,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “And I can reveal a secret: it’s not over yet.” She noted that Mesko has stepped up its production volumes in response to demand. Last year, it could produce “several hundred” systems annually; that has now risen to 1,500, and is set to grow even further. Last week, PGZ and the state assets ministry signed an agreement to support Mesko’s expansion with around 370 million zloty from the state Capital Investment Fund (FIK). It will help bring production capacity to around 2,500 per year. 🗣️ "Obiecywaliśmy, że lista kupujących z całej Europy będzie się powiększać i mamy tego żywy dowód. A mogę zdradzić sekret, że to jeszcze nie koniec. Dzisiejsza umowa to umowa w ramach zakupów w mechanizmie SAFE"@magdasobkowiak o zestawach Piorun dla Holandii ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/sTxG5SwnbZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 23, 2026 Growing demand for Pioruns resulted in Mesko last year posting the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year. The EU’s SAFE programme is providing a total of €150 billion in loans at preferential rates for member states to use on defence-related spending. Poland, with around €44 billion, is the largest single recipient. While most SAFE purchases are conducted individually by member states, some are also carried out jointly. Such joint procurement can also involve certain non-EU countries, such as Norway. World.title: Public astronomical observatory opens in Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday. Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment. The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall. “Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening. “Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added. The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express. “The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper. “We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added. Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation. The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking. This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions. The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope. The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 The observatory also features a computer coordinating its measurements, a camera showing almost the entire sky, and a weather monitoring system. Observations will depend on atmospheric conditions and visibility. “Examples of how this telescope might be used include photographing the cosmos and conducting simple research, such as measuring changes in the brightness of stars and producing graphs illustrating these changes,” explained Ewa Konarzewska from Gocław Culture Terminal. Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last year, the country launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest-ever contract with the European Space Agency, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Meanwhile, 2025 also saw astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski become the second-ever Pole to travel into space, as part of an ESA mission to the International Space Station. Earlier this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new ESA centre focused on civil security and resilience, with the agency’s head declaring that “Poland has rapidly become one of the driving forces in Europe’s space sector”. They added that preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia. The objects struck at three different locations in southeastern Poland – Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Mołodycz – not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. No injuries or damage to infrastructure was reported as a result of the strikes on Poland. Dubna is home to MKB Raduga, the Russian aerospace firm that produces Kh-101 missiles. “Kremlin trolls will once again try to convince Poles that these are not Russian missiles,” wrote Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, “but the evidence nips those lies in the bud.” Ireneusz Nowak, the operational commander of the Polish armed forces, revealed on Friday that the three missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before hitting the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which are helping patrol Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, had attempted to intercept the missiles. However, the pilots were unable to confirm the identity of the objects in time, largely because of “extremely difficult weather conditions”, said Nowak, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily. World.title: FedEx-led consortium completes €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm. Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange. The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK. A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private. InPost has delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Founder Rafał Brzoska stays on as CEO, and the company remains headquartered in Poland. pic.twitter.com/HWigKVPC3w — IPO Newsroom (@IPONewsroom_) November 20, 2026 Under the deal, FedEx and Advent, an American private equity firm, each hold 37% of InPost. A&R Investments, Brzoska’s own investment vehicle, has 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. PPF, A&R and Advent were previously already stakeholders. The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion. In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team. “InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent. They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another. “InPost has built a leading position in Europe’s out-of-home delivery segment,” said FedEx’s CEO and president, Raj Subramaniam. “Connecting our global network…with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth.” Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”. President Macron has thanked Polish delivery giant InPost for its latest investment in France The firm, which already operates over 9,000 parcel lockers in France through its subsidiary Mondial Relay, will now spend a further €500m to expand its presence https://t.co/caOGNQemfm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 InPost is the largest operator of parcel lockers in Europe, with around 70,000 across the continent. That includes roughly 30,000 in Poland and 16,000 in the UK, including in branches of the British Post Office, with over 23,000 more in the seven Eurozone countries where InPost operates. In the second quarter of 2026, InPost had revenue of 4.18 billion zloty (€970 million), up 18.2% year on year, while its number of parcels handled rose 16% to 380.9 million. The strongest revenue growth came in the eurozone, where sales increased 37.9%, followed by Poland, with 12.7% growth. Revenue in the UK and Ireland rose 9.8%. World.title: Christmas Trees You Can Replant After the Holidays Are Available in Prague
World.content:
Christmas trees do not have to end up on the pavement once the festive season is over.

In Prague and Brno, residents can buy small fir trees with intact roots and take part in planting them back in the forest the following spring.

The Forests of the Capital City of Prague (Lesy hl. m. Prahy) are running their Christmas Fir with a Future project for the tenth consecutive year.

Sales began on November 23, with each potted silver fir priced at 150 CZK.



The trees are approximately 50 centimetres tall and come from the forest nursery in Čimický háj. Unlike cut Christmas trees, they retain their roots and can be planted in the forest once the holiday season is over.

The organizers do not promise perfectly shaped Christmas trees. Some are smaller, others have irregular branches, and no two look exactly alike. The idea is to give people a tree that can continue growing rather than be discarded in January.

The project also supports the return of silver fir (Abies alba) to Czech forests. The species is native to the country but declined significantly during the 20th century, partly because of air pollution, forestry practices and excessive numbers of wild animals.

Trees are available at several locations in Prague, including the Ďáblice Garden Center, the Prales eco-centre and forest lodges in Hostivař, Chuchle, Šárka, Běchovice, Kunratice and Čimice.

How to Keep a Potted Christmas Tree Alive

A potted fir needs more attention than a conventional cut tree, particularly when moving between cold outdoor conditions and a heated home.

The tree should remain outside, preferably on a balcony or in a garden, for as long as possible. Before bringing it indoors, allow it to adjust gradually to the higher temperature.

Once inside, keep it in a room where the temperature does not exceed 20 degrees Celsius. Regular watering is essential, and misting the needles with water can also help prevent them from drying out.

After Christmas, the tree should be moved back outdoors gradually, rather than exposed immediately to a sudden change in temperature.

World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

You can visit META stand at Schola Pragensis, Prague’s high school fair, taking place from 26 to 28 November at the Prague Congress Centre

– stand number 245 on the 2nd floor.

The META team of professionals will help you explore the options and answer all your questions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: EF English Proficiency Index: Brno Speaks Better English Than Prague
World.content:
Prague has improved its English proficiency score, but it still trails Brno, according to the latest EF English Proficiency Index (EF EPI).

The Czech capital gained nine points over the past year, while Brno recorded a slight decline. Despite the contrasting trends, the South Moravian city remains ahead.



The Czech Republic ranked 24th out of 117 countries and regions in this year’s global index, published by education company EF Education First. Its score of 569 points represents a drop of 13 points and one place compared with the previous year.

The country remains in the high-proficiency category, although several neighboring states performed better. Austria ranked second worldwide with 613 points, followed by Germany in fourth place with 611. Slovakia came 11th with 594 points, while Poland ranked 15th with 587.

Slovakia’s performance is particularly notable. The country has gained 49 points since 2016, making it one of Europe’s most improved performers over the past decade. Although its score fell slightly compared with last year, it still leads the Czech Republic by 25 points.

Brno Maintains Its Lead Over Prague

Brno scored 613 points in this year’s assessment, placing it 28 points ahead of Prague, which recorded 585.

The gap between the two cities has narrowed, however. Prague improved from 576 points last year, while Brno fell from 620.

Brno’s result is particularly strong in an international comparison. Its score matches Austria’s, which ranked second among the countries included in the global index.

The regional figures also support Brno’s position. The South Moravian Region recorded 606 points, the highest score among Czech regions.

Sweden Takes First Place in Global Rankings

The Netherlands has lost its position at the top of the global English proficiency rankings, with Sweden taking first place this year with 615 points.

The Dutch finished fifth with 609 points. Austria, Denmark and Germany occupied the places between them, scoring 613, 612 and 611 points, respectively.

The survey was conducted through the Ipsos Instant Research application and focused on respondents’ self-assessments of their language abilities.

World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Colours of Ostrava official 💛 (@colours_cz)

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Prague’s Abandoned Vyšehrad Station Begins Its Transformation Into Apartments
World.content:
Work has begun on the redevelopment of Prague’s historic Vyšehrad railway station, set to become part of a residential complex with 138 micro-apartments, shops and two new buildings.

Developer Karlin Port Real Estate, led by Milorad Mišković and his business partner Miki Goldshtein, began preparatory work at the end of October.

The company plans to start the main renovation and construction works in March 2027.



The developer acquired the station and surrounding land in early 2024 from Cyprus-based company Miquelira Limited, which has been linked to businessman František Savov. The deal followed months of negotiations and extensive checks, as the listed historic building was in a serious state of disrepair.

The plans include the restoration of the original station building and construction of two additional buildings. The development will offer 138 micro-apartments, around 50 underground parking spaces and up to 13 retail units on the ground floor.

The apartments will be sold rather than operated as rental accommodation. According to Mišković, they could appeal to students, young professionals, investors and families looking for temporary accommodation for children studying in Prague.

The developer also wants to improve the wider neighbourhood, including the streets connecting the station with Albertov and the Vltava riverfront.

More projects planned across Prague

Karlin Port Real Estate is also preparing other residential developments in the capital. In Hostivař, the company plans to start construction of the Výhledy Košík project in 2027. It will include 228 apartments and approximately 1,500 square metres of retail space.

The company is also exploring opportunities involving former railway properties and preparing to enter Prague 9, where it plans to focus on the redevelopment of former industrial sites.

Mišković said brownfield regeneration remains his main interest, although the company is now considering projects across Prague rather than concentrating exclusively on the city centre.

World.title: 9 Czech Castles and Chateaux to Visit During Advent 2026
World.content:
Christmas markets are not the only way to enjoy the festive season in Czechia.

Across the country, castles and chateaux are preparing special Advent programmes, with decorated interiors, traditional markets, candlelit tours and activities for families.

Here are nine places worth visiting in the weeks leading up to Christmas and during the holiday season.



1. Loučeň Chateau

Located in Central Bohemia, Loučeň Chateau is hosting a Christmas exhibition titled The Story of the Christmas Tree until January 17, 2027.

Visitors can also explore the illuminated Labyrinths of Light in the castle park. One of the main highlights will take place on November 28, when the country’s largest Advent wreath will be blessed in the courtyard.

Special Advent tours and children’s programmes will run throughout December.

2. Karlštejn Castle

One of Czechia’s most famous castles will also welcome visitors with Christmas decorations.

From November 27, 2026, to January 3, 2027, selected tours of the Imperial Palace will include festive decorations and an introduction to Christmas traditions associated with the court of Charles IV.

The castle will be closed from December 21 to 25.

3. Sychrov Chateau

Sychrov Chateau in the Liberec Region will host its traditional Advent Market on November 28 and 29.

The market will feature Christmas decorations, seasonal products and food stalls in the castle courtyard.

Visitors planning a trip during the Christmas holidays can also explore the decorated interiors through self-guided tours from December 27 to January 3, 2027.

4. Křivoklát Castle

Křivoklát Castle, one of the most important medieval castles in Central Bohemia, will host its traditional Royal Advent event on December 5–6 and 12–13.

The programme includes an Old Bohemian Christmas Market, with artisan stalls selling traditional products, dried fruit, Christmas biscuits, sausages and mulled wine.

Visitors will also be able to explore the castle interiors at their own pace.

5. Hrádek u Nechanic

Built in the Windsor Gothic style, Hrádek u Nechanic will open its doors for Advent visits on selected weekends between November 28 and December 13.

The decorated interiors will feature Christmas trees, traditional ornaments, nutcrackers and nativity scenes. Guided tours will also explain how Christmas was celebrated in the past.

Special candlelit evening tours are scheduled for November 28, December 4 and December 11, while Advent concerts will take place on December 5 and 12.

The castle kitchen will also serve traditional English punch.

6. Dětenice Castle

Dětenice Castle in the Jičín area will offer a festive programme throughout December.

On December 5, children can take part in a St. Nicholas celebration in the medieval tavern. Visitors can also see Krampus performances on December 4, 5 and 12.

The castle’s medieval entertainment programme runs daily from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.

More Advent Destinations Across Czechia

Other places organising seasonal events include Třeboň Chateau, which will host Advent markets on December 5 and 6, and Jindřichův Hradec Castle, where a weekend programme of theatre, music, dance and traditional crafts is planned for the same dates.

In South Moravia, Valtice Chateau is displaying 30 Christmas trees decorated with more than 2,500 handmade glass ornaments. The exhibition runs until December 23.

Villa Stiassni in Brno is also offering special Christmas tours, featuring period decorations and an exhibition of historical toys.

World.title: Budapest finishes at the bottom of air pollution rankings among European capitals
World.content:
Budapest has placed 30th out of 40 European cities in a new air quality ranking by international environmental organisation Clean Cities, performing particularly poorly on measures designed to reduce pollution from transport.

Air quality needs to improve in the Hungarian capital

The organisation’s Free to Breathe study compared cities across four areas: current air pollution levels, compliance with EU air quality limits due to take effect in 2030, improvements over the past decade, and policies encouraging cleaner urban transport.

The research focused on two pollutants with significant health impacts: nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅), consisting of particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres. According to the report, nine in ten Europeans breathe air that exceeds World Health Organisation recommendations.

Budapest scored 25.6 out of a possible 60 points. It received 18 out of 30 for current air quality and 5.6 out of ten for improvements over the past decade. However, it received no points for meeting the EU’s 2030 air pollution limits and only two out of ten for transport policies. That category assessed measures including low- and zero-emission zones, protected cycle lanes, electric buses and restrictions on traffic around schools.

Budapest trails several regional capitals

The Hungarian capital was outperformed by several neighbouring cities. Vienna ranked ninth, Bratislava 19th and Ljubljana 29th. Budapest nevertheless finished ahead of Prague, which came 31st, Warsaw in 33rd place and Zagreb in 38th.

Copenhagen topped the ranking with 54.8 points, followed by the Stockholm region with 50.8 and the Helsinki region with 48.9. These were the only cities assessed as meeting all the EU air quality limits examined for 2030. Bucharest and Athens occupied the bottom two positions, scoring 17.9 and 13.8 points respectively.

Cleaner transport linked to better air

The study found that average nitrogen dioxide concentrations across the 40 cities fell by more than a third over the past decade, while fine particulate pollution declined by more than a quarter. Cities introducing stricter transport measures generally achieved greater improvements. Stuttgart, for example, almost halved its nitrogen dioxide levels despite its location in a basin where polluted air can accumulate.

However, none of the 40 cities met all WHO air quality recommendations. Only the Stockholm region complied with the WHO’s annual guideline for fine particulate matter. Clean Cities estimates that air pollution costs the EU economy around EUR 600 billion annually, equivalent to approximately four per cent of its economic output.

The organisation is calling for wider low-emission zones, more walking and cycling infrastructure, fully electrified bus fleets by the early 2030s and traffic-calmed areas around schools by 2030. It argues that relatively affordable measures can also improve urban air quality, provided local authorities receive sufficient powers and funding.

World.title: Hungarian man brutally murdered teenage sister, prosecution seeks harsher sentence
World.content:
Hungary’s Appellate Chief Prosecution Office in Budapest has called for a harsher sentence for a man convicted of murdering his 17-year-old sister, whom he had persuaded to run away from their family home in Szeged to the capital in 2008.

Prosecution seeks to postpone parole date

The man, now aged 42 or 43, was sentenced to life imprisonment at first instance, but prosecutors are seeking to postpone the earliest date on which he could be considered for parole. The case dates back nearly two decades and remained unresolved for years after the teenager disappeared.

According to the prosecution’s statement, the man had been living in Budapest with his partner between 2006 and 2008, moving between rented properties while avoiding authorities. In October 2008, he visited his parents in Szeged, where his younger sister was also living, and persuaded her to leave home and join him in the capital. Police subsequently listed the girl as a missing person.

Murder came after months of abuse

According to an RTL article back in 2023, the first-instance court found that, while living in Budapest, the 17-year-old girl had to die because she resisted when her brother, with whom she was hiding, tried to force her into prostitution. The two men assaulted her and drowned her in a bathtub at their flat, then disposed of her body. The man has since become a father of three and has been working as a bus driver.

The teenager was officially declared dead by a court in 2014, but investigators did not obtain substantial information linking her disappearance to a suspected murder until 2023. The Budapest Chief Prosecution Office brought charges against the two men in spring 2025.

On 3 June 2026, the Budapest Metropolitan Court sentenced the older defendant to life imprisonment, stipulating that he could first be considered for parole after serving at least 25 years. His accomplice, who was under 18 at the time of the crime, received a 13-year sentence in a juvenile detention facility for murdering the young girl, and both men were also banned from exercising public rights for ten years.

In case you missed it: Hungary to ratify Istanbul Convention as government unveils women’s rights reforms

Appeal could mean longer imprisonment

Prosecutors, both defendants and their lawyers appealed against the first-instance ruling. The Appellate Chief Prosecution Office is now asking the second-instance court to set a later earliest date for the older man’s possible release on parole than the 25-year minimum imposed previously.

Both defendants remain in custody while the appeal proceedings continue. The final outcome of the case has therefore yet to be determined.

World.title: New express bus service to connect Budapest and Pécs from December!
World.content:
A new express bus service will connect Budapest and Pécs from 13 December, offering passengers an additional way to travel between the two cities as concerns over the condition of the railway line continue. The buses will run every two hours, alternating with InterCity (IC) trains to ensure an hourly connection throughout the day.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced the new service on Facebook on Tuesday. The express buses will travel along the M6 motorway, departing from Népliget in Budapest and stopping at Kelenföld before reaching Pécs.

In Pécs, passengers will be able to get off both at the railway station and the main bus station. The buses will require reserved seats, and tickets must be purchased in advance.

Direct airport connections also planned

The new timetable will include an early-morning and a late-evening service extending to Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport. This will allow passengers travelling from Pécs to catch some of the capital’s earliest flights and return home after late-night arrivals.

Vitézy added that if demand is high, two buses could depart together on a service. However, passengers will still need to book their tickets beforehand.

Railway problems behind the new service

The new bus connection comes as the government prepares maintenance work on the main railway line between Budapest and Pécs. In a video accompanying his announcement, Vitézy said that the current condition of the line could not remain unchanged in the long term.

Maintenance work is due to begin in the autumn, while the journey times of IC trains between the two cities have been increased in the new timetable to reflect the condition of the tracks.

The minister stressed that routine repairs alone would not solve the railway line’s underlying problems. A more comprehensive reconstruction is planned, but it will take several years to complete.

The express bus service is intended to provide a more frequent and reliable connection in the meantime, ensuring that passengers can travel between Budapest and Pécs at least once every hour by train or bus.

World.title: Hungary to spend an extra EUR 325 million on public roads in 2027
World.content:
Hungary will allocate HUF 120 billion (approximately EUR 325 million) to renovating and maintaining its public road network in 2027, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy has announced.

Nationwide road renovation to receive more funds in 2027

The programme will include HUF 100 billion (close to EUR 271 million) in state funding for comprehensive road renovation projects, alongside an additional HUF 20 billion (around EUR 54.2 million) for Magyar Közút, the state road maintenance company. The latter allocation will cover routine maintenance, including pothole repairs.

According to the Ministry of Transport and Investment, the HUF 100 billion will complement projects co-financed by the European Union. The government says the combined funding represents a fivefold increase in the amount allocated from the state budget for major road renovations compared with this year.

In a statement reported by the MTI, the ministry said the previous government had provided Magyar Közút with only HUF 20 billion in state funding this year to maintain the country’s main and secondary roads.

Government promises continued motorway investment

The ministry also stressed that motorway maintenance and development would continue alongside the renovation programme. Its announcement comes amid plans to end the existing motorway concession system.

The ministry argued that cancelling the concession arrangements would not mean stopping road construction, but rather dismantling a system under which the state committed to purchasing infrastructure operation and maintenance services at high cost for decades.

Work has already started

Vitézy has also highlighted ongoing work on the 67 main road in Baranya County as an example of the renovation programme already under way. Magyar Közút began repairs on a nearly 1.3-kilometre section near Mozsgó on 19 November.

The project involves replacing the two upper asphalt layers, using approximately 2,400 tonnes of new asphalt. Roadside verges will also be repaired and new road markings applied. Work is expected to continue until mid-December, weather permitting.

During construction, traffic is subject to a 40km/h speed limit and alternating one-way control, with possible delays during daytime working hours. Vitézy said the increased funding would allow the state road company to undertake more extensive repairs across the country in 2027, covering both major routes and smaller roads.

World.title: Hungary approves extra EUR 2.7 million in support for ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia
World.content:
Hungary will provide an additional HUF 1 billion (approximately EUR 2.7 million) to support the ethnic Hungarian community in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region before the end of 2026. The one-off funding was approved in a government resolution published in Tuesday’s issue of the Hungarian Gazette.

The resolution instructs the Minister of Finance to make the money available this year through the Bethlen Gábor Fund, which finances national policy programmes and support for Hungarian communities abroad. It also allocates a further HUF 1.05 million for operational expenses.

Zrínyi Ilona Social Development Fund to be established

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced the additional support on Tuesday during his visit to Ukraine, where he met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Uzhhorod.

The prime minister said the Tisza government had decided to establish the Zrínyi Ilona Social Development Fund for ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia, providing HUF 1 billion on top of existing support from the 2026 state budget.

The fund is intended to help the community maintain its presence in the region and support healthcare, education and cultural activities.

Read our article about Magyar and Zelensky’s discussions: Magyar and Zelensky discuss energy, trade and EU membership as Hungary and Ukraine seek closer ties

Separate HUF 1 billion humanitarian aid package for Ukraine

The additional funding for Transcarpathian Hungarians is separate from Hungary’s humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, also announced by Magyar during his visit.

Hungary is providing Ukraine with medical and energy equipment, medicines and transport vehicles worth a further HUF 1 billion. The shipment includes patient monitoring equipment, generators and vehicles, among other supplies requested by the Ukrainian side. Magyar stressed that the donation does not include military equipment.

The two support packages bring Hungary’s newly announced assistance to a total of HUF 2 billion, with one half specifically earmarked for the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia.

World.title: Magyar and Zelensky discuss energy, trade and EU membership as Hungary and Ukraine seek closer ties
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held what the Ukrainian leader described as a “friendly conversation” in Berehove (Beregszász) on Tuesday, discussing energy cooperation, railway development, agricultural trade and Ukraine’s EU ambitions.

The meeting, held at the Ferenc Rákóczi II Transcarpathian Hungarian University, followed the two leaders’ joint wreath-laying ceremony in Uzhhorod earlier in the day. It marked an important step in efforts to improve relations between the neighbouring countries.

Zelensky thanked Hungary for condemning Russia’s aggression and supporting an end to the war. He also expressed appreciation for the joint tribute to Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict.

Energy supplies and railway links among key topics

According to 444.hu’s report, energy was one of the main issues discussed, with Ukraine needing diesel and looking to Hungary for support. Magyar said Hungary had also brought generators and other energy equipment as part of a HUF 1 billion (approximately EUR 2.7 million) humanitarian aid package, which includes medicines, patient monitoring equipment and vehicles.

The leaders also discussed modernising existing railway infrastructure, building new border crossing points and developing healthcare and social projects in Transcarpathia.

Agricultural trade was another topic. Zelensky offered to supply maize to drought-hit Hungary, while Magyar highlighted a shortfall of around two million tonnes in this year’s Hungarian maize harvest, which has caused difficulties for livestock farmers. He said the two countries should explore purchases of Ukrainian maize under state supervision and with appropriate checks. Food security was also discussed.

Magyar calls for faster implementation of minority rights deal

Magyar said Ukraine’s parliament had approved the ten-point programme agreed by the two countries to improve the situation of ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia, including their language, education and minority rights. He called for its implementation to be accelerated.

The Hungarian prime minister said the two countries had a long way to go and that trust would have to be built continuously. He also raised the issue of the Turul statue, which was removed from Mukachevo Castle in 2022, saying he would like to see it restored.

Hungary maintains reservations about Ukraine’s EU funding

The leaders also discussed Ukraine’s European Union membership prospects. Magyar reiterated that Hungary would continue providing humanitarian assistance but could not support linking Ukraine’s financing directly to the EU budget in a way that would oblige member states to participate in joint borrowing. He argued that each country should retain the freedom to decide how it supports Ukraine.

On EU accession talks, he stressed that membership must be based on merit and that there would be no fast-track process. He pointed to Hungary’s own 13-year path towards membership and Serbia’s lengthy accession process, adding that resolving minority rights issues was a prerequisite for Hungary to support opening the relevant negotiating cluster.

Magyar also said the visit had helped halt political escalation and put the relationship on a path towards good-neighbourly cooperation. The two leaders even joined students for a game of volleyball during their visit to the university.

The meeting follows two earlier discussions between Magyar and Zelensky: one on the sidelines of the European Council meeting in Brussels on 16 October and another at the European Political Community summit on 12 November. Magyar had said the two leaders wanted to meet in November, with Transcarpathia chosen as the location.

World.title: Young Hungarian talent Martin Molnár to race in Formula 3 from 2027
World.content:
Hungarian racing driver Martin Molnár will step up to the FIA Formula 3 Championship in 2027, joining the renowned Italian team Prema Racing and becoming a regular competitor at Formula 1 grand prix weekends.

Hungarian driver in Formula 3

The 18-year-old’s move marks a significant milestone in a career that has progressed through the British junior single-seater championships. Formula 3 is an important stage on the development path towards Formula 1, bringing together some of the most promising young drivers in international motorsport.

Molnár has already worked with his new team, completing 256 laps across two official post-season tests in Jerez and Barcelona. The sessions gave him an opportunity to get acquainted with Prema’s engineers and the demands of the category ahead of his first full campaign.

“I made a very good impression on them during the tests, and I am happy that we will be working together,” said Molnár at the announcement. He added that the reality of reaching this level became clear when he began testing and simulator preparation.

What are Formula 3 cars capable of?

According to the official website of the FIA Formula 3 championship, the cars are the same for every driver. They are capable of reaching 100km/h in around 3 seconds, and have a top speed of 300km/h, depending on their settings. This is comparable to modern day supercars, but thanks to the leightweight chassis and the downforce the cars create, they can turn far more quickly than any roadgoing car.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

A prestigious team and a demanding step up

Founded in 1983, Prema is one of the best-known teams in junior motorsport. It has won five FIA Formula 3 teams’ championships since 2019 and has helped develop several drivers who went on to reach Formula 1, including Charles Leclerc, Oscar Piastri, Oliver Bearman and now world champion Andrea Kimi Antonelli.

Prema chief executive Stephen Mitas said Molnár had made a strong impression during the Jerez and Barcelona tests. He said the team was looking forward to helping the Hungarian make the most of his first season in the championship.

Molnár’s move follows three seasons of progress in British single-seater racing. He began competing in British Formula 4 in 2024 with Virtuosi, finishing eighth overall in his debut year and becoming the leading rookie. He improved to third in the standings in his second season before moving to the GB3 Championship, commonly referred to as British Formula 3.

Racing for Rodin, he finished fourth overall after claiming seven podiums during the season. He was also the team’s highest-placed driver. The 2027 FIA Formula 3 championship is scheduled to begin in March, with ten rounds on the calendar. The opening event is due to take place in Bahrain, and all rounds are held as part of Formula 1 race weekends.

Read also: Budapest faces new rival in race to host the 2036 Olympic Games

Hungarian backing and a new ownership structure

Molnár will continue to receive backing from 4iG Group and One Hungary, which have supported his career since 2024 and are set to act as his main sponsors in 2027. The announcement also included a change in the business structure behind the driver. Through its investment subsidiary, 4iG intends to acquire full ownership of MOTAM Kft., the company managing Molnár’s career. The transaction remains subject to domestic and international competition approvals.

MOTAM’s management is expected to remain unchanged, with Tamás Őry continuing as managing director and former professional racing driver Pál Tamás Kiss leading its sporting programme.

Kiss said the tests showed that Molnár was technically ready for Formula 3, although adapting to the car and tyres will be a major challenge. With limited track time, drivers must learn quickly and extract maximum performance from each session. Physical and mental preparation will therefore become increasingly important.

Molnár will be the second Hungarian to contest the FIA Formula 3 championship after László Tóth, who competed in 2021 and 2022. Kiss previously raced in the series’ predecessor, GP3, where he won a race.
