World.title: Politicians differ over how to power Estonia's data center 'boom'
World.content:
That figure is nearly double Estonia's peak electricity demand of 1,700 megawatts, sparking debate over power prices, grid stability, and matching domestic generation.

Since data centers require uninterrupted, round-the-clock power for high-density servers and constant cooling, adding large campuses without new domestic generation would increase Estonia's reliance on cross-border imports — particularly from Finland, where a parallel data center boom could tighten supply and push Nordic prices higher.

Unlike Finland, which is considering requiring developers to add matching power generation, Estonia imposes no such obligation. Minister of Economic Affairs and Communications Erkki Keldo (Reform) said he wants to discuss with developers how projects can benefit Estonian society, whether through additional taxation or new domestic generation.

Call for pairing campuses with renewables and grid planning

MP Marek Reinaas (Eesti 200) said developers are unlikely to start construction unless their energy supply is secured, predicting data centers will be built alongside wind, solar, and battery storage. He added that growth in data processing is inevitable and that Estonia is better off hosting the infrastructure.

Center Party Riigikogu group chair Lauri Laats also backed attracting data centers, citing Sunly's planned solar-and-battery project as an example of developers covering part of their own demand. However, Laats warned that renewable output can fall short for large industrial consumers, urging the state to review its energy development plan, upgrade the transmission grid, and maintain existing oil shale capacity — which he noted provides around 1,000 megawatts during peak demand.

Jevgeni Ossinovski. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Social Democratic Party (SDE) deputy chair Jevgeni Ossinovski said Estonia should compete to attract data centers rather than lose them to Latvia and Lithuania, which would still affect regional electricity prices without bringing local benefits. He called for defining "critical consumers" in law, noting that developers are currently reserving grid capacity and obtaining building rights without linking projects to new power generation. Ossinovski urged drafting a six-month national plan mapping where and on what scale data centers should be built over the next five to 10 years, tying new demand to renewable generation through power purchase agreements.

Warnings over power bills and baseload supply

Isamaa's Priit Sibul warned that data centers could drive electricity prices "through the roof." While adding major consumers could lower per-unit grid fees, Sibul said solar farms cannot supply year-round power and Estonia cannot rely on imports from Finland once large data centers are built there too.

Parempoolsed deputy chair Siim Kiisler said projects can only go ahead if electricity prices make commercial sense, arguing that Estonia must expand cross-border links with Finland and Latvia to enable new domestic generation. While wind farms and storage can help offset seasonal swings in solar output, Kiisler said Estonia must ultimately look to nuclear power in the long run.

MP Rain Epler (EKRE) argued that intermittent wind and solar cannot meet around-the-clock server demand, adding that Estonia must first secure surplus baseload and dispatchable capacity — such as oil shale or nuclear power — before connecting major new consumers. Otherwise, he warned, the grid could face rationing decisions over whether to disconnect industrial plants or data centers.

Rain Epler on Wednesday's edition of 'Otse uudistemajast'. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Background:

Transmission grid operator Elering has already signed connection agreements for 600 megawatts and issued active offers for another 1,300 megawatts, with pending data center applications reaching 3,300 megawatts against Estonia's 1,700-megawatt peak demand, leaving the operator close to the limit of new offers it can issue. Most proposed multi-billion-euro campuses are clustered along high-voltage lines in western Estonia's Lääne-Nigula and Lääneranna municipalities — around Risti and Lihula — alongside major planned sites in Tapa, while Estonia's sole existing next-generation facility, Greenergy Data Centers in Hüüru near Tallinn, currently draws 2 megawatts with plans to scale to 200 megawatts by early 2028.

Energy analysts and Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) researchers warn that bringing even a fraction of the proposed capacity online without matching domestic generation would deepen Estonia's reliance on Finnish imports and raise consumer electricity prices, while rapid load swings could strain the small grid unless facilities are sited near major backbone substations and contribute to system balancing.

World.title: Share of special needs students growing rapidly in Estonian schools
World.content:
While the Ministry of Education wants local schools to teach all children, rural schools struggle to recruit support specialists and pressure to perform well in school rankings undermines inclusive education in urban schools.

When the concepts of enhanced and special support were introduced into legislation eight years ago, just over 9,000 students, or 6.1 percent of all students, required such support. By the previous academic year, that figure had exceeded 15,600, or 9.6 percent.

Jürgen Rakaselg, head of the Ministry of Education and Research's inclusive education department, told ERR that the upward trend is continuing, with similar developments observed elsewhere in Europe.

While the number of children requiring special support, the highest level of assistance, has increased only slightly, the proportion of students requiring lower levels of support has grown considerably.

Rita Punning, principal and mathematics teacher at Krootuse School in Põlva County, which has 68 students, said her experience also reflects the growing proportion of children with special educational needs.

However, she believes smaller rural schools may be better equipped to accommodate these children than large urban schools.

"We have fewer children and teachers know their students, understand their individual characteristics and know how to deal with them," Punning said.

Tõnu Piibur, principal of Tallinn's Pelgulinna School, believes children with difficulties have always been around, but schools have become better at recognizing their needs.

"Things haven't gotten worse, they've gotten better. We no longer abandon these students or label them bad boys or lazy," he said.

According to Rakaselg, improved identification of special educational needs, which are also linked to additional funding, partly explains the increase. However, perceptions of what constitutes normal behavior have also changed.

"What we consider normal has, in a sense, become narrower. Things that previously did not receive as much attention now qualify as requiring support," he said.

Rakaselg also pointed to changing parenting practices, insufficient sleep and difficulties developing concentration and work habits as contributing factors.

Meanwhile, Krootuse School has been unsuccessfully searching for a special education teacher for several years.

"In recent years, we've even offered a full-time position with a teacher's salary, but that hasn't helped either," Punning said.

A University of Tartu study published in 2024 confirmed that shortages of educational support specialists are particularly acute in rural areas. Although the number of support specialists working in Estonian schools has doubled over the past decade, many graduates do not end up working in educational institutions.

Rakaselg stressed that inclusive education should not come at the expense of other students' learning. Schools can employ teaching assistants, adapt teaching methods or organize lessons in smaller groups.

"The benchmark is that teachers must be able to teach and everyone in the classroom must actually be learning," he said.

However, Rakaselg acknowledged that requests for additional classroom assistance often go unanswered by school management or local governments.

"Everyone in this chain hopes the problem will somehow go away or the student will move to another school. We're burning out teachers who are left without support. Much of this is a management issue," he said.

Under Estonian law, a child's designated local school is required to admit and educate them regardless of their support needs. Nevertheless, the ministry receives complaints about schools attempting to pressure families into leaving.

"Parents are not always aware of their rights or that the school is obliged to educate their child, regardless of what level of support they need," Rakaselg said.

Piibur believes such practices are a consequence of school rankings. He compared schools seeking the best examination results by selecting the strongest students to hospitals attempting to reduce mortality rates by admitting healthier patients.

"The purpose of a school cannot be to select the best learners," Piibur said, calling for a more equitable education system and an end to school rankings.

"We're not expecting money from the minister. We're expecting the school system to be put right," he added.

The University of Tartu study found that current funding is insufficient to offer competitive salaries or recruit enough support specialists, teaching assistants and other support staff.

Rakaselg noted, however, that state funding for the operating expenses of students requiring additional support increased from €17.5 million in 2018 to €36.5 million in 2025.

Funding is calculated using a coefficient of two for students requiring enhanced support and four for those requiring special support, meaning allocations increase alongside overall education expenditure.

To alleviate the shortage of support specialists, the ministry is also planning to relax qualification requirements, allowing schools to employ specialists before they complete their university studies.

There are currently no signs that the growing proportion of children requiring educational support will level off, with similar trends evident among preschool children.

Nevertheless, Rakaselg believes the education system is moving in the right direction, as more children who would previously have been educated separately are now attending mainstream schools with additional support.

"As one school principal put it, I'm happy to practice inclusion, but there's no longer a uniform group to include anyone in, because everyone is so different," he said.

World.title: Latvian PM: Estonia rushed to close its border with Russia
World.content:
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs says Estonia should have consulted the other two Baltic states before deciding to close its border with Russia.

Riga is weighing closing its own Russian border as well, Kulbergs added, speaking to local broadcaster TV3's "900 sekundes" show.

Kulbergs said the Latvian government and relevant authorities are considering several possible scenarios for closing the border with Russia, with a final decision on next steps expected on Thursday.

The remarks follow the Estonian government's decision last week to suspend all road border crossings with Russia for six months starting Tuesday, December 1, in response to a wave of GRU-linked arson attacks targeting Estonian defense companies, including drone maker Threod Systems and Milrem Robotics.

The Latvian prime minister stressed that the issue must be carefully considered, including how closing the border would affect freight shipments and traffic flows, since some goods are already in transit.

Kulbergs also criticized Estonia for rushing into its decision to close the border ahead of next spring's elections. He said all three Baltic states should coordinate discussions on the issue, as rerouting traffic and freight could affect both Latvia and Lithuania.

Latvia also has yet to decide whether to halt the transit of Russian grain.

He noted that grain transit is tied to both support for Ukraine and efforts to reduce Russia's economic gains, adding that a final decision will be made once all circumstances have been assessed.

Kulbergs said the issue would be discussed in a broader context in the coming weeks, including in cooperation with Ukraine.

While Estonian opposition parties including EKRE, Center, and Isamaa have called for temporarily reinstating checks or full border controls with Latvia — noting that several suspects detained in the recent sabotage plots entered Estonia from Latvia itself — coalition leaders have rejected the move as unnecessary and overly resource-intensive. Interior Ministry Secretary General Tarmo Miilits has estimated that restoring controls along the southern border would cost roughly €65 million, arguing that the funds would be far better spent doubling Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) patrols and strengthening Internal Security Service (ISS) counterintelligence.

Meanwhile, Latvia's State Border Guard expects longer vehicle queues and extra overtime at its own Russian crossings once Estonia's eastern checkpoints close next week.

Both countries have an eastern border with the Russian Federation, while Latvia also shares a border with Belarus, whose regime is aligned with Moscow.

World.title: Estonia's minimum wage rises to €997 in 2027
World.content:
Estonia's minimum wage will rise by 5.4 percent next year to €997 per month and €5.93 per hour, under an agreement struck by the Estonian Trade Union Confederation and the Estonian Employers' Confederation.

In 2026, the minimum wage was set at €946 per month and €5.67 per hour. It was introduced on April 1, instead of the customary January 1, as it took longer than usual to reach an agreement.

This means a monthly increase of €51 and an hourly rise of 26 cents next year.

Estonian Employers' Confederation CEO Hando Sutter said the minimum wage will rise by 5.4 percent next year, more than twice the forecast rate of price increases.

"At the same time, outside Harju and Tartu counties, the new minimum wage will exceed 50 percent of the regional average wage, and an even faster increase could lead to job losses in several regions of Estonia. The minimum wage can only rise sustainably alongside productivity, but in recent years wages have grown faster than productivity. To increase productivity, businesses need a stable tax environment and decisions from the state that support investment, while employees can most reliably increase their wages by developing their skills," he said.

Estonian Trade Union Confederation head Kaia Vask said employees and their families may spend the majority of their wages on bills and food.

"It makes a big difference whether they receive higher wages for work done in January or have to wait until spring. The wage increase may provide exactly the amount they are short of to pay their winter heating bill, as the purchasing power of Estonia's minimum wage remains the lowest in the European Union," she said.

Vask estimates that around 37,000 people in Estonia earn the minimum wage or close to it.

The government must now approve the change.

World.title: Opposition parties seek 5% pay rise for Estonia's teachers
World.content:
After pay talks failed, the opposition Center Party, Isamaa and Social Democrats (SDE) have each called for raising teachers' minimum wage by 5 percent, Postimees reported .

The three parties have called for this rise instead of the 3 percent the education ministry proposed, ahead of the state budget's final reading before year-end.

The fourth opposition party, the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE), has indicated it would be on board with the hikes conditional on other specific budget cuts being made.

Mediation talks between the Estonian Education Personnel Union (EHL) and the Ministry of Education on Tuesday collapsed without agreement, giving teachers the legal right to strike in 2027 unless the Riigikogu allocates additional pay funding during December's final state budget vote.

"We think the 3 percent proposed by the ministry is too low, so we added another 2 percentage points. By our calculations, this would cost €13 million," Riigikogu Cultural Affairs Committee member Vadim Belobrovtsev (Center) told the daily.

Vadim Belobrovtsev (Center) Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Cultural Affairs Committee member Helle-Moonika Helme (EKRE) said her party would propose €1.1 billion in budget cuts, adding that if these passed, there would be no problem raising teachers' pay.

Tõnis Lukas (Isamaa), deputy chair of the Cultural Affairs Committee, said teachers' pay should at least keep pace with the average wage to prevent the gap from widening further. "With the average wage forecast to rise by 5 percent next year, we propose adding another 2 percentage points to the planned increase in teachers' pay."

SDE wants €17 million from the state budget to ensure pay rises for teachers, rescue workers and police officers keep pace with the average wage. The party says increasing needs-based student grants and creating additional places in higher education would require another €15 million.

Under next year's draft state budget, which has passed two readings in the Riigikogu, the minimum salary for teachers would rise by 3 percent to €2,030.

The third and final state budget reading is due to take place before the Riigikogu breaks up for its winter recess in mid-December.

Reemo Voltri. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Union boss: Opposition's proposed pay rise would avert teachers' strike

EHL Chair Reemo Voltri told ERR later on Wednesday morning that the opposition's proposed 5 percent raise represents the bare minimum teachers would accept to keep pace with Estonia's average wage amid a worsening teacher shortage.

"As far as we know, many of the parties in the Riigikogu believe teachers' pay should not fall relative to the average wage. Amendments to that effect have now been proposed to the budget," Voltri said. "We'll see how that process plays out, and the Estonian Education Personnel Union's council will meet in mid-December to decide whether we need to take stronger action and, if so, what form it should take."

Voltri noted that the union has been arguing for 15 years that teachers' starting pay should at least match the national average, making a 5 percent increase the lowest acceptable floor at this late stage of the budget process.

"No teacher ever really wants to go out on strike. But [a 5 percent pay raise] would at least mean they wouldn't have to. It would keep their situation from getting worse," he said.

While the EHL's ultimate goal is to bring the minimum salary for teachers with a master's degree in line with Estonia's projected average wage of €2,312 per month, the ministry maintained during Tuesday's failed mediation talks that the budget lacks funds for a larger increase.

Teachers most recently held a one-hour warning strike in September.

World.title: Psychiatrist: We have nowhere to send people for rehab
World.content:
Although Estonia's national development plan pledges to reduce drug-related deaths to zero by 2030, 83 people had already died of drug overdoses as of September this year.

"In Tallinn, we don't really have a dedicated detoxification service where we can refer patients for treatment," said psychiatrist Kaiti Redlich. "Children access psychiatric care through an e-consultation via their family doctor's office, but there is no specific place where someone can simply walk in off the street and say, 'Hello, I have this problem. Can you help me?'" Redlich said.

In her view, the problem is not that help is unavailable in Estonia, but rather that there is no clear system or structure in place to guide people on where to turn when they need help.

At the same time, rapid access to treatment is critical. "Someone who uses drugs won't wait two weeks or two months. When they realize they need treatment and are ready for it that very day, there has to be somewhere for them to go," Redlich explained.

Sharing his own experience, 19-year-old rapper Jan-Martti Kaljuvee, who has overcome addiction, confirmed that help was also unavailable in his hometown of Haapsalu.

"I've been through rehab and when I made that decision, I essentially had to move to an entirely different county, more than 50 kilometers from home," Kaljuvee recalled. He eventually found help online by signing up for the Village of Hope (Lootuse Küla) rehabilitation program.

Choices had to be made after cutbacks

Ministry of Social Affairs public health adviser Kristiin Mikko acknowledged that treatment capacity was inadequate but attributed this to state budget cuts.

"Unfortunately, this sector has not been spared the budget cuts made due to security needs and we have tried to preserve the services we consider the highest priority," Mikko said.

She confirmed that detoxification treatment is unavailable in Tallinn and that Viljandi Hospital has just seven beds for such treatment. "With funding for the sector having been cut, we simply don't have the resources to create additional treatment places, even if we wanted to," Mikko added.

According to Mikko, long-term inpatient addiction treatment in Estonia is currently available at only a handful of facilities in Narva and at Viljandi Hospital, which is clearly insufficient. Budget cuts also cost the harm reduction organization Ööhaldjad (Night Fairies), which previously worked in cooperation with the National Institute for Health Development (TAI), its state funding this year.

Actor Jan Uuspõld, who previously received help at a psychiatric clinic ward on Paldiski maantee, said it took a whole team — a doctor, psychologists and therapists — to help him overcome his addiction, but gaining admission was extremely difficult.

"I'm surprised the private sector doesn't offer this kind of service, given that there would seem to be demand for it," Uuspõld said.

At the same time, Uuspõld pointed out that constant support from loved ones can sometimes do more harm than good for someone struggling with severe addiction, as they may take advantage of it.

"It was much easier for me to get out of it once I'd hit rock bottom, when I no longer even had clothes of my own and never knew where I'd wake up. And at some point, I started asking myself whether I wanted to live or die," Uuspõld said.

Comedian Aleksander Eeri Laupmaa, who used drugs for 10 years, stressed that overcoming addiction requires finding in real life the feeling that drugs once provided. He also called for greater investment in harm reduction and public awareness efforts.

"Most people who fall victim to this kind of addiction are missing something in their lives — the feeling that the substance gives them," Laupmaa explained. "When you find something greater than the substance itself — whether that's faith, extreme sports or music — those are typically the ways people stop using drugs and move on to more productive pursuits," Laupmaa said.

World.title: Bomb squad prepares to destroy 250-kg WWII German explosive found in Pärnu County
World.content:
Bomb disposal experts are preparing to destroy a 250-kilogram World War II aerial bomb found in a Pärnu County field at an Estonian Defense Forces' training area, Postimees reported .

The bomb, reportedly a German-made device from World War II, was transported under police escort to the central training area in Harju County on Tuesday.

The Western Estonia Bomb Disposal Unit (Lääne-Eesti pommigrupp) is now preparing to render the device safe.

A metal detectorist had discovered the 250-kilogram aerial bomb about 30 centimeters underground in a field in Lemmetsa village just north of Pärnu City on Sunday.

Thanks to its considerable destructive power, the bomb could not be destroyed at the Rescue Board's usual demolition site in nearby Potsepa.

"The bomb disposal team is preparing to destroy the bomb using a special charge," said Aivar Post, head of the unit.

He added that the aim is to make the explosive burn rapidly through a process known as deflagration, avoiding a larger blast.

The SD250 Luftwaffe aerial bomb weighs 250 kilograms, contains about 80 kilograms of explosives, and was kept in a secluded, locked storage site before transport.

Post praised the metal detectorist, who reported the find to 112 shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday, for acting responsibly after realizing what the object might be and leaving it untouched.

"With finds like this, the most important thing is to leave the dangerous object untouched and report it immediately," Post said, noting that a similar aerial bomb has been found near Lemmetsa before.

The recovered bomb measured about 90 centimeters long because its tail fins were missing—compared with 1,638 millimeters in length and 368 millimeters in diameter in its original configuration — illustrating how metal detectorists searching for historical artifacts can uncover dangerous wartime ordnance.

The original Pärnu Postimees story is here.

What should you do if you find what may be an unexploded bomb or other ordinance?

Bomb disposal experts remind the public that all explosive ordinance is dangerous, regardless of its age or condition. Even an object that looks rusty and damaged can explode if moved, causing serious injury or death. Anyone who finds an explosive device or suspects they have found one should leave it untouched, mark the location, move to a safe distance, warn people nearby and call the emergency number 112. They should wait for the bomb disposal team at a safe distance and keep others from approaching the find.

World.title: Two months old, and Gaza’s meningitis wave has found him
World.content:
GAZA STRIP: Mustafa Hisham Halawin is two months old. For the past nine days he has been in Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza, being treated for meningitis.

His mother, Umm Mustafa, says the illness started with a fever of 39 degrees. Then a rash spread across the infant’s face and he began vomiting. She carried him to Al-Rantisi, where doctors took a sample of fluid from his spine. The results, she said, were “very bad.”

She added: “Unfortunately, the pain keeps getting worse, and he hasn’t settled. To this day he is not responding, even though they keep changing his treatment. The doctors here are not falling short at all. They are doing everything they can. But I know how hard life is for us.”

She said it is the second time this month that Mustafa has been infected with meningitis, and the second time she has stayed at the hospital with him. Coming back, she said, has become normal for families like hers.

The family lives in a tent by the sea. “I live in a tent. The conditions are tragic, with pollution and no way to keep clean,” she said. “We live by the sea in a tent, and the cold alone brings us diseases, not just for my son.”

Mustafa is one of a fast-growing number of patients. Local authorities say Gaza recorded 30 to 50 meningitis cases a month from the start of the year. From September to November, monthly cases rose eightfold. In October, 270 cases were recorded. About 75 percent were viral and 25 percent bacterial. In November, viral cases stayed at a similar level, while bacterial cases rose to 100.

The authorities have issued an early warning, saying the health system could not cope if meningitis turned into a full outbreak, and calling on the world to take responsibility. They link the rise to drinking and washing water mixing with sewage, a lack of sterilization and hygiene supplies, and severe overcrowding in shelters. Children are the most vulnerable, they said. Winter has only just begun, and they expect case numbers may rise further.

At Al-Rantisi, consultant pediatrician Dr. Sharif Yasser Matar said the hospital has been dealing with a wave of infectious disease for about a month. The infections are affecting children’s lungs, stomachs and nervous systems. Meningitis is part of that wave, and he said there is no sign yet that it is ending.

“Every day, new meningitis cases are admitted,” he said. Lab tests on the children’s spinal fluid show cell counts ranging from low to the thousands.

“We are talking about an infectious disease, and Gaza’s environment is an incubator for any infectious disease,” Matar said. “Expect anything contagious to spread.” He pointed to how crowded Gaza is, tents that offer no protection, and schools and nurseries that have reopened and are helping infections spread. He said nobody is checking the water children drink or the medicines they take. Many children are malnourished, which weakens their immune systems and leaves them open to infection.

So far, Matar said, the hospital has had enough drugs for the cases coming in. “No child has come to us needing meningitis treatment and been told it isn’t available,” he added.

The bigger problem is that many children are not responding to the standard treatment. “We had to bring older drugs back into use, ones we had not used for a long time,” he said.

The pressure on Al-Rantisi is also growing. Many of Gaza’s other children’s hospitals are out of service, so their patients now come to Al-Rantisi. “No other field hospital in the area can test for meningitis or take in these cases,” Matar said. “So, every case like this comes to Al-Rantisi.”

For Umm Mustafa, the medicine is only part of the problem. “I know how hard our life is,” she said.

World.title: Saudi Arabia's history, national heritage showcased at 'Bridge of Civilizations' art exhibition in Cairo
World.content:
RIYADH: The "Bridge of Civilizations" art exhibition opened in Cairo, highlighting the power of art to foster closer ties between civilizations and peoples, reported the Saudi Press Agency on Monday.

The exhibition features more than 60 visual artists from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Russia, with prominent artists and art enthusiasts in attendance.

An artwork featured at the exhibition in Cairo. (SPA)

At the three-day exhibition, around 30 Saudi visual artists will present a diverse collection of works highlighting the Kingdom's history, national symbols, and heritage passed down through generations.

The Saudi artists' paintings document Islamic heritage, the Prophet Muhammad's biography, and historical sites associated with the Two Holy Mosques. They also highlight the Kingdom's development achievements, including the Haramain High Speed Railway, as well as its cultural and architectural heritage, such as Najdi Sadu weaving and Al-Masmak Palace.

Participating Saudi artists told SPA that they aim to introduce audiences to the Kingdom's history, identity, and heritage through contemporary artistic approaches while highlighting the development of visual arts in Saudi Arabia.

This article was first published in Asharq Al-Awsat.

World.title: Iraq’s top court says Baghdad can deploy troops to secure borders in Kurdistan region, state TV reports
World.content:
Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court ruled that Baghdad can deploy federal troops to secure Iraq’s international borders, including those in territory administered by the Kurdistan region, Iraqi state television reported on Wednesday. Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take over border crossings run by the ‌Kurdistan region after an ‌oil smuggling investigation at ‌the state-run North Oil Company.

The court said federal authorities could oversee the agencies operating at all border crossings, including those in the Kurdistan region. It said Baghdad must coordinate with regional and provincial governments on customs administration, state television reported.

Zaidi also ‌on Tuesday ‌ordered the federal oil ministry to manage its ‌fields in areas under Kurdish ‌security control in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Diyala and Salahuddin provinces.

The court said the federal oil ministry can oversee and audit oil and ‌gas fields, while Baghdad shares responsibility for managing the oil and gas they produce with regional governments and producing provinces, state TV reported. The Kurdistan Regional Government on Wednesday rejected what it called “military language and threats” in the Iraqi military spokesman’s statement and called for talks with Baghdad. It said it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption and called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq.

World.title: The Groves returns to Riyadh with whimsical spirit, global flavors, festive charm
World.content:
RIYADH: With glowing lights, whimsical decorations, international restaurants and lively performances, The Groves has returned for Riyadh Season 2026, providing visitors with an experience that combines dining, entertainment and cultural diversity.

The Groves has stepped up its offerings, transforming the destination into an immersive setting where every corner invites visitors to explore, take photographs and discover something new.

From the moment visitors enter, the atmosphere feels almost theatrical. Elaborate decorations, illuminated pathways and carefully designed dining spaces create a setting that resembles a storybook village, while music and performances bring the destination to life.

Among the additions is Opa Kefi, a Greek restaurant that brings Mediterranean flavors and a lively dining atmosphere to Riyadh.

Beyond its menu, the restaurant offers an entertaining Greek wedding-inspired performance, turning an ordinary dinner into a celebration of music, dance and tradition.

Another addition is Anne Oja, a Turkish restaurant that combines traditional cuisine with live music, offering visitors a taste of Turkish hospitality in a setting designed around entertainment and social gatherings.

Together, the restaurants reflect The Groves’ growing emphasis on international dining experiences, where food is accompanied by cultural performances and distinctive surroundings.

However, the attraction is not limited to its restaurants.

Walking through the park has become an experience in itself, with visitors moving between decorated pathways, entertainment areas and outdoor spaces designed for families and groups of friends.

One of the attractions is Luca Park, where visitors can interact with dogs in a playful environment.

For families, this combination makes The Groves particularly appealing. Children can enjoy interactive activities while parents explore restaurants, watch live performances or simply relax in the outdoor surroundings.

The destination also provides a setting for visitors who prefer a leisurely evening, with its illuminated gardens and decorative installations offering opportunities for photography and quiet walks away from the busier entertainment areas.

For returning visitors, the changes are noticeable.

Diana Zeineddine, who has visited The Groves in previous seasons, told Arab News that the destination continued to attract her because of its variety and welcoming atmosphere.

“This is my second time visiting The Groves. I usually come every year,” she said.

“Despite everything that’s happening, actually we feel safe. We feel like it’s very easy to go out and hang out.”

Zeineddine said the combination of dining, entertainment and people from different backgrounds made The Groves stand out among Riyadh’s seasonal attractions.

“This place is really special. There’s a lot of variety of restaurants, people, entertainment and food, especially food,” she said.

“I’m very, very happy to be here.”

Another notable feature this season is the festive atmosphere, with Christmas-inspired decorations adding a holiday spirit to parts of the destination.

The colorful displays and illuminated installations have become attractions in their own right, drawing visitors to stop and photograph the decorations and enjoy the seasonal surroundings.

For Zeineddine, the decorations reflect the increasingly diverse cultural experiences available in the Saudi capital.

“There’s a lot of holiday spirit here. You can see there’s a lot of Christmas decorations and people enjoying their time and their holidays,” she said.

She added that she appreciated how Saudi Arabia was embracing cultural diversity through its entertainment destinations.

She said: “It’s really, really nice where we are these days and how Saudi Arabia especially is embodying all this change and embracing all the change and the variety of people and food and culture.”

The international appeal of The Groves is also reflected in its visitors.

Vatika Joannes, a visitor from Malaysia, returned to the destination after enjoying her experience during the previous season.

“For me, this place is very nice, very beautiful. And the ambience is also very good,” she told Arab News.

Joannes said the decorations and restaurant settings were among the features that encouraged her to return.

She said: “Actually, this is my second time coming here. Last year I came here and then today. I will come more.”

She added that she particularly enjoyed the restaurant surroundings and their elaborate designs.

“The restaurant here and the decoration; it’s very nice, very beautiful,” she said.

Her experience highlights how The Groves has developed an identity that encourages repeat visits, with its visual appeal becoming just as important as the food and entertainment.

As Riyadh Season continues to expand the capital’s entertainment landscape, destinations such as The Groves demonstrate how dining spaces are increasingly being designed as experiences rather than simply places to eat.

World.title: UN warns of growing risk of atrocities by Israel against Palestinians
World.content:
GENEVA: The United Nations warned Wednesday of a growing risk of atrocity crimes being committed by Israel against the Palestinians, and urged all states to take immediate preventative action.

UN rights chief Volker Turk said ongoing Israeli attacks, policies and violations against Palestinians indicated a “widening risk of further atrocity crimes” in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

“Israeli government representatives at highest levels have time and again spelled out policies of annexation, ethnic cleansing and collective punishment in the West Bank,” he said in a statement.

“Across society, the incitement to hatred and to perpetration of violations amounting to atrocity crimes — war crimes, crimes against humanity and even genocide — has been appalling.”

Turk said his office had repeatedly warned about the risk of Israel’s actions in Gaza posing a “real threat to the continued existence” of the Palestinians as a group.

Most of Gaza’s population of 2.1 million live displaced in tents or makeshift shelters in the territory, where Israel’s military says it controls more than 60 percent of the land.

“I am extremely worried about the increasingly widespread and systematic nature of the violations being perpetrated across both the West Bank and Gaza,” Turk said.

“Our warnings have not been heeded, and atrocity crimes continue to recur,” said the UN high commissioner for human rights.

“Civilians continue to be killed, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, with senior Israeli officials indicating intent for such displacement to be permanent.”

Violence in the West Bank, occupied by Israel since 1967, has surged since Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war.

“All states have the obligation to act, now, to prevent further atrocity crimes against the Palestinians,” said Turk.

“There must be independent investigations, and those responsible must be held to account. The work of the international courts in this regard must be supported by all states.”

Turk also reminded Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups of their obligations under international law, including to protect civilians and to respect the safety of humanitarian operations.

World.title: Saudi, Bahraini defense officials discuss Houthi and Iranian attacks
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman discussed Houthi attacks on the Kingdom and Iranian attacks on Bahrain in a phone call on Wednesday with Bahrain’s national security adviser, the Saudi Press Agency reported.

The Bahraini official also serves as secretary-general of the country’s Supreme Defense Council.

During the call, the two sides reaffirmed their solidarity in taking measures to protect the security and stability of both countries, SPA said.

The call came a day after a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial center injured 11 people, according to Saudi Civil Defense. Bahrain has also intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks in recent days.

World.title: Saudi cities climb global rankings with Riyadh up 16 places since 2022
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi Arabia’s capital has again risen in Kearney’s Global Cities Index, having now jumped 16 places since 2022 to rank 54th in the 2026 list.

Dammam recorded the biggest rise in the Middle East in the Global Cities Outlook list, which gauges their future potential, advancing 18 spots year on year to 64th.

The report showed Riyadh rose two places from 2025, improving across four of five dimensions, while Dammam’s progress was driven by gains in economics and innovation.

The findings come amid Riyadh’s growing prominence as an international business hub.

In September, the capital entered the top 50 of the Oxford Economics Global Cities Index for the first time, climbing 47 places and ranking fourth globally for human capital.

The Kingdom’s Regional Headquarters Program has also attracted more than 700 international companies, surpassing its 2030 target of 500.

Valentin Lavaill, executive director of Kearney Foresight Middle East and Africa, told Arab News that Saudi cities are benefiting from the Kingdom’s wider economic transformation under Vision 2030.

“Riyadh demonstrates the difference deliberate policy can make,” Kearney said in its report, highlighting investments in international schools and educational capacity.

Economic diversification

“Between 2021 and 2025, real non-oil activity grew by approximately 34%, reflecting the progress made in not only diversifying, but strengthening the economy,” Lavaill said.

Since 2020, the average scores of the five Saudi cities assessed have improved across four dimensions, with cultural experience rising 204 percent, information exchange increasing 120 percent and human capital growing 56 percent.

“Education helps people develop the skills and capabilities needed in a changing economy, while new industries offer them opportunities to put those skills into practice,” he said.

Lavaill noted that these investments help cities attract and retain businesses, investors and talent while building a more diverse economic base.

Makkah recorded the largest annual improvement among Saudi cities in the index, climbing six places, while Jeddah slipped two spots to 85th despite gains across three dimensions.

Innovation gains

Dammam’s rise in the outlook was supported by a 34-place improvement in economics and a 91-place jump in innovation.

“This year, the city rose from 142nd to 51st in the innovation dimension, driven primarily by strong anticipated performance on patents production,” Lavaill said.

He highlighted Dammam Valley’s biotechnology startup program and university-led patent and entrepreneurship support as initiatives that could advance industrialization and strengthen smaller businesses’ contribution to the non-oil economy.

The report also found that Dammam attracted increased foreign direct investment in 2025, while Riyadh and Jeddah lost ground despite operating under the same broad national conditions.

Future opportunities

Lavaill noted that Jeddah and Dammam benefit from international trade connections, while Riyadh is emerging as a hub for businesses and governments.

“The opportunity is to convert these strengths into broader global influence,” he said.

“In the global AI race, Saudi cities can also strengthen their position by investing in digital infrastructure, including data centers.”

He added: “Each city can build its own pathway to global prominence, laying the foundations to challenge established cities that have long dominated the top 30 of our index.”

World.title: Migrant arrivals in Spain’s Canary Islands break single-day record
World.content:
MADRID: A ‌record 2,100-plus migrants arrived in Spain’s Canary Islands over 24 hours in overcrowded boats, maritime rescue service data showed on Wednesday, exacerbating a situation the regional government described as unsustainable earlier this month.

One migrant was found dead in a boat and another gave birth during the perilous crossing from West Africa, the rescue service said.

The daily arrivals surpassed the previous record of about 1,500 set two weeks ago.

Most ‌of the boats ‌arrived at El Hierro island, ‌home to about 11,400 residents and one of Europe’s key entry points for migrants arriving from West Africa.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has faced tough criticism of his open stance on migration during the campaign ahead of Sunday’s parliamentary election, said on Wednesday Europe needed a comprehensive approach to migration, including stronger border controls ‌in cooperation with Senegalese ‌and Gambian authorities. Still, he said Spain needed “to open legal ‌migration pathways” for workers in sectors such as ‌housing that are short of qualified labor.

The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the ‌journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.

Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favorable for crossings.

Arrivals so far this year had climbed to 28,103 as of late November, more than last year’s total but still well below an all-time high of 46,843 recorded in 2024, when most crossings occurred during the first nine months of the year. Nearly 21,000 people have reached the archipelago in the last two months.

World.title: Iraq inaugurates first fiber optic cable factory in Diyala
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s first production facility for sixth-generation fiber optic cables was inaugurated on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at the Diyala State Company under the patronage of Minister of Industry and Minerals Mohammed Nouri.

The opening ceremony was attended by Minister of Communications Mustafa Jabbar Sanad, Undersecretary of the Ministry of Industry for Planning Affairs Ahmed Abdul-Jabbar Al-Karim, Diyala Governor Adnan Al-Shammari, the head of the provincial council, and senior officials from both ministries and local government.

Executed in partnership with the private sector under license from the specialized Chinese telecommunications firm FiberHome, the new production line carries a design capacity of 15,000 kilometers of optical fiber cables annually across multiple specifications and gauges.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Undersecretary Al-Karim stated that the project reflects the Ministry of Industry and Minerals’ strategic drive to modernize state factories, diversify domestic manufacturing, localize advanced technology, and expand private-sector partnerships to strengthen the competitiveness of Iraqi-made products in the local market.

Minister of Communications Mustafa Jabbar Sanad affirmed his ministry’s full commitment to purchasing locally manufactured fiber optic cables and integrating them into upcoming national telecommunications projects.

On the sidelines of the inauguration, the Ministries of Industry and Communications—represented respectively by the Diyala State Company and the General Company for Communications and Informatics—signed a formal cooperation agreement to supply domestic optical cables for state infrastructure projects, ensuring reliable local demand and supporting national industrial output.

World.title: Baghdad to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered on Tuesday the federal Ministry of Oil to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control, triggering an immediate rejection from the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and escalating a broader campaign to centralize state power.

Al-Zaidi’s directives follow an investigation into massive crude oil smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company.

The federal Oil Ministry in Baghdad must take over Kurdish-secured fields in four northern provinces—Kirkuk, Nineveh, Diyala, and Salah al-Din.

Erbil is prohibited from approving crude or refined product exports without federal ministry sign-off.

Iraq’s Border Ports Authority is instructed to take over all official border crossings in the Kurdistan region of Iraq, while security forces close informal crossings and unpaved roads connecting Iraqi Kurdistan to neighboring provinces.

The Iraqi prime minister suspended top executives at the North Oil Company and dismissed the head of the border authority pending further probes.

Last week, Baghdad threatened military action to enter the Iran-backed armed group Kataib Hezbollah’s stronghold in Jurf al-Sakhar after investigators linked the militia and senior officials to a multi-hundred-million-dollar oil smuggling network.

According to reports, al-Zaidi is attempting to curb non-state armed groups and rein in regional autonomy to stabilize Iraq for foreign investment.

World.title: Iraqi security seizes two drone launchers in Maysan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security forces seized on Tuesday two drone launchers and drone engine components hidden in an agricultural area in the southeastern province of Maysan.

The operation was announced by Iraq’s Security Media Cell and carried out by a specialized intelligence and technical team supervised by the director of Maysan Intelligence and Counterterrorism.

Following intelligence reports, security forces deployed to cordon off and search the farmland, the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.

Alongside the two concealed launch platforms, authorities recovered scattered remnants and components of a drone engine.

Authorities have seized the equipment and initiated legal and technical procedures. Officials have not yet identified who placed the launchers or confirmed whether they had been used in previous attacks.

After a drone attack targeted a pipeline in Saudi Arabia in September, which Riyadh and Baghdad said was launched from Iraqi territory, Iraqi security forces have discovered drone launchers near the border with Iran.

World.title: Iraqi political blocs name nominees to replace Communications and Transport Ministers
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Political factions within Iraq’s Coordination Framework have finalized their nominees to replace key cabinet members in an upcoming ministerial reshuffle led by Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, including the portfolios of Communications, Transport, and Oil, according to a coalition source speaking on Tuesday, November 24, 2026.

The source disclosed that the Islamic Supreme Council of Iraq (ISCI), headed by Humam Hamoudi, has put forward several candidates—prominently Ahmed Abdul-Jabbar and former Health Minister Saleh Al-Hasnawi—to assume the Ministry of Communications in place of incumbent Minister Mustafa Jabbar Sanad.

Meanwhile, the Badr Organization, led by Hadi Al-Amiri, has selected Mohammed Al-Zubaidi as its nominee for the Ministry of Transport to succeed current Minister Wahab Al-Hassani.

The nominations follow revelations by a government source on Monday, November 23, confirming a political and executive agreement to carry out a phased cabinet reshuffle immediately after Parliament settles the federal general budget bill. Driven by formal performance evaluations and consultations with nominating blocs, the first phase is expected to target three portfolios for distinct reasons:

Ministry of Transport: The planned replacement of Minister Wahab Al-Hassani is attributed to health reasons.

Ministry of Oil: Prime Minister Al-Zaidi is weighing the dismissal of Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi due to operational shortcomings across multiple files and recent revelations of crude oil theft and smuggling networks across several Iraqi cities. Alongside naming new ministers, the government is considering merging the Ministries of Oil and Electricity into a unified “Ministry of Energy”, potentially placing both portfolios under the current Electricity Minister.

Ministry of Communications: Coalition sources confirmed the move to replace Mustafa Sanad, though specific official grounds for the change have not yet been detailed.

The impending shakeup comes roughly six months after the Council of Representatives granted confidence to Al-Zaidi’s cabinet on May 14, 2026, and just over a month after the government completed its 25-ministry lineup on October 15.

World.title: Baghdad to take over border crossings in Iraqi Kurdistan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities on Tuesday to take control of all border crossings in Iraqi Kurdistan and directed the Oil Ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salah al-Din, and Nineveh provinces as part of a crackdown on oil smuggling.

The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) was instructed to approve crude oil and petroleum product exports only through the federal Oil Ministry.

Baghdad also announced plans to monitor oilfields with cameras and deploy Oil Ministry personnel at checkpoints leading into the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

Al-Zaidi directed the federal border crossings authority to assume control of all crossings in the Kurdistan region of Iraq. He also instructed the Border Forces Command to close unofficial international border crossings and ordered the shutdown of seasonal roads and unpaved routes connecting the four provinces and Iraqi Kurdistan.

The prime minister removed the head of the border crossings authority, suspended the director general of the state-owned North Oil Company and his deputies pending investigation, and dismissed several security officials in Kirkuk.

The directives followed an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company and a wider campaign against illicit oil networks—including alleged smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar linked to the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, which denied the accusation.

World.title: Iraqi PM meets Egyptian businessmen in Cairo
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi affirmed on Monday that Iraq has a promising investment environment and opportunities in several sectors.

Al-Zaidi’s remarks took place during his meeting with a group of Egyptian businessmen in the Egyptian capital, Cairo, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

The meeting is part of the Iraqi government’s efforts to strengthen the economic partnership between the two countries and expand investment cooperation.

The Iraqi government is striving to increase the presence of the private sector, recognizing its critical role in bolstering the country’s economy and attaining progress, according to al-Zaidi.

The Iraqi prime minister noted that the Iraqi investment law offers investors benefits and protection, including tax and customs exemptions.

Al-Zaidi listened to the views, recommendations, and suggestions put forward by Egyptian business leaders to increase investments in Iraq.

Egyptian business leaders conveyed their gratitude for the incentives that Iraq provides to investors as well as their interest in the available investment prospects.

World.title: Iraq, Egypt sign several memoranda of understanding
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly oversaw a ceremony held to sign 10 bilateral cooperation documents and memoranda of understanding (MoUs) on Monday in Egypt’s New Administrative Capital.

The ceremony followed the fourth session of the Egyptian-Iraqi Joint Higher Committee, co-chaired by both leaders during Al-Zaidi’s first official visit to Egypt since taking office.

The two countries signed a treaty to prevent tax evasion and eliminate double taxation on income and capital.

Health and trade officials finalized a MoU covering medical supplies and pharmaceuticals.

Regulators inked deals for radio and TV broadcasting cooperation alongside nuclear and radiation oversight.

Additionally, both sides signed five other documents establishing joint programs in fisheries, scientific research, national planning, youth, and sports.

Prior to the ceremony, al-Zaidi met President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to expand economic cooperation and coordinate diplomatic efforts on regional security.

World.title: US exports to Iraq reach $727 million in first nine months of 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – U.S. exports to Iraq surpassed $700 million during the first nine months of 2026, reaching a cumulative total of $727 million across the first three quarters of the year, according to U.S. Census Bureau figures published via the International Trade Centre’s (ITC) Trade Map platform on Tuesday, November 24, 2026.

Quarterly data shows that bilateral shipments held steady through the first half of the year before gaining momentum in the third quarter:

Q1 2026: $238 million

Q2 2026: $238 million

Q3 2026: $251 million

Nine-Month Cumulative Total: $727 million

The $727 million export volume spans a diverse range of industrial, energy, agricultural, and healthcare goods shipped to the Iraqi market.

Primary export categories include pharmaceuticals and medical products, heavy industrial equipment, gas turbines, machinery and appliances, petroleum derivatives, and agricultural staples such as rice.

World.title: Saharanpur showdown: Why Akhilesh's 1st candidate list in UP has rattled Congress MP Imran Masood
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

MP Imran Masood is breathing fire at the

after

's first candidate list for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. The list includes two constituencies that the Congress leader considers his political turf.

The SP's decision to renominate sitting MLAs from Behat and Saharanpur, both seats sought by Congress in alliance negotiations, has turned a seat-sharing disagreement into a personal and political confrontation.

Released on Tuesday night, hours after another round of seat-sharing talks between the two parties in Delhi, the five-name list features four Muslim candidates from western Uttar Pradesh and an OBC nominee from Bundelkhand.



The four Muslim candidates are sitting MLAs Umar Ali Khan from Behat, Ashu Malik from Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan from Kairana and Mehboob Ali from Amroha. Jyoti Lodhi has been named from Lalitpur.

The move has particularly rattled Masood, who represents Saharanpur in the Lok Sabha and is the Congress's Uttar Pradesh working president. Having won the Saharanpur parliamentary seat in 2024, Masood sees the two qssembly constituencies as important to Congress's claim to political space in the region. His sharp response has raised a pointed question: does the SP want to take on the BJP or its INDIA bloc ally?

The Saharanpur war

The SP renominated four sitting legislators: Umar Ali Khan from Behat, Ashu Malik from Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan from Kairana and Mehboob Ali from Amroha.





The fifth candidate, Jyoti Lodhi, has been named from Lalitpur.

All four Muslim candidates are from western UP, where the SP is keen to retain its traditional support base and expand its PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) coalition.

But Behat and Saharanpur make the list particularly sensitive for Masood.

The Congress MP won the Saharanpur Lok Sabha seat in 2024 with 5,47,967 votes, defeating the BJP's Raghav Lakhanpal by 64,542 votes.

He secured 44.57% of the vote, against the BJP candidate's 39.32%.

His performance was particularly strong in the two assembly segments now at the centre of the dispute. Masood led by 44,626 votes in Saharanpur and 38,229 in Behat in the parliamentary election. Both, however, had elected SP MLAs in 2022.

Umar Ali Khan won Behat with 1,34,513 votes, defeating the BJP's Naresh Saini by 37,880 votes. Ashu Malik secured Saharanpur with 1,07,007 votes, defeating the BJP's Jagpal Singh by 30,745 votes.

The contrast is the main disagreement point between the allies. Congress is banking on the 2024 Lok Sabha mandate, while the SP is relying on its assembly-level victories and sitting legislators.

For Akhilesh, the two seats are established SP territory. However, for Masood, they are part of the space where Congress can consolidate after his parliamentary victory.

Masood and Malik were involved in a public exchange during a district development coordination and monitoring committee meeting earlier this year.

After the SP announcement, Malik said he was under "no fear or pressure" and would contest the election strongly.

Masood's nephew Hamza Masood was more combative. He asserted that Congress would contest all seven assembly seats in Saharanpur district, adding that his uncle's support was crucial in the region.

"BJP ko Saharanpur se Imran Masood hi hara sakte hain," he said.

The Akhilesh-Masood equation

The latest confrontation is another turn in a political relationship that has changed parties, positions and equations more than once.

Imran Masood left Congress and joined the SP in January 2022, ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. But the association lasted barely nine months. After the SP did not give him or his associates a ticket, Masood quit the party in October 2022 and joined the BSP.

Mayawati appointed him coordinator of the BSP's western Uttar Pradesh unit, with additional responsibility for working among Muslims in Uttarakhand.

That stint, too, ended abruptly. In August 2023, the BSP expelled him, accusing him of indiscipline and anti-party activities. Masood returned to Congress in October that year.

The return proved electorally significant. In 2024, Congress fielded him from Saharanpur as part of the INDIA bloc arrangement, with SP support. He defeated the BJP, giving Congress a prominent Muslim face in western UP.

But the parliamentary victory did not necessarily settle the question of who would control the political space in the region.

The unease has been building for months. Congress's decision to appoint Masood as Uttar Pradesh working president in October was viewed by some SP leaders as an attempt to strengthen its bargaining position in seat-sharing negotiations. The Indian Express reported that sections of the SP were uncomfortable with Masood's public criticism of Akhilesh and his demands for an early alliance decision.

In August, another development added to the strain. Imran Masood's son-in-law, Shayan Masood, joined the SP, citing ideological differences with his father-in-law.

Shayan subsequently criticised Masood for targeting Akhilesh instead of the BJP.

The candidate announcement has now brought the personal and political tensions into the open.

"When you make such an announcement against me, I don't understand whether you want to fight me, the Congress, or the BJP," Masood said, questioning the SP's seriousness about the alliance.

He also rejected the idea that Congress was seeking charity from the SP.

"We are not beggars," he said, objecting to the party's unilateral announcement of candidates while negotiations were still underway.

Elder brothers or stepbrothers?

The public sparring quickly drew reactions from both camps, with some leaders attempting damage control and others adding fuel to the fire.

SP leader ST Hasan urged restraint, describing the two parties as elder and younger brothers.

"We are like elder and younger brothers. We should not talk like two stepbrothers fighting over division of property," he said.

SP MP SP Singh Patel, however, was less conciliatory. He dismissed Congress's electoral strength in Uttar Pradesh and said the party would only be able to win by relying on the SP.

"The Congress should simply accept whatever number of seats they are allocated in the alliance," he said.

Masood hit back, invoking Rahul Gandhi's role in Patel's political rise. He argued that Patel was an MP because of the political impact Rahul Gandhi had created after 2019.

The exchange has exposed a fundamental disagreement over the alliance's power structure. Congress wants its improved Lok Sabha performance recognised; the SP believes its much larger Assembly-level organisation should determine the terms.

The voter math

Strip away the personal exchanges and the five-candidate announcement points to a larger contest over political representation in western Uttar Pradesh.

The region has considerable electoral significance for both parties.

Saharanpur district, according to Census 2011 data, had a Muslim population of 41.9% and a Scheduled Caste population of 22.1%. These are district-wide population figures, not constituency-level voter shares, but they underline the social context in which the two parties are positioning themselves.

For the SP, the PDA formula is an attempt to bring backward classes, Dalits and minorities into a broader electoral coalition.

Renominating four Muslim sitting MLAs in its first list reinforces the party's commitment to that strategy.

Congress, meanwhile, sees its 2024 performance as an opportunity to rebuild its own Muslim-Dalit political base, particularly in western UP. Masood's Saharanpur victory gave the party a prominent regional leader around whom it can attempt to build that presence.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The competition is not limited to the two INDIA bloc partners either.

The Samajik Parivartan Morcha, a new alliance between AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Chandrashekhar Azad's Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram), is another political formation seeking space among Muslim and Dalit voters.

The BSP, too, remains part of the wider political equation, even as its organisational position has changed since the 2022 election.

The SP has released a list of five, but the questions they have raised go well beyond Behat and Saharanpur. Who speaks for western UP's Muslim voters? How much space will Congress get within Akhilesh Yadav's PDA framework? And can two allies compete for the same electoral ground without undermining the alliance they are trying to build?

For now, the SP has made its choices clear. Whether Congress accepts them, and whether the two parties can turn this confrontation into a workable seat-sharing arrangement, remains the bigger test.

World.title: UP polls: SP, Congress seat talks turn into public tug-of-war; BJP calls it 'thugbandhan'
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Relations between

and

appeared to sour after the latter jumped the gun on Tuesday and announced its first list of candidates for the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.

The list was released even as deliberations over a seat-sharing deal were still ongoing between the two parties.

To make matters worse, the list included candidates on two constituencies that featured on Congress' wishlist.

Congress fumed over its poll partner's decision and said the high command must decide whether seat-sharing talks with SP should continue. In a sharp rejoinder the grand-old-party also reminded SP that they are not beggars and must be treated respectfully.



Samajwadi Party, on the other hand, defended the announcements and maintained that announcing candidates for seats already held by the party was âa normal and expected processâ in all alliance deals.

The BJP, on the other hand, seized on the developments to highlight divisions within the opposition camp months ahead of a high-stakes electoral contest.

What triggered the rift

The latest round of tensions began on Tuesday night when SP chief

issued a lengthy public message to Congress, urging the party to prioritise "winnability" over the number of seats it wanted to contest.





In a social media post on X, Akhilesh also asked Congress to hold "serious discussions" on the seat-sharing deal.

"We propose that, by carefully considering public expectations and ground realities, we engage in serious deliberations to ensure the victory of our 'alliance' across the majority of the constituencies. Among the seats contested by us, the number of seats won should exceed the number of seats lost," he said.

Moments later, Samajwadi Party declared its first list of candidates, retaining its sitting MLAs Umar Ali Khan from Behat, Ashu Malik from Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan from Kairana and Mehboob Ali from Amroha, while naming Jyoti Lodhi as its candidate from Lalitpur.

Tej Narain Pandey alias Pawan Pandey was declared the party's candidate from Ayodhya in August.

Behat and Saharanpur were reportedly on Congress' wishlist.

The Saharanpur region is particularly significant for Congress, as the party's Uttar Pradesh working president, Imran Masood, won the Saharanpur Lok Sabha seat in the 2024 general elections.

Congress has been seeking a larger share of assembly seats falling within parliamentary constituencies it won in the Lok Sabha polls. It has cited its improved performance in the 2024 general elections to strengthen its claim for a greater share of seats in the alliance.

Congress cries foul

The list has started a fresh exchange of sharp remarks. Imran Masood objected to the SP's reported offer of just 26 "winnable" seats to Congress.

Imran Masood expressed strong objections to the SP's decision to offer Congress just 26 "winnable" seats.

"Where is the alliance? If you are acting like this, then where is the alliance? Our leadership will decide what we need to do; I just don't understand it.

Here you say one thing, and there something else happens," Masood told news agency IANS.

Making it clear that the final call would rest with the Congress leadership, the MP said he would abide by whatever decision the party takes.

"This decision has to be taken by our party. What Akhilesh Ji is doing or not doing is not a big issue for me; I am bound by my party, and whatever my party says, I have to do that," Masood said.

"When you are holding talks on one hand and making announcements on the other, it shows that you are not serious," he added.

Questioning the intention of their ally, Masood said, "I do not understand whether you want to fight me, the Congress or the BJP. It needs to be decided whether we want to fight the BJP or fight among ourselves."

AICC in-charge of UP Rajendra Pal Gautam also expressed displeasure over the Samajwadi Party's decision and said this should have been avoided while seat-sharing talks were ongoing.

"They should have avoided that and waited (for the talks to be over).

Nevertheless, this had also happened in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, and some candidates were withdrawn as well," Gautam said.

"I hope everything will go in the right direction," Gautam added.

Congress leader Hamza Masood, nephew of Congress MP Imran Masood, also questioned SP's approach towards its alliance partner, asking whether the SP wanted to fight Congress or BJP.

Hamza alleged that SP leaders, supporters, former ministers and MPs were continuously targeting Congress leaders on social media, including Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, despite Congress maintaining silence and adhering to the principles of the alliance.

"First, they should decide whether they want to fight against us or against the BJP. If you check Twitter, their supporters, leaders, former ministers and MPs continuously target our leaders and make remarks against Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi," Hamza told IANS.

"We remain silent and follow the alliance principles, and will continue to do so on Rahul Gandhi's instruction, but Saharanpur is our strong district, in 2012 our candidates fought on these two seats strongly, in 2017 our MLAs won," he added.

SP advises Congress to 'exercise patience'

Samajwadi Party, however, said that the it was already agreed between both the parties that there would be no compromise on seats held by each other.

"It was clear from the outset and known to all. Don't really know what the objection is all about," Samajwadi Party MP Rajiv Rai said.

Another SP MP Ramjilal Suman said that the party said that announcing candidates for seats already held by the party was âa normal and expected processâ in all alliance deals.

"Don't know what the brouhaha is about? The SP has merely announced candidates on seats held by the party. What's wrong with that and why so much hullabaloo?"

SP MP Shiv Pal Singh Patel weighed in on the controversy and refuted Congress's claim that SP's seat tally improved due to leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi.

"My advice to him (Imran Masood) is to exercise patience and refrain from making such direct, provocative statements.

I did not become an MP because of the Congress party; I belong to the Samajwadi Party. We contested the election under the leadership of Akhilesh Yadav, not Rahul Gandhi. Therefore, such claims should not be made. We were part of an alliance, from which the Congress party also benefited," Patel said.

"Letâs be direct: how many of your candidates won? Out of 17 candidates, 6 of yours won--thatâs 30%--whereas 37 of our candidates won out of 63, which is about 70%.

You can do the math yourself; so, please donât claim that we won because of them," he added.

Samajwadi Party MP Awadhesh Prasad, however, refuted speculation over the seat-sharing talks, saying that nothing of the sort was discussed in Tuesday's meeting and dismissing reports of discord between the alliance partners.

"Nothing of the sort was discussed in yesterdayâs meeting. These are just baseless rumours, mere talk in the air.

It would be best not to pay any heed to such talk. These are just rumours, and rumours simply vanish into thin air,â Prasad told ANI.

Reiterating that the coalition remains united around the core objective of ousting the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), he added, âThere has been no such statement. Instead of focusing on such baseless rumours, consider what is actually significant: the decision to remove the BJP from power has been finalised.

It is a settled matter that, under the leadership of Akhilesh Yadav, a good government will be formed in Uttar Pradesh.

â

Outlining the progress of the seat-by-seat review, Prasad noted that further rounds of discussions would follow as the entire discussion could not be concluded. He added that the matters raised were discussed constructively.

âThe matters raised during the meeting were discussed constructively and in a cordial atmosphere.

The core objective is to defeat the BJP at any cost and, in its place, make Akhilesh ji the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh. To this end, seat-by-seat discussions took place, though the entire discussion could not be concluded," Prasad said.

BJP's sharp jibe

Meanwhile, BJP took a jibe at the opposition and sought to highlight that all was not well in the opposition camp.

"They should perhaps focus on their own seat-sharing numbersâwhether the Samajwadi Party is offering them 5 seats or 26," BJP leader Sudhanshu Trivedi said at a press conference.

"Akhilesh Yadav began his campaign from Raebareli. Then, the SP announced they would provide 26 seats, but following this they released a list of five names without any consultationâthree of which could prove quite problematic for the Congress party. In doing so, they have clearly signalled their priorities," he added.

Reacting to the seat-sharing talks between SP and Congress, the deputy chief minister said whether the deal cooks up or not makes no difference to BJP.

"SP has shown Congress its standing; now let Congress show SP its standing. Whether their deal cooks up or not, it makes no difference to us."

"Such theatrics keep happening between the two parties (SP and Congress), but it will have no impact on the BJP's health," he added.

The deputy chief minister said the people of Uttar Pradesh were politically aware and would stand âfirmly behind the BJPâ.

"That is not an alliance but a 'thugbandhan (alliance of deceivers)â of goons, criminals, corrupt people and rioters.

Its condition is neither good today nor is it going to improve in the future," Maurya said.

"Voting for the Samajwadi Party is like inviting trouble, while voting for the Congress would once again push the country towards decline. People are standing strongly with the BJP, and the party will form the government in Uttar Pradesh for the third time with a massive majority," he said.

Inside the seat-sharing deadlock

Reportedly, the first round of talks, which ended on Tuesday at Congress veteran Pramod Tiwari's Delhi residence, remained inconclusive.

Congress is demanding 120 constituencies, including the Gandhi family's traditional strongholds of Amethi and Raebareli, and is unwilling to settle for fewer seats, news agency ANI reported, citing party sources.

Congress conveyed its demand during a meeting with SP leaders in Delhi, where it submitted a list of 120 constituencies it wants to contest, sources told ANI.

Meanwhile, Akhilesh has called for mutual understanding between the alliance partners and said candidates should be selected based on their electoral prospects. He also emphasised the need for consensus candidates representing the PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) framework on every seat to take on BJP.

SP has also sought details about Congress's prospective candidates and their electoral prospects in other constituencies claimed by the party.
