World.title: China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.content:
China has successfully tested two large unmanned cargo aircraft: one with a 5-ton payload capacity and the other capable of flying 3,000 kilometers, laying the groundwork for future commercial and emergency transportation systems.

On Tuesday, the country announced that the Changying-8, a domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, had completed a test delivery. Three days prior, another domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, the W5000, also completed its maiden flight.

The milestones come as China’s drone market is expected to exceed 140 billion yuan ($19.6 billion) by the end of 2026, with the industrial drone segment alone projected to reach 84 billion yuan, up 12.5% from last year.

China began testing large cargo drones as early as 2017 and incorporated the concept of the “low-altitude economy” into government policy in 2021. The Civil Aviation Administration of China has also laid out a roadmap to establish an air transportation system for unmanned aircraft by 2035.

During its delivery test, the Changying-8, developed by China North Industries Group Corporation, released a cargo pallet at an altitude of 300 meters before returning to its base.

The aircraft, whose maiden flight took place in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, on March 31, has a maximum range of over 3,000 kilometers, measures 17 meters in length, has a 25-meter wingspan, and an 18-cubic-meter cargo compartment volume, domestic media reported.

In the event of extreme disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and mudslides destroying roads and bridges, the aircraft can be used to transport up to 3.5 metric tons of goods, equal to over 700 disaster-relief tents, the head of the Changying-8’s development team told state news agency Xinhua.

According to its engineers, future applications could include transportation of regional cargo, emergency supplies, and cold-chain deliveries, domestic media reported.

On Saturday, the W5000, an unmanned cargo aircraft developed by Chinese aviation company Air White Whale, also completed its maiden flight in northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

The aircraft flew for about 30 minutes at an altitude of 1,000 meters, completing a series of test maneuvers before landing. The test focused on the aircraft’s flight stability and the coordinated operation of its propulsion, flight control, electronics, and ground-based monitoring and control systems.

With a maximum payload capacity of 5 metric tons, the W5000 is billed as one of the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft by payload capacity. Made of carbon fiber and weighing less than 6 metric tons, the aircraft measures over 22 meters in both length and wingspan and can fly at a cruising speed of 526 kilometers per hour, with a maximum range of 2,600 kilometers, domestic media reported.

Hu Zhendong, founder, chairman, and CEO of Air White Whale, said the W5000 could reduce logistics costs per ton-kilometer by more than 60% compared with comparable crewed cargo aircraft.

The W5000 is expected to begin commercial operation by the end of next year, according to domestic media.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: The W5000, billed as the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft, on display at Airshow China 2024 in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, Nov. 12, 2024. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.title: Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.content:
One of the wildest boss fights in China’s latest hack-and-slash blockbuster game begins with a calligraphy brush. Soul, the protagonist of Phantom Blade Zero, released late last month, dots the eyes of a lion-dance head, performing a traditional Chinese ritual believed to awaken the eponymous beast.

Cue the violence. Two performers animate the lion, lunging at Soul with blades spinning on its head and flames pouring from its mouth. The fight then spills onto elevated wooden poles, where Soul and the lion-dance master leap from perch to perch, trading blows to pounding Chinese drums and screaming electric guitar.

In the game its creator originally envisioned, Soul had just 66 lives to survive this fight and every other. Use them up, and hours of progress across the campaign would be gone for good.

The restriction was meant to mirror the game’s story: Soul has just 66 days to find a replacement for his damaged heart. But Beijing-based developer S-Game eventually abandoned the compulsory death limit, introducing three difficulty settings and making the original challenge optional.

S-Game founder Liang Qiwei called the compromise “one of the countless difficult decisions we made in developing Phantom Blade Zero.” His studio spent four years and a reported 300 million to 400 million yuan ($45 million to $60 million) creating a game it hoped would introduce wuxia — Chinese martial arts fantasy — to audiences around the world.

To bring its combat to life, S-Game recruited Hong Kong action star Donnie Yen, enlisted martial arts experts, and brought traditional performers into motion-capture studios. The finished game features more than 50 bosses and 55 weapons, each offering different ways to fight.

The scale of the undertaking drew inevitable comparisons with Black Myth: Wukong, China’s breakout global gaming hit of 2024. Chinese gamers even dubbed Phantom Blade Zero “the village’s second college student,” hoping the conditions for success would align twice.

So far, it has. Video game rating site IGN gave Phantom Blade Zero a 9 out of 10, praising its “memorable boss fights, compelling combat, and limitless swagger.” Its PC version scored 88 on review aggregator Metacritic, surpassing the 81 Black Myth: Wukong received.

Released on Oct. 29, with a standard edition priced at 268 yuan ($40) and a deluxe edition at 328 yuan, the game sold more than 4 million copies in its first 72 hours, topping Steam’s bestseller chart and generating an estimated 1 billion yuan in gross sales.

Unlike Wukong, which drew on the beloved Chinese classic “Journey to the West,” Phantom Blade Zero had to win over players with a far less familiar fictional universe, one Liang had spent two decades developing.

Punk fiction

In 2006, while studying architecture at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, Liang began developing Rain Blood, an independent role-playing game inspired by Taiwanese wuxia novelist Gu Long. Built using software intended for amateur game developers, it introduced Soul, an assassin serving the Order, a secretive organization of martial artists.

Over the following years, Liang, who later earned a master’s degree in architecture from Yale University, expanded the fictional universe through a series of PC and mobile games, retaining its characters, history, and storytelling conventions. In 2017, he began developing concepts for Phantom Blade Zero.

This time, Soul is fighting for his own survival. Framed for the murder of the Order’s leader and gravely wounded, he is kept alive by a venom-infused replacement heart that will last just 66 days. He must uncover the conspiracy, clear his name, and find a way to survive.

His search takes him through a bleak, rain-soaked world where ancient Chinese temples house enormous machinery, and traditional martial arts coexist with mechanical prosthetics. Liang calls the distinctive blend of wuxia and industrial technology “kungfupunk.”

Geng Youzimin, a researcher at Peking University’s Video Game and Art Research Center who has followed the series for years, recognized much of the old Rain Blood universe in the new game, from its character names and dialogue to its cold, gray atmosphere.

While many Chinese wuxia games emphasize storytelling over action, Geng was particularly impressed by Phantom Blade Zero’s side quests and the portrayal of jianghu — the loosely governed world of wandering martial artists, rival factions, and secret societies familiar to readers of wuxia fiction.

“The jianghu often represents a world in which an existing power structure governing a region has collapsed, while a new one has yet to emerge,” he said.

In one such quest, a Shadow Warden sent to capture Soul instead seeks his help to escape the organization he serves. He even discards the numerical identity assigned by his masters and chooses a name for himself. Though he ultimately fails to break free, he secretly helps Soul defeat his enemies, even at the cost of his own life.

Yet not all of the older series’ conventions have been as warmly received. Some players mocked the game’s grandiose names as adolescent melodrama, including “Dark Demon Castle,” where Soul fights a boss portrayed by Donnie Yen. Others found its dialogue overly straightforward.

Geng, who welcomed those familiar touches as a longtime fan, said the pushback underscores how tastes have shifted since the franchise’s indie beginnings. “When this IP first emerged, these elements were popular,” he said, adding that today, the same stylistic quirks have become “baggage” that risks alienating a wider audience.

For Cao Yuan, a game content creator in his 30s who had never played S-Game’s earlier titles, the moral ambiguity of its world struck a chord. “The game incorporates many such blurred boundaries between good and evil,” he said.

Cao also found Soul’s struggle more relatable. “I have no weapons, no resources, nothing at all, but I still have to fight my way into the jianghu,” he said. “That experience feels very close to real life.”

The fire-breathing lion that confronts Soul took shape in a Shanghai motion-capture studio, where a troupe from China’s southern Guangdong province performed a traditional lion-dance routine. Combat director Yang Liu and his team used the recordings to develop the fight, exaggerating the performers’ head tosses and tail swings into attacks.

Even the vegetables suspended above the arena draw on cai qing, or “plucking the greens,” a southern Chinese lion-dance ritual in which the lion retrieves greenery symbolizing prosperity and spits it out to spread good fortune.

In the game, Soul can collect the vegetables to boost his power; later, when the lion-dance master finally breaks free of the force controlling him, he offers Soul the greens.

The music, helmed by Bo Caisheng, a composer who’s worked on animated productions and video games, draws on the same traditions, beginning with drums performed live before introducing percussion evocative of the northern Shanxi province and electric guitar. Bo described his approach as “using Chinese music as the skeleton and Western music as the flesh.”

Tang Zhi, 35, grew up in central China’s Hunan province, where he was familiar with lion dancing from neighboring Guangdong. A Beijing-based developer relations executive, he’s followed Phantom Blade Zero since its early trailers.

“When you jump around on the plum blossom poles and fight the boss, it immediately reminds you of the martial arts performances you watched as a child,” he said.

Game theory

For all the intricate martial arts choreography onscreen, pulling off spectacular moves in Phantom Blade Zero requires surprisingly few commands.

In a fight against a wooden puppet, flashes of blue signal an attack the player can block, while red warns of one that must be dodged. Each response takes a button press, though timing is crucial: dodge at precisely the right moment, and Soul executes “ghoststep,” instantly slipping behind his opponent.

Another button unleashes an elaborate finishing sequence, launching the puppet into the air before Soul slashes its neck as it lands.

Liang wanted to make such combat accessible to newcomers while giving experienced players room to test their skills and explore its depth. Those less interested in mastering the fighting system could concentrate on the story or simply enjoy the cinematic choreography.

“And in the era of livestreaming and short videos, the gameplay itself will become content for a wider audience,” Liang wrote on social media.

Players can combine 30 primary weapons and 25 secondary weapons, including broadswords and twin daggers, each with their own moves and finishing animations. A sha qi, or “killing intent” meter, replenished by well-timed blocks and weapon switches, encourages fast, aggressive combat.

For Zhang Yingshen, 35, a game content creator who works in public relations for a foreign gaming company, the combat was exhilarating without the frustration he associated with learning other action games.

“It’s a game where positive feedback practically spills out of the screen,” he told Sixth Tone.

But Zhang admitted that he eventually wanted more of a challenge. “About halfway through the game, I felt it was a little easy, so I switched to the highest difficulty setting. But even that wasn’t challenging enough,” he said.

Players can switch between three difficulty settings as they progress, but the toughest challenge is reserved for those who complete the main story. Only then can they unlock “66 Days,” a separate mode that limits them to 66 lives — the restriction Liang originally intended for every player.

But Zhang’s experience at a Phantom Blade Zero playtest in Beijing left him with reservations about the combat system’s staying power. “We (and other uploaders) were worried that players might feel exhausted after 10 to 20 hours of gameplay,” he said.

Yet he found that the game’s more than 50 bosses and interconnected, three-dimensional maps gave players plenty to explore across Liang’s sprawling jianghu world.

“Throughout the game, you constantly feel like you’re discovering something new around every corner, and you always maintain a sense of freshness about the world,” Zhang said.

He Wei, a professor at Beijing Normal University’s School of Arts and Communication, sees Phantom Blade Zero’s fusion of wuxia and industrial machinery as an attempt to create a distinctive style that international audiences can readily embrace.

But he argued that incorporating Chinese traditions was only part of the challenge. “Gameplay is the vessel, while culture is the soul. Only when the two are integrated can a game spread culture far and wide,” he said.

He nevertheless considers Black Myth: Wukong stronger in artistic vision and cultural depth, particularly in its character designs. “From the character concept art to the finished designs, the illustrated portraits of characters are more sophisticated and demonstrate greater depth,” he said.

Geng, from Peking University, cautioned against expecting other Chinese developers to reproduce Wukong’s extraordinary cultural impact. “Black Myth: Wukong was a phenomenon. The cultural discourse it carried, or the cultural responsibilities it took on, were things that neither the game itself nor its development team could ever have fully anticipated,” he said.

Nor did the commercial success of Wukong and Phantom Blade Zero resolve Geng’s doubts about the sustainability of AAA development. Such games demand enormous investment and large-scale production, and require high returns to justify their costs.

“AAA games will always represent the ultimate ideal for many game developers, the crown jewel of their ambitions. But commercially, they are increasingly more like luxury goods,” he said.

For Liang, bringing a fictional world he had spent two decades developing to a mass audience meant balancing his desire for creative expression with his responsibilities to paying players. After a playtest in Beijing, he described himself as “a service provider” who had to give players more than their money’s worth.

“Making games is a process of dissolving one’s own ego and sinking it into the earth,” he wrote on social media, “where it can grow into a flourishing tree nourished by the soil.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A scene from the video game “Phantom Blade Zero.” From @影之刃零 on Weibo)

World.title: Mandarin Oriental is reborn, 12 years and a pandemic later
World.content:
The 275-room luxury hotel reopens its doors just across the street from its old home, this time as part of the Ayala Triangle development

MANILA, Philippines – When the last guests checked out of the Mandarin Oriental in September 2014, the hotel promised to be back in six years.

Makati would have to wait twice as long – with a pandemic in between that set back its original 2020 opening date – but the day has finally arrived.

On Thursday, November 26, Ayala Land opens the new Mandarin Oriental at Ayala Triangle, making good on a promise made more than a decade ago.

The original Mandarin opened on Makati Avenue in 1976, just in time for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Designed by National Artist for Architecture Leandro Locsin, it was among the first Mandarin Oriental hotels outside Hong Kong, arriving at a time when Makati was not yet the skyscraper-lined business district it is today.

That iconic structure has since been demolished, and in its place rises Park Central Towers, another Ayala Land development, billed as an ultra-luxury residential twin tower. (READ: Luxury condo resilience: Half of Ayala’s Laurean buyers staying despite pause)

Still, its successor, built just across the street, keeps a connection to the old Mandarin. American architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed the new hotel in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, the practice founded by the late architect.

REINVENTION. The 275-room Mandarin Hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati City is owned by Ayala Land Hospitality and managed by Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group. Ayala Land handout

The new Mandarin is considerably smaller, at 275 rooms compared with its predecessor’s 413. That was part of the plan from the beginning, when Ayala Land first announced the project in June 2014.

The return of the Mandarin is also part of Ayala Land’s continuing reinvention of Ayala Triangle. Once part of Nielson Airport, the property went on to first house the Makati Stock Exchange and has today evolved into a hub anchored by Ayala Triangle Gardens Towers, with upscale restaurants and landscaped gardens – and finally, a luxury hotel to round it all out.

With the Mandarin, Ayala Land is also making a wager on the Philippines’ place in Asia’s luxury tourism market. The company believes Filipino culture and creativity can be a selling point in their own right, rather than looking to Singapore, Hong Kong, or Bangkok for a blueprint.

Filipino art, craftsmanship, and design feature prominently throughout the property. Ayala Land said it was designed around the idea that “the Philippines need not imitate other luxury destinations to compete with them.”

In the first nine months of 2026, Ayala Land’s leasing and hospitality revenues grew 8% year-on-year to P37.8 billion. Recurring-income businesses also now account for a greater part of the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), standing at 55% and up from 44% in the same period last year. – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines’ biggest HiFi exhibit set this weekend
World.content:
Admission is free for all audio and music lovers, and there's no need to pre-register

(This is a press release from the November HiFi Show organizers.)

A team of Filipino audio experts is holding a HiFi show this weekend in Makati City.

The November HiFi Show is the Philippines’ biggest hi-fi exhibition, the country’s premier gathering for music lovers and audio enthusiasts that has been around for 24 years.

Each year, it brings together leading and local international brands showcasing the finest in high-fidelity and high-quality sound systems, speakers, amplifiers, turntables, and more.

Beyond the gear, it’s also a treasure trove for collectors, with rare finds, vinyl records, and CDs waiting to be discovered. More than just an exhibition, the November HiFi Show is a celebration of sound culture — where innovation, passion, and community converge.

“Since 2008, my team of Filipino audio experts and I have been doing this purely for the love of the hobby—no commercial agenda, just a shared mission to build world-class, 100% Filipino-made DIY high-end audio gear,” said veteran business journalist and Rappler columnist Val Villanueva.

The November HiFi Show 2026 will be held on November 28 to 29 at the Makati Diamond Residences, 118 Legazpi Street, Legazpi Village, Makati City.

Parking can be found nearby Greenbelt Malls, and street side parking is available in Legazpi Village.

Admission is free for all audio and music lovers, and there’s no need to pre-register. Just walk in and enjoy what the November HiFi Show has to offer.

Whether you’re a seasoned audiophile or just curious about great sound, swing by Room 802. Let’s talk gear, swap stories, and enjoy the music. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pope Leo calls COP31 failure ‘troubling,’ urges action on climate change
World.content:
Pope Leo gestures from the popemobile during the weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, November 25, 2026.

'This situation calls for a renewed sense of shared responsibility, new forms of solidarity among nations and fundamental changes in behaviors, socio-economic systems, and the governance of our societies,' says the Pope

VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday, November 25, sharply criticized the failure of UN climate talks over the weekend, calling the outcome “troubling” and urging world leaders to step up efforts to combat climate change.

“In the face of the growing frequency of extreme environmental events linked to the climate crisis, it is troubling that COP31 ended without the international community adopting clear commitments to address it seriously and responsibly,” the pope told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square.

“This situation calls for a renewed sense of shared responsibility, new forms of solidarity among nations and fundamental changes in behaviors, socio-economic systems, and the governance of our societies,” said the Pope.

The COP31 talks collapsed on Sunday, November 22, as the European Union and others rejected a final deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted was after a summit in Copenhagen in 2009.

Leo is known for speaking carefully in public and makes appeals to the international community in his weekly audiences on a less frequent basis than his predecessor, Pope Francis.

Leo, the first US-born pope, has urged the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics to protect the Earth. Last year, he approved a new Catholic rite of Mass that exhorts people to care for creation, in a first for the global Church. – Rappler.com

World.title: More connected but lonelier than ever: How do we navigate an AI-reliant world?
World.content:
Mental health advocates say that tools like AI chatbots normalize isolation and provide a false sense of connection. Where do we draw the line, especially for the youth?

Childhood looks different for many kids nowadays in the age of artificial intelligence and social media.

Toys are no longer the only things keeping them busy. Screens dominate their free time. And when they want to play with their friends, they don’t always just head outside anymore; they log onto gaming platforms instead.

And when they become lonely and need someone to open up to, it’s no longer a human hearing them out — but an AI chatbot. For mental health advocates like actress and She Talks Asia co-founder Iza Calzado, the rise of these tools is alarming. Under the guise of connection and offering safe spaces, AI chatbots often just work to normalize isolation, and it’s a reality that many humans who have fallen for the trap have to face.

“It’s safer to chat with a bot in this landscape. It agrees with you all the time. It does not judge you. It’s never disappointed when you say something. So imagine a child, who perhaps does not feel as confident or as safe in their own home, is lonely, starts talking to a bot, and then eventually becomes friends with a bot,” Calzado illustrated during a panel discussion at Rappler’s 2026 Social Good Summit last Saturday, November 21.

“Because you know what? This friend will not unfriend me, will not spread rumors about me in school, and will not bully me. That’s how it begins, and that to me is very concerning.”

Even among adults, AI chatbots have become pseudo-therapists who help rationalize their thoughts, make sense of whatever they’re going through, and validate their feelings — even when they may be in the wrong. The chatbot pulls you in by making you feel seen, and before you know it, you’ve been completely hooked.

But why does it do this?

For Empath CEO and founder Steph Naval, it’s simple: AI chatbots are there to make money.

Steph Naval at We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

“Chatbots, when you go there for a replacement of therapy or well-being, what happens is that you don’t get the benefit of having difficult conversations and corrective behavior. Because that’s something that you do in therapy,” Naval said, adding that it was in her painful therapy sessions that she was actually able to heal and grow most.

It’s the same with social media, which has become a fierce breeding ground for insecurity. Naval said these apps can detect that through your images and videos, and “responds by pushing certain products or content that can exacerbate these negative thoughts.

“For example, it takes a lot of photos of your body or the gym and then they can detect if you feel insecure. Then they’ll push products to you. So I find that’s something to definitely take note of because that has really caused and affected a generation,” said Naval.

When technology comes before policy

Social media and chatbots, however, don’t just offer you a false sense of companionship and feed on your biggest vulnerabilities. They have also doubled a platform for groups to promote violence among young children — and this is something that has become apparent in the alarming rise of school shooting incidents in the Philippines.

Still, Akbayan Representative Perci Cendaña believes that the growing reliance on these chatbots isn’t something you can blame on those who turn to it, especially in countries like the Philippines where mental health services are scarce. From then on, it only leads to a bigger set of issues that the country is not yet equipped to properly address.

“We lack mental health assistance, that’s why our countrymen go online instead. They rely on chatbots. They rely on the warmth and affirmation they get from these platforms, and this phenomenon, combined with other social realities, are fueling these isolated incidents,” Cendaña said in a mix of Filipino and English.

“Nauuna ang teknolohiya sa polisiya. Nauuna ang teknolohiya sa government framework (Technology is prioritized over policy. Technology is ahead of the government framework),” he added.

Perci Cendaña at We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

This is what Cendaña hopes to address through the National AI Governance Act — which is anchored on human-centeredness. It contains the AI Bill of Rights, which holds that humans should have the authority to override platform systems.

Cendaña then believes that tech executives and government officials shouldn’t be the only ones making decisions about AI governance. Because it’s human well-being at the very core of it all, civil society should have a seat at the table, too.

Back to your community

The solutions to the impact of AI and technology on community mental health requires an intensive systemic approach. But these policies are not what we should only rely on, because these safeguards should start at home.

“Home should be the safest space. That’s the first line of defense — families, friends… So let’s make sure that we are that for our children,” Calzado said.

Iza Calzado at We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

Parents need their own community, too, however. It takes more than a village to raise a child in this era, and parents also need their own kind of support and human connection so they can come home strong to their kids.

For Naval, one of the best ways to do that is to dedicate time to activities that will allow you to interact with other human beings. Take a wellness class. Join clubs for your hobbies. Make the effort to see your friends in person.

Technology and AI are here to stay. Decentering it, then, requires us to go back to our roots as humans and hone in on that. – Rappler.com

World.title: The Green Report: Worst COP ever? What went down at 2026 UN climate talks

World.title: FACT CHECK: ICC chamber order on ‘Incident 57’ doesn’t mean Duterte will be released
World.content:
While the ICC Trial Chamber III did order the removal of ‘Incident 57’ from the list of incidents in the charges against Duterte, this does not mean the entire case itself has been dismissed or that Duterte is set to be released

Claim: Former president Rodrigo Duterte is set to be released after the International Criminal Court (ICC) dropped one drug-related killing, “Incident 57,” from his crimes against humanity case.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel bearing the claim has already received 823,000 views, 12,500 reactions, 1,400 shares, and 1,200 comments as of writing. It was posted on November 17 and continues to gain traction up to this date.

The video shows a photo of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, who is currently detained at the ICC facility in The Hague, Netherlands. The text on the photo reads, “Tuluyan nang ibinasura ng ICC ang Incident 57 drug war charges laban kay PRRD dahil sa sablay ng petsa.”



(The ICC has definitively dismissed the ‘Incident 57’ drug war charges against [former president Rodrigo Roa Duterte] due to an error in the date.)

Additional text overlaid on the reel claimed that the ICC junked the case and that the Vice President has urged their supporters to pray for her father’s safety upon his supposed return.

The facts: While the ICC Trial Chamber III’s order to drop “Incident 57” from the list of incidents in the second count of charges against Duterte is genuine, it is not true that he is set to be released following this directive.

Duterte remains detained in ICC custody. There are no credible news reports or official announcements saying that Duterte can now return to the Philippines or that his case has been dismissed.

In an October 9 ruling, the ICC Trial Chamber III ordered prosecutors to remove Incident 57, a single alleged drug-related killing involving a “high-value target,” because it fell outside the confirmed timeframe of the second charge against Duterte.

The prosecution then complied with the order. In a document dated October 20, the prosecution said that all references to Incident 57 are now removed from the trial brief and replaced with redacted information.

Duterte is currently facing three counts of crimes against humanity, including murders in and around Davao City allegedly committed by the “Davao Death Squad” while he served as mayor between 2013 and 2016, targeted killings of alleged high-value targets during his presidency between 2016 and 2017, and murders and attempted murders during barangay-level anti-drug operations between 2016 and 2018.

List of incidents: Aside from Incident 57, which the ICC chamber ordered removed, there are many other active incidents included in the charges against Duterte. In October, the ICC trial chamber approved the addition of seven new incidents to the charges, raising the total number from 49 to 56.

Duterte was arrested in March 2025 for crimes against humanity. He is set to face trial on November 30.

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

World.title: Senate prioritizes feeding program in push for higher 2027 DepEd budget
World.content:
BUDGET DEBATES. Senator Bam Aquino and Education Secretary Sonny Angara during the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Education on November 24, 2026.

Senator Bam Aquino wants to increase the school-based feeding program's budget to P28.7 billion. Meanwhile, the ARAL Program has no allocation in the Senate committee report.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Bam Aquino recommended making the school-based feeding program the top priority for an additional budget among other Department of Education (DepEd) programs in 2027.

Overall, the Senate finance committee recommended P915.49 billion for the proposed new general appropriations of the DepEd and its attached agencies.

That amount is P4.91 billion higher than the P910.5 billion approved by the House of Representatives, but P1.25 billion lower than the P916.75 billion in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

Among the changes, the Senate panel added P11 billion to the school-based feeding program, pushing the proposed allocation to P22.4 billion.

But Aquino, as the DepEd’s budget sponsor, plans to seek an additional increase for the program. “At the proper time, this representation, alongside some other colleagues, will introduce an amendment to increase the budget for the school-based feeding program by P6,265,478,145,” he said during the plenary deliberations.

That would raise the program’s budget to P28.7 billion, higher than the P25.7 billion in the 2026 national budget.

The additional funding would also expand the universal feeding to cover kindergarten to Grade 2, reaching another 1.8 million students in 2027. This follows the phased implementation under the national children’s nutrition bill, which has been ratified but not yet signed into law.

The P28.7-billion budget would cover 124 feeding days, or from June to December in 2027, at P30 per meal.

Aquino remains hopeful that they can still set a higher budget for the education sector.

“I have spoken to the Senate President multiple times to share my frustration with the fiscal space provided for this important agency,” he said in the plenary.

“We have proposed a much bigger budget only to be met with an answer that we didn’t like, which was that the fiscal space is very limited — which we understand. Mr. [Senate] President, I believe that we can still increase this before the period of amendments,” he added in a mix of English and Filipino.

ARAL Program’s low disbursement

Aquino also supports funding for the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program in 2027. There is no separate line item for it in the 2027 NEP.

However, in the Senate committee report, the ARAL Program remains unfunded.

“Talo pa tayo ng House. P300 million, nakalagay sila. Tayo, wala,” Senator Joel Villanueva said during his interpellation. (The House outdid us. They allocated P300 million. We did not put anything.)

Villanueva noted that 11 million students have been identified as needing remediation sessions in school year 2026-2027.

Aquino told senators that the ARAL Program still has unspent funds from this year. During the 2026 budget talks, it was the Senate that pushed P8.9 billion for the learning recovery initiative.

“More than half of the P8.9-billion budget for this year was released very late, only in July and August. Therefore, because of the late release, meron pa pong pondo, ‘yon ang gagamitin (there is still funding, which will be used) next year,” he explained.

He added that the disbursement rate, which refers to actual payments made, is only at 13%.

According to Aquino, the DepEd is already in the process of disbursing the funds in the next few weeks, with Education Secretary Sonny Angara promising a faster process. Angara was standing beside the senator during the deliberations.

“We know that it can work. We’ve been talking about our learning gaps for so many months. The main solution to the learning gap is really a remediation program,” Aquino said. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Trump did not praise Davao City’s energy security efforts
World.content:
Reports from news outlets quoted the US leader saying, ‘We have more energy than any country in the world by double.’ The misleading posts misinterpret ‘double’ as ‘Davao.’

Claim: US President Donald Trump praised Davao City for its energy security efforts.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook reel bearing the claim was posted by the page Baste Duterte fan on November 21. The video has received 76,000 views, 1,700 reactions, 517 shares, and 139 comments as of writing.

The video shows Trump in a bilateral talk with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on November 18.

Text overlaid on the video reads, “[Number one] energy save security Davao City in the world.” The post further claimed that Marcos was supposedly taken aback when he heard Trump mention Davao City, the stronghold of his political rivals, the Dutertes.

Another Facebook reel, which has already garnered an estimated 704,000 views, also claimed that the US government will provide Davao City with a new energy project.

The facts: Nowhere in Trump’s statements during the bilateral talks did he say that Davao City was number one in the world for its energy security efforts. He also did not mention any new US government energy project for the city. No global rankings or news reports identify Davao City as a top city for energy conservation and security, contrary to the claim.

Reports from news outlets such as GMA News quoted Trump saying, “We have more energy than any country in the world by double.” The misleading post misinterpreted Trump’s pronunciation of “double” as “Davao.”

Trump was actually referring to US energy production. He claimed that the country is now the leading producer of oil and natural gas, surpassing the combined supply of Russia and Saudi Arabia, with the US leader also referencing its “acquisition” of Venezuela’s oil reserves. Trump also said the US aims to increase energy exports to Pacific allies, including the Philippines.

Trade deal: The posts circulated following Trump’s arrival in Manila on November 17 for a state visit and to participate in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations-US Special Summit, as well as the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue leaders’ summit.

During his visit, the US leader highlighted what he described as the “biggest trade deal” between the Philippines and the United States. The US is strengthening its defense partnership with the Philippines while signaling interest in expanding cooperation on energy security, particularly in nuclear energy.

US energy production: Trump’s remarks appeared to refer primarily to the United States’ energy production, particularly oil and natural gas. He has previously made the claim that the US is producing more oil and gas “than Russia and Saudi Arabia combined.” According to an article by PolitiFact, this remark is “mostly true,” but added that the US lead over the two countries “is built on the other liquids, not crude oil.”

According to Our World in Data, a project by UK-based nonprofit Global Change Data Lab, when considering total energy supply across different sources, including coal, oil, natural gas, renewables, and nuclear energy, China ranks first globally, with approximately 45,000 terawatt-hours in 2025.

World.title: LTFRB, OSG: Loophole in the law allows foreign firm to operate taxi fleet
World.content:
LTFRB Acting Chairperson Greg Pua Jr. (FILE PHOTO)

MANILA, Philippines — A loophole in the law apparently allowed a Vietnamese firm to fully operate a taxi fleet using electric vehicles (EVs) in the country despite the 1987 Constitution limiting foreign ownership, according to the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG).

During the House of Representatives committee on transportation hearing on Wednesday, several lawmakers questioned why the foreign firm was allowed to operate locally, raising concerns whether it was still in accordance with the Constitution, which limits foreign ownership to 40 percent in specific sectors and reserves at least 60 percent for Filipino citizens or entities. The committee discussed proposed amendments to Republic Act No. 11697 or the Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act.

Quezon Rep. Reynante Arrogancia asked LTFRB Acting Chairperson Greg Pua Jr. how the Vietnamese company was allowed to operate without any Filipino representation within the firm.

Article continues after this 

In response, Pua noted that there is a loophole in the law as Republic Act No. 11659, or the amendments to the Public Services Act, defined public utility vehicles (PUVs) as vehicles that transport people from one point to another using internal combustion engines (ICE).

With this definition, EVs, which do not have ICEs, would not classify as PUVs.

“Under RA No. 11659, for the first time, public utility vehicles were defined under section 2(k) because the definition of a [PUVs] is that there is an internal combustion engine. With an electric vehicle, there’s no internal combustion engine,” Pua said.

He added that R.A. No. 11659 differentiated public utility and public service — a concept that used to be the same under the original Public Service Act– and indicated that foreign ownership rules do not apply to PUVs.

“Under Section 4(d) of RA No. 11659, they were able to differentiate public utility and public service. So public utility, specifically mentioned are [PUVs], and if you will read the foreign ownership restrictions under our Philippine Constitution, Section 11 of Article XII, what was stated there is public utility,” Pua explained.

Article continues after this 

“So that’s the reason why in 2024, LTFRB under the leadership of then Chairman Teofilo Guadiz issued that for electric vehicles without an [ICE], foreign ownership (rule) does not apply,” he added. “In fact in RA No. 11659, specifically mentioned there is that foreign ownership rules under our constitution are not applicable to public service. Only to [PUVs].”

Assistant Solicitor General James Cundangan of the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) agreed that there is a gray area in the legislation which makes the foreign company able to operate in the country.

Article continues after this 

“I agree with you Mr. Chair, it’s really a gray area […] because we never thought that the time will come that there will be an electric vehicle, we only saw that in cartoons before. Now it is happening […] because this is an advent of change which was not contemplated at the time that the constitution was passed,” Cundangan said.

“As of now, as we speak, all is legitimate, that’s it. So in order for us to address it squarely we need to pass a law to reconcile all of this one. So on that note, the OSG will submit its position paper on the matter, for the perusal of the chairperson as well as the committee,” he added.

Arrogancia did not mention what specific taxi company he was referring to, but committee chairperson and Quezon City Rep. Franz Pumaren said that it was Green and Smart Mobility (GSM) Philippines Inc.,, This was confirmed by Arrogancia.

Green GSM is a subsidiary of Vietnam-based Green and Smart Mobility Joint Stock Company founded by Vingroup chairperson Pham Nhat Vuong.

According to Green GSM’s website, they are a “green and smart transportation vehicle rental unit” operating in either electric car rental or travel services using EVs.

READ: Inside the green taxi: When the shift to electric becomes a question of survival

Green GSM uses vehicles from VinFast, the company which is also under Vingroup.

However, Pumaren noted that the committee has received several complaints about Vinfast, from commuters and workers themselves.

Pumaren said drivers and workers believe the company does not prioritize their welfare because it is not Filipino-owned.

READ: LTFRB suspends e-taxi unit after driver joins viral robbery prank

Amend or declare unconstitutional?

Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro, a member of the committee and also the chairperson of the House committee on justice, quizzed Cundangan about their stand on the matter. When Cundangan reiterated the presence of a gray area and the need to ensure that the definition of PUVs will include EVs, Luistro said that the constitutional provisions should prevail.

According to Luistro, regardless of the absence of EVs in the definition of PUVs, the constitutional provision mandating that Filipinos own 60 percent of public utilities should still holds true.

“I don’t think that there is a question about the constitutional provision. That is very clear, the 60-40 for the transportation industry. What gives rise to that issue is the subsequent laws defining the ICE or the public utility vehicle,” Luistro said.

“We have an existing principle in statutory construction, that all subsequent laws need to be aligned with a constitutional provision. So notwithstanding the fact that we see the issue that is created by the subsequent legislation, I think it should be the constitutional provision that must prevail, OSG, am I correct?” she asked.

“Yes, I agree Madam Chair that the superior law is always the Constitution,” Cundangan replied.

However, when Luistro said that the 60-40 ownership share provision can be implemented while amendments are pending since the Constitution has to be followed — therefore making the Green GSM operation unconstitutional — Cundangan said there is a presumption of regularity as of now.

Cundangan noted that there needs to be a declaration that the operations are unconstitutional, and this can only be done by the Supreme Court.

“Notwithstanding the issues which were created by this Public Service Act on the definition of PUV, I don’t think there is (anything) wrong if as early as now, even prior to the subsequent legislation, we will already give consideration to the 60-40 constitutional provision on the transportation industry,” Luistro said.

“In as much as it is an existing law, there should be a categorical declaration that it is unconstitutional, because presumption of regularity will apply. Otherwise we will be wreaking havoc on the stability of laws. So I agree with you Madam Chair that it is unconstitutional, but there should be (a declaration),” Cundangan noted.

Cundangan reminded the lawmakers that the power of Congress is to craft and amend laws, and not deem a law unconstitutional.

“We will be trekking on dangerous grounds wherein Congress itself is declaring a law to be unconstitutional. With all due respect, Madam Chair, I agree with your position. I agree, I definitely agree. That is precisely the reason why the OSG will give its position paper,” he said.

However — thank you for agreeing with me Madam Chair, I appreciate it — only the Supreme Court can declare a law unconstitutional. So there must be a court action for that matter, it will take time,” he added./ts

World.title: LTO must sustain reforms amid Manibela corruption concerns – Dizon
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said the Land Transportation Office (LTO) must prove the public wrong by sustaining reforms, following transport group Manibela’s warning that corruption could return to the agency after a leadership shakeup.

The concerns were raised after LTO chief Markus Lacanilao was transferred to the Maritime Industry Authority (Marina), where he will serve as administrator.

Former Naga City Administrator Noreen San Luis, meanwhile, was appointed as the new LTO chief.

Article continues after this 

Manibela had opposed Lacanilao’s transfer, with its president, Mar Valbuena, condemning the “appointment of rotten individuals in the government.”

The group launched a transport strike and a series of protests on Monday, Nov. 23, including a march to the LTO main office to express its support for Lacanilao.

Manibela later called off its scheduled third day of protest on Wednesday due to bad weather, although its transport strike continued.

READ: Manibela extending protest, strike until Wednesday

In a press conference on Wednesday, Dizon acknowledged the public’s persisting perception of corruption in government, saying it would take sustained reforms for people to regain confidence in government agencies.

Article continues after this 

“The perception of corruption in the government, unfortunately, is there,” he said.

“And it will be there. It will persist until people start feeling that the reforms have been put in place and will be lasting.”

Article continues after this 

Dizon said the LTO must demonstrate that the changes introduced under its previous leadership would continue, while expressing confidence in the newly appointed officials.

“You will be surprised by what he [Lacanilao] is about to do there [Marina]. For Asec. (Assistant Secretary) Noreen, her job now is to continue the reforms that were started,” he said.

READ: Dizon to meet transport groups as Manibela readies 2-day strike

San Luis said she “did not know” where Manibela’s doubts about the possible return of corrupt LTO personnel were coming from.

“I thank Manibela for observing and keeping watch over the agency. I hope they continue monitoring us so they can see the various reforms we will be implementing at the Land Transportation [Office],” she said.

Drawing from her previous stints as director of LTO Region 4-A Office 5, San Luis said she would strengthen discipline among personnel, scrutinize their records and ensure that corrupt officials would not return.

She also addressed concerns about the possible return of Dermalog Identification Systems GmbH as the LTO’s information technology (IT) provider, saying she was unaware of the basis for the claims.

“During our time, we modernized the IT system [of the LTO]. And regarding the Dermalog, its contract already ended last May [2026],” she said.

READ: LTO says Dermalog already ceased LTMS support; firm’s new proposal hit

Dizon, meanwhile, described the LTO’s previous IT system as “chopsuey,” referring to its mix of different service providers.

He said the government plans to integrate the agency’s systems with the eGov app to make transactions easier for motorists and driver’s license holders.

Dizon added that the integration would be carried out through an open and transparent public procurement process, with the goal of eliminating the need for fixers in LTO transactions.

“That’s open, that’s transparent, and that will be really responsive to the goal of making it easier for everybody, every motorist, every driver’s license holder. So that, fixer won’t be needed for the LTO systems anymore.” /gsg

World.title: Ejercito aims for P100-B PhilHealth subsidy target
World.content:
Sen. JV Ejercito —File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate has realigned P19.8 billion from the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) to increase the subsidy for PhilHealth under the proposed 2027 national budget, Sen. JV Ejercito said in a statement on Wednesday.

With the realignment, Ejercito, chair of the Senate Committee on Finance, noted that the PhilHealth subsidy has increased from P73 billion to P94.2 billion, bringing the allocation closer to Ejercito’s target of P100 billion to strengthen healthcare coverage and ensure that more Filipinos benefit from the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act.

“As the author and principal sponsor of the UHC Act, this is one of my priorities. UHC is my baby, and I will definitely make sure that its implementation is given the funding it needs,” Ejercito said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ejercito pushes funding for health, education, infra in 2027 budget

“It’s not enough that we have a Universal Health Care Law. Every Filipino should feel this. If anyone in the family is sick, where to get the money to pay for the hospital should not be the first problem. What they should first think about is how someone they love would get well,” Ejercito said in Filipino.

According to Ejercito, the realignment of the MAP funds amounting to P9.9 billion will channel financial aid directly to hospitals to support the implementation of Zero Balance Billing (ZBB). This includes P7.6 billion for Department of Health (DOH) hospitals, P2 billion for legacy hospitals, and P1 billion for local government unit (LGU) hospitals.

In addition, the Senate version of the 2027 budget realigned another P9.9 billion from the increase in AICS allocation introduced by the House of Representatives in its version of the General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

According to Ejercito, the Senate version also provides P5.49 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) to support the improvement of provincial government hospitals and locally funded health facilities.

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, the proposed 2027 budget also allocates P1.099 billion for health promotion and P1.599 billion for immunization programs to strengthen preventive healthcare and help protect Filipinos from preventable diseases. Another P736 million is provided for the Sulu Transition Program.

READ: PH health care ranks 87th of 110 in global index

Article continues after this 

“Our goal is simple: Better hospitals, more affordable medicines, and fewer families who get deep into debt because of illness. This is the spirit of universal health care, and this is what we want to implement in the 2027 budget,” he said.

The Senate version allocated a total of P378.6 billion budget for the DOH and its attached agencies and corporations. /atm

World.title: BOC-Naia seizes P369.44M worth of kush from Thailand
World.content:
The cargo declarations listed truck side mirrors and assorted children’s plastic toys. But customs personnel found kush, or high-grade marijuana. —Photo from the Bureau of Customs

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Customs at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (BOC-Naia) seized 307.866 kilograms of high-grade marijuana, or kush, worth an estimated ₱369.44 million in two shipments from Thailand on Monday, Nov. 23.

The shipments were bound for consignees in Bulacan and Caloocan City.

Customs personnel flagged both shipments based on information from Thailand Customs and cargo profiling. X-ray screening revealed suspicious images, and the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) conducted a K9 inspection of the shipments.

Article continues after this 

READ: PDEA seizes P1.5-M kush in Rizal bust

During the physical examination, customs personnel found kush in 164 boxes. The cargo declarations listed truck side mirrors and assorted children’s plastic toys. /atm

World.title: Ombudsman upholds graft charges vs ex-Bohol town mayor, 6 others
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday said it has upheld its decision to file graft charges against former Guindulman, Bohol Mayor Albino Balo and five other local officials over alleged irregularities in a 2023 billboard construction project.

In a statement, the ombudsman said it also affirmed the dismissal of Balo and the five other officials who were found administratively liable for grave misconduct.

The five other officials are Municipal Engineer Rodney Jones Labang, Municipal Treasurer Jean Janiola, Municipal Engineer Ariston Beronio, Administrative Aide III Evelyn Hinatuan, and Administrative Aide II Dennis Theodore Besinga.

Article continues after this 

The ombudsman noted that a private contractor, Emilio Bernaldez, is also facing graft charges for his alleged participation in the questioned transaction.

READ: Ombudsman affirms preventive suspension order vs Dalaguete mayor

The case stemmed from a complaint filed by a resident of Barangay Mayuga, Bernard Banal, regarding the municipality’s “Multi-Purpose Billboard Cell” construction project in 2023.

The ombudsman said it found that a “giant Christmas tree” constructed in November 2022 was later “presented to the municipality as a newly procured multi-purpose billboard” in May 2023.

It maintained that there was “probable cause” against the seven respondents for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, given “evidence of alleged bad faith, manifest partiality or gross inexcusable negligence.”

Article continues after this 

“The investigation cited the participation of several municipal officials in the inspection, acceptance, and processing of documents supporting the project, including the inspection and acceptance report, certificate of acceptance, payment certifications and other supporting documents,” the ombudsman said.

It noted that Balo and the others have sought the reconsideration of the order, arguing that the project “underwent proper procurement procedures and that they acted in good faith.”

Article continues after this 

The ombudsman, however, said it rejected their arguments as there was “no sufficient basis to overturn its earlier determination of probable cause.”

READ: Ombudsman orders filing of graft case vs ex-Dumaguete water district GM

It added that the respondents will be given the opportunity to answer the charges before the appropriate court, with the criminal case to proceed separately from administrative proceedings.

“With the denial of the motions for reconsideration in the criminal case, the ombudsman affirmed its directive to file the corresponding informations against the six municipal officials and Bernaldez before the appropriate court,” the ombudsman said.

In a 2025 statement, Balo said there was no corruption under his administration.

World.title: DAR to distribute over 4,800 land titles in Negros Oriental
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — A total of 4,850 land titles are set to be distributed to farmers in Negros Oriental, the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) said Wednesday.

READ: DAR: Decades-long farm lot distribution program may be completed in 2027

In a statement, the DAR said land titles will be distributed on Nov. 26 as the government advances its agrarian reform program, pairing secure land ownership with debt relief

Article continues after this 

The distribution will be held in Dumaguete City, along with a trade exhibit giving agrarian reform beneficiary organizations an opportunity to showcase and market their products.

Meanwhile, Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III said farmers must also receive continuing assistance after obtaining their titles so they can develop their land.

“Kasi hindi naman sapat na lupa ang ibibigay mo sa ating magsasaka,” Estrella said.

(Land alone is not enough for our farmers.)

“Secure ownership gives families greater certainty over the land they cultivate. Farmers also need planting materials, production skills, working capital and access to buyers to turn their harvests into income,” he added.

Article continues after this 

The DAR chief also stressed farm-to-market roads, machinery, livestock and access to credit are among the forms of assistance that help beneficiaries make productive use of their farms.

Estrella said the activity on Thursday aims to bring all these concerns together by combining title distribution with opportunities for farmer organizations to promote their agricultural products.

Article continues after this 

The distribution forms part of the current administration’s continuing implementation of land acquisition and distribution and the Support to Parcelization of Lands for Individual Titling or SPLIT project.

Through the project, DAR facilitates the subdivision of collective Certificates of Land Ownership Award and the issuance of individual titles, subject to applicable procedures and safeguards.

World.title: 7 wanted persons in Bukidnon arrested
World.content:
Bukidnon police personnel undergo a regular rank inspection. The Bukidnon police arrested seven wanted persons from Nov. 20 to 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy of PNP Bukidnon)

VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — Police arrested seven wanted individuals, including four listed as most wanted persons, in separate operations across Bukidnon and Manila from Nov. 20 to 24, 2026.In Manila, operatives from the Valencia City Police Station, Bukidnon Provincial Police Office, Regional Intelligence Unit 10, and Baseco Police Station nabbed Bukidnon’s eighth most wanted person at the provincial level on Nov. 23 at 11:00 a.m.The 36-year-old construction worker from Barangay Sinayawan, Valencia City was arrested at Baseco Compound, Port Area, Manila for four counts of rape with no bail recommended.

He is detained at the Baseco Police Station.In Malaybalay City, two city-level most wanted suspects were captured in separate operations on Nov. 20.

They are 27-year-old Jake Vequizo Jadraque, alias Jake Lim Jadraque, who is wanted for rape with no bail recommended, and a 39-year-old married woman, who is facing a child abuse case with bail set at P180,000.In Manolo Fortich, police arrested the town’s fifth most wanted person on Nov. 23 in Zone 1, Barangay Mambatangan, a 30-year-old suspect wanted for statutory rape and sexual abuse, with no bail recommended.

In Lantapan, a 20-year-old student known as “Padot” was arrested on Nov. 24 for illegal drug charges under Sections 5 and 11 of RA 9165 with no bail recommended.In Don Carlos, a 29-year-old man known as “Totoy” from Dangcagan was also arrested on Nov. 24 for failing to appear in court over an illegal gambling case.In Talakag, a 23-year-old resident known as “Bebing” was arrested on Nov. 23 also for illegal gambling, with bail recommended at P5,000.All suspects arrested in the province are currently detained.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Myanmar’s China Dilemma: Turning Beijing’s Need Into Leverage Requires Legitimate Leaders
World.content:
Anyone seeking clarity on China-Myanmar relations must first ask one crucial question: does China need Myanmar, or does Myanmar need China?

Some argue that Beijing’s often-cited desire for access to the Indian Ocean through Myanmar is overstated. Others contend that China barely needs Myanmar at all, and that the relationship matters far more to Naypyitaw than to Beijing.

The reality is more complicated.

The Malacca Dilemma

Some analysts state that China needs Myanmar to secure overland access to the Indian Ocean, bypassing the Malacca Strait chokepoint. Others dismiss this view, saying the chokepoint is no longer a problem for a country which now boasts the world’s largest navy.

Chinese leaders began wrestling with the “Malacca Dilemma” in the early 2000s under President Hu Jintao. Around the same time, Beijing and Myanmar’s previous junta began talks on pipelines to transport oil and gas from the Bay of Bengal to Yunnan Province. Agreements were reached in 2007-2008, and construction began in June 2010.

At that point, China had yet to commission a single aircraft carrier. Its first carrier — a Soviet-made ship bought from Ukraine in 1998 and modified — did not enter service until 2012. Today, China operates three aircraft carriers and is reportedly building a fourth, which is expected to be nuclear-powered.

In other words, the strategic calculations underpinning the China-Myanmar energy corridor were made before Beijing emerged as a major naval power.

More than one energy corridor

In reality, China has never relied on a single route to meet its vast energy needs. Myanmar’s gas and oil pipelines provide a direct energy corridor from the Indian Ocean, but are only one piece of a much larger network. Beijing also imports oil through the Kazakhstan-China pipeline and receives oil and gas from Russia via overland routes. Meanwhile, the Central Asia-China pipeline network pumps natural gas from Turkmenistan and other Central Asian states into western China. Additional pipelines from Central Asia and Russia are planned or under construction.

For a country the size of China, a single pipeline or supply source is never enough. Beijing’s strategy is diversification.

Why Myanmar matters

Those who argue that China does not need Myanmar often point to Beijing’s expanding network of rail, road and pipeline connections across Eurasia.

China has rail links with Laos, Vietnam, Russia, Mongolia and Central Asia. It has energy corridors stretching north into Russia and west into Central Asia. On paper, Myanmar is only one route among many.

Yet, China is not an economic monolith; its interests vary sharply from province to province. Here is where geography gives Myanmar a unique advantage.

For inland provinces such as Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou, Myanmar provides the most direct route to the Indian Ocean. It is also the closest overland entry for energy imports arriving from the Middle East and Africa.

A railway or trade corridor through Myanmar would offer southwestern China a global shipping link that is shorter, cheaper and likely more efficient than ports to the east.

It would also help bridge the yawning gap between the country’s wealthy coastal provinces and its underdeveloped inland regions. Coastal provinces like Guangdong have prospered through direct access to ports, global shipping networks and export markets, outpacing inland neighbors facing higher logistics costs and weaker international connectivity.

For Beijing, plugging southwestern China into international markets is not simply a foreign-policy objective, but part of a broader strategy to reduce economic inequality inside China itself.

This is where Myanmar enters the picture.

The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor, Kyaukphyu projects, road links, railways and pipelines are not intended for China as a whole. They are aimed at accelerating development in China’s southwest including Yunnan, Sichuan and other inland regions seeking easier access to the Indian Ocean and global markets.

A relationship of mutual interests

When it comes to foreign investment, countries only inject capital where they see strategic or economic returns.

During the so-called reform period between 2011 and 2020, Myanmar failed to attract large-scale investment from Western countries despite their stated commitment to the country’s democratization. They were reluctant to invest because the prospects of economic returns were low.

Beijing invests because it sees a tangible benefit — access to the Indian Ocean that will integrate China’s landlocked southwest into global trade networks.

In return, Myanmar gains infrastructure, jobs, technology transfer and improved connectivity. The ousted National League for Democracy government recognized the benefits in 2020 when it signed agreements for the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor.

A well-governed Myanmar could turn China’s need for access into an opportunity, negotiating terms that serve its national interests, and ensuring a win-win situation for both. The question is whether military-ruled Myanmar is in a position to do so today.

The real question

The argument over whether China needs Myanmar or Myanmar needs China misses the point. Both need each other.

China needs Myanmar as an Indian Ocean gateway, a trade partner and a critical link in the development of its southwestern provinces. Myanmar needs investment, infrastructure and access to the world’s second-largest economy. The ingredients for a mutually beneficial relationship are in place.

The real question is whether Myanmar has leaders capable of translating that potential into national gains rather than debt, dependency and unequal agreements.

A military regime lacking a public mandate, mired in corruption, and facing war crime accusations cannot negotiate from a position of strength — or ensure that Chinese investment serves Myanmar’s national interests.

China’s need for Myanmar is real. The challenge for Myanmar is ensuring that need works in its favor.

World.title: Arakan’s Next Battle Is for Legitimacy, Not Territory
World.content:
The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) November 19 ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations marks a historic moment for international justice. But its implications extend beyond Myanmar’s military and the courtroom in The Hague.

For the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA), which now controls most of Arakan (Rakhine State) in western Myanmar, the judgment raises a fundamental question: Can a movement that has achieved remarkable military victories build a political system that protects the rights of all communities, including the Rohingya?

The ICJ judgment is legally binding on Myanmar, not directly on the ULA/AA, which was not a party to the case. Nevertheless, the organization now controls much of the territory from which hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Its policies will influence the prospects for reconciliation, refugee repatriation and Arakan’s international engagement.

The ULA/AA’s next challenge is therefore not simply territorial control, but establishing political legitimacy through responsible governance.

The politics of identity

One of the most sensitive issues facing the ULA/AA concerns the terms “Rohingya,” “Bengali” and “Muslim.”

For Rohingya communities, their name represents ethnic identity, historical belonging and the right to recognition. Arakan political actors and the people of Arakan, however, reject the term “Rohingya,” preferring “Bengali” because of competing interpretations of the region’s history and migration.

The ULA/AA has sometimes encouraged the use of “Muslim” as a less politically contentious term in efforts to improve relations between communities.

Such an approach may help reduce tensions, but it cannot resolve the underlying disagreement. “Muslim” describes religious affiliation, while “Rohingya” represents ethnic self-identification. The terms are not interchangeable, and not all Muslims in Arakan identify as Rohingya.

The ICJ’s treatment of the Rohingya as a protected group under the Genocide Convention underscores the significance of their collective identity.

Yet peaceful coexistence does not require every community to agree on a single historical narrative. It requires accepting that disagreements over identity cannot justify discrimination or the denial of fundamental rights.

For the ULA/AA, respecting ethnic self-identification while ensuring equal treatment would demonstrate political maturity rather than weakness.

Social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures

Decades of discrimination, communal violence and displacement have created deep mistrust between Arakanese (Rakhine) and Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Some local initiatives under ULA/AA administration, including intercommunal meetings, sporting activities and limited Muslim participation in local governance, suggest efforts to rebuild relations.

These developments may be constructive, but genuine social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures.

It depends on freedom of movement, access to education and healthcare, protection of property, fair administration and meaningful participation in decisions affecting communities.

The ULA/AA also faces serious human rights scrutiny. United Nations reporting has raised allegations of abuses against Rohingya civilians in areas under Arakan Army control, including arbitrary detention, forced labor, forced recruitment and restrictions on movement.

The organization has disputed allegations of wrongdoing, while citing security threats from armed groups operating near the Bangladesh border.

Such threats require legitimate security responses, but they cannot justify collective punishment or discrimination against civilians. The actions of Rohingya/Muslim armed organizations must be distinguished from the rights of Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Credible investigations, accountability and transparent administration would do more to build trust than political assurances alone.

International engagement is not recognition

The ULA/AA’s territorial advances have transformed the political landscape along the Myanmar-Bangladesh border.

Bangladesh, which hosts more than a million Rohingya refugees, has publicly acknowledged communicating with the AA as part of efforts to address the refugee crisis.

This creates opportunities for practical engagement with regional governments, the United Nations and international humanitarian organizations.

China and India also have strategic interests in Arakan, particularly concerning regional stability, trade and infrastructure development.

However, practical engagement and formal diplomatic recognition are fundamentally different.

Governments and international organizations may cooperate with authorities exercising effective territorial control without recognizing them as sovereign governments.

The ICJ judgment does not confer international recognition or political legitimacy upon the ULA/AA. Nor does it guarantee that regional governments or the United Nations will recognize the organization.

Nevertheless, the ULA/AA could strengthen its international standing by demonstrating respect for human rights, facilitating humanitarian assistance and establishing credible policies for all communities.

The opportunity is significant, but international credibility must be earned through conduct rather than military victories alone.

Preparing for the Rohingya challenge

The Rohingya issue remains one of the most complex long-term challenges facing the ULA/AA.

Refugees in Bangladesh continue to face uncertainty over citizenship, security, freedom of movement, destroyed homes and the possibility of renewed persecution.

Although the ULA/AA cannot independently resolve Myanmar’s citizenship framework or confer internationally recognized Myanmar citizenship, it exercises considerable influence over local security, administration and conditions affecting eventual refugee returns.

Rather than waiting for formal international recognition or a nationwide political settlement, the ULA/AA should develop a comprehensive and transparent policy addressing the Rohingya issue.

Such a framework should prioritize equal protection, respect for ethnic self-identification, intercommunal dialogue and safeguards against discrimination.

It should also establish credible mechanisms to investigate alleged abuses, protect housing and land rights, preserve residency records and consult Rohingya representatives, including refugees in Bangladesh.

Cooperation with Bangladesh, relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organizations could help prepare the groundwork for future repatriation.

Any return process must be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable. Premature repatriation without adequate security and rights protections would risk repeating past failures.

These steps would not immediately resolve historical grievances or guarantee international recognition. But they would demonstrate that the ULA/AA is preparing to govern a diverse society rather than merely administer territory captured through war.

The real test of Arakan’s future

The ICJ judgment concerns Myanmar’s legal responsibility for genocide. It does not determine Arakan’s constitutional future or confer recognition upon the ULA/AA.

Yet it presents the organization with an important political opportunity.

For decades, Arakanese communities have pursued greater autonomy, political rights and self-determination. Those aspirations remain central to Arakan’s political struggle.

But self-determination becomes more credible when it respects the rights and identities of other communities sharing the same territory.

The ULA/AA has demonstrated its military capabilities. Its next challenge is to establish institutions capable of protecting people regardless of ethnicity, religion or political affiliation.

International engagement may expand as the organization becomes increasingly relevant to regional security, humanitarian operations and the Rohingya refugee crisis.

However, lasting legitimacy will depend on whether it can translate territorial control into inclusive governance, accountability and peaceful coexistence.

The ULA/AA has won control of territory. Its next battle is to earn the trust of all the people who live there.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader to Attend Regional Talks in Vietnam
World.content:
HANOI, Vietnam—Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing will attend regional talks in Hanoi on Saturday, Vietnam said. It will be his first multilateral meeting since taking civilian office this year.

The event comes days after the UN’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar committed genocide with its 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.
