Min Aung Hlaing was head of the armed forces at the time, before leading a 2021 coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged Myanmar into civil war.

The prime ministers of Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and hosts Vietnam will also take part in the talks held under two regional cooperation mechanisms, ACMECS and CLMV, the Vietnamese Foreign Ministry said in a statement late Tuesday.

Min Aung Hlaing was installed as nominally civilian president in April following widely criticized elections in which pro-military parties won a landslide.

He has since been touring regional capitals, including in neighboring Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia, in what analysts say is a quest for legitimacy.

The four nations are part of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, but which agreed this month to seek “calibrated engagement.”

ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn will attend Saturday’s talks in Hanoi alongside Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and Laotian Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith.

According to Vietnamese state media, the discussions are expected to focus on economic connectivity, notably infrastructure, logistics, trade and supply chains as well as the environment.

The meetings will comprise the 12th Cambodia-Laos-Myanmar-Vietnam (CLMV) summit and the 11th Ayeyawady-Chao Phraya-Mekong Economic Cooperation Strategy (ACMECS) summit.

Myanmar’s regime has always denied genocide, saying its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents, and described the ICJ ruling as “a great disappointment” and “not fair”.

World.title: Malaysia to Repatriate Thousands More Myanmar Migrants
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia—Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Tuesday the country will send more than 6,500 migrants back to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations.

The Southeast Asian Muslim-majority country has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar by persecution or conflict but has been keen to resolve a long-running refugee challenge involving foreign asylum seekers.

Malaysia already sent back around 1,500 migrants back to war-torn Myanmar in late September in an opaque scheme that rights groups have raised concern about.

The fresh repatriation comes five days after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

“The foreign minister has approved three naval ships to transport back on December 6 and 7, 1,500 Myanmar citizens,” Anwar told the Malaysian parliament.

“And for the month of December, 5,303 will be brought back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government,” he added.

The UN’s highest court, based in The Hague, has ruled that Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

Kuala Lumpur said in late October it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country were being held in military detention.

Anwar did not mention the request for clarification, but he said Malaysia reiterated its stance over concern about the Rohingya and other ethnic groups, which was also underscored by the ICJ’s ruling.

Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize their status.

AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fueling xenophobia and intimidation.

Turkey rebuffs Rohingya resettlement

Separately, Anwar said Turkey was not prepared to consider taking in 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, following an announcement by his deputy that was later rowed back.

Malaysia said Friday it was seeking to resettle the refugees in Turkey through a structured skills training program, but the statement was subsequently deleted from Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s Facebook page without explanation.

In his initial statement, Ahmad Zahid said the proposal aimed to address Malaysia’s Rohingya refugee situation in a more “coordinated, effective and humane” manner.

“So if they [Turkey] say that ‘we are not ready,’ I respect that decision,” he said.

In response to a lawmaker’s question on whether Ankara had agreed to take in 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, Ahmad Zahid said Turkey “is not ready to consider [the request].”

He added that Turkey is currently hosting “more than 4 million refugees from Gulf countries, Arab countries and several neighboring countries.”

Malaysia will explore third-country resettlement options, including among members of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, he continued.

World.title: UK Sanctions 5 Regime Generals Following ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
The United Kingdom on Monday sanctioned five more senior Myanmar military officers after the United Nations’ top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya community in 2017.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced its ruling in the case on November 19.

The UK stated on Monday that it formally recognized the ICJ ruling and announced a major package of measures in response, imposing sanctions against five Myanmar military officers for atrocities against civilians since the 2021 coup.

The new UK sanctions target Brigadier General Myo Htut Hlaing, Major General Myo Min Tun, Major General Myat Thet Oo, Major General Kyaw Soe and Major General Kyaw Swar Oo.

The UK announced asset freezes, travel bans and director disqualifications in response to ongoing violence and repression against civilians across the country.

“Today, we are imposing new sanctions on those suspected of involvement in repression of the civilian population and other serious abuses of human rights in Myanmar,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The UK claimed that Brig-Gen Myo Htut Hlaing, deputy commander of Northwestern Regional Command, is responsible for serious cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of detainees in Chin State.

Maj-Gen Myo Min Tun, Eastern Military Command chief in Shan and Karenni states, was involved in repression of the civilian and threatens the peace, stability and security of Myanmar, it said.

Former head of the Northern Command in Kachin State and ex-ambassador to Laos Major General Myat Thet Oo, who was reportedly removed and jailed in 2024, was sanctioned for his role in enabling military authorities to repress civilians.

Maj-Gen Kyaw Soe, commander of the Western Command in Rakhine State, was sanctioned for involvement in airstrikes on civilians and medical infrastructure.

The UK said Maj-Gen Kyaw Swar Oo, former head of the Western Command, was responsible for repression of civilians including through an airstrike on Mrauk-U General Hospital that killed 33 civilians, including a baby, and left many others injured.

London also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar.

Alongside the sanctions, the UK is providing £5 million (US$6.53 million) in new aid for about 350,000 people, including Rohingya and other communities in Rakhine State, while a further £3 million will go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.

The United Kingdom has already imposed sanctions on 42 individuals and 39 entities, including individuals responsible for atrocities against the Rohingya, since the 2021 coup.

The UK earlier welcomed the ICJ ruling and ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché, Captain Soe Aung, from London.

World.title: 2 More Chinese Scam Syndicates Raided on Military-Linked Land in Yangon
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has raided two more Chinese scam syndicates operating at sites on military-owned land or believed to have military-linked ownership in the commercial capital Yangon.

The regime raided two residential houses in Mayangone Township and a Golden City Condo in Yankin Township on November 20 and November 22 respectively, arresting over 120 people, according to regime reports.

Observers believed the series of scam raids was prompted by tip-offs provided by Beijing.

On Sunday night, the regime raided Golden City Condo in Yankin Township and arrested 16 people on suspicion of involvement in an online gambling scam, the regime reported on Monday.

During raids on four condo rooms, the regime seized 15 laptops, 26 smartphones and three Wi-Fi routers. All four units were linked to Chinese national Jiang Hong Feng, who allegedly operated online casino and sports betting platform Zaw Play.Com.

Golden City condo sits on military-owned land leased in 2013 under a long-term Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) agreement with the military’s Office of the Quartermaster General.

In 2016, Singapore-based Emerging Towns & Cities Singapore (ETC) entered the development by taking a 70-percent stake. The other 30 percent is held by a military-linked local partner, Nature Link. The project generates revenue for the Myanmar military through land-use premiums and ongoing lease payments.

In 2023, two years after the coup, ETC took steps to sell its stake in a subsidiary linked to the project to Grand Ally Pte Ltd, which is owned by Li Bo, a Chinese citizen who is the vice president of sales and marketing for ETC, and the company’s regional sales and marketing director for Myanmar.

Justice For Myanmar (JFM), a rights watchdog, pointed out that ETC’s related-party sales risk maintaining ties to the military through personnel and stakeholders.

Nature Link belongs to Yangon-based Jewellery Luck, a group owned by regime crony Kyaw Sein with interests in real estate, hospitality, mining and forestry.

This scam syndicate not only sits on military-owned land, but is also just 500 meters from police housing compounds, a local resident told The Irrawaddy. The condo sheltering the scam center also shares a compound with the military-owned Myawaddy Media Center, formerly the Military Records Department. It is also located 600 meters from the regime’s No. 2 Police Security Command Headquarters located at the corner of No. 1 Industrial Road and Sayar San Road.

Following Sunday night’s raid, word spread in real estate circles, with agents warning other agents who had rented properties to Chinese nationals to flee the area, a local resident noted.

Real estate agents have a lot of incentive to rent to Chinese nationals in the Golden City condo, she added.

“To enter the condo, you have to pass a security gate and do a face scan,” she said.

Prior to Sunday’s raid, some media—citing resident accounts—had reported a previous regime raid on the condo on November 13, in which suspected scammers were also detained. But the regime has not made any public announcement about the earlier raid.

On the night of November 20, the regime raided suspected Chinese scam syndicates based in two residential buildings in Mayangone Township’s Ward No. 5, arresting 33 Chinese, two Thai and 70 Myanmar nationals.

The two compounds at 19/A and 43/1 Ma Soe Yein Street were just under 1 km from military bases including Military Intelligence Assistant Unit 1. Military defectors claimed the land housing the scam centers is linked to retired military officers and others in military circles.

A Chinese analyst claimed this raid, too, came in response to a tip-off from China.

Although the regime has pledged to keep fighting scam operations and act in accordance with the law, online critics are widely questioning how authorities could remain unaware of large numbers of people living in such compounds while Myanmar nationals face strict overnight guest registration rules and constant surveillance.

“When we register overnight guests, we have to provide the regime ward administrators with portrait photos of guests with their personal identities,” a Yangon resident said.

“Why don’t the ward administrators and authorities know about that?” he said.

Online critics urged authorities to check the many other places in Yangon where Chinese nationals live or rent together, alleging they could be running online scams.

On the night of November 12, the regime raided nine rooms at Golden River Residence condo in Thaketa Township and arrested 52 Chinese nationals, including Su Fu Quan, who was wanted by China, along with eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar nationals.

According to the regime’s reports, the syndicates targeted Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian nationals with romance and investment scams.

The regime reported the arrest of 323 people—302 Chinese nationals and 21 Myanmar women—during a raid on a makeshift online scam and gambling compound in southern Shan State’s Kyethi Township on Monday morning.

In a January 2026 report, the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar (ISP-Myanmar) said scam syndicates in Shan State were relocating from the China-Myanmar border to central Shan State and major urban centers such as Yangon and Mandalay.

ISP-Myanmar also said crackdowns on scam compounds in Karen State had pushed syndicates to relocate to other areas.

On November 19, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army’s Commander-in-Chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

World.title: After the Genocide Verdict, Myanmar’s ‘Foreign Intruder’ Scare Returns
World.content:
Since November 3, when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced the date for its judgment in Myanmar’s Rohingya genocide case, one word has surged across Burmese-language social media: “khoe win”, meaning “illegal entrant.” It is routinely paired with “Bengali,” the label Myanmar’s military establishment uses to deny the Rohingya their chosen identity. Sometimes it comes with “kalar,” a slur against Muslims and people of South Asian descent.

The message is familiar. The timing should worry anyone who remembers where it led.

On November 19, the ICJ ruled, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the military’s 2017 operations in northern Rakhine State.

Rather than reckon with that finding, pro-military nationalist circles are again urging Myanmar people to look for “Muslim outsiders” in their own neighborhoods.

Over the past three weeks, I have been monitoring Facebook and TikTok, Myanmar’s most-used social media platforms, and found hundreds of posts demanding that “Bengali intruders” be expelled, questioning Muslim businesspeople’s identity cards or calling for household members’ lists or guests’ lists inspections.

Some propose an Operasi-style campaign, borrowing the Malay term for enforcement operations against undocumented migrants, including Myanmar workers. An old video of former spy chief Khin Nyunt denying Rohingya identity has resurfaced on TikTok. None offers evidence of an influx from Bangladesh.

From social media to parliament

The posts are not all anonymous. On Facebook, veteran pro-military journalist Myat Khine encouraged guest-list checks, suggesting they would expose intruders.

Since November 19, the day of the ruling, Ashin Agga Dhamma, a famous nationalist Buddhist monk, has posted at least 12 interview videos featuring two Muslim businessmen. One of them, Htay Aung, claims Yangon is seeing an influx of illegal Muslim immigrants and rejects Rohingya identity. The monk and Htay Aung are widely seen as close to Ma Ba Tha, the ultranationalist Buddhist movement, and have previously appeared at anti-Rohingya rallies.

On November 15, the Burma Human Rights Network warned that Ma Ba Tha-backed groups were reportedly preparing nationwide protests against the ICJ ruling. It documented threats demanding that Myanmar Islamic organizations deny Rohingya identity, backed by calls to boycott Muslim-owned businesses if they refused.

Separately, UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie warned on October 29 that groups behind earlier anti-Muslim agitation were becoming more active online and in political spaces under military control. On November 18, citing reports from inside Myanmar, she told journalists in Dhaka that authorities in Naypyitaw were acting alongside Ma Ba Tha and other Buddhist nationalist organizations previously involved in spreading hatred and inciting violence.

On November 10, before the judgment, the inflammatory language reached the military-controlled parliament. Lawmaker Hla Swe accused the Arakan Army of letting undocumented entrants cross from Bangladesh. Deputy Immigration Minister Lin Zaw Tun outlined plans for inspections and arrests of people described as undocumented “Bengali” migrants. No independently verified evidence of the alleged influx was presented, but online demands to “check papers” had acquired an official counterpart. On November 20, the regime rejected the judgment and again called Rohingya “Bengalis.”

The road to 2017

This same deadly playbook has unfolded before. A UN fact-finding mission cited a government inquiry recording 192 deaths during the 2012 Rakhine violence, which displaced more than 140,000, mostly Rohingya. Anti-Muslim mobs killed at least 44 in Meiktila in 2013, according to Human Rights Watch. False online rape allegations helped ignite Mandalay riots that killed two in 2014, according to the US State Department.

These attacks occurred under former General Thein Sein’s military-backed government. Military hardliners and nationalists exploited religious fears during the political opening, presenting the army as the country’s protector. They used the same message against Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy before its 2015 landslide.

The violence of 2012–2014 was part of a broader campaign of hatred and discrimination that culminated in the military’s far larger assault on the Rohingya in 2017. By then, Aung San Suu Kyi led a civilian government, but the military still controlled security operations. The generals carried out the atrocities while her government bore much of the international backlash. That outcome also served the military’s political interests.

The ICJ’s judgment now shows how far the military took this approach. Citing UN investigators, it noted that 36 military-linked Facebook pages posted 10,485 anti-Rohingya hate-speech items, including repeated material, during six months of 2017.

Why revive the rhetoric now?

Min Aung Hlaing, president since April after a military-dominated election, faces pressure on several fronts. On the battlefield, while Chinese pressure helped Naypyitaw secure fragile ceasefires in parts of northern Shan State, major regime counteroffensives in Rakhine and Kachin states have stalled against fierce ethnic and resistance forces.

Diplomatically, ASEAN still bars the junta’s political representatives from summits, while Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun, who is loyal to the pro-democracy parallel government, still holds Myanmar’s UN seat. At home, the economy is in deep distress, with the kyat plunging toward 5,000 to the U.S. dollar and driving severe inflation.

The ICJ judgment brings another humiliation for a military establishment that has long portrayed itself as the sole defender of Myanmar’s sovereignty. Inciting public anger toward supposed foreign infiltrators is a tactic used by successive generations of generals. But repeating it today carries a far deadlier risk. Myanmar is far more heavily armed than during the communal riots a decade ago. Since the 2021 coup, the military has equipped and mobilized local militias, including Pyithu Sit and Pyu Saw Htee groups, to fight the resistance. In Meiktila in 2013, mobs carried machetes and petrol bombs. Today, the same crowd has access to guns and grenades. Another massacre is not inevitable, but hatred in a country with so many armed groups could be harder to contain.

The opposition has responsibilities too. The National Unity Government and Karen National Union welcomed the ruling. Yet some democracy supporters still reject Rohingya identity. Opposing military rule is not enough if we still deny the minorities’ rights and identity.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Myanmar’s generals have spent decades teaching people to fear one another, and those divisions have repeatedly helped the military justify its grip on power. Myanmar’s people have seen where campaigns against supposed outsiders can lead. The genocide judgment should be a reason to confront that history, not repeat it. A demand to inspect someone’s identity card must not become the first step toward another burning village.

Nyein Chan Aye is a Burmese journalist based in Washington, D.C., who previously worked for the BBC and Voice of America. He writes on Myanmar, U.S. policy, China and regional affairs.

World.title: Tokayev to Visit Moscow for Talks with Putin and AI Journey 2026 Conference
World.content:
ASTANA – President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will pay a working visit to Moscow on Nov. 25-26 at the invitation of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Aibek Smadiyarov, the president’s press secretary, announced on his Telegram channel.

During the visit, the two leaders are scheduled to discuss strengthening the strategic partnership and alliance between Kazakhstan and Russia.

Tokayev will also participate in the AI Journey 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence.

World.title: IEA Says Hormuz Shock Could Reshape Oil Trade for Years
World.content:
ASTANA – The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has triggered the largest energy supply shock in history and could reshape oil trade long after tankers can again move freely, the International Energy Agency said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 released on Nov.19.

As of November, disruptions in the Gulf had cost the world a cumulative 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic meters of gas supply, according to the IEA. Before the crisis, approximately 80% of the oil that passed through Hormuz went to Asia.

“We have already seen a multitude of short-term responses to lessen the impacts on energy systems, economies, businesses and households. Energy producers both inside and outside the Gulf stepped up to bring additional supplies to market via alternative routes and expanded production. China, the world’s largest oil importer, massively reduced its purchases from international markets,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in the report’s foreword.

Longer-term responses from governments included change in policies or changes in “perceptions of risk.” Birol also noted the countries’ efforts to build new pipelines to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil production in Kazakhstan dropped by 8.3% in nine months of 2026, reaching 69.4 million tons, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said at a government meeting in October. This decline, he noted, is among the factors hindering the country’s economic growth.

“This year, the economy is facing a number of headwinds. First, there is a decline in oil production and a negative contribution from the oil sector to GDP growth,” Zhumangarin said.

The decline in production was recorded in Kazakhstan’s largest fields. The Tengiz field on the Caspian shores posted a 12% decrease to 26.7 million metric tons. Kashagan’s output fell by 6% to 12.8 million metric tons and Karachaganak by 18% to 7.5 million metric tons.

For Kazakhstan, the most important oil route runs through the Black Sea. The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which carries Kazakh crude to a terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, repeatedly suspended flows after attacks on tankers near the terminal. The pipeline handled around 81% of Kazakhstan’s crude exports in 2025, according to KazMunayGas national oil and gas company.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which carries Kazakh crude to a terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, repeatedly suspended flows after attacks on tankers near the terminal.

Askar Ismailov, an independent oil and gas analyst and founder of PACE Analytics, counts eight attacks on CPC facilities and tankers carrying Kazakh oil since January. According to him, storage tanks could absorb a one-day export halt with little effect on annual production. In his scenarios published in a Telegram post, he estimated a weeklong shutdown could cut output by as much as 650,000 metric tons. A three-week shutdown could cost two million tons.

Ismailov expects Kazakhstan to produce 94 million to 95 million tons of oil and gas condensate this year, below the government’s November target of 96 million tons.

“A high Brent price can’t make up for the oil that Kazakhstan will physically be unable to produce and export in the remaining 40 days,” he wrote.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin told a government meeting in October that lower oil production was already weighing on economic growth. Export disruptions were one of several pressures on producers. A January fire and power outage temporarily halted production at Tengiz, Kazakhstan’s largest oilfield.

Rough seas can also keep tankers from loading. By late May, the CPC had recorded 680 hours of weather-related downtime at its tanker terminal near the Russian port of Novorossiysk. Even after a tanker leaves the terminal, it must pass through the Bosporus and Dardanelles to reach the Mediterranean. Dense fog regularly halts traffic in the Turkish Straits, usually for hours and there is no other sea passage out of the Black Sea.

Kazakhstan can bypass the Black Sea by shipping crude across the Caspian from Aktau to Baku and sending it by pipeline to Türkiye’s port of Ceyhan. KazTransOil shipped 1.16 million tons toward the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline in January–September, up 24% from a year earlier. By the end of October, shipments had reached 1.32 million tons, exceeding the 1.26 million tons shipped in all of 2025.

Overall, the IEA projects that oil output across the Caspian region stays flat at around three million barrels a day through 2050 in its Current Policies Scenario.

Why a gas producer is buying more gas

Kazakhstan imported 6.4 billion cubic meters in the first nine months of 2026, more than the 4.7 billion it bought in all of 2025, according to the Energy Ministry. The ministry cited rising domestic consumption.

In 2025, total natural gas production in Kazakhstan reached a record high of 68.1 billion cubic meters but only 27.4 billion cubic meters was ready for sale, according to the Energy Ministry. Much of the country’s gas comes from the Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak fields, where it is produced alongside oil and condensate. Domestic processing capacity limits how much of that raw gas can be treated and piped to homes, factories and combined heat and power plants.

Producers reinjected 52% of the gas they extracted in January–September to maintain pressure in oil reservoirs, according to the ministry.

IEA also expects Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to take a larger share of extra Russian gas exports as domestic demand rises and output from mature fields declines.

Writing on his Tradereport Telegram channel, a trading and investment analyst Yernar Serik put gas imports at $1.08 billion and exports at $812 million in January-September. Kazakhstan also spent more than it earned on petroleum products and electricity. Russia supplied around 80% of the country’s energy imports by value, according to his analysis.

Overall, Serik indicated Kazakhstan exported $35.5 billion of energy goods in the first nine months of 2026 and imported $2.6 billion. However, when removing crude oil, exports of everything else fell 25% to $1.8 billion while imports rose 44% to $2.6 billion, leaving a deficit of $832 million, according to calculations by Serik.

World.title: EDB Plans to Invest at Least $500 Million in Uzbekistan in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) plans to invest at least US$500 million in Uzbekistan in 2027, with its total investment volume in the country potentially reaching US$3 billion by 2031.

The plans were discussed during a Nov. 25 meeting in Tashkent between EDB Chairman Nikolai Podguzov and Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev. According to the bank, the talks focused on expanding investment cooperation, implementing prospective projects and the bank’s country strategy for 2027-2031.

The EDB is currently considering 10 potential projects in Uzbekistan with a combined investment volume that could exceed US$1 billion, Podguzov said.

“Uzbekistan is one of the EDB’s key investment destinations. In 2027, we intend to invest at least US$500 million in projects in Uzbekistan,” he said.

He added that using non-sovereign financing instruments could help attract private and international capital without increasing the country’s direct sovereign debt burden.

The officials identified five priority areas for cooperation: transport and logistics infrastructure, water and energy resilience, industrial development and production cooperation, digitalization, and financial instruments. The latter includes support for small and medium-sized enterprises, export financing, green finance and Islamic finance.

The meeting also covered opportunities to expand cooperation with state-owned companies and private investors through project financing and syndicated lending.

Uzbekistan joined the EDB in 2025, becoming the bank’s third-largest shareholder with a 10% stake. In May, the bank opened its representative office in Tashkent and began operations in the country.

The EDB is a multilateral development bank investing in Eurasia. By the end of June, its cumulative portfolio comprised 348 projects worth US$22.1 billion, covering transport infrastructure, digital systems, green energy, agriculture, manufacturing and mechanical engineering.

World.title: Rybakina Named ESPN’s Best WTA Player of 2026 After Historic Season
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has been selected as the WTA Player of the Year in ESPN’s review of the 2026 professional tennis season. ESPN, a U.S.-based sports media company covering major sporting events worldwide, published its selection following a remarkable year in which Rybakina won two Grand Slam titles and finished as world No. 1.

The 27-year-old won the Australian Open in January and the US Open in September, bringing her career Grand Slam tally to three. She defeated Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka in both finals.

According to ESPN’s season review, Rybakina stood out for her powerful serve, composure under pressure and consistent performances against the world’s leading players.

She beat Sabalenka in a three-set final, 6-4, 4-6, 6-4. The victory marked her second Grand Slam title, following her 2022 Wimbledon success.

Rybakina continued her strong run, reaching the final at Indian Wells and winning the Stuttgart Open in April. She also advanced to the final of the Canadian Open in Toronto.

Despite an Achilles injury that forced her to retire in the Cincinnati Open quarterfinals and disrupted her US Open preparations, Rybakina returned to competition in impressive form.

At Flushing Meadows, she defeated U.S. Coco Gauff in the semifinals before overcoming Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the final to secure her second Grand Slam trophy of the season.

Her US Open victory also propelled her to the top of the WTA rankings on Sept. 14, ending Sabalenka’s 99-week reign as world No. 1.

Rybakina further strengthened her position by winning the Ningbo Open in October, bringing her season title tally to four. She finished the year with a 54-14 win-loss record and secured the year-end No. 1 ranking for the first time in her career.

According to the WTA, she became the 17th player in the organization’s history to finish a season at the top of the women’s singles rankings and the first athlete representing Kazakhstan, in either men’s or women’s singles or doubles, to achieve the milestone.

Separately, Rybakina was nominated for the official WTA Player of the Year award, with the winner to be announced during the week of Dec. 14.

ESPN also highlighted the unpredictability of the 2026 season, with several players making major breakthroughs. Russia’s Mirra Andreeva claimed her first Grand Slam title at the French Open, while Czech player Linda Noskova won Wimbledon.

Meanwhile, Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, who had dominated the men’s Grand Slam tournaments in recent years, faced injury setbacks during the season.

The WTA also shared a video featuring Rybakina with the trophy recognizing her as the year-end world No. 1 in women’s singles. In the video, she thanked fans for their support throughout the season and said she hoped the achievement would be only the beginning.

“I just want to say a big thank you to everyone for the support throughout the year. It’s been an amazing year. … Hopefully, this is just the beginning. Thanks again, and see you next year,” she said.

Rybakina’s achievements mark another significant milestone for Kazakhstan’s presence in international tennis, placing the country at the top of the sport’s women’s singles rankings.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan Launch Joint Startup Hub in London
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Astana Hub and Uzbekistan’s IT Park have launched a joint Eurasia Growth Hub in London to help technology companies from both countries enter the British market and connect with international clients, investors and business partners.

The hub will provide practical support to startups, from arranging initial business meetings and finding potential customers to identifying partners for pilot projects, Astana Hub reported on Nov. 24.

At the first stage, Eurasia Growth Hub will focus on helping Kazakh and Uzbek technology companies establish a presence in the United Kingdom. Its London-based team will identify potential clients, investors and industry partners and organize meetings tailored to each company’s needs.

The hub also plans to develop a soft-landing program to help startups assess demand for their products, build local partnerships and address operational issues when entering the British market.

It will also organize business missions, industry forums and webinars to facilitate business connections. In the future, the initiative aims to expand its support model to other European markets.

“British companies, in turn, will be able to explore the technology sectors of our countries and find teams for joint projects,” said Tanat Uskembayev, managing director of Astana Hub.

The initiative will also help British companies access the markets of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and develop joint projects with local technology teams.

“Companies will have different needs. One may need to identify potential buyers in the United Kingdom, while another may be looking for a partner for a pilot project. The meetings and on-the-ground support will depend on each team’s goals,” said Muzaffar Karabayev, CEO of Eurasia Growth Hub.

Astana Hub, IT Park Uzbekistan and Eurasia Growth Hub signed a memorandum of cooperation on Oct. 2. The London hub expands their network of joint international hubs, which already operate in China, the United Arab Emirates, Malaysia and the United States.

World.title: Kazakhstan Reaffirms Commitment to Strengthening Cooperation With OIC
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening cooperation with the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), as Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi discussed future engagement with OIC Assistant Secretary-General Bagdat Amreyev during a Nov. 25 meeting.

Tileuberdi highlighted Kazakhstan’s particular attention to its relations with the organization and outlined promising areas for cooperation, according to the ministry.

He also emphasized the importance of adhering to the OIC’s fundamental principles and Charter, as well as consistently implementing decisions adopted at OIC summits and ministerial meetings.

The officials also discussed the calendar of upcoming OIC events and confirmed their readiness to continue effective cooperation between Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry and the OIC General Secretariat.

Amreyev was elected OIC assistant secretary-general for administration and finance in October during the organization’s 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers session in Baghdad.

World.title: Flowers on My Way to University: Learning What It Means to Feel Safe
World.content:
Every day, on my commute from the place I am still learning to call home to the university, I find flowers. Not the kind of flowers people expect to receive on a special occasion, carefully wrapped in florist’s paper and given with a particular purpose. These are different. They are little mosaic roses, scattered throughout Ravenna, waiting along familiar paths and hidden in the tiniest streets. I keep finding them in places I might have otherwise walked past, and somehow, these small encounters have become something I look forward to on my way to university.

When you move somewhere new, you start to notice things you might never have paid attention to before. Small things become significant. A familiar route, the same morning light, something beautiful that you happen to come across on your way somewhere.

I think it is the feeling they leave me with that makes me remember them. My usual commute has become a small reminder, almost every day, that I am not alone. There is something comforting about finding them along the way, especially on mornings when everything feels unfamiliar, when being far from home feels heavier than usual, or when I am reminded of just how much it takes to build a life somewhere new. Moving to another country is not only about the excitement of discovering a new place or the growth that comes with it. It is also about allowing yourself to feel the difficult parts: the uncertainty, the loneliness, the days when you question your decisions, and the moments when you don’t yet feel like you belong. These little roses remind me that all of it is part of the journey, that what I am doing matters, and that I am allowed to feel everything along the way – the highs and the lows – without having to make either one smaller.

I came to Ravenna to pursue a master’s degree in Protection of Human Rights and International Development. It is a city known as la città amica delle donne – a city friendly to women. And as Nov. 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, approaches, I have begun to think more about what that phrase really means. What makes a city a friend to women? What does it mean to feel safe somewhere? To move freely, to walk without fear, to exist without constantly calculating the risks of simply being a woman?

Only after I started noticing the roses did I realize they weren’t there by chance. They were part of something larger, a message woven into the city itself. Suddenly, the flowers I had been finding on my way to university meant more.

The mosaic roses are part of I Fiori di Ravenna – Città Amica delle Donne, or The Flowers of Ravenna – A City Friendly to Women. The anti-violence association Linea Rosa developed the initiative with Ravenna’s mosaic artists and cultural community. It uses the city’s centuries-old mosaic tradition to create a visible message of solidarity with women and awareness of gender-based violence. The roses are placed across the city, on buildings and along streets, turning its artistic heritage into something more than a reminder of its past.

The project began in 2011, bringing together artists, associations, cultural institutions and the city itself. The roses are not simply decoration. They are a promise that women should feel welcome, that violence should not be ignored, and that a community has a responsibility to notice. That’s why I find them so touching. They don’t ask you to know the story behind them before you see them. They are just there, on your way somewhere. And then, one day, you discover what they mean.

As the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women approaches, I started to think about the place I come from. There, domestic violence remains a deeply serious issue. In 2024 alone, the Kazakh Ministry of Internal Affairs received around 100,000 reports of domestic violence. According to United Nations Women, approximately 72,000 protective orders were issued, and 16,000 court decisions were made. Legislative changes introduced in April 2024 reinstated criminal penalties for battery and minor bodily harm in domestic violence cases, marking an important shift in the country’s legal response. These changes matter. But laws, as necessary as they are, cannot alone change what happens behind closed doors, what a girl is taught to tolerate, what a woman is afraid to report, or what society still sometimes chooses not to see.

Coming from Kazakhstan and now living in Italy, I often find myself thinking about how differently we speak about women, and how similar many of our silences are. We speak about safety as if it were a privilege, about freedom as if it was something that can be negotiated, and about violence as if its absence was the responsibility of women themselves – to be careful, to avoid certain places, to dress differently, to make better choices.

But safety should not be something a woman has to earn through caution. It should not depend on how well she knows a city, how carefully she walks home, whether someone is waiting for her, or whether she can afford to leave. It should be something she is entitled to simply because she exists.

I am still learning Ravenna. I am learning its streets, its language, its habits. I am learning how to feel at home somewhere that was once only a point on a map. And perhaps that is why the roses matter to me more than I can explain. They remind me that belonging is not only about being familiar with a place. It is also about knowing that the place, in some way, is making room for you.

On my way to university, I pass these roses without always stopping. I have places to be, books to read, deadlines to meet, and a life that is still very much in progress. But I know they are there. And I like to think that somewhere, a woman passing one of these mosaics for the first time might need to see it. That she might be walking through a city she doesn’t know, carrying something she has never told anyone, and find a small flower on a wall that says she is welcome. That someone thought of her. That help exists. That she is not alone.

Maybe a city cannot promise that no woman will ever experience violence within its streets or homes, but it can decide not to look away. It can make the message visible, put it on its walls, in its institutions, in its schools, in its conversations. It can create places where women are listened to, believed and protected. And perhaps it can begin with something as small as a flower.

World.title: IEA Highlights Gas Supply Pressures in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Stable Caspian Oil Output
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan face growing pressure on their natural gas supplies as domestic demand rises and production from mature fields declines, according to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026.

The report, released on Nov. 19, notes that Russia is expected to marginally increase its natural gas exports to the Caspian region, with a significant share going to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. It says the two countries face “rising domestic demand and declining output from mature fields,” pointing to growing pressure on their domestic gas balances.

The report also projects modest growth in Turkmenistan’s gas supply as new phases at the country’s giant Galkynysh gas field come online.

“Turkmenistan sees modest supply growth as additional phases of the giant Galkynysh field are developed,” the IEA says.

Caspian oil output remains stable

In its Current Policies Scenario (CPS), which reflects existing policies and regulations, the IEA projects that Caspian oil production will remain broadly stable at around 3 million barrels per day through 2050. This is a regional projection and does not represent Kazakhstan’s oil production alone.

The report also highlights Eurasia’s position as a major oil-exporting region. In 2025, the region’s net exports amounted to approximately 7.1 million barrels per day of crude oil and around 1.9 million barrels per day of oil products.

Energy security and global outlook

The report examines how changes in energy policy, investment and geopolitical conditions could affect global supply and demand. It presents several scenarios rather than a single forecast, including pathways based on current policies, announced government measures and more ambitious energy transitions.

One area of concern is the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and gas shipments. Under the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), around 20 million barrels per day of oil flows through the strait in 2035. In the Low Hormuz Capacity (LHC) scenario, which assumes severely disrupted transit through the waterway, flows fall to around 2 million barrels per day.

The IEA notes that approximately 7 million barrels per day of new pipeline capacity is under construction or under consideration, which could help reduce reliance on the strait.

The report also points to the expanding role of renewable energy. Renewables currently account for around 33% of global electricity generation. Their share is projected to reach 45-50% by 2035 under the CPS and STEPS scenarios, and a higher level under the Accelerating Renewables Case (ARC).

Nuclear energy is also gaining momentum, with nearly 90 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity under construction worldwide as of mid-2026, the highest level in more than 35 years. In Central Asia, Uzbekistan has begun construction of its first nuclear power plant.

The IEA emphasizes that its scenarios are not predictions but explore how different policy choices and developments could shape the energy system. For Kazakhstan and its neighbors, the outlook highlights the importance of balancing rising domestic energy demand with production capacity, infrastructure development and regional energy security.

World.title: Fake videos and leaked personal data: Georgian journalist Tornike Razmadze targeted in digital harassment campaign
World.content:
Georgia’s first AI smear campaign against an activist

Tornike Razmadze, a journalist and critic of Georgian Dream, has become the target of a smear campaign. Between 21 and 23 November, anonymous social media accounts circulated AI-generated videos portraying him as a drug dealer.

His phone number was also published, accompanied by suggestions that people could use it to buy marijuana. The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) described the incidents as a targeted harassment campaign.

Fact-checkers say this is one of the first cases in Georgian politics in which highly realistic AI-generated videos have been used in such a coordinated campaign against a government critic.

Tornike Razmadze is a journalist, blogger and civic activist. He regularly publishes videos criticising representatives of the Georgian Dream party, which attract large audiences. He also hosts two programmes on the Mismane YouTube channel.

What happened?

According to Myth Detector, on 21 November an anonymous Facebook page called Politikani published a video featuring Razmadze’s name. The page has previously been involved in smear campaigns against the opposition. The video shows a man who resembles Razmadze asking a drug dealer to hire him as a courier. It was accompanied by the caption: “Now it’s clear why he became friends with Akhobadze” (Giorgi Akhobadze is a Georgian doctor and activist who faced charges of illegally purchasing and possessing a particularly large quantity of drugs, but was later acquitted by a court – JAMnews).

On 22 November, a TikTok account called DaDash Pirveli published a video showing a man entering the stairwell of a residential building and bending down near the gas meters (apparently to leave a drug package – JAMnews). The video carried the caption: “Wasn’t it Tornike Razmadze who said, ‘It wasn’t me’?”

‘Threat of censorship’: What we know about Georgia’s new Interior Ministry department overseeing public communication

Georgian blogger says Interior Ministry wants to punish him for insulting Russian propagandists

On the same day, the Facebook page Ganulebuli Opozitsia published a photograph of Razmadze with a woman dressed in black. The post presented the woman as the mother of a young man who had died of a drug overdose. She blamed his death on “drug dealers like Razmadze”.

The Myth Detector fact-checking service concluded that the first two videos had been generated using artificial intelligence. According to InVID, there was a 96% probability that the video posted by Politikani was AI-generated. Sightengine put the probability for the TikTok video at 77%.

Fact-checkers note that both the anonymous pages and the TikTok account mentioned above had previously taken part in campaigns targeting government critics.

On 23 November, Razmadze’s phone number was also published on social media.

What does Razmadze say?

Razmadze has filed a complaint with the Interior Ministry. “The attacks against me have crossed the line into criminal activity. This is no longer just propaganda,” he said.

Speaking to TV Pirveli, he described the possible consequences of the digital harassment campaign: “This extremely dirty campaign could end with a physical attack on me or with someone planting something on me.”

Razmadze believes the authorities are behind the harassment. He says Dimitri Samkharadze, a Georgian Dream MP, discussed the possibility of physically attacking him in social media comments.

The activist links the campaign to his recent videos. In one, he recalls the case of Barbare Rapaliani (a 10-month-old girl whose tragic death in Georgia shortly before the 2012 parliamentary election became one of the country’s most high-profile and politicised unsolved cases in recent history – JAMnews). In another, he mocks comedians from pro-government television channels. Razmadze says both videos attracted widespread attention. He is now consulting lawyers.

How pro-government media covered the story

The campaign against Razmadze extended beyond social media to pro-government media outlets.

On 22 November, the Facebook page Pirveli Ambebi published footage of a residential building collapse in Batumi in 2021, presenting the incident as if it were happening at the time. The post claimed that hundreds of people were trapped under the rubble and that 30 had died.

The Interior Ministry denied the report, saying the post was intended to spread panic among the public.

Pro-government media outlets subsequently claimed that the Pirveli Ambebi page, which had circulated the false information, was allegedly linked to Tornike Razmadze. Their only evidence was that the page had previously published videos featuring him. None of the reports identified the people who ran the page.

Razmadze denies publishing the post and says he has no connection to the page. According to him, the page was created a long time ago and regularly published videos featuring other opposition figures. Razmadze has demanded that the Imedi, Rustavi 2 and POSTV television channels remove the false information and apologise.

What do human rights organisations say?

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) described the actions targeting Razmadze across various platforms as “a coordinated, targeted and systematic harassment campaign”.

The organisation says the materials published as part of the campaign amount to identity theft, as the videos reproduce Razmadze’s appearance and voice without his consent.

GYLA notes that the videos contain no elements of satire or parody, which “aggravates the negative impact on Tornike Razmadze’s rights – his rights to honour, privacy, identity and security”.

The organisation says the state has an obligation to assess such risks promptly, take protective measures and provide effective legal remedies for violations of these rights.

Reaction on social media

The story sparked widespread discussion on social media. Razmadze faced a wave of insults and accusations that echoed the narrative promoted by the fake videos. At the same time, many users expressed their support. Other bloggers and government critics voiced solidarity with Razmadze, warning the authorities that such campaigns could have dangerous consequences. YouTube bloggers and sports commentators also expressed their support.

Comedian Onise Okriashvili wrote on Facebook that this appeared to be the first case in Georgia in which someone had tried to discredit a person using hyper-realistic AI-generated videos rather than satirical ones.

Background: fined over remarks about Russian propagandists

A month before the campaign began, Razmadze was fined 3,000 lari. In September, the Interior Ministry opened administrative proceedings against him. The case concerned a Facebook comment containing obscene language directed at Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov. They had previously described Georgian King Erekle II as a ruler who “knelt down”. Razmadze’s video addressed those remarks.

A newly established Interior Ministry unit responsible for combating “hate speech” initiated the case. The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association described it at the time as a precedent for censorship.

Razmadze says he expected a campaign against him after the authorities opened the case.

What happens next?

Razmadze is discussing further legal action with his lawyers. The Interior Ministry has yet to say whether it has launched an investigation following his complaint.

Georgia’s first AI smear campaign against an activist

World.title: Georgia awarded contracts worth nearly $499m without competitive tenders – TI
World.content:
Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

Between January and October 2026, almost half (45%) of tenders announced in Georgia attracted only one bidder. The lack of competition meant that these contracts cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) more.

This is according to a new study by Transparency International Georgia.

According to the study, in the first ten months of 2026, government agencies awarded contracts worth a total of 4.09 billion lari (approximately $1.57 billion) through 16,222 electronic tenders.

A total of 7,364 tenders – 45% of all those announced – attracted only one bidder, either a company or an individual entrepreneur. The contracts were worth a combined 1.31 billion lari (approximately $499 million), accounting for almost a third of all public procurement spending.

According to the organisation, the winning bids in single-bidder tenders were, on average, just 4.3% below the initial estimated value set by the authorities. By comparison, prices in competitive tenders fell by an average of 15.4%.

TI estimates that if prices in non-competitive tenders had fallen by the same proportion, public contracts would have cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) less.

The study also found that in 2,883 tenders, worth a total of 572 million lari (approximately $219.6 million), the winning bid exactly matched the estimated value set by the government in advance. In these cases, the state made no savings.

The largest public procurer using non-competitive procedures is the Special Penitentiary Service

According to TI, in 2026 the Special Penitentiary Service was the largest public procurer using non-competitive tenders. Through this mechanism, the agency awarded contracts worth a total of 203.7 million lari (approximately $78.6 million).

Almost the entire amount – 201.4 million lari – went towards two contracts for providing meals to prisoners.

In May 2026, the Special Penitentiary Service awarded contracts worth 152.4 million lari to Giorgi 2020 and 49 million lari to Delfood.

Both companies were the sole bidders in their respective tenders. Moreover, their bids exactly matched the estimated values set in advance.

The contracts were awarded amid a scandal over the quality of food served in Georgian prisons. Earlier, in March, the Special Penitentiary Service terminated its contract with Ili Group, which had been responsible for providing meals to prisoners.

According to TI, Giorgi 2020 had never previously won a public procurement tender.

On 3 April 2026 – the day the tender was announced – the company’s owners transferred 33% of its shares to Irakli Letodiani free of charge.

According to the TV Pirveli television channel, Letodiani is a former employee of the State Security Service.

Which sectors have the least competition?

According to the study, several sectors have particularly high proportions of tenders with only one bidder:

Transport services – 85%;

Software and information systems – 81%;

Repair and maintenance – 78%;

Medical equipment and medicines – 59%.

The proportion of construction tenders attracting only one bidder was relatively low, at 29%. However, construction ranked first in terms of the total value of contracts awarded.

Non-competitive construction contracts were worth a total of 517.9 million lari (approximately $199.8 million).

Tbilisi and Batumi account for the largest sums in non-competitive procurement

According to TI, 43% of tenders organised by municipalities – including those run by mayors and bodies established by them – attracted no competition. The figure for central government agencies and other state institutions was 48%.

Municipalities awarded contracts worth a total of 625 million lari (approximately $241.1 million) without any competition.

In monetary terms, Tbilisi ranked first, with 277 million lari, accounting for 38% of the capital’s procurement spending. Batumi came second, with 63 million lari, or 30% of its procurement spending.

In terms of the proportion of non-competitive tenders, the highest figures were recorded in Ambrolauri (61%), Terjola (59%) and Khulo (55%).

The risk of tailoring tender requirements to specific companies

TI notes that one possible reason for the high proportion of tenders with only one bidder is that authorities tailor procurement requirements to suit specific suppliers. The organisation cites several examples of this practice.

In June 2026, TI reported on five road repair tenders announced by Batumi’s Department of Infrastructure and Improvement.

Under the terms of the tender, bidders had to either own an asphalt plant within a 30km radius of the work site or provide a contract with such a facility. This requirement applied to a tender worth 29.2 million lari (approximately $11.3 million), in which Gza was the sole bidder.

Another example is a security services tender announced by Georgian Railway in 2023. To qualify for the contract, worth 7.8 million lari (approximately $3 million), bidders had to demonstrate at least 20 years of uninterrupted experience.

According to Transparency International (TI), only two companies in the entire country met this requirement. The sole bidder was Intersecurity Georgia LLC, owned by Ioseb Alavidze, a former head of the Tbilisi police. The company’s bid exactly matched the estimated contract value.

The organisation also cites a tender for the provision of social canteen services announced by Rustavi City Hall in 2022.

In that case, the company offering the lowest price was excluded from the tender because its revised price schedule listed figures to four decimal places instead of two. The contract was ultimately awarded to a company whose bid was 155,000 lari (approximately $59,800) higher.

The problem extends beyond large-scale tenders

TI says that a lack of competition in public procurement is not a new problem. The organisation refers to a 2024 study which found that half of the large tenders – those worth more than five million lari – announced between January and July 2024 attracted no competition.

Figures for 2026 show that the problem is not limited to large-scale procurement: only one bidder took part in half of all tenders worth up to 100,000 lari.

The organisation also criticises reports prepared by the State Procurement Agency. TI notes that although the agency’s reports point to an increase in competition, none of its annual reports published since 2019 has mentioned that almost half of all public tenders attract only one bidder.

Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

World.title: NEST Centre: 408 Azerbaijani citizens killed while fighting in Ukraine for Russian forces. What is known in Baku?
World.content:
Azerbaijani citizens killed while serving in Russian army

At least 408 Azerbaijani citizens who fought in the ranks of the Russian army have been killed in Russia’s war against Ukraine. The figures come from a study published on 23 November by the independent think tank NEST Centre (New Eurasian Strategies Centre). The study draws on registered death records obtained through a data leak from Russia’s Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).

According to NEST Centre’s calculations, 6,947 foreign nationals who fought on Russia’s side were confirmed killed between 24 February 2022 and 29 September 2026. Azerbaijan ranks sixth in the number of fatalities, after Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

Earlier this year, the authorities in Azerbaijan acknowledged that a “significant number” of the country’s citizens had died in the war between Russia and Ukraine, but did not specify how many. The leaked data help to fill some of this information gap.

What does the figure of 408 deaths tell us, what does it leave out, and how does Baku view the deaths of its citizens in this war?

How did the data leak happen?

In late October, the Belarusian hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian group Silent Crow said they had gained access to Rosstat’s information systems. The agency confirmed that it had come under cyberattacks between 29 October and 1 November, but denied that hackers had breached its databases or leaked confidential information.

Several international media outlets and research centres subsequently analysed the database. Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said there was no longer any doubt about its authenticity. Bloomberg, meanwhile, reported that it had been unable to verify the data using cryptographic methods, but had found no signs of falsification.

Why could the death toll be higher than 408?

NEST Centre stresses that the list of fatalities is incomplete and that the figures do not reflect the true scale of Russia’s losses. There are several reasons for this.

First, the figure of 408 includes only Azerbaijani citizens. According to a Bloomberg analysis based on the same database, more than 6,000 of the 11,335 foreign-born servicemen killed had acquired Russian citizenship before their deaths. Russia offers foreigners a simplified and accelerated path to citizenship in exchange for military service. The figures for Azerbaijan do not include people born in Azerbaijan who died as Russian citizens.

Second, researchers say that if Russian civil registry offices did not register a foreign national’s death, the information may have remained only in the Ministry of Defence’s internal records. Third, the database contains no information about people missing in action. In 2025, the average delay in registering deaths exceeded four months.

How did they end up in the Russian army?

NEST Centre provides no specific information about how Azerbaijani citizens joined the Russian army. However, the study says that recruiters promised foreigners – primarily migrants from Central Asia – civilian jobs, help with paperwork or release from detention centres, before sending them to military units. In some cases, researchers say, recruiters used threats and physical violence to force migrants to sign military contracts.

There have also been individual reports of Azerbaijani citizens ending up on the front line under similar circumstances. In August this year, the Azerbaijani news website Modern.az published a video in which an Azerbaijani man serving in the Russian army claimed that authorities had unlawfully sent him to the combat zone.

What does Baku say?

Azerbaijan criminalises participation in armed conflicts abroad. On 3 February 2026, the State Security Service (SSS) said that “a significant number of citizens of the Republic of Azerbaijan have taken part in hostilities between Russia and Ukraine, been killed, gone missing or been wounded, while some remain in captivity”. According to the agency, in January that year authorities detained four Azerbaijani citizens suspected of fighting on the side of Russia or Ukraine. A court ordered their pre-trial detention.

The SSS warned citizens that “participation in such armed conflicts entails criminal liability in the Republic of Azerbaijan”. However, it did not specify how many Azerbaijani citizens had been killed, gone missing or been taken prisoner.

Azerbaijanis are also fighting on Ukraine’s side. In September 2024, Galib Osmanly, a representative of the United Azerbaijani Diaspora of Ukraine, told the Turan news agency that at least 60 ethnic Azerbaijanis had been killed while serving in the Ukrainian army since the start of the war. They included both Ukrainian citizens and Azerbaijanis who held residence permits in the country.

Against the backdrop of tensions with Moscow

The figures on those killed have emerged amid tensions between Baku and Moscow. The crash of an AZAL passenger plane in December 2024 and the disagreements that followed undermined trust between the two countries. In September this year, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists on its wanted list.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry and State Security Service have yet to comment on the findings of the NEST Centre study. Russia’s Defence Ministry, meanwhile, does not disclose figures for the number of foreign nationals serving in its army or the casualties among them.



Azerbaijani citizens killed while serving in Russian army

World.title: Opinion: ‘Pashinyan’s proposal is aimed at Russia, not Armenian opposition’
World.content:
Who did Pashinyan address his referendum proposal to?

Experts in Armenia are debating Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s proposal to the parliamentary opposition. He suggested that opposition MPs vote to put the draft of a new constitution to a referendum. In return, he promised to resign as prime minister regardless of the referendum’s outcome.

Local analysts describe the offer as a “deal” with the opposition. Under its terms, if opposition MPs do not obstruct the constitutional referendum, Pashinyan will voluntarily step down. Opposition figures have repeatedly stated that their main goal is to remove him from office. Pashinyan, meanwhile, wants to change the Constitution. He believes a new version would allow Armenia to live in peace and resolve conflicts with its neighbours.

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan, discussing the opposition forces that could theoretically vote in favour of the referendum, highlights the following points:

“They are part of, and even lead, political forces that have ‘united’ to overthrow the government;

The political capital of these forces lies neither in their members, nor in their standing at home, nor in the other groups they have joined forces with.”

According to the analyst, the political capital of both opposition factions – “Strong Armenia” and “Armenia” – lies in “Moscow’s patronage”.

“They will only be able to respond to Pashinyan’s proposal after agreeing on their answer with the Kremlin. In reality, Russia is the party responding to the proposal,” Robert Gevondyan argues.

The political analyst also puts forward scenarios in which Moscow might allow the pro-Russian opposition to “make a deal” with the Armenian authorities.

“The opposition rejects the offer of its dreams”

In recent days, Armenia’s prime minister has repeatedly presented his proposal in public appearances. Pashinyan is asking opposition MPs to vote in favour of holding a referendum on the draft Constitution. In return, he promises to resign if voters reject it. If they approve it, the ruling party will not nominate him for prime minister in the next election.

The opposition factions “Armenia” and “Strong Armenia” have rejected the offer.

They believe the incumbent prime minister will step down anyway and refuse to accept his proposed “deal”.

Opposition figures describe the draft of the new Constitution as “Aliyev’s Constitution”. They believe Armenia is changing its supreme law at Azerbaijan’s request.

Azerbaijan refuses to sign a peace treaty until Armenia changes its Constitution. Baku considers the reference in its preamble to the Declaration of Independence problematic. The declaration calls for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. The new draft omits this reference. Parliament must first approve the proposal to put the draft Constitution to a referendum. At least two-thirds of MPs must vote in favour. The ruling Civil Contract party does not have enough seats to secure the required majority. It is six votes short.

Commenting on the opposition’s refusal, ruling party representative and Speaker of the National Assembly Ruben Rubinyan said that, for them, “obstructing peace matters more than removing Pashinyan from power”.

He also suggested that the opposition was seeking to “make peace impossible and incorporate Armenia into another state – the Union State of Russia and Belarus”.

Pashinyan himself describes his proposal as an unprecedented opportunity for the opposition.

He explains the opposition’s refusal by saying that “their mission is to prevent the country from achieving both peace and independence”.

Analysis

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan has outlined his views on the issue in an article titled “The new Constitution and Pashinyan’s proposal to Russia”:

“Pashinyan apparently understands that the Kremlin will make the final decision on the issue he has raised.

The proposal, made just days before three visits to Moscow scheduled for December this year, is addressed not to Armenia’s parliamentary opposition, but to the Kremlin.

The Armenian prime minister has announced that he will visit Russia on 3, 11 and 22 December. According to a preliminary agreement, Pashinyan will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on 3 December. The Armenian prime minister also said that a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, bringing together the heads of government of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), is scheduled for 11–12 December. The annual meetings of the leaders of the EAEU and Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries will take place in St Petersburg at the end of the year.

There is little doubt that Armenia’s new Constitution will be on the agenda when Pashinyan meets Putin. The draft was published ahead of the planned visits.

But under what circumstances could Pashinyan secure the six votes he needs with Russia’s help? There are two theoretical scenarios.

First, Moscow could give the green light to a constitutional referendum if the new Constitution takes Russia’s interests and demands into account.

However, the draft has already been published, and it contains provisions that are clearly problematic for Moscow. In particular, removing the reference to Armenia’s Declaration of Independence from the preamble is primarily a geopolitical issue. But another provision, which bars political parties from operating with foreign funding, would directly limit Russia’s ability to exert influence in Armenia.

Under the current Constitution, the Constitutional Court may ban only parties that have advocated violence or used it to overthrow the constitutional order. The new draft introduces the following additional grounds for banning a political party: receiving funding from foreign sources;

advocating the renunciation of state independence;

inciting ethnic or religious hatred;

taking actions that obstruct the free expression of voters’ will.

The second way to secure Moscow’s approval for the six votes needed to hold a constitutional referendum would be to reach agreements on other issues.

These could include Armenia’s railway network, the construction of a new nuclear power plant, Russia’s 102nd military base in Gyumri, Armenia’s European integration process and other matters.

In other words, if Pashinyan and Putin reach agreements on key issues, Russia could “give the green light” to a referendum on constitutional amendments. The question is whether Yerevan is prepared to pay such a price.”

Who did Pashinyan address his referendum proposal to?

World.title: Georgian Dream propaganda network ran coordinated campaign against Metropolitan Iov – ISFED
World.content:
Campaign against Metropolitan Iov in Georgia

Following a sermon that included criticism of the Georgian government, a coordinated disinformation campaign against Metropolitan Iov was launched on social media. Dozens of social media pages published posts with identical content at almost exactly the same time.

As part of the campaign, at least 20 paid s appeared on Meta platforms, generating between 77,600 and 107,180 views in total.

Pro-government media outlets, Facebook pages and individuals affiliated with Georgian Dream’s propaganda network stepped up the campaign against Metropolitan Iov following his critical sermon.

The campaign was investigated by the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED).

The organisation analysed how identical quotes targeting the metropolitan spread across dozens of pages within minutes of each other; how videos from previous years were used in a new context; and how paid advertising complemented the campaign’s organic reach.

What Iov said and why it led to a confrontation with the authorities

The confrontation followed a sermon that Metropolitan Iov delivered at Urbnisi Cathedral on 10 November. He called government officials “non-believers” and “alien to the Church”, saying that the government had exhausted its potential and that the Georgian people should choose more worthy leaders in the future.

The metropolitan criticised the Church’s dependence on state funding, saying that the authorities were trying to merge Church and state.

He also raised issues such as corruption, the prevalence of drug addiction among young people and the widespread popularity of gambling. In addition, he referred to information allegedly leaked from the State Security Service in 2021, which contained details of surveillance of members of the clergy.

In his sermon, Iov also mentioned Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the Georgian Dream party. He also referred to the previous administration, saying: “We know what the previous government was doing; everything is obvious – the people voted against it.”

Metropolitan Iov’s remarks attracted particular attention because he had previously supported Georgian Dream.

On 21 November, during another sermon, he explained that although he had supported the ruling party, he believed it had since changed course, making criticism necessary.

“I supported Georgian Dream and stood by them, but I saw that they had gone astray. The situation had changed, and it became necessary to speak out against such actions. If they put things right, take these remarks into account and bring about change in Georgia – if they change the course of these developments – I may support them again,” he said.

Metropolitan Iov was also among the candidates for the post of patriarch in May 2026. Metropolitan Shio Mujiri was elected patriarch.

Identical posts and quotes from ‘experts’

According to ISFED’s monitoring, representatives of Georgian Dream were the first to react to Metropolitan Iov’s sermon.

MP Levan Machavariani called it “irresponsible”, saying that a senior clergyman should not use the pulpit to make political statements. Meanwhile, MP Mariam Lashkhi, responding to journalists’ questions, remarked: “May God forgive him.”

Meanwhile, pro-government figures began posting their views on social media.

On 11 November, news agencies and television channels linked to Georgian Dream published the same quote from a Facebook post by Gia Abashidze. He claimed that Bishop Iov was using the church pulpit to call for a change of government.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Thirteen minutes after Abashidze’s statement, a quote from Davit Kartvelishvili was circulated. He accused the metropolitan of having links to Saakashvili’s political forces, referred to criminal cases involving the metropolitan’s diocese and raised the issue of the seizure of agricultural land.

According to ISFED, these allegations came without references to specific sources or any particular case. Nevertheless, the text appeared on 14 pages within a few hours.

Screenshots of the posts. Source: ISFED

Tamta Megrelishvili, Davit Chikhelidze and Zaal Anjaparidze also joined the campaign. In their posts, they accused Metropolitan Iov of making political statements against the government, supporting Saakashvili and taking a position that ran counter to the country’s interests.

Davit Chikhelidze even linked the metropolitan’s diocese to harbouring criminals and “gangland-style disputes”.

A fake Facebook profile also took part in the campaign

The campaign also involved a Facebook profile that Myth Detector had previously identified as fake. The account, registered under the name Ketevan Mikiashvili, published two posts targeting Bishop Iov, just a few hours apart.

In her first post, Mikiashvili addressed the metropolitan ironically, referring to the election of the new patriarch. She remarked that Bishop Iov had “dropped his mask” after Shio became patriarch. The post included an archive television report captioned “Call to release Saakashvili”.

In her second post, she shared a video recorded on 25 September 2019, titled “Bishop Iov on Petre Tsaava”, implying that the footage revealed the metropolitan’s true motives.

These posts highlighted another narrative promoted by the campaign: Bishop Iov’s criticism of the authorities was presented not as a political or ecclesiastical disagreement, but as a personal grievance stemming from his defeat in the patriarchal election.

Mikiashvili later published another post portraying Bishop Iov’s sermon as yet another attempt to stage a revolution.

Personal attacks also appeared in posts by other figures.

On 11 November, Lasha Natsvlishvili, a Georgian Dream supporter and propagandist, published a Facebook post containing insults directed at Metropolitan Iov. [Fact-checkers say Lasha Natsvlishvili is behind the fake “Ketevan Mikiashvili” profile – JAMnews].

The post prompted a strong reaction, including from members of the clergy.
