World.title: Arab and DAC development partners chart closer ties on fragile contexts, blended finance at 2026 Oslo Dialogue
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 25. Members of the Arab Coordination Group (ACG) and of the OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) met in Oslo on 24 and 25 November 2026 for the 2026 Arab-DAC Dialogue on Development. Held at a critical juncture for international development co-operation – marked by shifting geopolitical priorities, a widening financing gap for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and compounding crises – the Dialogue reaffirmed the value of a long-standing and trusted partnership, and focused on how Arab providers and DAC members can deliver more, and better, together.

The Dialogue was co-chaired by Ms Gunn Jorid Roset, Director General of the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (Norad); Mr Fawzi Yousef Alhunaif, Director General and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development (AFESD) and Chair of the ACG; and Mr Carsten Staur, Chair of the OECD DAC. Enriched by the contributions of international experts, discussions addressed two themes: the future of international development co-operation and ways of working, and scaling up blended finance for sustainable development, including in fragile contexts.

Partnerships built on horizontality and country ownership

Participants agreed on the need to build on proven models of co-operation and to work in broader partnerships to overcome the fragmentation of the development landscape. They stressed that horizontality – equal and mutually respectful relationships between partners – should lie at the core of these partnerships, together with country leadership, local ownership and alignment with national priorities.

Fragile contexts: a priority for joint engagement

Fragile contexts emerged as a key area for strengthened co-operation. Participants underlined the importance of applying development effectiveness principles in these settings, drawing on the complementary experience of Arab providers and DAC members, and of ensuring coherence across humanitarian, development and peace efforts. They exchanged views on support for recovery and reconstruction, including in the Syrian Arab Republic, and highlighted the value of information sharing, closer coordination and complementary engagement in support of ongoing international and regional initiatives. Consultations on these questions will continue.

Blended finance: from mutual learning to scale

Participants discussed how to mobilize additional and innovative resources, including private capital, while safeguarding development additionality – in areas such as youth employment and decent work, climate and infrastructure. They called for greater standardization of mobilization instruments and structures to enable scale, combined with the context-sensitive implementation that fragility demands, and for fuller use of the complementarities between development agencies, national and regional development funds, development finance institutions and multilateral development banks. Participants underlined that blended finance complements, and does not substitute for, concessional public development finance.

Participants welcomed the continuation and expansion of mutual learning under the Arab-DAC Partnership on Blended Finance for Sustainable Development, and expressed openness to further practical collaboration, including through joint blended finance country platforms, country policy dialogues, capacity-building workshops and joint participation in high-level events.

World.title: Iran spends $150B annually on energy consumption - Pezeshkian
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 25. The costs of energy consumption are very high in Iran, with about $150 billion spent per year, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said.

According to the Iranian president’s official information portal, he made the remarks on Wednesday, November 25, at Ferdowsi University in Mashhad city, in the northeastern Razavi Khorasan Province.

"Even saving just 10% of these funds could make it possible to allocate substantial resources to improving public welfare and addressing the country's problems," he noted.

Pezeshkian said there is considerable potential for energy savings in the country. Changing consumption patterns could reduce energy consumption by 30-40% in certain sectors. This is because uncontrolled consumption not only depletes the country's national resources but also harms the environment.

"It is clear that the current level of government support for citizens is insufficient. Solutions must be found to increase government support. One such solution is the proper use of the country's resources, saving energy through more efficient consumption, and directing the funds saved toward improving people's living conditions. Universities can play an effective role in this regard," he noted.

Iran's annual gas production previously stood at 297 billion cubic meters. However, following the US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran, production fell to 242 billion cubic meters per year. In other words, damage to the country's infrastructure reduced annual gas production by 55 billion cubic meters.

Before the aforementioned attacks, Iran already faced an annual natural gas supply deficit of 45 billion cubic meters. Following the attacks, the country's gas deficit increased to 100 billion cubic meters per year.

World.title: Kazakhstan targets tenfold increase in freight transportation with China
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 25. Kazakhstan aims to increase freight transportation volumes with China tenfold, according to a press release from the Ministry of Transport following a meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Asel Zhanasova and a delegation from Chinese company Guo JingAn.

The meeting focused on expanding freight transportation between the two countries and developing transport infrastructure.

The parties discussed rail freight transportation between Kazakhstan and China, a proposal to build a broad-gauge railway line on Chinese territory, and the implementation of the Center-West highway project.

According to the ministry, expanding the Nur Zholy border crossing on the Chinese side is expected to increase its capacity to 1,500 trucks per day, compared with the current 800. The Chinese side is also considering extending the operating hours of the Khorgos border crossing by three hours through the end of December.

The meeting also addressed cooperation with CITIC Group on the Center-West highway project.

Zhanasova proposed establishing a distribution hub in Kazakhstan, based in Khorgos and the city of Alatau, to accelerate the delivery of Chinese goods to markets in Central Asia, the South Caucasus, Türkiye, Iran, and Pakistan. She also proposed setting up Chinese laboratories in Kazakhstan to certify agricultural products.

The parties agreed to establish rapid-response working groups and continue developing specific proposals.

World.title: Libya vows retaliation over Ukrainian strikes as Russian deaths near 500,000
World.content:
Ukraine has defended its right to self-defence after launching a series of lethal air strikes on Russian ships in Libya as the deadly conflict threatens to escalate beyond eastern Europe.

Two Libyan army personnel have since died from wounds sustained in Sunday's drone attacks that sunk a Russian ship and damaged another at the Benghazi naval base in the country's east.

The Libyan National Army (LNA), which controls the country's eastern portion and has ties to Russia, has threatened to retaliate over the strikes.

Meanwhile, leaked data has shed light on the extent of Russia's losses in Ukraine, with Russian government statistics revealing nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers have died fighting on the frontline since 2022, the BBC and The Guardian have reported.

It comes as both countries traded a fresh wave of drone strikes on Tuesday night that targeted energy infrastructure and caused widespread power outages.

Libya threatens to respond

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said both Russian vessels, a navy corvette and a cargo ship transporting military equipment, were valid targets and Sunday's operation embodied a legitimate act of self-defence.

Loading...

"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Mr Sybiha said on the Telegram messaging app.

"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasise that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people."

He said international law did not limit the right to self-defence to the territory where the aggression takes place, but could also be exercised on the territory of the aggressor or in international waters.

The naval attacks caused concern at the United Nations mission in Libya, which warned against turning the country, still recovering from civil war, into a "battleground for foreign conflicts".

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani also expressed concern about exporting the conflict to "just a few kilometres from Italy's coastline", while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot backed Ukraine in its "absolute right to self-defence".

The LNA command confirmed on Tuesday that two of its military personnel had succumbed to wounds sustained in the attack. In a statement, the LNA said its response to the strike would come "at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means".

The Libyan strikes came just days after Kyiv attacked a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. (Reuters/Finnish Border Guard)

Norway has also urged caution after Ukrainian drones attacked a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.

"All attacks would stop immediately if Russia stopped this war," Norwegian Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said.

"That said, we are focused on the fact that Ukraine must do this [these actions] within the rules of international law. So we take this matter up with them."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the operation had struck a legitimate military target.

"Every vessel with a Russian flag, everything that carries weapons or any sanctioned cargo that can carry God knows what, it is a legitimate target for us in Russian territorial or neutral waters," he told Bloomberg.

Close to 500,000 Russians killed in war, data shows

Leaked data from Russia's statistics agency has revealed nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The numbers, leaked by hackers in September and analysed by the BBC and The Guardian, vastly surpass previous estimates and do not account for soldiers declared missing.

It paints a picture of a war which has grown increasingly deadly.

According to The Guardian, Russia recorded nearly 20,000 military deaths in the war's first year, and 50,000 in 2023. The toll hit more than 134,000 in 2024, and rose further to almost 200,000 in 2025 in what was the deadliest year of the war so far.

Ukraine's military losses are estimated at around 115,000 since 2022 with 105,000 missing, according to the online UA losses project.

Fresh wave of strikes cause sweeping power outages

Ukraine and Russia carried out a series of drone strikes on Tuesday night targeting energy and industrial infrastructure in both countries.

Ukraine's Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said Russian strikes caused overnight power outages in five regions, including Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and Kharkiv.

Ukraine's access to Starlink communications disrupted again Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service is affecting the Ukrainian front line.

The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant lost external power for the 17th time this year and switched to diesel generators, Mr Nekrasov said.

In Russia's Samara region, industrial facilities also came under attack with a Ukrainian drone strike killing one and triggering power cuts.

Regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said air defence forces downed 145 Ukrainian drones overnight. Unverified reports suggested two oil refineries were the subjects of the attack.

ABC/Reuters/AFP

World.title: Video shows harrowing moments in lead-up to electric motorbike death
World.content:
Shocking aerial footage has been released to the public for the first time, showing the lead-up to the death of a woman who was fatally struck by an electric motorbike in a suburban Perth park.

WARNING: The following story contains details and vision that may distress some readers.

The video was shown in the Perth Children's Court during the trial of a teenager who was allegedly riding the motorbike in an Edgewater park in July last year when he collided with 59-year-old nurse Shelley Spinks.

Ms Spinks was taken to Joondalup Hospital, but died from her injuries.

The teenager, who cannot be identified as he was 17 at the time of the incident, has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter.

Loading...

The 25-minute clip shows the teen riding at speed through suburban streets, veering onto the wrong side of the road and narrowly avoiding other vehicles, before cutting across a park.

At several points, he mounts footpaths while continuing to ride at speed and rides close to a group of pedestrians.

At 2:40pm the vision shows the teen veering across the road and into Picnic Cove Park, and two minutes later his motorbike can be seen lying on its side, as Ms Spinks lies on the grass near a footpath.

The teen was seen riding on the wrong side of the road. (Supplied: Perth Children's Court)

The moment of impact was obscured from the police camera vehicle by trees in the park.

A police officer is then seen approaching the teen, while several bystanders tend to Ms Spinks and call for help.

Police officer Alessandro Caratozzolo gave evidence in the trial and said he was riding his police motorcycle when he first came across the teenager.

Officer Caratozzolo said the accused flipped him "the bird" in a car park, which he told the court was a "clear gesture."

The court heard that the police officer later arrested the motorbike rider, and his body-worn video was played to the court.

The 17-year-old accused can be heard repeatedly asking in the video, "Why'd she jump in front of me?" and "Will she be okay?"

As the footage was played in court, the accused and his family were visibly emotional.

Earlier in the day, the court heard from witnesses who saw the boy riding his bike before the collision.

What is the difference between an e-bike and an e-motorbike? If you're bamboozled by the talk of e-bikes, e-motorbikes and rules around them, you're not alone. Here's what each jurisdiction says about them.

Linda Hughes told the court she was walking two dogs with her partner when she saw a bike in the park travelling with "astonishing speed".

Ms Hughes said her partner Mario Geisner ran to the scene to give first aid to a woman.

Her partner also gave evidence and said he heard the motorbike first, describing it as "so quick".

Another witness, Julian Harris, told the court he had been jogging in Picnic Cove Park before the fatality.

After hearing a police helicopter, Mr Harris said he then heard the sound of a motorbike.

Mr Harris said the motorbike was travelling "quite fast".

"I was quite worried that it was going to hit someone," he said.

In his opening address, defence lawyer Simon Watters said the footage showed the teenager was "in control of his bike throughout the pursuit" and that he was "seeking to avoid the deceased" at the time of impact.

The trial continues.

World.title: Police confirm no sign of kitesurfer missing off WA's north west coast
World.content:
The search for a 62-year-old kitesurfer missing off Western Australia's north west coast will resume on Thursday, with no sign of the man a day after he disappeared.

Eric Metrot was last seen near Five Finger Reef, just outside Coral Bay and about 1,000 kilometres north of Perth, on Tuesday afternoon.

Authorities were notified of his disappearance just after 8:40pm, and the search got underway shortly after.

Eric Metrot went kitesurfing near Five Finger Reef. (Supplied: WA Police)

Mr Metrot's kite was found washed up on a reef earlier on Wednesday, but no other signs of him have been found after he failed to return.

Pilbara Police Sergeant Danny Richmond said the kite was found on Wednesday morning stuck on a reef, with the assumption it had washed ashore.

He said the co-ordinated search would resume on Thursday morning, prioritising areas along the shore near where the kite was found.

Danny Richmond says the search for Eric Metrot will resume on Thursday. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"I am always hopeful that we find people in distress, always hopeful," Sergeant Richmond said.

"At some stage we have to be realistic, and sometimes it gets to a stage where it's beyond anything more than a recovery.

Various groups, including the police air wing, water police and volunteer marine rescue crews, are involved in the search. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"But at this stage I'm treating it as a search and rescue."

Divers were part of the coordinated search. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

The Australian Maritime Safety Authority is also assisting with the search and spotted Mr Metrot's kite.

The 62-year-old was last seen wearing a blue rash vest and board shorts.

He is about 182 centimetres tall, of medium build, with short brown hair and eyes.

Anyone with information is urged to contact police on 131 444.

World.title: Indigenous groups alarmed as NT flags fresh child protection overhaul
World.content:
The Northern Territory is considering further child protection changes that would limit judicial oversight of care arrangements and give child protection workers the ability to issue domestic violence orders, the ABC can reveal.

Other proposals, outlined in a consultation paper, include moves to establish a pathway for the permanent adoption of children in care.

Indigenous groups told the ABC they hold grave fears the changes will make family reunifications for Aboriginal families in the out-of-home care system more difficult.

The paper outlined "several possible reform options" for stakeholder feedback but said these were not settled government policy.

They included:

removing the courts' ability to make orders requiring the Department of Children and Families (DCF) to facilitate family contact, visits to community and kinship assessments;

preventing family from proposing an alternative carer for their child in court proceedings, leaving that solely to DCF;

lowering the threshold for courts to grant long-term parental responsibility to non-family or non-kinship carers;

allowing DCF child protection workers to issue interim Domestic Violence Orders, a power currently held only by police; and

establishing a specific pathway for permanent carers to apply to adopt a child after a minimum period of time.

Several organisations told the ABC they only received the consultation paper on Tuesday, with a deadline for response by Sunday.

The DCF's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot told the ABC targeted consultation was underway with stakeholders who bring specialist knowledge and cultural expertise.

"The consultation process provides the appropriate forum for stakeholders to raise concerns about the proposed reforms, which we will carefully consider as we determine whether and how any legislative changes progress," she said in a statement.

Minister Robyn Cahill says the first tranche of reforms made child safety the 'front and centre principle'. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Limiting judicial powers

The consultation paper said courts were currently making broad orders directing DCF to do things which were "impractical, and impose significant logistical, human and financial resource burdens on DCF".

It gave examples of court orders that required DCF to ensure children have regular visits with their parents or their grandparents, fund a child's travel to their home community or order particular kinship assessments.

Cindy Torrens, a Warlmanpa and Wambaya woman, said these orders were "really critical when we're needing to think about keeping kids connected to family".

The DCF paper suggested removing or limiting these powers, so that courts would only be able to make directions about services and supports for the child, but not their placement or contact arrangements.

The paper also suggested changes so that only DCF, and not family, could propose to the court which person should be given daily care and control or parental responsibility for the child.

"Restricting the ability to formally put forward alternative carers in child protection proceedings further limits options for families to keep kids within their family groups," Ms Torrens said.

"You're taking Aboriginal kids away from the people who love them and putting them with people who've got no biological connection to them."

The paper also proposed lowering the threshold for courts to grant long-term parental responsibility to non-family or non-kinship carers.

It said courts have interpreted the law to mean they should only grant this when they are satisfied "there would never be a time when a parent would be better suited to exercise parental responsibility".

Instead, it suggested this test be lowered so courts only need to be satisfied "there is no other person better suited to exercise that responsibility at the time".

Ms Torrens said such a change would create enormous pressure on parents hoping to be reunited with their children.

"Keeping kids for Aboriginal families feels like it's going to be almost impossible with these changes and I think that's the whole plan, the whole idea," she said.

"Even more frightening … is that we know that the government isn't set up for these changes.

"So [they're] taking kids away from family and putting them into a system that's not established, not culturally safe, not ready for them."

Caitlin Wetherby-Fell says the government has not allowed enough time for meaningful consultation. (ABC RN: Kristina Kukolja)

'Significant expansion of power'

Authorised child protection officers would be given the power to issue interim domestic violence orders (DVOs), similar to those issued by police, according to one option put forward.

The DCF acknowledged this would represent a "significant expansion of power … including the ability to impose immediate restrictions on a person without a court order first being made".

Caitlin Weatherby-Fell, CEO of the Top End Women's Legal Service, said child protection workers were not adequately trained to make these assessments.

"Our fear here is that introducing another player to make a DVO is going to overburden our court system and be contrary to victim survivors' needs and wants," she said.

"We have presentations every day where police have taken out a DVO and it is not right for that family … and the restrictions within it mean that the family unit is unworkable."

She said the changes could also make it harder for victims of domestic violence to seek help.

"We have real fears that parents, and particularly mothers impacted by gender-based violence, will be even more reticent [to come forward] and increasingly distrustful of authorities."

Clara Mills is concerned adoption changes could permanently break up Aboriginal families. (Supplied)

The DCF has also flagged changes to the territory's Adoption of Children Act.

It would establish a specific pathway for permanent carers to apply to adopt children who are "unable to safely return to the care of their birth parents".

The paper said a birth parent would need to consent to the adoption "unless that consent is dispensed with by the court under the existing provisions of the Act."

Clara Mills, principal lawyer at the North Australian Aboriginal Family Legal Service, said she feared it could lead to children in care being adopted against the will of their families.

"How is the court going to test whether a parent can reasonably consent when they've been excluded from their child in totality through the child protection system?" she asked.

She said such an outcome would be a "national shame" and cause intergenerational harm.

More than 800 children were in out-of-home care in the Northern Territory as of June 2025, about 90 per cent of whom are Indigenous.

Less than 18 per cent of those Indigenous children were placed with relatives or kin, according to an analysis by First Nations children's peak body SNAICC.

The NT government passed the first tranche of child protection changes in July, leading to an outcry from Indigenous groups and several high-profile resignations.

Ms Broadfoot said the government was committed to keeping children safe and strengthening the laws that protect them.

"The options being considered have been identified through reviews underway since 2025, including issues raised through stakeholder submissions and operational experience," she said.

"The consultation papers do not represent final government policy or legislative changes."

World.title: Deloitte suspended by WA government after AI report debacle
World.content:
The WA government has suspended accounting firm Deloitte from the bulk of its government work for up to three months over an AI-riddled report it produced on a controversial university merger plan.

Deloitte was enlisted to deliver a taxpayer-funded cost-benefit analysis of its proposed merger of three of the state's public universities — Curtin, Murdoch and the University of Western Australia.

But last month it was revealed that the report was littered with errors generated by artificial intelligence, prompting the government to order the firm to refund its $166,000 fee.

WA's university merger explained The University of Western Australia, Murdoch University and Curtin University could be merged under a WA government proposal. What's behind the plan, how will it work and what comes next?

Now the government has gone a step further, banning Deloitte from most government work for up to three months.

"While the errors contained in the report do not affect the modelling or the findings, they are nonetheless disappointing," a state government spokesperson said.

"The WA government had made the decision to suspend Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu from the Audit and Financial Advisory Services Common Use Arrangements and Information and Communications Technology Services Common Use Arrangements."

Minister embarrassed

The ABC understands the firm was told about the decision today.

The action follows comments from Tertiary Education Minister Tony Buti earlier this week saying the refund requested for the report had not yet been paid back.

Tony Buti says he was embarrassed by the report. (ABC News: Keane Bourke )

"We are demanding that the refund be looked at, but if that doesn't take place, there are other measures that we can put in place," Mr Buti said on Monday.

"I'm incredibly disappointed at Deloitte's [conduct] … I'm very embarrassed by what happened, but incredibly disappointed in their performance."

Mr Buti said discussions had "taken place" but noted a "satisfactory outcome" had not been reached with the firm.

Deloitte labelled the errors in the report "minor" at the time they surfaced and said they did not affect the findings of the cost-benefit analysis.

WA moves ahead with university merger plans Premier Roger Cook says a potential merger could create a "once-in-a-generation" opportunity as all three universities raise concerns about the move.

However, the firm has previously been caught using AI in consultancy reports for government.

Last year, Deloitte used AI to produce a $440,000 federal government report that contained similar errors and made-up quotes.

The firm apologised, reissued the report and has paid back nearly $100,000.

The ABC has contacted Deloitte for comment.

The government has said data from Deloitte's merger report, along with new information, will be "interrogated by the university reform business case".

Plan continues

Mr Buti has continued to pursue the proposed university merger despite concerns raised by two of three parties — Curtin and Murdoch.

Graduates' satisfaction with degrees at record lows Australian students are less satisfied with their university degrees than ever before, according to a long-running survey.

Students and staff have also been vocal in their objection, taking to the steps of parliament last month to protest.

According to the WA government website, potential benefits of the merger include "creating a globally competitive university of scale that receives more research funding, has increased domestic student numbers, higher regional representation and better course completion rates".

"We often as politicians get criticised for thinking short term," Education Minister Sabine Winton told reporters on Tuesday.

"It is energising to be part of a government that is having a long-term think around what is best for this state, and I welcome that contest of ideas."

World.title: Google faces $220m claim in Malaysia over harmful YouTube content
World.content:
Malaysia's communications regulator has filed two lawsuits against Google, seeking a combined 600 million ringgit ($240 million) in damages over its alleged failure to adequately address harmful online content.

The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) said Google had failed to adequately address content related to online gambling, scams and fraud on its YouTube platform.

It also accused the technology giant of failing to take proactive measures against content posted by a prominent Malaysian blogger.

Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Malaysia is a Muslim country where gambling is largely illegal. (Supplied: Naim Fadil)

The regulator said the damages sought reflected the substantial resources and manpower required to address more than 50,000 instances of harmful online content.

The commission is also seeking several injunctions against Google, including an order requiring the company to maintain the suspension of a YouTube account associated with blogger Wan Muhammad Azri Wan Deris, known as Papagomo or Sir Azri.

It wants Google to identify and remove similar content featuring the blogger within 24 hours, including material uploaded through third-party accounts and YouTube live streams.

The commission is also seeking interest on any damages awarded and legal costs.

Gambling is heavily restricted in Malaysia, with strict exceptions for licensed operators serving non-Muslims.

Google had recently announced major investments In Malaysia, including clean energy projects and improving water security. (AP: Matt Rourke)

The lawsuits come just weeks after Google announced it would invest 61 billion ringgit ($22.4 billion) in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028.

The investment will go towards data centre campuses, clean energy projects, improving water security and training workers.

Malaysia's government has had a rocky relationship with major social media companies, including TikTok and Facebook, accusing them of failing to remove content it considers harmful.

Australia moves to strengthen online safety laws

Communications Minister Anika Wells announced a deal had been reached with the Greens on Tuesday. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Malaysian lawsuits come as Australia moves to give individuals greater power to hold social media companies to account for harmful online content.

Labor, Coalition find common ground on AI copyright A parliamentary inquiry has backed finding a new way to compensate Australian artists for their work being used to train AI, but the music industry remains opposed to any changes.

Australia's digital duty of care legislation passed parliament on Wednesday after Labor reached a deal with the Greens on Tuesday to increase penalties for technology giants and strengthen protections for social media users.

The new laws will also give Australians a "private right of action" that will allow them to directly sue social media companies for harm suffered online.

YouTube is among the platforms subject to Australia's social media minimum age restrictions introduced last December. Companies face penalties of up to $49.5 million for failing to take reasonable steps to prevent under-16s from holding accounts.

In March, the eSafety commissioner identified YouTube as one of five social media platforms raising significant compliance concerns.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Bowen details how the words 'fossil fuels' derailed COP31
World.content:
Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen has revealed his frustrations over the outcome of COP31.

The climate negotiations in Türkiye broke down and ended without a deal after several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept a final proposal that did not mention fossil fuels.

The deal was rejected on Sunday afternoon at the summit at which Australia and Türkiye shared leadership.

In the aftermath Mr Bowen has been under attack from political rivals and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor called for Mr Bowen to resign.

Mr Bowen, speaking in his first interview since the conference, told 7.30 that the outcome of COP31 left him frustrated after Australia had spruiked plans for its own targets, including electrification.

"The COP negotiations were going quite well, then got caught up in the use of the words 'fossil fuels'," Mr Bowen told 7.30.

"Frustration [was the feeling] at that point ... and a strong degree of disappointment that we were so close, had done so much work, and an issue then arose.

"Countries dug into positions and it was very, very hard to move because of the consensus model at COP."

That consensus model means that all nations attending the climate summit have to agree on the resolution.

At COP28 that included a final deal with "historic" references to "transition away from fossil fuels", a pledge to triple renewable energy and a commitment to stop adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere by mid-century.

At COP31 that language was dropped as Mr Bowen blamed the consensus system and existing geopolitical tensions for stopping a final proposal that mentioned fossil fuels.

People attend the closing plenary at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, November 22, 2026. (Reuters: Murad Sezer)

"In our first draft decision, we did have language about transition away from fossil fuels, and a number of countries indicated we then consult with every country," Mr Bowen said.

He also said Australia wanted that language in the final agreement but existing tensions soon kicked in.

"There were some countries, EU and others who said, 'these words must be in' and Saudi Arabia said 'these words must be out'," Mr Bowen added.

"And both parties were saying, 'we will veto it if they're in or veto it if they're out'.

"That's not unusual at a COP [but] the difference this year was that countries were a lot harder to budge from their position.

"I felt a lot of geopolitical tension in the room on other issues infecting the conversation and making it so much harder to negotiate.

"The views were more dug in and dislike between parties much stronger this year than I've seen previously. "

This COP was held amid tensions in the Middle East and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.

Mr Bowen confirmed Russia played a role and was making "conservative" arguments on the issues at hand but that the negotiations went down to the wire.

Australia's 2030 target looking good

At home, the government is set to release its annual climate change statement on Thursday.

Mr Bowen was the lead negotiator at COP31. (Reuters: Murad Sezer)

Mr Bowen said Australia is meeting its carbon reduction targets for 2030, but that meeting its target of reducing emissions to 62-70 per cent below 2005 levels by 2035 remains an issue.

"[The report] will show 6.2 million tonnes of carbon reduction in the last year. Which is about 1.5 times higher than the average over the last 10 years," Mr Bowen said.

"It'll show we've also got more work to do.

"The Climate Change Authority Advice will say Australia's doing well, but needs to do better on emissions reduction.

" We've got to keep going and accelerating to meet our targets. We are largely on track for our 2030 target; we have a lot of work to do to get the 2035 target. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Cape York residents swelter through heatwaves and nightly water outages
World.content:
Remote communities at the tip of Cape York are having their water turned off overnight as reservoirs run critically low during a prolonged heatwave.

Mains water has been cut, often with only a few hours' notice, across the five communities of Queensland's Northern Peninsula Area (NPA) since early September.

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued heatwave warnings for the peninsula district for several weeks, the most recent forecasting temperatures in the low 40s and overnight minimums in the mid-20s until Friday.

Residents in the coastal NPA town of Seisia, near the northernmost point of the Cape, say the rolling restrictions are having a significant impact on their lives.

Kawia Akinsola, 45, said the outages, from 9pm to 6am on allocated days, were disrupting activities including cooking, cleaning and taking medication.

A new backup generator has ben installed at the Bamaga Water Treatment Plant to assist during power outages. (Facebook: NPARC)

The Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council (NPARC) uses its Facebook page to provide updates, but Ms Akinsola said not everyone in the communities was receiving the messages.

"Some of us, especially older people or people with disabilities, are not on social media, so they don't get told until the last minute most of the time," she said.

The raw water pond near Bamaga Water Treatment plant was 50 per cent full earlier this month. (Supplied)

"Our elders and people with disabilities don't know the water's turned off and go to the toilet and we have to wait for the next day to flush it or clean it."

She said many households were also overcrowded, and stored water could run out quickly.

According to the 2021 Census, the Peninsula region is home to about 2,800 people living in 1,090 dwellings, with residents in New Mapoon, Injinoo, Umagico, Bamaga and Seisia impacted.

The Jardine River provides the NPA's mains water. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

Critical levels

Veolia, the council's water contractor, warned in early November that storage levels at the region's reservoirs were at critically low levels after power outages disrupted pumping from the Jardine River.

The council has since installed an emergency backup generator to allow reservoirs to recharge, but it has been switching off water supplies to alternating communities overnight.

Upgrades underway

Premier David Crisafulli described the restrictions as "completely unacceptable" and said his government had invested in water pumps and pipes in New Mapoon and Bamaga.

David Crisafulli, in the Far North this week, said his government had invested in NPA water infrastructure. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

The $10 million joint federal-state Northern Peninsula Area Water Supply Project includes upgrades to the Bamaga Water Treatment Plant, increasing capacity to a proposed nine megalitres a day, replacing asbestos-cement water pipes and connecting a new water main in New Mapoon.

A spokesperson for Federal Water Minister Murray Watt said the investment would support long-term improvements to water supply infrastructure in the region.

But Cook MP David Kempton said it remained unclear whether the planned works would resolve the council's ongoing supply issues.

David Kempton says water security will be an ongoing issue for the NPA. (ABC Far North: Christopher Testa)

"That's the plan, but we don't know what the state of some of those other asbestos pipes are, but as things fail, of course, we'll fix them," he said.

The solutions

The ABC has contacted Veolia and NPARC for comment.

In March, the council's Local Resilience Action Plan identified securing a second pipeline from the Jardine River as a critical infrastructure priority. The project remains unfunded.

The council has also said it is considering a second raw water pond, estimated to cost $4 million, to increase storage capacity.

World.title: Crews battle tough conditions in race against time to save trapped miners
World.content:
WorldAsiaMining Crews battle tough conditions in race against time to save trapped miners Zach Hope and Karuni Rompies November 25, 2026 — 10:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Singapore/Jakarta: Indonesian rescuers have pulled six bodies from a flooded gold mine south of Jakarta and are struggling to reach at least 20 other fossickers who have been trapped since Monday. The abandoned mine’s terraced shaft was so narrow and slippery teams could not immediately get down oxygen tanks, according to Desiana Kartika Bahari, the head of the Jakarta branch of the nation’s search and rescue agency, BASARNAS. A rescue worker entering the narrow passage, which may stretch 100 metres below the ground. BASARNAS “We also need to bring lamps as it is very dark – and right now the rain is pouring in heavily,” she said. She said it was still unclear if diving experts would be needed from overseas, like in this year’s Laos cave rescue and the Thailand rescue of the Wild Boars youth football team in 2018.



The mine used to be operated by state-owned company PT Antam, Desiana said. The fossickers were searching for gold illegally in one of the “thousands” of closed shafts in Bogor, West Java, when the nearby Ciseureuh River overflowed. She said the shaft was possibly 100 metres deep. Rescuers are working through tough conditions. “We don’t know for sure [how many people were down the mine] but we talked to illegal miners here and they gave 26 names, so maybe there are 26 people,” she said. “We don’t know for sure because they are illegal. They are quite stubborn, these illegal miners, because they have been warned frequently for not doing what they are doing.”



Monday night and most of Tuesday went by before rescue crews from Bogor arrived and attempted to pump the water out. “In fact, they found pumps inside the pit believed to be belonging to the illegal miners. It means these people know that it is dangerous to go down there,” Desiana said. Related Article Indonesia ‘We seem to be going nowhere’: Indonesian president is losing his people A press release from BASARNAS on Wednesday said three bodies were recovered earlier in the afternoon at a depth of between 30 and 40 metres. World.title: One of 2026’s best openings is from two chefs you’ve never heard of
World.content:
Eating outFood One of 2026’s best openings is from two chefs you’ve never heard of They’ve worked at Honto, The Lodge and Bentley Group, among many others. Now they’re bringing all that experience to bear in an unexpected northside spot. Matt Shea November 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Don’t know of Burak Cakir and Inal Erdener? You probably need to. If you ask where these two chefs emerged from, the pithy answer would be Turkey. But what you’re asking, of course, is where have they’ve worked – and that’s because their work at Lokanta is very, very impressive. Lokanta launched in Albion in mid-October. Markus Ravik Lokanta launched in mid-October – launched as opposed to opened because this is a continuation of Olive Thyme, which existed in the 293 Sandgate Road space for eight years, and which Cakir and Erdener bought in July. But the two chefs, over three months, have completely reworked the restaurant and its menus – the rebranding was simply the final step. Cakir and Erdener both earned a reputation in Sydney working for Efendy Group: Cakir for Efendy Restaurant and Erdener for Anason. Their respective moves to Brisbane began when Cakir took a job at Honto in 2021, becoming part of a Jake Pregnell-led kitchen team that helped that restaurant hit its post-pandemic stride.



Related Article Red Hill welcomes one of Brisbane’s most exciting new restaurants “They offered me sponsorship at Honto because at that time, they wanted to do yakitori and I’m Turkish. I know barbecue charcoal,” he says, laughing. “I said, ‘after permanent residence, straight away I’m quitting. I don’t want any more hospitality.’ And the day I received my visa, I said, ‘thank you so much’.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up But Cakir did do more hospitality, most notably pop-ups at Niky in Newstead and BNE Baracca in Tarragindi. Meanwhile, Erdener followed Cakir from Sydney, leaving high-end Bentley Group to take a sous chef position at The Lodge on James Street for two years underneath Matt Lambert and James Evangelinos. The dining room recalls Olive Thyme but Lokanta is a different beast. Markus Ravik It was through BNE Baracca owner Umut Gunday that the two chefs found out Olive Thyme was on the market. On first pass, the 100-seat venue scanned as too large for their needs, but the offer was ultimately too good to pass up, Cakir says.



Lokanta’s fitout is a simple evolution on Olive Thyme, with new paint outside, and a rearranged kitchen with barbecue charcoal added to the mix. Light fittings have been changed, and the linen removed from the tables, the timber of the furnishings and the heritage-listed Albion Building’s floorboards now accounting for much of the charm. Co-owner and chef Inal Erdener in Lokanta’s open kitchen. Markus Ravik It makes for an amiable setting to share a plate or four or five, the venue’s large bay windows enabling it to commune with the street life outside. Cakir may still be in restaurants, but he’s moved away from back-of-house to run the floor, while Erdener oversees the food menu, which is anchored in Turkish cuisine, but includes broader Levantine and Mediterranean inspirations and goes large on plant-based dishes. Ora King salmon pastirma served with pickled onions and chilli oil. Markus Ravik



Expect things to continually evolve, but you might order smoked pork sausage with a Turkish tomato ezme; charred cabbage with Moroccan harissa and coriander; or a salmon pastirma served with pickled onions and chilli oil that Cakir and Erdener are particularly proud of. “We apply the salt, hang it, marinate it with fenugreek, hang it again,” Erdener says. “It takes five days, six days. We say it’s Mediterranean but we’re using Ora King salmon [from New Zealand].” Heirloom tomatoes with ricotta cream and shallot oil. Markus Ravik Larger plates include beef manti with garlic yoghurt and a fermented chilli sauce; chicken shish served with a tomato risoni, smoked labneh and pickles; and slow-cooked lamb shoulder with a zhoug salsa and jus. For drinks, there’s a tight wine list that roams across Australasia, Europe and Anatolia, with most drops available by the glass to keep it local friendly. There’s also a Mediterranean and Middle Eastern-inflected cocktail list, and a short raki menu.



Slow-Cooked lamb shoulder with zhoug salsa and jus. Markus Ravik The transition from Olive Thyme means Lokanta has flown under the radar slightly since the rebrand, but this is a restaurant that deserves the city’s attention – not just Albion’s – even if it’s yet another ambitious, locally angled venue in the broad approach of Red Hill’s Sofia (which opened earlier this month) and Pici in New Farm (which opens any day now), among many others. “People are always wary of change,” Cakir says. “But after trying the food, almost everyone leaves happy.” Lokanta occupies two original tenancies at the northern end of the heritage-listed Albion Building. Markus Ravik “And we saw at Ruby’s Wine Shop next door that there are plenty of young people who have moved to the area,” Erdener adds. “It was just about making the right moves to get them to come into the restaurant.”



Open Tue-Wed 5pm-9pm, Thu-Sun 12pm-3pm, 5pm-9pm 293 Sandgate Road, Albion, (07) 3862 4599 lokanta.au

World.title: Police confirm body found in Albion is missing Perth man
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Police confirm body found in Albion is missing Perth man Louise Harris November 25, 2026 — 9:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A “deeply loved” Perth man missing for almost two weeks has been found dead in Brisbane, but police are not treating his death as suspicious. Simon Thuijs was last seen leaving a Brisbane hospital on November 14, after flying in from Perth five days earlier. Queensland Police confirmed late on Wednesday that a body found in the inner-Brisbane suburb of Albion last Thursday was that of Thuijs. Simon Thuijs (right) with partner Agustin Garcia Haag. Facebook The 32-year-old’s family also posted a message to Facebook confirming his death.



“It is with a profound sense of loss and sadness we share with you that our much loved partner, son, brother and uncle, Simon Thuijs, has passed away following a tragic accident,” the post reads. “We take comfort in knowing that Simon was so deeply loved, that his life touched so many people, and that the memories we share will remain with us always.” Thuijs, who worked as an AI behavioural experience specialist for mining giant BHP, had travelled to Brisbane for a work conference. He was due to return to Perth on November 13, but missed his flight after suffering a medical episode in the hotel where he was staying in the CBD. He was taken by ambulance to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital and discharged about 11pm the same day.



He returned to the RBWH the following morning and left about an hour later. He did not take a backpack containing his phone, laptop and wallet with him, and had not been seen or heard from since. His partner, Agustin Garcia Haag, said he last heard from Thuijs on the day he first went to hospital, when he received a text that read “love you lots”. Simon Thuijs, whose body was found in Albion last week. Facebook Haag, who flew to Brisbane with Thuijs’s parents to search for him, previously said they were worried he may have become disoriented because he did not know Brisbane. He also said he didn’t have access to his medication. During the search, Haag said the response from locals and businesses had been overwhelming, with people displaying flyers and sharing appeals across social media.



In their Facebook post, the family thanked Queensland Police and all those who helped in the search “and held us in your thoughts this past week”. “Please know we are truly grateful and deeply humbled by your outpouring of love, care and concern.” Police are preparing a report for the coroner. London: British police have charged two men with trespassing and intention to steal at the country home of the Prince and Princess of Wales after finding intruders at the property. Officers rushed to the home on Monday night (early on Tuesday morning, AEDT) to deploy drones, rescue dogs and a police helicopter to find and detain the suspects, who are believed to be Albanian. Police are investigating a break-in at the family’s country home, Anmer Hall, in Sandringham. The alleged break-in took place at Anmer Hall on the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England. The Norfolk Constabulary said they had charged the two men with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site.



The police named the men as Mirgen Doku, 34, of Courtfield Gardens in London, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, of no fixed address. Prince William, Princess Catherine and their children were not in the home at the time of the alleged incident, as their main residence is Forest Lodge, near Windsor Castle, west of London. Norfolk Constabulary said in a statement that police were called to the estate just before 6pm on Monday (5am on Tuesday, AEDT) following a report of suspicious activity. The police named the men arrested shortly before 10am on Wednesday (9pm on Wednesday, AEDT). “Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area,” the police said.



“Two men were arrested on the estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass. They remain in police custody.” The Sun newspaper reported the two men were Albanian nationals and that one of them had made a claim for asylum that had lapsed. Anmer Hall is a 10-bedroom house on the Sandringham estate, given to William and Catherine as a wedding gift by the late Queen Elizabeth II. King Charles was photographed driving past Anmer Hall with an aide on Tuesday. The break-in heightens concerns about royal security after a series of recent incidents.



Related Article Catherine, Princess of Wales Princess of Wales opens up about cancer treatment in new documentary A 39-year-old man was sentenced to 32 weeks in prison this year after twice breaking into the grounds of Kensington Palace. In 2024, intruders entered Windsor Castle grounds and stole two farm vehicles. A man wielding a crossbow climbed a fence at Windsor Castle in 2021 and made threats to the life of Queen Elizabeth. The man, Jaswant Singh Chail, 21, was later convicted of treason and sentenced to nine years in prison. An incident at Sandringham earlier this year highlighted the risks to the royal grounds. Police arrested a man after Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former Duke of York, was allegedly threatened near his home on the royal estate in May.



Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, have been seeking greater security from British authorities since moving back to the UK earlier this year. Kensington Palace, the official base for the Prince and Princess of Wales, does not comment on security arrangements. Prince visits Downing Street News of the intrusion came as William made a rare visit to No 10 Downing Street to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at his office in the heart of London. Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with Prince William after a meeting at 10 Downing Street. Getty Images

World.content:

“Discussions about when certain shopping bags were used as status symbols (C8), reminds me of an article I read, while scrolling through old newspaper archives, about the humble string bag being referred to as ‘the symbol of feminine bondage in Australia’ by the US Consul at a NSW Agricultural Bureau conference in 1950,” writes Mary Carde of Parrearra (Qld). “Worse still, was the panic they caused on the tram, when they became hooked on a button, which was not yours, but a man’s trouser button and your stop was coming up!”

“Having been swotted numerous times by leather strap-wielding Jesuits for not cleaning my shoes at Perth’s St Louis School, instead of rebelling after graduating and favouring dirty footwear, I still zealously polish them to a mirror shine, says Greg Flynn of Turramurra. “I’m worried this makes me the poster boy for corporal punishment.”

Ball tampering (C8) is a balls-up, according to Col Burns of Lugarno: “Oh what we 1970s schoolboys wouldn’t have given for a real ‘six-stitcher’. Andrew Cohen would’ve bagged a ‘six-for’ every innings had he been afforded the privilege of bowling a chipped five-match-old ‘cork’ ball on an uneven coir mat pitch. Even my wayward ‘donkey-drops’ once got me two wickets in an over, albeit alongside three wides and two no-balls.”

For Noel Birrell of Dundas Valley, “the West Ryde Rovers C grade of 1980 figured out the best way to rough up the ball, although not always to our advantage. The trick was to make the opposing batters hit sixes onto the adjoining road. By the time the batter was worn out (and had scored a million) the ball was scuffed enough for our seamers to take over. Needless to say chasing 500 runs in a one-dayer was well beyond our capabilities, but we didn’t bend the rules.”

Lindy Babb of Colo Vale remembers pulling out all the stops for the Princess Royal (C8): “I was probably at the same 1970 event as Wendy Bull. Staff at the General Assembly Library, of whom I was one, were seconded to serve sandwiches. Being pre cling-wrap days, tinned spaghetti sandwiches were covered with damp tea towels to preserve freshness.”

World.title: Victorian hot seats: Terrifying incident at his front door convinced a police officer to enter politics
World.content:
When masked intruders tried to break into Paul Pribilovics’ family home last year, the veteran police officer decided something needed to change.

“We had a few people dressed in hoodies and masked up, carrying torches and trying to get in the front,” he tells me. “It was a scary moment for the family. That’s what inspired me.”

And so after three decades on the force, Pribilovics took leave from Victoria Police to contest the seat of Hawthorn for One Nation, attributing crime as the catalyst for his candidacy.

World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes in which to work from home Shona Hendley November 25, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Since the pandemic, working from home has become the norm for many employees, with some working full-time from home offices and others taking a hybrid approach. Whether you’re working or studying, having the right set-up is key. A dedicated space with few distractions, good lighting, reliable connectivity, ergonomic comfort, and room to store any resources or equipment is essential. Here are five of our luxury homes in which to work from home that are on the market. 4 Linlithgow Road, Toorak, Vic



Created by Melbourne design royalty Christopher Doyle, Davies Henderson and Paul Bangay, this impressive Toorak residence features a home office fit for royalty. With a built-in bookshelf that is not only practical but also makes an interesting visual feature for any Zoom call, a desk, hardwood floors, an arched window and a grand piano, the room offers a stylish space for working from home. Located on Linlithgow Road, the home also features a private cinema, full-scale entertaining areas, a gym, two additional bedrooms, and turnstile parking for six cars. This luxurious residence has a price guide of $28 million to $30 million. 14 Weeroona Avenue, Woollahra, NSW



This grand Tudor Revival residence in Woollahra includes a study with lots of period charm. A large bay window features a built-in seat overlooking greenery. The room has high ceilings, a split system, a lounge area, a built-in desk and shelving, and abundant natural light. Other highlights include a dedicated wellness zone with a hot tub, sauna and cold plunge, as well as a custom-designed children’s playhouse with its own climbing wall. 6 Mary Street, St Kilda West, Vic



Set over two levels, “Lady of St Kilda” is an Edwardian home renovated by Bojan Simic Architecture. The result is a blend of original period features, such as fireplaces and leadlight windows, and contemporary additions, including the home office, which is located on the first floor. The room features a large built-in desk with seating for two and sits in a quiet corner of the home. Other highlights include the dramatic central void, designer lighting and a stone kitchen that connects to the outdoors through oversized dual sliding doors to an al fresco deck, framed by bespoke perforated screens and deep, private gardens.



House 6, 161 Raglan Street, Mosman, NSW The upper level of this two-storey Mosman home features four bedrooms, two with their own balconies, and a study. The study includes dual desks, built-in shelving and cupboards, making it an ideal spot to work from home, study or for multiple family members to work side-by-side. Located in the gated Tregoyd Estate on Balmoral Slopes, the freestanding Torrens Title home features a Hamptons-style interior and a tropical garden.



The property includes access to a swimming pool, a tennis/pickleball court and a rainforest walkway. 93 Macquarie Street, Teneriffe, QLD The largest of the Catalina homes, the residence was originally conceptualised by Hong Kong- and Southern China-based architect Wilfred Wong. The three-level home includes an impressive library with built-in shelving, cupboards and a desk.



With enough room for a lounge and plenty of natural light through the windows, you can kick back and relax after a long day of working from home. It features panoramic views across the Brisbane River towards Hawthorne and Hamilton, plus a 976-bottle temperature-controlled wine cellar and, outdoors, a 25-metre heated swimming pool.

World.title: 74 lashes for a woman in Iran who dared to sing without a hijab
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIran 74 lashes for a woman in Iran who dared to sing without a hijab Ephrat Livni and Leily Nikounazar November 25, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

An Iranian woman received 74 lashes this week for singing publicly in 2024 without a mandatory hijab, according to her lawyer in comments to an Iranian news outlet. The singer, Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, had performed without her hair or shoulders covered in a video that spread quickly online and drew the ire of Iranian authorities, who mandate that women must wear a veil in public. Singing by women is also highly restricted in Iran, and they are banned from singing solo in public. A screenshot from YouTube of a performance by Parastoo Ahmadi. Internet Ahmadi and four others connected with the performance appeared at the prosecutor’s office in the city of Qom, where they were lashed, Ahmadi’s lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the news outlet, Emtedad, on Monday. They were also banned from performing for two years and from leaving Iran during that time. A person in Tehran familiar with Ahmadi’s case, speaking on the condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the Iranian government, confirmed that she had received the lashes.



Ahmadi’s performance in 2024 was at a historic site in Qom. There was no audience, but it was shown live online in what she called an “imaginary concert” in the post of the livestream. The video of the event reached 3.3 million viewers. Related Article Analysis

Middle East tensions ‘Biggest moment in Iran since 1979’: World on edge as protests grow Wearing a long, black gown, Ahmadi sang Iranian folk songs. “I am Parastoo, a girl who wants to sing for the people I love,” she wrote in a caption with the post. “This is a right I could not ignore, singing for the land I love passionately.” The initial ruling, issued in June, sentenced Ahmadi and eight others involved with the concert to flogging. It was unclear if the others would be flogged at a later date or had already received their penalties. News outlets affiliated with the government have reported that Ahmadi and her colleagues were accused of “offending public decency” and of failing to adhere to legal and cultural norms.



Ahmadi’s punishment, nearly two years after her performance, comes amid an ongoing government crackdown against dissent. “What used to lead to international outrage, now it barely registers because of attention on the war.” Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights. Authorities brutally suppressed mass protests in January, killing thousands of demonstrators, according to human rights groups. Iran has continued to execute and arrest dissidents in the months since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. The war has reduced the political cost of repression for the Islamic Republic, said Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, a nonprofit in Norway. “What used to lead to international outrage, now it barely registers because of attention on the war,” he said. Women in Iran can be arrested or whipped for not donning the hijab, as Ahmadi’s case showed, but unveiled women are nonetheless seen throughout the country. In 2022, Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died in police custody after being arrested on grounds of breaking modesty laws involving the hijab.



Her death prompted nationwide protests that were called the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement. Since then, many more women have chosen to ignore the hijab rule. Unveiled women have even been seen on Iranian state media and at pro-government rallies amid the war. But Amiry-Moghaddam said that Ahmadi had pushed the boundaries, going further than just flouting the hijab rules, by demanding recognition of fundamental rights. He said that her punishment was part of a broader campaign to spread fear and deter others who were tempted to follow in her footsteps. “The main threat to the Islamic Republic doesn’t come from the United States or Israel,” he said. “It comes from young Iranians who want fundamental change, and that’s why what Parastoo does, as peaceful as it seems, it’s regarded as dangerous.” Loading Suppression of cultural expression has escalated in recent months, according to the Centre for Human Rights in Iran, a nonprofit in New York.



Related Article Opinion

Prisons When I was behind bars, time stopped. But you could never hide from the new year Kylie Moore-Gilbert Political scientist and writer The group last month called on governments and the United Nations to pressure Iran by demanding the release of cultural figures being held for their expression and urging an end to corporal punishment such as flogging. The group highlighted the cases of about eight cultural figures in Iran who had been arrested, detained incommunicado, prosecuted or imprisoned for songs, poems, paintings, books or social media posts in September and October alone. The group also noted that Ahmadi’s conviction, and those of eight musicians and crew members who participated in the virtual concert with her, were upheld by an appeals court in Qom in September. “These arrests must be understood as part of the broader and increasingly violent campaign of repression in Iran, aimed at silencing dissent and intimidating entire communities,” said Esfandiar Aban, director of research at the centre.



Yeganeh Torbati contributed reporting. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

Singapore/Jakarta: Indonesian rescuers have pulled six bodies from a flooded gold mine south of Jakarta and are struggling to reach at least 20 other fossickers who have been trapped since Monday. The abandoned mine’s terraced shaft was so narrow and slippery teams could not immediately get down oxygen tanks, according to Desiana Kartika Bahari, the head of the Jakarta branch of the nation’s search and rescue agency, BASARNAS. A rescue worker entering the narrow passage, which may stretch 100 metres below the ground. BASARNAS “We also need to bring lamps as it is very dark – and right now the rain is pouring in heavily,” she said. She said it was still unclear if diving experts would be needed from overseas, like in this year’s Laos cave rescue and the Thailand rescue of the Wild Boars youth football team in 2018.



The mine used to be operated by state-owned company PT Antam, Desiana said. The fossickers were searching for gold illegally in one of the “thousands” of closed shafts in Bogor, West Java, when the nearby Ciseureuh River overflowed. She said the shaft was possibly 100 metres deep. Rescuers are working through tough conditions. “We don’t know for sure [how many people were down the mine] but we talked to illegal miners here and they gave 26 names, so maybe there are 26 people,” she said. “We don’t know for sure because they are illegal. They are quite stubborn, these illegal miners, because they have been warned frequently for not doing what they are doing.”



Monday night and most of Tuesday went by before rescue crews from Bogor arrived and attempted to pump the water out. “In fact, they found pumps inside the pit believed to be belonging to the illegal miners. It means these people know that it is dangerous to go down there,” Desiana said. Expect things to continually evolve, but you might order smoked pork sausage with a Turkish tomato ezme; charred cabbage with Moroccan harissa and coriander; or a salmon pastirma served with pickled onions and chilli oil that Cakir and Erdener are particularly proud of. “We apply the salt, hang it, marinate it with fenugreek, hang it again,” Erdener says. “It takes five days, six days. We say it’s Mediterranean but we’re using Ora King salmon [from New Zealand].” Heirloom tomatoes with ricotta cream and shallot oil. Markus Ravik Larger plates include beef manti with garlic yoghurt and a fermented chilli sauce; chicken shish served with a tomato risoni, smoked labneh and pickles; and slow-cooked lamb shoulder with a zhoug salsa and jus. For drinks, there’s a tight wine list that roams across Australasia, Europe and Anatolia, with most drops available by the glass to keep it local friendly. There’s also a Mediterranean and Middle Eastern-inflected cocktail list, and a short raki menu.



Slow-Cooked lamb shoulder with zhoug salsa and jus. Markus Ravik The transition from Olive Thyme means Lokanta has flown under the radar slightly since the rebrand, but this is a restaurant that deserves the city’s attention – not just Albion’s – even if it’s yet another ambitious, locally angled venue in the broad approach of Red Hill’s Sofia (which opened earlier this month) and Pici in New Farm (which opens any day now), among many others. “People are always wary of change,” Cakir says. “But after trying the food, almost everyone leaves happy.” Lokanta occupies two original tenancies at the northern end of the heritage-listed Albion Building. Markus Ravik “And we saw at Ruby’s Wine Shop next door that there are plenty of young people who have moved to the area,” Erdener adds. “It was just about making the right moves to get them to come into the restaurant.”



Open Tue-Wed 5pm-9pm, Thu-Sun 12pm-3pm, 5pm-9pm 293 Sandgate Road, Albion, (07) 3862 4599 lokanta.au

World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Police confirm body found in Albion is missing Perth man Louise Harris November 25, 2026 — 9:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A “deeply loved” Perth man missing for almost two weeks has been found dead in Brisbane, but police are not treating his death as suspicious. Simon Thuijs was last seen leaving a Brisbane hospital on November 14, after flying in from Perth five days earlier. Queensland Police confirmed late on Wednesday that a body found in the inner-Brisbane suburb of Albion last Thursday was that of Thuijs. Simon Thuijs (right) with partner Agustin Garcia Haag. Facebook The 32-year-old’s family also posted a message to Facebook confirming his death.



“It is with a profound sense of loss and sadness we share with you that our much loved partner, son, brother and uncle, Simon Thuijs, has passed away following a tragic accident,” the post reads. “We take comfort in knowing that Simon was so deeply loved, that his life touched so many people, and that the memories we share will remain with us always.” Thuijs, who worked as an AI behavioural experience specialist for mining giant BHP, had travelled to Brisbane for a work conference. He was due to return to Perth on November 13, but missed his flight after suffering a medical episode in the hotel where he was staying in the CBD. He was taken by ambulance to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital and discharged about 11pm the same day.



He returned to the RBWH the following morning and left about an hour later. He did not take a backpack containing his phone, laptop and wallet with him, and had not been seen or heard from since. His partner, Agustin Garcia Haag, said he last heard from Thuijs on the day he first went to hospital, when he received a text that read “love you lots”. Simon Thuijs, whose body was found in Albion last week. Facebook Haag, who flew to Brisbane with Thuijs’s parents to search for him, previously said they were worried he may have become disoriented because he did not know Brisbane. He also said he didn’t have access to his medication. During the search, Haag said the response from locals and businesses had been overwhelming, with people displaying flyers and sharing appeals across social media.



In their Facebook post, the family thanked Queensland Police and all those who helped in the search “and held us in your thoughts this past week”. “Please know we are truly grateful and deeply humbled by your outpouring of love, care and concern.” Police are preparing a report for the coroner. World.content:

London: British police have charged two men with trespassing and intention to steal at the country home of the Prince and Princess of Wales after finding intruders at the property. Officers rushed to the home on Monday night (early on Tuesday morning, AEDT) to deploy drones, rescue dogs and a police helicopter to find and detain the suspects, who are believed to be Albanian. Police are investigating a break-in at the family’s country home, Anmer Hall, in Sandringham. The alleged break-in took place at Anmer Hall on the royal family’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England. The Norfolk Constabulary said they had charged the two men with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site.



The police named the men as Mirgen Doku, 34, of Courtfield Gardens in London, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, of no fixed address. Prince William, Princess Catherine and their children were not in the home at the time of the alleged incident, as their main residence is Forest Lodge, near Windsor Castle, west of London. Norfolk Constabulary said in a statement that police were called to the estate just before 6pm on Monday (5am on Tuesday, AEDT) following a report of suspicious activity. The police named the men arrested shortly before 10am on Wednesday (9pm on Wednesday, AEDT). “Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area,” the police said.



“Two men were arrested on the estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass. They remain in police custody.” The Sun newspaper reported the two men were Albanian nationals and that one of them had made a claim for asylum that had lapsed. Anmer Hall is a 10-bedroom house on the Sandringham estate, given to William and Catherine as a wedding gift by the late Queen Elizabeth II. King Charles was photographed driving past Anmer Hall with an aide on Tuesday. The break-in heightens concerns about royal security after a series of recent incidents.



Related Article Catherine, Princess of Wales Princess of Wales opens up about cancer treatment in new documentary A 39-year-old man was sentenced to 32 weeks in prison this year after twice breaking into the grounds of Kensington Palace. In 2024, intruders entered Windsor Castle grounds and stole two farm vehicles. A man wielding a crossbow climbed a fence at Windsor Castle in 2021 and made threats to the life of Queen Elizabeth. The man, Jaswant Singh Chail, 21, was later convicted of treason and sentenced to nine years in prison. An incident at Sandringham earlier this year highlighted the risks to the royal grounds. Police arrested a man after Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former Duke of York, was allegedly threatened near his home on the royal estate in May.



Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, have been seeking greater security from British authorities since moving back to the UK earlier this year. Kensington Palace, the official base for the Prince and Princess of Wales, does not comment on security arrangements. Prince visits Downing Street News of the intrusion came as William made a rare visit to No 10 Downing Street to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at his office in the heart of London. Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with Prince William after a meeting at 10 Downing Street. Getty Images
