“Discussions about when certain shopping bags were used as status symbols (C8), reminds me of an article I read, while scrolling through old newspaper archives, about the humble string bag being referred to as ‘the symbol of feminine bondage in Australia’ by the US Consul at a NSW Agricultural Bureau conference in 1950,” writes Mary Carde of Parrearra (Qld). “Worse still, was the panic they caused on the tram, when they became hooked on a button, which was not yours, but a man’s trouser button and your stop was coming up!”

“Having been swotted numerous times by leather strap-wielding Jesuits for not cleaning my shoes at Perth’s St Louis School, instead of rebelling after graduating and favouring dirty footwear, I still zealously polish them to a mirror shine, says Greg Flynn of Turramurra. “I’m worried this makes me the poster boy for corporal punishment.”

Ball tampering (C8) is a balls-up, according to Col Burns of Lugarno: “Oh what we 1970s schoolboys wouldn’t have given for a real ‘six-stitcher’. Andrew Cohen would’ve bagged a ‘six-for’ every innings had he been afforded the privilege of bowling a chipped five-match-old ‘cork’ ball on an uneven coir mat pitch. Even my wayward ‘donkey-drops’ once got me two wickets in an over, albeit alongside three wides and two no-balls.”

For Noel Birrell of Dundas Valley, “the West Ryde Rovers C grade of 1980 figured out the best way to rough up the ball, although not always to our advantage. The trick was to make the opposing batters hit sixes onto the adjoining road. By the time the batter was worn out (and had scored a million) the ball was scuffed enough for our seamers to take over. Needless to say chasing 500 runs in a one-dayer was well beyond our capabilities, but we didn’t bend the rules.”

Lindy Babb of Colo Vale remembers pulling out all the stops for the Princess Royal (C8): “I was probably at the same 1970 event as Wendy Bull. Staff at the General Assembly Library, of whom I was one, were seconded to serve sandwiches. Being pre cling-wrap days, tinned spaghetti sandwiches were covered with damp tea towels to preserve freshness.”

World.title: Victorian hot seats: Terrifying incident at his front door convinced a police officer to enter politics
World.content:
When masked intruders tried to break into Paul Pribilovics’ family home last year, the veteran police officer decided something needed to change.

“We had a few people dressed in hoodies and masked up, carrying torches and trying to get in the front,” he tells me. “It was a scary moment for the family. That’s what inspired me.”

And so after three decades on the force, Pribilovics took leave from Victoria Police to contest the seat of Hawthorn for One Nation, attributing crime as the catalyst for his candidacy.

World.title: After the day, in many ways, life will just go on
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters After the day, in many ways, life will just go on November 25, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. By this time next week, the Liberals will have prevailed or, against the odds, Labor will have clung to power. Whatever happens, we are unlikely to see any major changes in our lives. Shops and schools will still be open, public transport will continue to run, and people will keep going to work. People who expect big changes will surely be disappointed.

Whomever wins, the media will flood us with explanations, recriminations and prognostications for a while, then it will be business as usual, and much about the coming summer of cricket. As I see it, the main result of a change in government will be that the present apologists for the current Labor government will become fierce critics of the new government, and the denigrators of the Labor government will become champions of the new.

Al Morris, Doncaster Fearing the consequences of result

I’d be very sad to see a thoughtful state go down the gurgler, led by a party in bed with One Nation, and by a party that doesn’t take climate change seriously – even if it’s only for one parliamentary term; a lot can happen, be done and not done in four years.

David Anderson, Point Lonsdale Children will be in debt to legacy

Your correspondent (Letters, 24/11) lauds each of the successful projects completed under Labor and adds that his children and grandchildren will benefit for years to come.

Those same children and grandchildren, however, will be burdened forever by a state debt of more than $160 billion and attendant interest of $8.9 billion a year.

What a dire legacy we are leaving future generations.

Terry Black, Black Rock



On wrong side of history

Jess Wilson has pledged to end the Treaty. It’s such a shame that a relatively young politician, and the likely next premier, is deciding to put herself on the wrong side of history, the side of decades of neglect and abuse of the Indigenous people, instead of the future, which will eventually be one of hope, truth and reconciliation.

Matthew Hamilton, Kew Democracy is a good system

It looks like it will be party time for the Liberals on Saturday night and good luck to them, what goes around comes around. Labor has had a good run in government, it did some positive things: improved infrastructure, protected the community from the pandemic and invested in health and education. It did some bad things such as the Commonwealth Games and Big Build botch-ups.

In the usual course of governments, the longer they stay in power the more arrogant and lazy they get. That’s why democracy is such a good system, it gives people the opportunity to change governments and refresh the political parties.

My only pause is the rise of populist parties, particularly One Nation, that use legitimate concerns to ostracise minorities and distract from the cause of social disharmony – increasing inequality driven by the concentration of economic power and ridiculous income disparities.

Pier Paolo De Carlo, Ascot Vale If victory comes, expect the hard right to rise

The last time I voted Liberal we got Jeff Kennett with his school closures etc. He was front and centre at Jess Wilson’s campaign launch. The Liberals’ division between moderates and hard right has been swept under the carpet for the election. A few things have bubbled to the surface though with the proposal to scrap the Treaty and close the safe injecting room in Richmond. Come next week expect the hard right to come out of the closet and ride supreme over the moderates.

David Jones, Essendon THE FORUM A productive life

Ross Gittins (Comment, 25/11) succinctly lays out the key to productivity. However, the final paragraph of his article sums up what society should be thinking; he refers to his inner Salvo to state that there is more to life than productivity. One would hope that no matter what your religious leanings are everyone with any morals should be in total agreement.

Peter Roche, Carlton



Mutual help

Donald Trump owns shares worth millions in Nvidia. He pressures the board of Nvidia to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang, who then praises Trump (″⁣Huang back at helm of Nvidia as Trump steps in″⁣, 25/11).

A classic case of you scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours.

Chris Burgess, Port Melbourne Can’t go much lower

Donald Trump justified his blatant interference into Nvidia by saying after its recent share price collapse, following CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, that “I think it even affected the perception of our country in the world”.

I would have thought that his erratic second term as president had left little scope for the US’s international credibility to degenerate much further.

Kevin Burke, Sandringham Dealing with Trump

Deal or no deal? It seems that because of the businessman president Donald Trump, virtually every agreement or pact between nations is now called a ″⁣deal″⁣. Wrong. Important international arrangements should not be sullied with the language of business bargaining. Let’s tone down his influence in this area at least, and restore the dignity to ″⁣agreements″⁣.

Muriel Porter, Camberwell Common ground

Poor old King Canute. It’s bad enough he is so often wrongly referred to as an archetype of hubris, but now he is compared to Donald Trump (Letters, 24/11).

The wise, humble, and pious Canute did not – as is so often erroneously claimed – place his throne in the path of the incoming tide to command, out of supreme arrogance, that it retreat. His action was to silence the excessively obsequious, dishonest claims of flattering courtiers that his majesty and power were limitless, and to demonstrate how hollow is a king’s authority compared to nature and God’s eternal laws.

Trump may believe he has the deal-brokering power to alter the tides of human affairs, but it’s doubtful even he is deluded enough to believe he can command the ocean’s tides. Perhaps Canute and Trump, despite the former’s humility and the latter’s bombast, may have something in common after all.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East A woman’s fears

It used to be that falling pregnant was the greatest fear for young women engaging in sex. Now their greatest fear should be being killed or permanently disabled by strangulation during sex (″⁣The schoolyard strangulation story that shocked experts″⁣, 25/11).

Michelle Leeder, Trentham



Just a pipe dream

Chris Bowen claims he ″⁣left everything on the field″⁣ at COP31 (″⁣Bowen defends role in failed climate talks, blames deadlock″⁣, 25/11), yet the talks still imploded in public recrimination over four ″⁣largely symbolic″⁣ words on transitioning away from fossil fuels. Perhaps the deadlock wasn’t just the fault of stubborn European and Arab blocs. Rather, as independent MP Monique Ryan rightly pointed out, it came down to a lack of Bowen’s ″⁣moral authority″⁣.

When you arrive at a climate summit carrying the heavy baggage of new coal mine licences and long-term gas export contracts, preaching a clean transition is an impossible sell. To command genuine credibility on the world stage, one must both talk the talk and walk the walk. Right now, our climate change minister is talking-up electrification while dragging a long history in the opposite direction on fossil fuels. Until Australia aligns its domestic approvals with its international rhetoric, expecting global consensus will remain a pipe dream.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Workforce imbalance

While the article ″⁣Stabbings trigger new calls for specialist hospital services″⁣ (24/11) rightly highlights the need to review inpatient psychiatric care, the larger issue is an imbalance in our mental health workforce.

Psychiatrists and psychologists are increasingly overwhelmed by referrals for mild and moderate presentations, limiting their capacity to treat people with severe and complex mental illness. At the same time, many Australians are unable to access timely support for less acute concerns.

A practical solution exists. Australia has more than 20,000 professionally registered, master’s-qualified counsellors and psychotherapists, yet most remain excluded from providing Medicare-funded mental health services. Integrating this workforce would rapidly expand access to care, particularly in regional communities, and allow our scarce specialist resources to be directed where they are needed most.

This is not a workforce shortage alone; it is a workforce utilisation problem. At a time when at least nine Australians die by suicide each day, governments should focus on removing barriers to care and making better use of the qualified professionals already available.

Michael Saxon, Footscray A safe place needed

I agree wholeheartedly with your correspondent (Letters, 25/11) in relation to asylums. Yes, many places needed to be closed then. But what was said then, that many of these people will end up on the streets, has transpired. I had a friend who benefited enormously from her inpatient stays at Royal Park Psychiatric Hospital. It was an excellent hospital.

As an experienced mental health and disability nurse, I have found over those years, many of these very unwell, untreated and isolated people just want a place – with routine, with regular staff, and some certainty in their life – when in a crisis. These ″⁣institutions″⁣ provided that. Yes, there were reports of abuse, and unsafe practices, and those places needed to be shut down, but also rethought.

We desperately need public psychiatric hospitals, acute and general, in Victoria. For diagnosis, treatment, perhaps training, and most of all, to be able to place psychiatric patients somewhere.

Meredith James, Glen Huntly Lack of understanding

The decision by Jess Wilson and the Liberal Party to close Victoria’s only medically supervised injecting centre, with no intention of establishing another, says a great deal about their understanding of drug addiction and the people affected by it.

It also rather conveniently exposes the argument that the centre’s location, next to a school, is the real problem. If that were genuinely the concern, surely the obvious response would be to find a more appropriate location. Instead, there is no intention of providing an alternative. It seems they simply don’t want it anywhere.

This announcement demonstrates a staggering lack of understanding of the complex issues surrounding drug addiction, not to mention an apparent disregard for the success of the centre and the lives it has helped protect.

A few weeks ago, I had the opportunity to take part in one of the centre’s weekly tours. I saw an extraordinary level of care, empathy, professionalism and understanding of the needs of people who are often among the most marginalised.

This is not about condoning drug use. It is about recognising that addiction is a complex health and social issue, not something that disappears because a government decides it would rather not see it.

The centre provides dignity, support, medical supervision and, most importantly, saves lives.

Closing it without providing an alternative is not a solution. It is an ideological decision that puts politics ahead of public health, compassion and common sense.

Sue McNamara, Rye Identifying the error

The driver of the vehicle that drove in front of an incoming plane said he ″⁣misidentified his position″⁣ (″⁣Jet aborts take-off in near miss with ute″⁣, 24/11). I guess that’s a bit like our politicians who say they ″⁣accidentally misspoke″⁣. In other words, they got it wrong.

Merryn Boan, Brighton



Baffling position

I agree with your correspondent that clean energy is powering ahead despite a lack of political will (“COP31 failed yet fossil fuels are done for”, 25/11). The economic case for solar, wind and batteries is simply too compelling for households, business and industry to ignore.

It remains baffling, then, that parties and candidates from the Liberals to One Nation advocate for more expensive, polluting coal and gas, which will cost Victorians through both power bills and climate impacts.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Informally, not a donkey

The Age Sunday quiz (22/11) said that a donkey vote was an informal vote. They are not the same. A donkey vote is when the voter numbers all the boxes on the ballot from top to bottom sequentially. It has been completed properly and will be counted. An informal vote is when the voter does not complete the ballot properly, and so it will not be counted.

Jane Wright, East Malvern Unwrapping tradition

I was always led to believe it was not de rigueur to still have a Christmas tree up after New Year’s Day. Likewise, not to have decorations up before December.

Mark Hulls, Sandringham Photo: Matt Golding



AND ANOTHER THING Politics

If the Liberal Party is planning to close the safe injecting room, what sort of community are we? Where do these people go for help?

Raelene Spencer, Croydon I’m sure businesses have lost out in Richmond because of the Aldi and Woolworths stores on Victoria Street rather than the nearby safe injecting room.

Chris Hooper, Castlemaine First Nations people and addicted people thrown under the Jess Wilson election bus. Treaty and safe injecting room dead.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn The polls suggest we will be getting ″⁣a fresh start″⁣. How long after that we will have to endure the words, ″⁣We inherited a mess from the previous government″⁣?

Danny Van Vliet, Mount Eliza



It would be ironic if an incoming Liberal government decided to privatise our newly minted road and rail infrastructure assets to pay off our multibillion-dollar debt incurred under Labor.

Martin Newington, Aspendale As someone who tries to align their voting with their conscience, I despair at the lack of options. We need change, but I fear the coming Labor wipeout will present us with something even worse: a Gina Rinehart-controlled state.

Matt Dunn, Leongatha What are the chances that Jess Wilson will be rolled not long after she wins the election?

Simon Limjak, Reservoir I can cope with Labor losing the election. I can live with a Liberal government. But One Nation a clear second is a bridge too far.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Furthermore

Dan Tehan supports the continued use of fossil fuels yet criticises the COP outcome which in effect supports the use of fossil fuels?

Peter Baddeley, Portland



Next COP meeting Australia should send David Pocock.

Robin Jensen, Castlemaine Finally

Black Friday seems to be morphing into Black Fortnight.

Richard Crago, Burwood East

Since the pandemic, working from home has become the norm for many employees, with some working full-time from home offices and others taking a hybrid approach. Whether you’re working or studying, having the right set-up is key. A dedicated space with few distractions, good lighting, reliable connectivity, ergonomic comfort, and room to store any resources or equipment is essential. Here are five of our luxury homes in which to work from home that are on the market. 4 Linlithgow Road, Toorak, Vic



Created by Melbourne design royalty Christopher Doyle, Davies Henderson and Paul Bangay, this impressive Toorak residence features a home office fit for royalty. With a built-in bookshelf that is not only practical but also makes an interesting visual feature for any Zoom call, a desk, hardwood floors, an arched window and a grand piano, the room offers a stylish space for working from home. Located on Linlithgow Road, the home also features a private cinema, full-scale entertaining areas, a gym, two additional bedrooms, and turnstile parking for six cars. This luxurious residence has a price guide of $28 million to $30 million. 14 Weeroona Avenue, Woollahra, NSW



This grand Tudor Revival residence in Woollahra includes a study with lots of period charm. A large bay window features a built-in seat overlooking greenery. The room has high ceilings, a split system, a lounge area, a built-in desk and shelving, and abundant natural light. Other highlights include a dedicated wellness zone with a hot tub, sauna and cold plunge, as well as a custom-designed children’s playhouse with its own climbing wall. 6 Mary Street, St Kilda West, Vic



Set over two levels, “Lady of St Kilda” is an Edwardian home renovated by Bojan Simic Architecture. The result is a blend of original period features, such as fireplaces and leadlight windows, and contemporary additions, including the home office, which is located on the first floor. The room features a large built-in desk with seating for two and sits in a quiet corner of the home. Other highlights include the dramatic central void, designer lighting and a stone kitchen that connects to the outdoors through oversized dual sliding doors to an al fresco deck, framed by bespoke perforated screens and deep, private gardens.



House 6, 161 Raglan Street, Mosman, NSW The upper level of this two-storey Mosman home features four bedrooms, two with their own balconies, and a study. The study includes dual desks, built-in shelving and cupboards, making it an ideal spot to work from home, study or for multiple family members to work side-by-side. Located in the gated Tregoyd Estate on Balmoral Slopes, the freestanding Torrens Title home features a Hamptons-style interior and a tropical garden.



The property includes access to a swimming pool, a tennis/pickleball court and a rainforest walkway. 93 Macquarie Street, Teneriffe, QLD The largest of the Catalina homes, the residence was originally conceptualised by Hong Kong- and Southern China-based architect Wilfred Wong. The three-level home includes an impressive library with built-in shelving, cupboards and a desk.



With enough room for a lounge and plenty of natural light through the windows, you can kick back and relax after a long day of working from home. It features panoramic views across the Brisbane River towards Hawthorne and Hamilton, plus a 976-bottle temperature-controlled wine cellar and, outdoors, a 25-metre heated swimming pool.
