World.title: Legal expert says pressure from Ministry of Health altered response to asbestos contaminated sand
World.content:
Audio player for " Law Professor on abestos contamination investigation " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/health/2773396%2Flegal-expert-says-pressure-from-ministry-of-health-altered-response-to-asbestos-contaminated-sand

Law Professor on abestos contamination investigation Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

An Auckland University legal expert says behind the scenes pressure from the Ministry of Health altered toxicology & law experts' recommendations on the response to asbestos contaminated play sand.

This week a Consumer NZ investigation revealed conflicting claims and confusion among government agencies as concerns arose.

It said eight tonnes of the sand was sold over the last decade but Health NZ had baulked at proposals to monitor children exposed to the product.

Law Professor, Alex Sims told Checkpoint she worked alongside toxicologist, Professor Ian Shaw, in formulating recommendations for active monitoring of exposed children.

"The Ministry of Health were putting behind the scenes pressure for the briefing to be changed and, ultimately, it was changed. It's extremely disappointing.

"There were so many different government departments - they were all pointing fingers at other people. People don't seem to be doing what they're meant to do so it's all a bit of a mess," Sims said.

Sims said - despite initial claims the products were low risk - an Auckland University of Technology study would later find asbestos in the products could be inhaled when used.

"People didn't know the risks. It was thought that the asbestos wouldn't be freed unless [the sand] was mechanically compressed.

"When we changed the report we said 'you need more information' but then when the information came out later it showed that there really should be monitoring of those children," Sims said.

She said there were concerns that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's advisories about voluntary recalls were authored by suppliers such as Kmart and the company was told by WorkSafe that wording about the products was incorrect.

"If a recall notice has to go through, at a government department, it may take quite a while. So you might want an initial one but then there should be a thing then to look at and revise it as soon as you've got proper information and not just leave it there for, in this case, months," Sims said.

She said the country's systems for dealing with importing of potentially dangerous goods needed more teeth.

"There's no testing at the border. Since this has occurred there is a new notice that's not going to come in effect until the first of February, that's going to require suppliers of goods with sand in them, especially toys, that they have to get them tested.

"It's on the supplier to do that but the suppliers weren't following the existing law so what is there to make them follow that law?," Sims said.

In a statement, MBIE said the Consumer report raised important questions about how effectively agencies worked together and whether the country's product safety system had kept pace with global supply chains.

The Ministry of Health maintained its position that monitoring of people exposed to asbestos in sand was not recommended.

It advised people to discuss concerns with Healthline and avoid further exposure by removing the product safely.

The Ministry said concerns about an article authored by professors Sims and Shaw, recommending a public register, had been raised with Consumer NZ.

They said they questioned whether the academics had the technical expertise and qualifications to make clinical recommendations, and the article was subsequently amended by publishers, the Public Health Communication Centre.

Kmart said it acted quickly by removing affected products from sale, issuing recall notices and providing refunds and guidance based on regulatory advice at the time.

World.title: Building developer keen to take on fixing cracked heritage building
World.content:
An Auckland heritage building developer says he is interested in taking on fixing up the former Fitzroy Hotel on Wakefield Street, one of the region's oldest building.

Built in the mid-1850s, the building has cracks in its facade and is the subject of a dangerous building notice.

Earlier this month, owner The Fitzroy Hotel Limited and company director Terry Huang were fined $135,000 for failing to make it safe.

The developer of St James Theatre on Queen Street, Steve Bielby of Auckland Notable Properties Trust, said the former hotel has suffered after years of no maintenance.

"That comes home to roost at some point, and unfortunately the wheel's stopped, and the current owner is holding the prize."

The building needs a full restoration, Bielby said.

Auckland Council field operations manager for compliance, David Pawson said safety is the immediate priority and the dangerous building notice is still in place.

"While it's in its current state, we still need to keep Wakefield Street and Lyndock Street cordoned off to make sure that the public are safe."

The building is surrounded by high hoardings that have blocked the streets around it for years.

Huang told RNZ he could not get on with plans to prop the building until the council fixed the footpath next to the hotel, which he said was undermined.

Pawson said there had been numerous engineering reports, some potential issues were identified and investigated, and the council's investigations had shown there was no contributing cause from council assets that would be undermining the building.

A heritage assessment from 2010 showed there were cracks already present in the building before Huang's company bought it in 2015, Pawson said.

Auckland Council cannot compel the owner of a heritage building to carry out maintenance, he said.

"We can't force him to fix the roof, we can't force him to stop the water ingress which is making the problem worse. We can deal with the symptom through the building being dangerous and taking the action under The Building Act, with the dangerous building notices."

Auckland Council's spent $457,064 mitigating the risk to passersby from potential falling masonry.

Former Waitematā local board member Allan Matson pushed for heritage listing more than 20 years ago and has been watching closely. He said, with bills stacking up for Huang, one avenue could be he could sell the building.

Restoring the building is something Bielby would prepared to do.

"I have had discussions with the owner and the agent and I have put proposals forward to look at it.

"I think it is a significant place and I think it is worth saving and is capable of being saved, so I'd love to give it that opportunity if I can.

He estimated the work needed would cost between $1.5m and $2m.

A registered valuation Auckland Council presented as evidence at court earlier this month valued the property at $1.45m,

World.title: Worries about staffing and workload at Dannevirke clinic
World.content:
Worries about staffing and workload at clinic run by under-fire Tararua Health Group

Health NZ says it is aware of concerns

Primary health organisation holds talks about staffing and clinical capacity

Last onsite GP leaving Barraud Street Health Centre in Dannevirke.

Health officials are seeking assurances about staffing and care for patients at a Dannevirke health clinic, where the last onsite GP is leaving and telehealth services are relied on.

The doctor was working at the Barraud Street Health Centre in the Tararua town, but is moving to another practice.

RNZ understands this has left a small team of registered nurses, healthcare assistants and administrators at the centre, run by the troubled Tararua Health Group, whose operations in the district are under review by Health NZ.

Tony Wai, the chief executive of the The Primary Health Organisation (the PHO) - which contracts the Barraud Street Health Centre for its services - says a formal notice has been issued to the Tararua Health Group and talks were held on Wednesday morning about care options.

Tararua Health Group, owned by nationwide primary care provider Omnihealth, until October also ran the Dannevirke Community Hospital, which is next to the Barraud Street Health Centre.

Health NZ has since taken over operations at the community hospital after there was a temporary freeze on it taking new patients in September due to concerns about patient safety.

Tararua Health Group also previously ran the Pahīatua Medical Centre, which had seven staff resignations, due to overwork and safety concerns.

Earlier in November the medical centre was bought by Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua Trust.

In Dannevirke, which has a population of just over 5500 people, Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua recently took over the Tini Whetū Health and Wellbeing Centre - this clinic wasn't run by Tararua Health Group.

Health officials are watching the Barraud Street Health Centre, where the last onsite GP is leaving. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Reliance on telehealth

RNZ understands remaining onsite staff at the Barraud Street Health Centre are supplemented by GPs and a nurse practitioner offering telehealth services.

It Is understood that this week the telehealth GP was sick for a day, placing extra pressure on staff.

A source told RNZ the small team of staff at the clinic were responsible for daily primary healthcare tasks, including clinical assessments, follow-up care, administration and co-ordinating consultations with clinicians working remotely.

"The absence of onsite GPs and nurse practitioners creates additional challenges for patients requiring physical examinations, urgent assessments and ongoing management of complex medical conditions," the source said.

"While telehealth can be a valuable component of healthcare delivery, it cannot fully replace accessible, face-to-face medical services, particularly in rural communities where alternative options may already be limited."

The source said it was concerning to hear patients from the Barraud Street Health Centre turning to other clinics because they were unable to access care, and that raised concerns about whether the clinic could provide appropriate primary healthcare and whether staff were under too much pressure.

"Patients should not have to reach a point of crisis before they can access appropriate healthcare, nor should neighbouring healthcare providers be expected to absorb the consequences of an under-resourced medical centre."

The source said they would like to see the Barraud Street Health Centre transferred to a new or existing entity.

Tararua Health Group director Mark Wills was approached for comment, but did not respond.

Clinic operator on notice

Wai said the PHO was aware of "workforce and service delivery challenges" at the Barraud Street Health Centre, including the impending departure of the onsite GP.

It had previously issued the Tararua Health Group a formal notice about the situation and was working with it to address gaps in the service.

"We met again with the provider this morning and are progressing a range of options, including interim clinical cover, recruitment support, alternative models of care and arrangements that could enable other local healthcare providers to provide additional clinical capacity.

"Our immediate priority is maintaining safe and timely access to primary healthcare for the Dannevirke community," Wai said.

"Our clinical and regional teams are reviewing clinical rosters, workforce capacity, skill mix, clinical support arrangements, clinical oversight, patient access, escalation pathways and arrangements for patients who require face-to-face consultations.

"Where we identify gaps, we work with the provider to address them and, where necessary, develop alternative arrangements to maintain continuity of care."

Wai said the clinic, which had about 4500 enrolled patients, had limitations to its clinical capacity and some patients might experience difficulties in accessing care.

"This is precisely why we are actively intervening and working on additional clinical capacity and contingency arrangements.

"We are exploring options that would enable other local healthcare providers to support Barraud Street patients where necessary, while the practice works to restore sustainable clinical capacity."

Wai said the Tararua Health Group was best placed to comment on staffing levels and vacancies.

Telehealth was an established part of healthcare, but was no substitute for face-to-face appointments.

"Our immediate focus is on working constructively with Tararua Health Group to restore sufficient clinical capacity and ensure continuity of care for patients.

"This includes exploring alternative service delivery arrangements and how wider local general practice capacity could be utilised to support the community while the practice rebuilds its workforce."

Wai said the PHO's responsibility was for the needs of the community, rather than on a particular operating model at the clinic.

Health officials watch on

Health NZ central regional director for planning, funding and outcomes Geoff Gwyn said officials were aware of concerns about services at the Barraud Street Health Centre.

"The practice is operated by Omnihealth and questions about its day-to-day operations and staffing should be directed to Omnihealth," he said.

"Health NZ continues to work with the PHO to seek assurance that appropriate staffing, clinical oversight and contingency arrangements are in place to support safe and continuous care for patients.

"We will consider whether any further action is required once that information has been assessed."

A Barraud Street Health Centre patient told RNZ using telehealth wasn't as good as face-to-face meetings with clinicians.

"You cannot tell what state someone's in by having a phone conversation with them. It leaves room for error, misdiagnosis and isn't something they should be leaning on too heavily."

Other Dannevirke residents spoken to this week held a range of views about primary healthcare in the town.

Some were concerned about the recent problems, while others were more optimistic since the Tini Whetū Health and Wellbeing Centre was set up and Health NZ took over running the Dannevirke Community Hospital.

RNZ asked Health NZ about how long it expected to run that hospital, and if it was in negotiations with any other providers to take over.

"Health New Zealand continues to oversee service delivery at Dannevirke Community Hospital, with clinical governance and operational support provided by MidCentral," Gwyn said.

World.title: Two charged after $30k worth of drugs found in car off Cook Strait ferry
World.content:
About $30,000 worth of illicit drugs were found in a car following a ferry journey across the Cook Strait.

Last Friday, police were alerted to two people allegedly with a large amount of illicit drugs onboard a ferry heading to Picton.

Tasman police said after the ferry arrived, the car and two people of interest were found.

The car was searched a spokesperson said, and about $30k worth of illicit drugs were found including 200 MDMA tablets and 4kg of cannabis.

Detective Sergeant Lisa Brent said a 24-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman from Queenstown would reappear in Blenheim District Court on January 18, 2027.

World.title: Victim Support review reveals staff concerns over 'personal cost' of speaking out
World.content:
An independent workplace culture review of the country's lead agency supporting victims of crime and trauma says some staff believed speaking up about workplace concerns carried a "personal cost" including "isolation, being assigned extra work or changes in their relationship with their manager".

The review did not find evidence of an "organisation-wide" culture of bullying or toxicity at Victim Support but it also said that staff concerns could not be treated as "solely historical or as coming from a small number of dissatisfied individuals".

Although there was a "generally positive, values-led culture overall", the review found "uneven employee experience, with concerns particularly concentrated in certain local leadership relationships, psychological safety, and confidence in the outcomes of workplace concerns raised".

Eight of those spoken to as part of the review described "repeated conduct of undermining comments, aggressive behaviour, isolation, and informal consequences for speaking up".

The review made 12 recommendations and outlined five principal opportunities for improvement.

The external review came after reporting by RNZ in July over claims of a "toxic" and "bullying" workplace culture, four years after an investigation into similar allegations.

RNZ spoke to several current and former workers who raised concerns about the culture at Victim Support. One person described it as a "very unsafe environment".

The agency's chief executive James McCulloch earlier said the agency "does not accept that these claims reflect Victim Support today".

Then, in August, the agency announced it had agreed to commission a review of the organisation's workplace culture, confidence in people leadership and the processes for resolving workplace concerns.

The review, by Charlotte Stevens, heard from 57 current Victim Support employees between August and October. This represented about 36 percent of the workforce. The review did not include speaking to former staff.

Four people outside Victim Support, including representatives of the Ministry of Justice and Police, were also interviewed.

The overall assessment was that the agency had made "substantial organisational progress" since an earlier review.

"There are identifiable strengths in organisational culture, and considerable pride in Victim Support's purpose."

Employee experience was "not uniform and appears to be materially influenced by immediate leadership and local team dynamics".

"Employees generally understand how to raise concerns, but confidence in what happens after concerns are raised is less consistent, particularly among frontline employees."

It also said the evidence did not establish a "toxic and bullying workplace culture".

"The recurring concerns appear to reflect a mix of historical experiences, organisational change, differing expectations and understanding, and some current, localised issues."

Among the key findings of the review was that there was a "generally positive, values-led culture overall, with genuine pride in the organisation's purpose, but experience varies considerably depending on a person's specific team and immediate leader".

In relation to senior leadership, most participants who addressed the question had confidence in the Senior Leadership Team (SLT). Confidence was strongest among SLT and national office participants and some managers.

"Frontline views are more divided, partly because the SLT is less visible to frontline staff day-to-day, and some frontline staff do not know who is on the SLT."

The review also said McCulloch's initial communications to staff about media allegations regarding the culture at the agency "drew a mixed response" from staff with "some saying they contradicted their experience and made them less willing to approach him".

It also said that participants were "divided" as to why concerns continued to be raised about the organisation.

"Sixteen attributed the concerns to a small number of aggrieved individuals, 7 said the issues are real and unresolved, and 22 gave mixed explanations.

"Any concerns raised were generally associated with specific teams or working relationships, and most respondents did not describe them as widespread across the organisation."

Some key organisational strengths included "genuine pride" in Victim Support's purpose and commitment to victims as well as wellbeing support that participants valued and strong awareness of how and where to raise a concern.

Among the principal opportunities for improvement were closing the gap between raising a concern and seeing a visible outcome by providing clarity on process, privacy and legal limitations as well as individual staff responsibilities.

It also details improving awareness of the "established safe routes for raising concerns" and strengthening the capability of team leaders and district managers.

The review also identified increasing the visibility of senior leaders to frontline staff and making progress against earlier reviews visible to all people.

The review detailed several matters outside its scope including determining whether any individual allegations should be upheld.

It said there were several limitations, including that former employees were not included in the participant group "because the review is of the current culture".

The review details findings in relation to five themes that were explored including speaking up and management of workplace concerns.

It found that while there was "strong awareness" of how and where to raise a concern, there was "less confidence" that the process followed was "consistently fair, timely or visible to the person who raised it".

Sixteen participants, all frontline staff or managers, said they believed speaking up carried a "personal cost" the review said.

"Some apprehension about raising a concern is common in any workplace," the review said.

"However, several of these participants described more than a general apprehension: they provided examples of what they said had happened to them or to colleagues after raising concerns, such as isolation, being assigned extra work, or changes in their relationship with their manager. However, the Review has not tested individual accounts.

"The recurring concerns appear to reflect a mix of historical experiences, organisational change, differing expectations and understanding, and some current, localised issues."

Of the participants who commented, the largest group placed problems with particular teams, districts or relationships.

A smaller group described "current, unresolved problems in their own areas".

"The pattern points to a continuing gap in awareness about how concerns are handled, concentrated in certain places."

The review said WorkSafe defined bullying as "repeated and unreasonable behaviour directed at a worker or group of workers that can lead to physical or psychological harm".

Some managers described "ordinary management actions" being labelled as bullying by staff.

"Eight participants described repeated conduct of undermining comments, aggressive behaviour, isolation, and informal consequences for speaking up. If accurate, those accounts describe the kind of conduct the definition concerns.

"However, the Review has not tested individual accounts and cannot say which description applies in any particular case. The evidence shows that both kinds of experience were reported to the Review, and that a participant's view of "the culture" depends heavily on which they have encountered."

The review said participants who saw no visible outcome after raising "lower-level concerns" were most likely to conclude that raising further concerns was "pointless".

"And some said that people who feel unheard internally will eventually look elsewhere to raise them. Together with the perception gap, this helps explain why concerns may continue to be raised outside the organisation despite all the improvements since 2022."

In relation to McCulloch's initial email to staff about RNZ's coverage, the review said his response "should be considered in context".

"His first message to staff was a firm defence of the organisation and its people. A small number of staff (six) said it contradicted their own experience and made them less willing to approach senior leaders.

"The CE's all-staff email of 3 July 2026 took a different approach. It acknowledged that the coverage had been unsettling and that it was upsetting to hear that anyone felt this way. It said that no one should feel unheard, disbelieved or worried that raising a concern would make things harder for them."

The review said the second email was the kind of acknowledgement some participants said should have come first.

"For future responses, the lesson is to lead with acknowledgement and then set out the organisation's position."

The review said that the findings describe an organisation that had "largely completed the structural aspects of its change since 2022".

"What has not yet been achieved consistently is the day-to-day experience those structures are meant to produce: a direct manager who makes it safe to speak up, a concern that is visibly followed through, and progress that all frontline staff can see."

The 12 recommendations include further closing the loop on all concerns, providing clarity on the perception of repercussions, ensuring senior leaders are visible and accountable, making progress visible and ensuring follow-up where participants described unresolved issues.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the agency's board said the organisation was "committed to continue building a work environment where staff wellbeing is prioritised".

"The Board is pleased to see the pride our people have in Victim Support's important purpose. The review found many strengths in our organisational culture, and that substantial structural change has been delivered since a review in 2022," it said.

"The review found the evidence does not establish a 'toxic' and 'bullying' workplace culture. However, we recognise there is always room to improve. We are committed to listening to our people, understanding their experiences and strengthening our organisation. We will build on the progress we have made over the last four years and strive to be a workplace where staff wellbeing is at the forefront of everything we do."

The Board said the organisation was now focussed on implementing the review's recommendations.

McCulloch said the organisation would continue to strive to be a workplace where everyone had an "excellent experience". He said work on the improvement areas was underway.

"Our staff are passionate and dedicated, and their wellbeing is central to the support we provide to victims of crime and traumatic events - it matters deeply to me that we are a place where everyone should feel respected, heard, supported and able to do their best work for victims.

World.title: Cyber attacks: A month of hacks, breaches and shutdowns
World.content:
Crucial digital infrastructure systems have been under pressure over the past few weeks, with a number of high-profile hacks and network outages reported both globally and locally.

RNZ has not proven immune to this, with an apparent cyber breach of its own systems reported today, but it is far from the only organisation struggling to deal with such digital dilemmas.

While a new major breach seems to be revealed every day, they appear to have no direct connection, as hackers use AI technology to break into systems, while networks struggle and sometimes collapse after upgrades. The National Cyber Security Centre says frontier AI is accelerating cyber threats, with vulnerabilities able to be identified and exploited faster.

Here are some of the major technological breakdowns that have been reported in New Zealand and around the world in just the past month:

Frontier AI is reported to be accelerating cyber threats, with vulnerabilities able to be identified and exploited faster GORODENKOFF PRODUCTIONS/SCIENCE / GPR / Science Photo Library via AFP

Planes, banks and spies

The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence in the United States have been subjected to an apparent hack affecting unclassified information, it was reported today, with the intrusion hit a system the agencies draw on​ for open-source intelligence analysis.

Officials emphasised that no classified information was affected.

While it was not immediately clear when the hack occurred, who was responsible for it, or if it has been resolved, the incident does not appear to be related to an apparent hack of the FBI's nation-wide criminal information database reported on Friday.

The FBI breach - which targeted its nation-wide criminal information database that serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement - was the second attack on the federal agency in recent months.

The government agency hacks have followed a series of unrelated high-profile tech outages affecting banks and the FAA's air traffic control system.

All US flights were grounded for hours in mid-November after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. At about the same time, Chase Bank said thousands of its customers had trouble using online accounts, and several other banks reported issues.

Stranded travellers queue for rental cars at Salt Lake City International Airport during the nationwide ground stop. AFP / NurPhoto / Charles-McClintock Wilson

Big business, big tech issues

The biggest tech outage of the month saw several key Microsoft services become unavailable for almost a day. Offices around the world were disrupted when services such as Outlook and Teams were out of action for more than 20 hours.

Meanwhile, some of the world's most visited websites, including those of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax , CNN, Salesforce and Ikea, were compromised in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones.

Travel booking companies Bookit, Booking.com and Expedia have each recently confirmed data breaches, while in late October, Sony confirmed a data breach had compromised 2.5 million records containing current and former customers' personal information.

In Europe, grocery stores from Sweden to Portugal were hit by a suspected cyberattack on their freezer systems with food retailers forced to throw out produce that had spoiled or was at risk of spoiling after refrigerator temperatures soared overnight.

An employee throws away bags of spoiled food outside a Stockholm supermarket after a number of stores suffered problems with their refrigerators and freezers overnight. FREDRIK SANDBERG / TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP

New Zealand outages

Aotearoa may be geographically isolated, but is globally connected on a digital level, and has also suffered cyberattacks and breaches.

Local media outlets have been the latest targets of apparent cyber attacks in the past 48 hours - Allied Media publications including the Greymouth Star, the Hokitika Guardian, the Blenheim Sun, Southern Rural Life and The Ensign were all affected by an attack yesterday, with the Otago Daily Times coming close to close to not making its deadline for publication.

That was followed by news that RNZ had also been hit, with some staff were unable to access wi-fi, editorial systems, and the virtual private network.

Meanwhile, Forest & Bird was alerted to a hack last Wednesday, where people's names, phone numbers, and email addresses were accessed, while the NZ Defence Force also shut down its public websites after a breach on Friday of a database associated with a discount scheme for Defence Force families.

World.title: Port Chalmers Pool to remain open, council to consider how to reduce costs
World.content:
Dunedin's Port Chalmers Pool will remain open for now, with the council agreeing to investigate ways to make it more cost effective and involve the community in decisions about its longer-term future.

The Dunedin City Council was considering closing the pool after staff were asked to come up with operational savings costs as part of its long term plan.

A staff report said the pool received an average of 4735 visits per year, with the net operating cost amounting to $102.73 per visit.

At a meeting today, councillors agreed to keep the pool operating under its current seasonal lifeguarded model, with staff to report back to council by the end of January on ways to improve its financial sustainability.

A number of Port Chalmers residents and pool users showed up to the meeting in support of keeping the pool open. An online petition calling to halt its closure had received almost 2000 signatures.

Residents were unable to speak about the pool during the meeting's public forum because the council said it did not pre-consult on Long Term Plan proposals and the West Harbour Community Board had expressed disappointment that there was not a lack of meaningful engagement before the matter was brought forward to council.

A major point of debate was whether the reported pool attendance figures accurately reflected its use, and staff said they stood by the revenue and operating figures, but accepted there could be some variation in attendance numbers.

Councillors discussed to how reduce costs or increase use, including sponsorships and partnerships, volunteer lifeguards, longer opening hours, solar power and potentially a targeted rate for the Port Chalmers community.

The options before council were to close the pool after the summer season, create a new pool key access-only system or keep the pool open under the existing arrangements with lifeguards.

The staff report said the council had earmarked $577,000 for maintenance and upgrades in the invested in 2025-34 plan. Based on projected costs over the next decade, the unstaffed key access option would save about $72,000 per year, while closing the pool would save about $264,000 per year.

Councillor Steve Walker put through a motion that the council continue to operate the pool under its current seasonal lifeguarding model, pending further consideration by the council.

The Port Chalmers Swimming Pool opened in 1961. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Staff were directed to investigate further options to improve the financial sustainability of the pool, including pricing, utilisation and attendance data, sponsorship and partnership opportunities and alternative operating arrangements, with a report to come back to council before the end of January.

"Port Chalmers Pool is far more than a swimming facility and its value to our community cannot be measured by its operating cost alone," Walker said.

"In a country surrounded by water, swimming is not simply a recreational activity, it is an essential life skill. The pool provides local children with opportunities to learn to swim, develop confidence and acquire the water safety skills that could one day save their lives."

He said the pool was also an important rehabilitation facility for older people, post-surgical patients, people living with chronic pain and those with disabilities.

When it came to the finances, Walker said a staff report estimated that closing the pool would save approximately $264,000 annually, but also identifies ongoing costs of around $109,000 even if it was to close.

The motion was supported 14-1, with councillor Lee Vandervis the only one voting against it.

Vandervis said the same debate was had 15 years ago, over the number of pool users versus the extremely high cost of running the pool, which back then amounted to $83 per swim.

He said the council were paying to keep the pool open for 13 swimmers a day, with ratepayers outside of Port Chalmers, paying a $100 subsidy "every time somebody wants to have a swim".

Seeking another report would add further costs, he said, "for a pool whose operation is unsustainable and caters for a tiny minority of people relying on an enormous subsidy to keep the pool open".

Mayor Sophie Barker said pools were precious to communities and the council did want to hear from residents and ratepayers about what was important to them.

"We have to look at our levels of service and we have to look at the facilities that we provide. And it is heartbreaking in some ways to think about how we're going to do this."

Councillors Doug Hall and Marie Laufiso both referenced a letter that was sent in from a class of five and six year olds at Port Chalmers School.

"To the city council, we are the children in Ruma Tepetepe at Port Chalmers School," it read.

"Please keep our swimming pool open. We need it for swimming lessons to learn to swim and be safe in the water. We want to have it to play and to be with our friends and family. We can make new friends there too. If the pool closes we would feel sad, annoyed and upset about this. Please save our pool."

World.title: Man admits concealing body of 21-year-old Braydon Hepworth
World.content:
A Christchurch man has admitted his role in concealing the body of Braydon Hepworth.

The 21-year-old's body was found buried in a shed in Linwood on October 8 after he disappeared in early September.

A 34-year-old, one of two men charged with concealing Hepworth's body, appeared in the Christchurch District Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to one count of interfering with human remains.

Judge Jane Farish extended a temporary order for name suppression before releasing him on bail.

The man will be sentenced in April.

A 60-year-old man, whose name is also suppressed, pleaded not guilty to charges of manslaughter, concealing Hepworth's body and making a false statement when he appeared in the High Court at Christchurch last week.

He was remanded in custody with a trial tentatively set for late next year.

An independent review is being carried out into the care Hepworth received at the Christchurch City Mission after he was told to leave its Whakaora Kāinga transitional housing complex less than two months before he disappeared.

Mission board chairperson Jane Evans earlier said the review would examine Hepworth's time with the mission and the decision-making involved in his care.

"We take our responsibilities to our clients, our staff and the wider community very seriously," she said in an October statement.

"The mission is open to improving how it supports people in its care and looks forward to the outcome."

World.title: NSW hold on for epic draw against Queensland
World.content:
Forgotten Test spinner Mitchell Swepson has outshone Nathan Lyon to almost bowl Queensland to an unlikely Sheffield Shield victory, before NSW held on for a draw with two wickets in hand.

On a frantic final day in Sydney, Queensland raced from 2-106 to 6-306 on Wednesday morning, before declaring and setting NSW 282 for victory.

With rain a constant threat and at times interrupting, the Blues then initially chased after a win before slumping to 6-105 and going defensive in the final hours.

At one stage in the final hour the covers were brought on for 7 minutes, as Queensland players remained on the field and even put stumps back in themselves.

But the Blues ultimately held on, going to stumps at 8-152 after 56.5 overs.

In a match full of Test ramifications, Steve Smith was bowled by a big-turning Jack Sinfield off break on 13 on Wednesday, adding to his first-innings 12.

Sam Konstas charged the first ball he faced from Swepson and was caught at cover for 11, missing a final chance to ram home his chances of a Test recall.

Queensland were desperately close to a famous victory at the SCG. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe Photography)

For Queensland Jack Clayton did his chances no harm with an unbeaten 84, keeping the innings together alongside Hugo Burdon (98) and Michael Neser (61).

But the most notable aspect were Swepson's 11 wickets for the match and Lyon's four.

Swepson was able to get great turn out of an SCG wicket that he declared on Tuesday was back to its old spinning ways, before his fourth-innings 5-55.

In comparison Lyon was solid but failed to illicit any real turn or significant bite with his finger spin.

His overspin and bounce had Marnus Labuschagne caught behind sweeping on day three, before catching Burdon's edge with one that went straight on on Wednesday.

Lyon also had Neser caught in the deep as Queensland pursued quick runs late in their innings, but otherwise finished with 3-84 to go with his first-innings 1-86.

Lyon's status as Australia's No.1 spinner is not up for debate in the eyes of selectors, but his selection in Perth will likely come down to the nature of the wicket.

Although there have been questions asked of the 39-year-old in recent weeks, including a stinging attack from Stuart MacGill this week.

Swepson, meanwhile, is not in the Test frame but retains hope of earning a recall for the Border-Gavaskar Trophy in India later this summer.

His 11 wickets for the match was the best haul by a spinner in the Sheffield Shield since Stephen O'Keefe in 2014, and the best of his own career.

After producing the ball of the match to bowl Kurtis Patterson out of the rough on day two in first-innings figures of 6-73, he was again the destroyer on Wednesday.

He had a cutting Josh Philippe caught behind, bowled a leaving Ryan Hicks for a duck with one that went straight on, trapped Charlie Stobo lbw and then had Lyon caught low at slip late.

But the leggie was unable to get the two breakthroughs needed in the last over, as NSW held on.

AAP

World.title: Khawaja says he offered Sandpapergate peace proposal
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has revealed he proposed a "middle ground" peace deal to Todd Greenberg that could end the Sandpapergate feud that has ripped Australian cricket apart.

Speaking on The Grade Cricketer Podcast, Khawaja read out a text message he sent to Greenberg, the CEO of Cricket Australia (CA), that he hoped the entire squad could stand behind.

"We accept and acknowledge as a team that we knew we were ball tampering by artificially altering the condition of the ball in South Africa in 2018," Khawaja's proposed statement read.

"Whether it was sandpaper, or by any other means, is irrelevant. We knew what we were doing, and we take full responsibility as a team and squad for our actions, something we should have done eight years ago.

"Furthermore, we would like to acknowledge that Steven [Smith], Cameron [Bancroft] and David [Warner] paid an enormous price for the sake of the team for which we are sorry and eternally grateful."

Khawaja said he wrote the statement after thinking about the situation last Friday.

"I was driving to the mosque on Friday … and I was reflecting and thinking about, can we not just find a middle ground?" Khawaja said.

"I don't even care any more about what they say, what we say.

"Everything is just being drip-fed right now, and it feels like there's no end to it."

He even admitted that he had a "pipe dream" that the entire squad would take accountability one day.

Khawaja said Greenberg was initially receptive to the idea, but was not convinced that the statement would solve the issue, and said he would put it to "the other parties" involved.

In a wide-ranging interview on the cult podcast, Khawaja touched on multiple topics, including the threats he has received that meant he required a security guard at a charity cricket game in Cairns on Sunday.

Usman Khawaja said he still loves Pat Cummins. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney, file photo)

Khawaja said Pat Cummins's comments in his press conference were "really surprising" and that he had texted the Australian captain before his press conference in an attempt to try and find the middle ground.

"I was never expecting him to come out and attack me personally like that," he said.

"Attack what I said? Yeah. Personally, the way he did, for so long and he kept going and going and going I've never seen that side of Pat before.

"I didn't want to watch it, but I had to watch it. I wanted to turn it off so many times.

"I will always love Pat, and as much as he hurt me, I'm not going to judge him on a presser."

Khawaja said that he is "not convinced" that anyone else would have spoken about it when justifying the Sandpapergate chapter of his book, adding that he could understand why some people were angry that he wrote about the topic when some of his teammates were still playing.

"100 per cent, I definitely can. I'm not an idiot, I'm not devoid of empathy," he said.

"I get that side, and that's why I'm so happy now that CA has come out and said there's not going to be any sanctions, nobody's going to get in trouble, Pat Cummins remains as captain — I was actually really happy with that.

"I don't want to hurt anyone individually."

Usman Khawaja says he wants there to be a middle ground found. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Khawaja said that had he come out and spoken during his career he would have never played for Australia again.

"If I'm being brutally honest, if I came out and said that while I was playing, 100 per cent my career was over," he said.

"I couldn't play for Australia anymore.

"I'm not trying to hide from that. Call me selfish, maybe it was.

"The thing I've tried to do … is talk about Cameron Bancroft. How much longer do I wait? What do I do? Do I make him suffer for another five years?"

Khawaja said that he knew sandpaper was being used on the field in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, just by looking at the wear on the ball that was not consistent with normal wear and tear of a game.

Khawaja said he delayed coming on the podcast, he missed two previous appointments, because his appearances clashed with Pat Cummins's press conference and Cameron Bancroft's revealing West Australian article.

"I just thought that, if I came on at that time, I would inflame the situation so much more," he said.

"This was never about me versus Pat [Cummins], and I know that's what the media wanted but that was never my goal.

"As disappointed as I was about that presser, I was just, 'I'm going to stay away from this'.

"The Bancroft situation was the same … it was so deep, it was so full on."

World.title: Matildas keeper reveals career-threatening health scare
World.content:
A neurological disorder threatened to cut Teagan Micah's career short, but the Australian goalkeeper has overcome it with a little help from her Matildas friends.

The 29-year-old was diagnosed with autonomic dysfunction after suffering a concussion in March while training with her current French club, Lyon.

She previously sustained a serious head injury in 2022 with Swedish side FC Rosengård and the latest concussion forced the shot stopper to miss March's Asian Cup.

It also led to her developing the debilitating condition, which stops the nervous system properly regulating automatic body functions.

Micah has recovered and returns to Joe Montemurro's Matildas squad for their two-game series against Colombia, beginning in Canberra on Saturday night.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the Queensland product revealed the "big health scare" threatened to force her into early retirement.

"I had a lot of chats with my family, with doctors, my best friends … every day about retirement, and it was looking like that for a while," Micah said.

Teagan Micah plays for OL Lyonnes in the French top flight. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Lilou Cassin)

She experienced problems regulating her heart rate, which would rise to 190 beats per minute after walking for 2 minutes.

Micah consulted with specialists in Sydney, Geneva and France in a bid to get healthy and back on the field.

"It was probably about June, July time when I came home to [Australia] for about two weeks and I also saw my doctors here … it was kind of the turning point for me," she said.

"I sat down with my family and spoke a lot with them [about retiring] and it was just a matter of … get back healthy first and then making the decision.

"I didn't want to make a decision before that because I knew it wasn't going to be something I'd be comfortable with … I just knew I wanted to keep going."

Micah, who says she feels "alive again", credited ex-Lyon star Ellie Carpenter and other Australian teammates for getting her back on her feet.

"She got me through so many days," Micah said of close friend Carpenter.

"She sent me food to my apartment when I couldn't get out of bed for days.

"Steph [Catley], Ellie, Ras [Hayley Raso] were the main ones checking in all the time.

Hayley Raso (left) was one of Teagan Micah's key supporters during her lay-off. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"Also the coaching staff here, the Matildas, were incredible as well … and at Lyon, those girls made me smile on days where I didn't think I had it in me anymore."

Competing with Mackenzie Arnold for the number 1 shirt, Micah said she would do everything possible to nab a spot in Australia's squad for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil.

"I need to probably go back to the drawing board and write down what I want to achieve now with the rest of my career," Micah said.

"Now that I feel good and I'm ready to go it's like where do I want my career to take me … [I want] to use this second chance I have."

The friendlies in Canberra and Geelong are world number 15 Australia's last before the World Cup draw on December 11.

World number 19 Colombia have established themselves as the second-best South American team behind hosts Brazil.

Along with Micah, Australia have regained Mary Fowler, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Alanna Kennedy, Tameka Yallop and Kahli Johnson.

Everton attacker Holly McNamara [hamstring] is out until late December, while Clare Hunt and Charlie Rule remain sidelined.

AAP

World.title: Ireland lose skipper for Wallabies clash while Suaalii relishing centre role
World.content:
Ireland stand-in skipper Dan Sheehan will miss his side's final Nations Championship match against the Wallabies after being given a two-week suspension following his red card for a croc-roll against South Africa at the weekend.

Sheehan's initial yellow card eight minutes from the end of Saturday's 20-17 win was upgraded to a red after the match.

The 28-year-old has captained Ireland in the absence of injured Caelan Doris.

Sheehan, usually a hooker, played at number eight for the first time in his international career against the Springboks as the side were grappling with an injury crisis at the back of the scrum.

Ireland are already without at least three number eights through injury, with Jack Conan and Sean Jansen missing, as well as Doris.

Given the Wallabies' strength at the back of the scrum, the absentees will be cause for concern for the Irish.

Ulster's 23-year-old giant, James McNabney, should be fit to return after missing the Springboks clash after he was knocked out on debut against Fiji, although his Ulster teammate, backrow utility forward Nick Timoney, will likely start.

Ireland, which finished third in the Northern Hemisphere section, will face Australia at Twickenham in a play-off to decide fifth and sixth place.

Meanwhile, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii said he enjoyed the combination at centre with the experienced Len Ikitau as the debate over his best position for the Wallabies continued.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii says he enjoyed playing centre. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Suaalii played at centre in his first 22 starts for Australia, following his high-profile defection from rugby league, but new Wallabies coach Les Kiss moved him to wing for the 42-38 victory over South Africa in Perth in September and the first Bledisloe Cup clash against New Zealand last month.

The absent Hunter Paisami may be expected to challenge him for that outside centre spot, while Ikitau could benefit from a move to 13, with Carter Gordon at 12.

In the Nations Championship this month, he was picked on the wing against England but returned to the midfield against Scotland and last weekend's 29-26 win over Wales.

"I just love playing rugby and, being able to play 13, you get to be both sides of the ball. You can defend and attack and you're in the front line," he said in London.

"Playing alongside Lenny, he's great with his comms. He's quiet off the field but once he goes on the field, he helps you quite a bit."

The 23-year-old Suaalii has also been a regular fullback for the New South Wales Waratahs in Super Rugby but has not been picked at number 15 for Australia.

With the hosting of the World Cup now less than a year away, and where home hopes will rest heavily on his shoulders, where best to use Suaalii's powerful presence has stirred plenty of debate among Aussie pundits.

"I think my biggest thing is just, I'm still learning the game. I'm still trying to get better each week," he added.

"It doesn't matter what number I have on my back; I'm just trying to use the skill sets I have … defence, aerial attacking, ball in hand, breakdown.

"I see myself just growing my game in all that sense: the attack, defence, breakdown, transition. I'm really just focusing on putting my energy towards trying to get better in that sense and then position-wise, it's just up to the coach.

"I've always said that. I'm happy to play anywhere, just always just trusting what the coach is going to do and, at the end of the day, I'm playing for my country, so I'm always grateful for that."

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Indian teen wonder breaks List A record with 200 from 52 balls
World.content:
Indian cricket prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has broken yet more records, this time with the fastest century and double century in men's List A competitions.

The 15-year-old smashed a century in 28 balls, then 150 in 40 balls, and finally crossed 200 in 52 balls while playing for India A against the United Arab Emirates in the Asia Cup Rising Stars 50-over tournament.

All of those are records for List A competitions, the International Cricket Council confirmed, adding that Sooryavanshi's 200 was nearly twice as fast as the previous record of 103 balls.

The teen was caught soon after on 204 to end an innings boasting 28 sixes. India easily chased down the target of 250 set by the UAE to finish on 3-254. More than 80 per cent of the team's runs came off Sooryavanshi's bat.

List A cricket is the level below one-day international cricket. It covers the top level of one-day domestic cricket around the world as well as international games involving a top nation's development team, such as India A.

The records continue a spectacular year for Sooryavanshi. He scored 175 to win the Under-19 World Cup final for India in February, lit up the Indian Premier League and became the youngest player to represent India in a full international game, beating the record held by all-time great Sachin Tendulkar.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Players and umpires unite against Super Netball rule changes
World.content:
Super Netball players and umpires have released a joint statement opposing suggested rule changes to the competition.

It is a rare move from the umpires, who typically keep quiet on such matters.

Heading into its 11th season, there is a desire from stakeholders to increase entertainment value and keep pushing the sport forward in order to hold onto its tag as the world's best league.

However, there is a clear divide in how that should be done.

The Vixens and Thunderbirds contested the 2026 Super Netball Grand Final. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

In April, Netball Australia shelved plans for expansion and signed a five-year broadcast deal with Nine to return to free-to-air TV audiences.

These are the kinds of ideas the player and umpire group prefer.

"Netball has a bright future. Getting there will take big ideas and bold thinking," the statement read.

"We don't want less innovation. We want much more of it.

"Why not more teams, more games, new competitions and exciting formats? Why not fresh broadcast opportunities, technology, digital engagement and events that bring new audiences to our sport?"

Ruth Aryang of the Fever looks to block a super shot by Uneeq Palavi of the Mavericks. (Getty: Paul Kane)

The last rule changes fell six years ago when the super shot was announced six weeks before the 2020 season start. The decision was controversial and created distrust between the national governing body and the athletes, who felt their opinions had been disregarded.

Since then, England and New Zealand have also added two-point shots to their top-flight competitions.

Other innovations, such as tactical timeouts and rolling subs, have been much better received.

In May this year, Netball Australia ran a fan engagement survey, asking how they could elevate the 2027 spectator experience. Of the 3,000-plus fan submissions, there were consistent themes around speed, scoring and technology.

That same month, it formed a League Innovation Forum — comprised of Netball Australia staff, as well as Super Netball club, coach, umpire and player association representatives — to discuss potential modifications.

Former Big Bash League boss Anthony Everard is head of the project.

If the competition already has regular sell-out crowds, does it need more rule changes? (Getty: Matt King)

Although the sport has been reluctant to confirm details, three key proposals have been leaked:

Stop the clock: Time will be held when the ball is out of play in the last two minutes of a match.

Time will be held when the ball is out of play in the last two minutes of a match. A shoot-off: If a match is still tied at the end of extra time it will go to a shoot-off. Allowing two shooters each two attempts at a two-point super shot or giving one shooter three attempts at a regular goal.

If a match is still tied at the end of extra time it will go to a shoot-off. Allowing two shooters each two attempts at a two-point super shot or giving one shooter three attempts at a regular goal. The centre pass heist: Players can request two centre passes in a row up until the last two minutes of a match.

The last of the three was trialled in early November in Victoria's men's premier division. Those involved said it did not make a compelling case as it had little impact, interrupted flow, and created confusion and inconsistency in the game.

None of the All Australian umpires that officiate Super Netball were involved in the trials. (AAP: Scott Barbour)

When ABC Sport asked Netball Australia how these trials went, it was told that executives were finalising their recommendations to present at a December board meeting.

The players and umpires have concerns the trial didn't appropriately replicate the demands and standard of Super Netball and that fundamental changes will be made again without proper consultation.

By taking this stance now, they hope it's not too late to change the executive's minds.

"Netball is a team sport … That's it's magic," the statement read.

Loading Instagram content

"Reducing a hard-fought contest to a shootout involving a small number of players moves away from what makes netball great. It also unnecessarily exposes individual players to additional pressure and scrutiny.

"The centre pass heist raises similar concerns. Possession should be earned through the contest, with all players having the opportunity to influence the outcome. Close games should be decided by skill and teamwork.

"Rule changes aren't off the table. But surely we should first ask: What problem are we solving? Will it improve the contest, reward skill, entertain fans and grow the game? And have we considered those who play and officiate it?

"If the answers are convincing, let's get on with it. If not, let's keep exploring."

World.title: Senegal reinstated as African champions after appeal
World.content:
Senegal is once again Africa's soccer champion more than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final.

Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.

Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.

CAS has rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.

Senegal walked off the pitch during the final after a controversial refereeing decision. (Reuters: Amr Abdallah Dalsh)

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.

The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refused to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently".

Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.

Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to award a penalty sparked a massive protest. (Reuters: Siphiwe Sibeko)

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said.

"However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgement did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.

In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds, including a judge's integrity.

Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.

Fans and players clashed with security in chaotic scenes at the final. (Reuters: Siphiwe Sibeko)

The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.

Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart.

Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz, a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka", was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.

The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognised as the champion at that point.

Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.

Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.

The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally cannot be taken to the sports court.

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.

The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.

AP

World.title: Jannik Sinner set to miss Australian Open
World.content:
Jannik Sinner's planned Melbourne comeback is in considerable doubt, with the former world number one going back to the operating table for more surgery.

The two-time Australian Open winner had targeted the major for his big-time comeback after nearly six months out with a right knee injury.

Sinner last played in July at Wimbledon, where he won his fifth grand slam title. During his absence he has lost his world number one status to Alexander Zverev.

"Over the past few months, together with my team we've tried everything ⁠to ‌treat my ​injury without surgery," Sinner ​said in ‌a statement after the operation on Tuesday.

"After some very encouraging ​progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn't ​respond ​as we'd ​all hoped, that's ‌why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my ​iliotibial band."

Sinner is a five-time major winner. (Getty Images/Frey)

The thick band of connective tissue runs along the outside of the leg from the hip to the top of the shinbone. It stabilises the knee when functioning properly but can cause irritation when too tight, or when associated muscles are weak.

The winner in Melbourne in 2024 and 2025, Sinner said a fortnight ago: "The aim is to go to Australia."

But he now could be sidelined for months. The 2027 Australian Open main draw begins ​on January 17.

Jannick Sinner says he misses playing tennis. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Sinner ‌said recently that he had lost a significant amount of ​weight after having his tonsils removed and was in the process of rebuilding muscle.

"I have to respect the protocols because if we rush things we could have more serious problems," he said earlier this month.

"I have a ‌lot of faith ‌in the process, ⁠and I'm working toward that objective.

"Initially, we had an impossible goal for my ​return in mind, so we took a different path. I'm a tennis player, not a doctor, so my only option is to trust them.

"I miss playing tennis. Right now, however, it is crucial that I take care of my body, because I want to keep playing for another 10 to 15 years."

AAP

Tech.title: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This month’s Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual “Code Red” internally, Reuters reports. The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers.

In a memo to the teams responsible for Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson revealed the outage was the most significant in history for Microsoft’s customers. “Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” said Henderson. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.”

As part of this Code Red declaration, Microsoft is focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft now has a target of resolving future outages within an hour, and will reportedly deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose issues. Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly reviews.

In a separate memo, Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of M365 Core and Work IQ, said engineers had to work through a “fog of war” to help resolve the outage. I reported last week that Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call during the entire outage, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants.

Microsoft engineers had to exchange messages across 11 Teams chats and reportedly “struggled ​to maintain a cohesive picture” during the outage because of the fragmented internal tracking systems. Sources tell me the outage was marked as “sev0,” the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Engineers struggled to get servers back online because they had entered maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads.

Tech.title: US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. The Department of Defense, whose National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also reportedly impacted by the breach, declined to comment. The CIA and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month.

Americans have been on high alert about security incidents

FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.

FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.

Update, November 24th: Added response from Department of Defense.
